seal.def: A carved stamp, usually printed in red ink, that marks a work with an artist’s or owner’s name. Chinese paintings often collect many seals from the people who owned them.
seal.think: Think of a personal stamp or signature in red.

seascape.def: A painting whose main subject is the sea.

self-portrait.def: A picture an artist makes of themself.
self-portrait.think: Think of a selfie, but painted, drawn or printed.
self-portrait.seen: No. 87 Self-Portrait with Saskia; No. 105 Self-Portrait (Vigée Le Brun); No. 133 SelfPortrait as a Soldier; No. 140 The Two Fridas.

series.def: A group of artworks on the same subject or theme, made to be seen together, or a subject an artist returns to again and again. Monet painted the Saint-Lazare station many times; Cézanne painted Mont Sainte-Victoire dozens of times.
series.seen: No. 116 The Saint-Lazare Station; No. 125 Mont Sainte-Victoire; No. 141 The Migration of the Negro, Panel no. 49.

sfumato.def: A painting technique using many soft, hazy layers so edges melt into each other with no hard lines, like smoke. Italian for ‘smoky’. Associated with Leonardo da Vinci.

shanshui.def: Chinese for ‘mountainwater’: the Chinese tradition of landscape painting with mountains, rivers and mist, expressing harmony between people and nature.
shanshui.seen: No. 201 Travelers among Mountains and Streams.
shanshui.see: monumental landscape, literati, brush and ink.

sketch.def: A quick, rough drawing or painting used to try out an idea before a finished work.
sketch.think: Think of a first draft of an essay.

soak-stain.def: Pouring very thin paint onto raw, unprimed canvas so it soaks into the cloth, leaving soft, see-through pools of color. Pioneered by Helen Frankenthaler.
soak-stain.think: Think of spilled juice spreading into a tablecloth.

staged photography.def: Photographs where the artist carefully sets up the scene, costumes and poses, like a film still, instead of capturing a real moment.
staged photography.think: Think of a carefully planned photo shoot rather than a candid snap.

stencil.def: A sheet with shapes cut out of it, through which paint or ink is brushed or sprayed so only the open areas print. Braque stenciled letters into The Portuguese; Cotsiogo probably used stencils for some figures on his elk hide.
stencil.seen: No. 130 The Portuguese; No. 165 Painted elk hide.

still life.def: A painting of non-moving objects, such as fruit, flowers, cups or skulls, arranged by the artist.
still life.think: Think of a carefully styled food photo.
still life.seen: No. 96 Fruit and Insects; No. 110 Still Life in Studio.

support.def: The surface a painting or drawing is made on, such as wood panel, canvas, paper, silk, vellum, plaster or hide.
support.think: Think of the ‘what is it painted on’ answer.
support.seen: No. 122 The Scream (cardboard); No. 141 Migration Series (hardboard).

synthetic polymer paint.def: The museum-label name for acrylic and similar plastic-based paints. They dry fast and come in bright colors.

tarashikomi.def: A Japanese technique of dropping ink or paint onto an area that is still wet, so the colors pool and blur into soft, mottled patches.
tarashikomi.think: Think of dripping food coloring onto a wet paper towel.
tarashikomi.seen: No. 210 White and Red Plum Blossoms.

tempera.def: Paint made by mixing pigment with egg yolk (egg tempera). It dries fast to a matte finish with crisp detail, but can’t be blended smoothly. The main panel paint before oil.
tempera.think: Think of paint whose glue is literally egg yolk.
tempera.seen: No. 71 Madonna and Child with Two Angels; No. 72 Birth of Venus; No. 94 Screen with the Siege of Belgrade.

texture stroke.def: In Chinese painting, a type of brushstroke (cun) used to show the texture of rocks and mountains, such as ‘raindrop’ or ‘axe-cut’ strokes. Fan Kuan’s mountains are built from thousands of raindrop strokes.
texture stroke.seen: No. 201 Travelers among Mountains and Streams.
texture stroke.see: brush and ink, shanshui, monumental landscape.

triptych.def: A work in three panels, usually a central panel with two side wings, often hinged so the sides fold over the middle.
triptych.think: Think of a three-part fold-out greeting card.
triptych.seen: No. 66 Merode Altarpiece; No. 226 Horn Players.

underdrawing.def: The drawing an artist makes on a surface before painting over it. Scientists can often see it with infrared light.
underdrawing.think: Think of the pencil lines under a finished comic.

unprimed canvas.def: Canvas not coated with gesso or primer, so thinned paint soaks straight into the fabric. Helen Frankenthaler poured paint onto it in her soak-stain technique.

vellum.def: Fine, smooth parchment made from calfskin, used for the best medieval manuscripts. Some luxury manuscripts were dyed purple, the royal color.
vellum.seen: No. 50 Vienna Genesis (purple vellum); No. 55 Lindisfarne Gospels; No. 61 Bible moralisée; No. 64 Golden Haggadah.

vignette.def: A small scene or picture set within a larger composition or border. Four corner vignettes in the Virgin of Guadalupe painting tell the story of her appearances.

wash.def: A thin, watery layer of ink or paint brushed over an area to give a soft, even tone.
wash.think: Think of a drop of ink spreading in a glass of water.
wash.seen: No. 227 Summer Trees; No. 201 Travelers among Mountains and Streams.

watercolor.def: Paint made with pigment and a watersoluble gum binder, applied with water. Usually transparent, so the paper glows through.
watercolor.think: Think of the little paint trays from elementary school.
watercolor.seen: No. 208 Jahangir Preferring a Sufi Shaikh to Kings; No. 210 White and Red Plum Blossoms.

wing.def: A side panel of an altarpiece, often hinged so it can close over the center panel. Wings were often painted on both sides, with different scenes showing when open or closed.
wing.think: Think of the doors of a cabinet.
wing.seen: No. 66 Merode Altarpiece; No. 77 Isenheim altarpiece.

woodblock print.def: A print made by carving a picture into a block of wood, inking the raised surface and pressing paper onto it. Japanese color woodblock prints used a separate block for each color.
woodblock print.think: Think of a potato stamp, made by experts, with one block per color.

woodcut.def: A relief print from a carved wood block, especially in the European tradition. Its lines are often bold and blocky, and it could be printed cheaply in large numbers.
woodcut.think: Think of a rubber stamp carved from wood.
woodcut.seen: No. 79 Allegory of Law and Grace; No. 134 Memorial Sheet for Karl Liebknecht.

zoopraxiscope.def: A device Eadweard Muybridge built in 1879 to project his sequences of motion pictures, painted from his photographs onto a spinning glass disk, so they appeared to move. It was an early ancestor of film.
zoopraxiscope.think: Like a flipbook projected on a wall.
zoopraxiscope.see: chronophotography, photography. 4 Sculpture, objects and materials How three-dimensional things are made: carving, casting, firing clay, weaving, inlay. Also the names for common object types such as reliefs, reliquaries and masks.

abrasion.def: Shaping a very hard material by grinding it away, usually with wet sand rubbed on with a tool, instead of cutting it. Jade is too hard to carve with a knife, so it was worked this way.
abrasion.think: Like sanding wood, but on stone harder than steel, so one object could take months.

additive.def: Making a sculpture by building it up, adding material such as clay, wax or pieces of metal. The opposite of subtractive (carving away).
additive.think: Think of building with Lego or adding scoops of clay.
additive.seen: No. 10 Tlatilco female figurine; No. 237 Pisupo Lua Afe.

adlocutio.def: The pose of a Roman general or emperor with one arm raised, addressing his troops. The word is Latin for ‘speech’ or ‘address’.
adlocutio.think: Think of a coach with one arm up giving a pep talk before the game.

alabaster.def: A soft, pale, slightly seethrough stone that is easy to carve and polish.
alabaster.think: Think of a stone that looks like frozen milk.

alloy.def: A metal made by melting two or more metals together, such as bronze (copper plus tin) or brass (copper plus zinc). Inka metalworkers used gold and silver alloys.
alloy.think: A metal smoothie: blended to get the best qualities of each ingredient.

andesite.def: A hard, gray volcanic stone. Borobudur in Java was built from enormous numbers of andesite blocks, and its long relief panels are carved into them.

appliqué.def: A textile technique where cut shapes of fabric are sewn onto a larger cloth to make a design.
appliqué.think: Think of iron-on patches on a jacket, but stitched.

architectural sculpture.def: Sculpture made to be part of a building, such as figures on a roof, carved bands along a wall, or a carved panel over a doorway.
architectural sculpture.think: Think of statues and carvings that are built into the building rather than placed in front of it.
architectural sculpture.seen: No. 31 Temple of Minerva (Apollo of Veii); No. 38 Great Altar of Zeus and Athena; No. 58 Sainte-Foy tympanum.

armature.def: An inner skeleton of wire, wood or metal that supports a sculpture made of clay, plaster or other soft material while it is being built.
armature.think: Think of the wire frame inside a stuffed animal or a clay figure.

assemblage.def: A threedimensional work made by putting together found or ready-made objects and materials. The 3D cousin of collage.
assemblage.think: Think of a sculpture built from things you would find in a junk drawer.
assemblage.seen: No. 237 Pisupo Lua Afe; No. 245 Old Man’s Cloth.
assemblage.see: collage, found object, readymade, mixed media.

back slab.def: The block of stone left behind an Egyptian statue, joining the figures to their support. It keeps the statue stable and makes it look solid and eternal.

barkcloth.def: Cloth made by soaking and beating the inner bark of trees, such as paper mulberry, into thin sheets. In Polynesia it is called tapa (hiapo in Niue, masi in Fiji, ngatu in Tonga).
barkcloth.think: Like paper, but made by pounding bark instead of pulping it.
barkcloth.seen: No. 216 Staff god; No. 219 Hiapo (tapa); No. 223 Presentation of Fijian mats and tapa.

bas-relief.def: Another name for low relief: carving that sticks out only a little from its background. French for ‘low relief’.
bas-relief.think: Think of the raised face on a coin.
bas-relief.seen: No. 199 Angkor Wat; No. 198 Borobudur Temple.

basalt.def: A very hard, dark gray to black volcanic stone. Hard to carve, so it feels permanent and authoritative.
basalt.think: Think of the dark rock from cooled lava.
basalt.seen: No. 19 Code of Hammurabi; No. 157 Templo Mayor (Calendar Stone).

batik.def: A way of decorating cloth by painting hot wax on the areas you want to keep from the dye, then dyeing the cloth and removing the wax. Emily Kame Kngwarreye made batik for years before she painted on canvas.
batik.think: Like using tape to keep paint off part of a wall.

bi.def: A flat jade disk with a round hole in the center, made in China from Neolithic times on and often buried with the elite. Later Chinese texts link the bi with heaven; on Lady Dai’s funeral banner two dragons loop through one.
bi.seen: No. 194 Funeral banner of Lady Dai.

bitumen.def: Natural tar or asphalt that seeps from the ground in Mesopotamia. Sumerians used it as glue to hold inlay in place and to color hair and beards.
bitumen.seen: No. 14 Votive figures from Eshnunna; No. 16 Standard of Ur.

black-figure.def: A Greek vase-painting technique where figures are painted in black slip on the natural red-orange clay, and details are scratched in. It came before red-figure.
black-figure.think: Think of black shadow puppets on an orange background.

blackware.def: Pottery with a black, often glossy surface, made by firing the clay in a smoky, low-oxygen fire. Maria and Julian Martínez of San Ildefonso Pueblo made black-on-black pottery: shiny polished areas next to matte painted designs.
blackware.think: Think of two different blacks, one mirror-shiny and one dull, on the same pot.

blue-and-white porcelain.def: Porcelain painted with cobalt-blue designs under a clear glaze, perfected in China during the Yuan dynasty (1300s) and traded all over the world.
blue-and-white porcelain.think: Think of the classic blue-patterned dinner plate.

bone.def: Animal bone used as a material for carving or shaping. One of the earliest art materials.
bone.think: Think of a carved bone tool, made into a sculpture.
bone.seen: No. 3 Camelid sacrum in the shape of a canine.

brass.def: A gold-colored metal made by mixing copper and zinc. It can be hammered or cast, and it shines like gold when polished.
brass.think: Think of a trumpet or a doorknob.
brass.seen: No. 169 Wall plaque from Oba’s palace; No. 188 Basin (Baptistère de St. Louis).

bronze.def: A metal made by mixing copper with tin. It is strong, can be cast into detailed shapes, and lets sculptors make arms and limbs stick out without breaking.
bronze.think: Think of an Olympic bronze medal.
bronze.seen: No. 41 Seated boxer; No. 69 David (Donatello); No. 119 The Burghers of Calais; No. 202 Shiva as Lord of Dance.

burnishing.def: Rubbing a surface hard with a smooth stone or tool to make it shiny. Potters burnish clay before firing to make it gleam; printmakers burnish metal plates to smooth out areas and lighten them.
burnishing.think: Think of polishing a shoe until it shines.
burnishing.seen: No. 166 Black-on-black ceramic vessel; No. 106 Y no hai remedio.

bust.def: A sculpture of a person’s head, neck and usually shoulders and upper chest.
bust.think: Think of a statue that stops at the chest, often on a pedestal.

camelid fiber.def: Yarn spun from the hair of alpacas, llamas and vicuñas, the main material of Andean weaving. The finest vicuña cloth was reserved for the Inka elite.

carpet.def: A heavy woven floor or wall covering. In Persian knotted-pile carpets, millions of short yarn knots are tied around the warp threads, then trimmed to make a soft surface with a detailed design.
carpet.think: Think of a rug where every tiny dot of color is a separate knot.

carving.def: Shaping a sculpture by cutting, chiseling or scraping material away from a block of stone, wood, ivory or jade.
carving.seen: No. 57 Pyxis of al-Mughira; No. 129 The Kiss (Brancusi); No. 171 Ndop of King Mishe miShyaang maMbul.

cassone.def: A large, often richly painted wooden chest given at weddings in Renaissance Italy to hold the bride’s clothes and dowry. Plural: cassoni. In the Venus of Urbino, maids search one in the background.

casting.def: Making a sculpture by pouring a liquid material, such as molten metal or plaster, into a mold and letting it harden. Many copies can come from one mold.
casting.think: Think of making ice cubes in a tray.
casting.seen: No. 69 David (Donatello); No. 202 Shiva as Lord of Dance.
casting.see: lost-wax casting, mold, bronze, hollow casting.

ceramic.def: Any object made of clay and hardened by heat (firing). Includes earthenware, terracotta, stoneware and porcelain.
ceramic.think: Think of mugs, plates, flowerpots and bathroom tiles.
ceramic.seen: No. 10 Tlatilco female figurine; No. 166 Black-on-black ceramic vessel; No. 204 The David Vases.

chiasmus.def: The crossing balance in a contrapposto figure: the tense, working parts sit diagonally across from each other, and so do the relaxed parts. In the Doryphoros the straight weight-bearing right leg pairs with the bent, spear-holding left arm.
chiasmus.think: Named after the Greek letter chi (X): the tensions form a hidden X through the body.
chiasmus.see: contrapposto, canon of proportions, Classical Greek.

cinerary urn.def: A container for the ashes of a cremated person. The Etruscans made them of clay or stone, often with figures of the dead on the lid; the Sarcophagus of the Spouses may have held ashes.

cloisonné.def: A technique where thin metal strips are attached to a surface to make little walled cells (cloisons), which are then filled with colored enamel or cut stones like garnets.
cloisonné.think: Think of a stained-glass window shrunk onto jewelry.

closed-circuit video.def: Video sent live from a camera straight to monitors in the same place, without broadcasting it. Nam June Paik used it so viewers suddenly see themselves on screen inside the work.
closed-circuit video.think: Like a store’s security camera feed.

cobalt.def: A mineral that gives a strong deep blue when painted on ceramics and fired. Cobalt imported from Persia made the blue of Chinese blueand-white porcelain.

coiffure.def: An elaborate hairstyle. African masks often carve detailed coiffures to show beauty, status or the fashions of a time and place.
coiffure.think: A fancy word for a hairdo.
coiffure.seen: No. 173 Pwo mask; No. 174 Portrait mask (Mblo); No. 175 Bundu mask.

coiling.def: Building a pot by hand from long ropes of clay stacked in rings, then smoothing the walls, without a potter’s wheel.
coiling.think: Think of stacking snakes of Play-Doh into a cup.

colossal.def: Much larger than life size, sometimes many stories tall.
colossal.think: Think of the Statue of Liberty.
colossal.seen: No. 182 Buddha (Bamiyan); No. 197 Todai-ji (Great Buddha); No. 214 Moai on platform; No. 17 Great Sphinx.

combine.def: Robert Rauschenberg’s name for his works that combine painting with real objects attached to the surface, part painting and part sculpture. Jaune Quick-to-See Smith’s Trade follows the idea.

composite mask.def: A mask built from many separate parts joined together, often combining a human face with an animal. The Torres Strait buk is a composite mask.

cong.def: A Chinese ritual object of jade shaped like a tube that is square outside and round inside, often carved with faces. Made by the Liangzhu culture over 4,000 years ago; its exact use is unknown.
cong.think: Think of a square stone tube with a round hole through it.

convex mirror.def: A mirror that bulges outward, reflecting a wide view in a small, curved image. Van Eyck painted one on the back wall of the Arnolfini Portrait; Kusama’s Narcissus Garden is a field of mirrored spheres.
convex mirror.think: Like the curved safety mirror at a blind corner.
convex mirror.seen: No. 68 The Arnolfini Portrait; No. 148 Narcissus Garden.

Cor-Ten steel.def: A type of steel that forms a stable, rusty-orange outer layer, which protects the metal from further rust. Popular for outdoor sculpture since the 1960s.
Cor-Ten steel.think: Think of metal that is supposed to look rusted.

couching.def: An embroidery method in which threads are laid across the surface of the cloth and tied down with small stitches. The Bayeux Tapestry fills its figures with laid-and-couched work.

cowrie.def: A small, glossy sea-snail shell used as money across Africa and the Indian Ocean world for centuries. On objects it signals wealth.
cowrie.seen: No. 171 Ndop of King Mishe miShyaang maMbul.

cuirass.def: Body armor protecting the chest and back. Augustus of Prima Porta wears one carved with scenes celebrating the return of Roman battle standards from the Parthians.

dentate stamping.def: Decorating pottery by pressing a tool with a toothed, comb-like edge into wet clay, leaving rows of tiny dots. It is the signature technique of Lapita pottery.
dentate stamping.think: Like pressing the teeth of a comb into Play-Doh.

direct carving.def: Carving straight into stone or wood without first making a clay model to copy, letting the material guide the shape. Championed by early modern sculptors like Brancusi.
direct carving.think: Think of improvising a carving rather than tracing a plan.

drill.def: A tool spun quickly to bore holes into stone. Late Roman sculptors used drills heavily to cut deep pockets of shadow in hair, eyes and drapery.

Dutch wax print.def: Brightly patterned cotton fabric printed with a wax-resist method. Made in the Netherlands imitating Indonesian batik, it became popular in West Africa and is now seen as ‘African’ cloth, a story about colonial trade.
Dutch wax print.think: Think of a fabric whose ‘African’ look actually has a European and Asian back story.

earthenware.def: Pottery fired at a fairly low temperature. It stays slightly porous (it can soak up water) unless glazed. Terracotta is a kind of earthenware.
earthenware.think: Think of a red clay flowerpot.
earthenware.seen: No. 5 Beaker with ibex motifs; No. 166 Black-onblack ceramic vessel.

eﬀigy.def: A likeness of a person, especially a sculpture on a tomb or a figure used in a ritual. Among the cast-gold pieces hanging from the Golden Stool are eﬀigies of enemy rulers the Asante defeated.

embroidery.def: Decorating cloth by stitching designs onto it with colored thread.
embroidery.think: Think of a name stitched onto a baseball cap.
embroidery.seen: No. 59 Bayeux Tapestry; No. 183 The Kaaba (kiswa).

enamel.def: Powdered glass melted onto metal (or ceramic) to make a hard, shiny, colorful surface.
enamel.think: Think of the glossy colored coating on a pin badge.
enamel.seen: No. 58 Reliquary of Sainte-Foy; No. 23 Tutankhamun’s coﬀin.

ephemeral.def: Made to last only a short time, or to be destroyed after use. The event or experience matters more than keeping the object.
ephemeral.think: Think of a sandcastle or a fireworks show.
ephemeral.seen: No. 222 Malagan display and mask; No. 224 The Gates; No. 223 Presentation of Fijian mats and tapa.

equestrian.def: Showing a person on horseback. Equestrian statues of rulers were a classic way to show power and command.
equestrian.think: Think of a general on a rearing horse in a city square.

escudo de monja.def: Spanish for ‘nun’s shield’. A large painted badge worn on the chest by nuns in colonial New Spain, showing a religious scene such as the Annunciation. Sor Juana wears one in her portrait.
escudo de monja.see: New Spain, Viceregal art, Virgin Mary.

fabrication.def: Having an artwork physically made by assistants, workshops or factories from the artist’s design. Jeff Koons’s porcelain Pink Panther was fabricated by skilled craftspeople, not by Koons’s own hands.
fabrication.think: Like an architect who designs a building but doesn’t lay the bricks.

featherwork.def: Art made by tying, gluing or sewing feathers onto a backing to create garments, headdresses or images. Rare, bright feathers were a sign of high rank in Polynesia and Mesoamerica.
featherwork.think: Think of a coat made entirely of shimmering feathers.
featherwork.seen: No. 158 Ruler’s feather headdress; No. 215 ‘Ahu ‘ula (feather cape); No. 216 Staff god.

fiber.def: Threads or strands from plants (cotton, bark, pandanus, coconut husk) or animals (wool, camelid hair, silk) used for weaving, netting, tying and binding.
fiber.think: Think of string, yarn and rope.
fiber.seen: No. 162 All-T’oqapu tunic; No. 215 ‘Ahu ‘ula (feather cape); No. 221 Navigation chart; No. 223 Presentation of Fijian mats and tapa.

fiber art.def: Art made from fibers and textiles, such as yarn, cloth, rope and burlap, treated as fine art rather than craft. Magdalena Abakanowicz’s hollow burlap figures are an example.

fibula.def: A decorative pin or brooch used to fasten clothing at the shoulder, like a fancy safety pin. Plural: fibulae.
fibula.think: Think of a jeweled safety pin that shows off your wealth.

fieldstone.def: Rough stone gathered from the ground and used as found or barely shaped. Ordinary Machu Picchu walls are fieldstone, while the most sacred buildings got finely fitted, cut stone.

figurine.def: A small statue, usually of a person or animal, often small enough to hold in your hand.
figurine.think: Think of an action figure or a chess piece.

filigree.def: Delicate ornament made from very fine twisted wires of gold or silver soldered into lacy patterns.

firing.def: Heating clay in a kiln (a very hot oven) or fire so it hardens permanently. The temperature and amount of oxygen change the clay’s color and strength.
firing.think: Think of baking cookie dough until it can’t be squished.
firing.seen: No. 166 Black-on-black ceramic vessel; No. 193 Terra cotta warriors.

font.def: A basin that holds the water used in baptism. The Mamluk brass basin called the Baptistère de Saint Louis was later used as a baptismal font for French royal babies.

found object.def: An ordinary object, natural or manufactured, that an artist uses in a work of art, either as is or changed. Often called by the French ‘objet trouvé’.
found object.think: Think of turning a thrift-store item into art.
found object.seen: No. 144 Fountain; No. 138 Object (fur-covered cup); No. 245 Old Man’s Cloth.

freestanding.def: A sculpture that stands on its own, not attached to a wall or background, so you can walk all the way around it.
freestanding.think: Think of a statue in the middle of a plaza.

gilding.def: Covering a surface with a thin layer of gold, as gold leaf or gold paint. Something gilded is called ‘gilt’.
gilding.seen: No. 58 Reliquary of SainteFoy; No. 170 Sika dwa kofi (Golden Stool); No. 184 Jowo Rinpoche; No. 89 Ecstasy of Saint Teresa (gilt bronze rays).

gilt bronze.def: Bronze covered in a thin layer of gold, so it looks like solid gold but is far cheaper and stronger.

glass bead.def: A small bead of colored glass. Made in Venice and Bohemia, glass beads were traded worldwide by Europeans from the 1500s on, and Native American and African artists turned them into dazzling beadwork.
glass bead.seen: No. 163 Bandolier bag; No. 178 Aka elephant mask.

glaze (ceramics).def: A thin glassy coating melted onto pottery in the kiln. It makes the surface shiny, colorful and waterproof.
glaze (ceramics).think: Think of the glossy coating on a coffee mug.
glaze (ceramics).seen: No. 230 Pink Panther; No. 185 Dome of the Rock (glazed tile).

granite.def: A very hard, speckled stone formed from cooled magma. It takes a high polish and lasts almost forever.
granite.seen: No. 225 Vietnam Veterans Memorial; No. 167 Great Zimbabwe.

greywacke.def: A hard, dark gray sandstone. Egyptian sculptors used it for royal statues and objects because it could be polished to a smooth finish.
greywacke.think: Think of a dark, finegrained stone that polishes almost like metal.
greywacke.seen: No. 13 Palette of King Narmer; No. 18 King Menkaura and queen; No. 9 Ambum Stone.

gypsum.def: A soft mineral that is easy to carve and is ground to make plaster. Fine-grained gypsum is a kind of alabaster. The Sumerian votive figures from Eshnunna are carved mostly from gypsum.

hand-modeled.def: Shaped by hand, by pinching, rolling or coiling clay, rather than with a mold or a potter’s wheel.
hand-modeled.seen: No. 10 Tlatilco female figurine; No. 166 Black-on-black ceramic vessel.

headdress.def: An elaborate ornament worn on the head, often showing rank, power or a sacred role.
headdress.think: Think of a crown, but possibly made of feathers, beads or gold.
headdress.seen: No. 158 Ruler’s feather headdress; No. 196 Gold and jade crown.

helmet mask.def: A mask that covers the whole head like a helmet, rather than just the face. The Sande society’s sowei (Bundu) mask is a famous example.

hiapo.def: Tapa (bark cloth) from the island of Niue, painted freehand with fine, detailed geometric and plant designs.
hiapo.think: Think of a big cloth sheet made from tree bark, drawn on like graph-paper art.

high relief.def: Carving in which figures stick out far from the background, sometimes with parts almost fully separated. Gives strong shadows and drama.
high relief.think: Think of a figure half-stepping out of a wall.
high relief.seen: No. 47 Ludovisi Battle Sarcophagus; No. 38 Great Altar of Zeus and Athena at Pergamon; No. 200 Lakshmana Temple.
high relief.see: low relief, relief, in the round.

hollow casting.def: Casting metal so the finished sculpture is a thin shell with an empty inside. It uses less metal, weighs less, and cracks less as it cools.
hollow casting.think: Think of a chocolate Easter bunny that is hollow inside.

hood mask.def: A mask made of cloth, beads or fiber that is pulled over the whole head like a hood. The Bamileke Aka elephant mask is a beaded hood mask.

ikenga.def: A carved wooden shrine figure of the Igbo people of Nigeria, with ram’s horns, honoring a man’s right hand, his personal drive and success. A man kept one and made offerings to it.
ikenga.think: Think of a personal trophy for your own hard work and ambition.

imagines.def: Wax masks of a noble Roman family’s ancestors, kept in the atrium of the house and worn by actors in family funeral processions. They may help explain the stern realism of Roman portrait busts.
imagines.seen: No. 42 Head of a Roman patrician.

in the round.def: Sculpture that is fully threedimensional and meant to be seen from all sides, not attached to a background like relief.
in the round.think: Think of a statue you can walk all the way around.
in the round.seen: No. 27 Anavysos Kouros; No. 34 Doryphoros; No. 69 David (Donatello).

incising.def: Cutting lines or designs into a surface with a sharp tool.
incising.think: Think of scratching your initials into a tree.

inlay.def: Setting pieces of one material into cut-out spaces in another so the surface is flat and decorated, such as shell set into wood or silver set into brass.
inlay.think: Think of a puzzle where the pieces are different materials.
inlay.seen: No. 16 Standard of Ur; No. 14 Votive figures from Eshnunna (eyes); No. 41 Seated boxer (copper); No. 188 Basin (Baptistère de St. Louis).
inlay.see: pietra dura, mother-of-pearl, cloisonné, lapis lazuli.

iridescence.def: Shimmering color that changes as the angle of light changes, like a soap bubble or a peacock feather. The quetzal feathers of Aztec featherwork are iridescent green.

ivory.def: The hard, creamy-white material of elephant tusks (and some other animal teeth), prized for fine carving. Today the ivory trade is mostly banned to protect elephants.

jade.def: A very hard, usually green stone (nephrite or jadeite) prized in China, Korea and Mesoamerica for its beauty and associations with life, purity and power. It is so hard it must be ground with sand rather than carved with tools.
jade.think: Think of a stone so valuable it was worth more than gold in some cultures.
jade.seen: No. 7 Jade cong; No. 196 Gold and jade crown; No. 157 Templo Mayor (Olmecstyle mask).

jamb figure.def: A tall statue attached to the jamb (side post) of a church doorway. Those on Chartres Cathedral’s Royal Portal are stiff and column-like, almost part of the architecture.

joined-block construction.def: A Japanese technique (yosegi-zukuri) for making large wooden statues from many separately carved blocks fitted together, which makes them lighter and less likely to crack. Unkei and Kaikei’s Nio guardians at Todai-ji were made this way.
joined-block construction.think: Like building a statue from interlocking Lego pieces of carved wood.

kaolin.def: A fine white clay, the key ingredient of porcelain. Its name comes from Gaoling, a hill near the porcelain city of Jingdezhen in China.

kente.def: A colorful, strip-woven cloth of the Asante and Ewe peoples of Ghana. Narrow woven strips with bold geometric patterns are sewn together edge to edge. Once worn by royalty.
kente.think: Think of a blanket made by sewing together many brightly patterned ribbons.

kiswa.def: The black silk cloth that covers the Kaaba in Mecca, embroidered with Qur’anic verses in gold and silver thread. A new one is made every year.
kiswa.think: Think of a giant ceremonial covering made fresh each year.

kline.def: A couch used by Greeks and Etruscans for reclining while eating and drinking at banquets. The Etruscan Spouses recline on one.

knot.def: In carpet weaving, each short tuft of yarn tied around the warp threads. The more knots per square inch, the finer and more detailed the carpet. The Ardabil Carpet has roughly 26 million.
knot.think: Like pixels: more knots means higher resolution.

kore.def: An Archaic Greek statue of a standing clothed young woman. Plural: korai. Often an offering to a goddess.
kore.think: The female partner of the kouros, but always dressed.

kouros.def: An Archaic Greek statue of a nude young man standing stiffly, one foot forward, arms at his sides. Plural: kouroi. Used as grave markers and offerings.
kouros.think: Think of the Greek remix of an Egyptian standing pharaoh.
kouros.see: kore, archaic smile, frontal, in the round.

krater.def: A large, wide-mouthed Greek vase used to mix wine with water at parties.
krater.think: Think of a big punch bowl.

lamassu.def: A huge Assyrian guardian figure with a bull or lion body, eagle wings and a bearded human head, placed at palace gateways. Some have five legs so they look correct from the front and the side.
lamassu.think: Think of a giant winged bouncer guarding the door.
lamassu.see: high relief, in the round, alabaster.

lapis lazuli.def: A deep blue stone with gold flecks, mined in Afghanistan and traded across the ancient world. Very costly; it was also ground to make the paint color ultramarine.
lapis lazuli.think: Think of a stone the color of a midnight sky.
lapis lazuli.seen: No. 16 Standard of Ur; No. 23 Tutankhamun’s coﬀin.

life mask.def: A cast taken directly from a living person’s face, usually in plaster, so a sculptor can get a precise likeness. Houdon made a life mask of George Washington at Mount Vernon in 1785.

limestone.def: A fairly soft, usually pale stone formed from shells and sea creatures, easy to carve. Widely used for sculpture and buildings.
limestone.think: Think of the beige stone of many old buildings.
limestone.seen: No. 15 Seated scribe; No. 22 Akhenaton, Nefertiti, and three daughters; No. 129 The Kiss (Brancusi).

lost-wax casting.def: A way to cast metal. The artist makes a model in wax, covers it in clay, and heats it so the wax melts out (‘is lost’). Molten metal is poured into the empty space, and the clay is broken away.
lost-wax casting.think: Think of a candle shape replaced by bronze.
lost-wax casting.seen: No. 202 Shiva as Lord of Dance; No. 169 Wall plaque from Oba’s palace; No. 69 David (Donatello).

low relief.def: Carving in which figures stick out only slightly from the flat background. Also called basrelief.
low relief.think: Think of the raised design on a coin.
low relief.seen: No. 13 Palette of King Narmer; No. 36 Grave stele of Hegeso; No. 155 Yaxchilán (lintels); No. 30 Audience Hall (apadana).
low relief.see: bas-relief, high relief, sunken relief, relief.

lukasa.def: A hand-held wooden ‘memory board’ of the Luba people (Congo), covered in beads, shells and metal pins. Trained experts touched it while reciting history, king lists and sacred knowledge.
lukasa.think: Think of a beaded map you read with your fingers to remember history.

marble.def: A hard, fine-grained stone, often white, that takes a high polish and can be carved in great detail. The favorite sculpture stone of Greece, Rome and the Renaissance.
marble.think: Think of a gleaming white statue in a museum.
marble.seen: No. 34 Doryphoros; No. 37 Winged Victory of Samothrace; No. 89 Ecstasy of Saint Teresa; No. 104 George Washington.

mask.def: A covering for the face (or worn on top of the head) used in performance, ritual or dance to transform the wearer into a spirit, ancestor or character. In many cultures the mask works together with costume, music and movement.
mask.think: Think of a costume that turns the wearer into someone, or something, else.
mask.seen: No. 164 Transformation mask; No. 173 Pwo mask; No. 175 Bundu mask; No. 218 Buk (mask).

Mblo.def: A portrait mask of the Baule people (Côte d’Ivoire) carved to honor a specific admired person, danced in entertainment performances while that person watches.
Mblo.think: Think of a carved tribute to a local celebrity, worn in a dance.

metalwork.def: Objects made from metal by casting, hammering, cutting, inlaying or soldering, such as jewelry, vessels and crowns.
metalwork.think: Think of a jeweler’s or blacksmith’s craft.
metalwork.seen: No. 188 Basin (Baptistère de St. Louis); No. 196 Gold and jade crown; No. 53 Merovingian looped fibulae.

mixed media.def: A work made from several different materials combined, such as paint, photos, fabric and found objects.
mixed media.think: Think of a project using everything in the craft cupboard.
mixed media.seen: No. 233 Trade (Gifts for Trading Land); No. 237 Pisupo Lua Afe; No. 247 Preying Mantra.

moai.def: The huge stone heads-and-torsos of Rapa Nui (Easter Island), carved from volcanic tuff and set on ahu platforms, facing inland. They represent important ancestors.
moai.think: Think of giant stone ancestors watching over the village.

mobiliary art.def: Portable prehistoric art, such as carved figurines or decorated stones that could be carried, as opposed to paintings fixed to cave walls. Also called portable art.

modeling (sculpture).def: Shaping a soft material like clay or wax with hands and tools to make a sculpture. It is additive, building form up.
modeling (sculpture).seen: No. 10 Tlatilco female figurine; No. 29 Sarcophagus of the Spouses.

modular.def: Built from standard, interchangeable parts. The Terracotta Warriors were assembled from mold-made legs, torsos, arms and heads, then finished by hand so each looks individual.
modular.think: Like a car assembled from standard parts, then given custom paint.

mold.def: A hollow form into which liquid material like clay, plaster or metal is pressed or poured to make a shape. Molds let makers produce many matching parts.
mold.think: Think of a jelly mold or an ice-cube tray.
mold.seen: No. 193 Terra cotta warriors; No. 228 Androgyn III.

monolith.def: A single large block of stone, or a statue or monument carved from one. Each moai was carved from a single block of volcanic tuff.

mosaic.def: A picture or pattern made by setting many small pieces of colored stone, glass or tile (tesserae) into plaster or cement.
mosaic.think: Think of a picture made from thousands of tiny colored tiles, like pixels.
mosaic.seen: No. 40 Alexander Mosaic; No. 51 San Vitale; No. 52 Hagia Sophia; No. 185 Dome of the Rock.

mother-of-pearl.def: The shiny, rainbow-colored inner layer of some seashells, cut and inlaid into wood, lacquer or paintings.
mother-of-pearl.think: Think of the shimmer inside an oyster shell.
mother-of-pearl.seen: No. 95 The Virgin of Guadalupe; No. 94 Screen with the Siege of Belgrade.

multichannel video.def: A video artwork in which several separate video sources play at once on different screens. Paik’s Electronic Superhighway runs dozens of channels across more than 300 TV monitors.

neon.def: Glowing, gas-filled glass tubes bent into lines or letters, as in signs. Paik outlined the U.S. states in neon in Electronic Superhighway.

nephrite.def: One of the two minerals called jade, the kind used in ancient China. It is extremely tough and was shaped by abrasion.

ochre.def: Natural earth pigment colored by iron oxide, ranging from yellow to red to brown. It is one of the oldest paints humans used.
ochre.seen: No. 2 Great Hall of the Bulls; No. 4 Running horned woman.

openwork.def: Carving or metalwork pierced with holes so you can see through it, making a lacy pattern.
openwork.seen: No. 218 Buk (mask); No. 222 Malagan display and mask.

operculum.def: The hard, round ‘trapdoor’ lid a sea snail closes over its shell opening. New Ireland carvers set opercula as gleaming eyes in malagan figures. Plural: opercula.

opus sectile.def: Latin for ‘cut work’. Pictures or patterns made from pieces of colored marble or stone cut into specific shapes, rather than the small, even cubes used in mosaic.
opus sectile.think: Like a jigsaw puzzle in stone.

opus vermiculatum.def: Latin for ‘worm-like work’. The finest Roman mosaic technique, using tiny tesserae laid in curving rows that follow the outlines of forms, allowing painterly shading.

orrery.def: A mechanical model of the solar system that shows the planets orbiting the sun. Joseph Wright of Derby painted a lecture demonstrating one by lamplight.
orrery.seen: No. 100 A Philosopher Giving a Lecture on the Orrery.

pandanus.def: A tropical plant whose long leaves are dried, split and woven into mats, baskets and sails across the Pacific. Fine pandanus mats are valuable gifts.
pandanus.seen: No. 223 Presentation of Fijian mats and tapa.

paper mulberry.def: A tree whose inner bark is beaten into barkcloth (tapa) across Polynesia, and made into paper in East Asia.

patina.def: The thin film, often green or brown, that forms on bronze or copper over time, or is added on purpose with chemicals to color the metal.
patina.think: Think of the green color of the Statue of Liberty.

pedestal.def: The base that raises a statue above the ground. Rodin wanted his Burghers of Calais set low, without a tall pedestal, so the figures would stand at the viewer’s own level.

pestle.def: A heavy tool for pounding or grinding food or other materials, usually in a bowl. The Ambum Stone may have been used as one.

pieced fabric.def: Cloth made by sewing together many smaller pieces, as in quilting and patchwork.

pietra dura.def: Inlay of cut and polished colored stones fitted together into marble to make flowers, vines and patterns. Italian for ‘hard stone’.
pietra dura.think: Think of a flower picture made from jigsaw pieces of gemstones.

pile carpet.def: A carpet made by tying short tufts of yarn (knots) around the warp threads so that their cut ends stand up and form a soft, velvety surface.

plaque.def: A flat panel, often of metal or stone, decorated with relief and attached to a wall.
plaque.think: Think of a commemorative sign on a building, but sculpted.
plaque.seen: No. 169 Wall plaque from Oba’s palace.

plaster.def: A paste of lime or gypsum, sand and water that hardens as it dries. Used to coat walls (for fresco), to model details and to make casts.
plaster.think: Think of the material in a cast for a broken arm.

polychromy.def: Painting a sculpture or building in many colors. Greek and Roman marble statues were originally painted; the color has mostly worn off. Adjective: polychrome.
polychromy.think: Think of ancient statues that once looked more like painted action figures than plain white marble.
polychromy.seen: No. 27 Anavysos Kouros; No. 28 Peplos Kore; No. 62 Röttgen Pietà; No. 193 Terra cotta warriors.

porcelain.def: Fine, hard, white ceramic made from a special clay (kaolin) fired at very high heat. It can be so thin light glows through it. First perfected in China.
porcelain.think: Think of a delicate teacup that rings when you tap it.
porcelain.seen: No. 204 The David Vases; No. 230 Pink Panther; No. 250 Kui Hua Zi (Sunflower Seeds).

portrait.def: A likeness of a specific person, showing their appearance, status or character. It can be painted, carved, cast or photographed, and it can be naturalistic or symbolic.
portrait.think: Think of an oﬀicial headshot, but with a message about who the person is.
portrait.seen: No. 42 Head of a Roman patrician; No. 171 Ndop; No. 174 Mblo; No. 205 Portrait of Sin Sukju.

portrait mask.def: A mask that represents a specific, named person, such as the Baule mblo masks honoring individuals admired for their beauty or achievements.

Prussian blue.def: A deep blue synthetic pigment invented in Berlin around 1706. Imported into Japan, it gave Hokusai the intense blues of the Great Wave.

public art.def: Art installed in public spaces, like parks, plazas or streets, where anyone can see it, often paid for by governments or communities.
public art.think: Think of a sculpture in a city park.
public art.seen: No. 150 Lipstick (Ascending) on Caterpillar Tracks; No. 225 Vietnam Veterans Memorial; No. 224 The Gates.

Pwo.def: A female mask of the Chokwe people (Angola and Congo) honoring the ideal woman and the founding ancestress. Ironically, it is danced by men, dressed as women.
Pwo.think: Think of a tribute mask of the perfect ancestor-mother.

pyxis.def: A small round box with a lid, used for jewelry, cosmetics or perfume. Plural: pyxides.
pyxis.think: Think of a fancy jewelry box shaped like a cylinder.

quillwork.def: Native American decoration made from dyed porcupine quills, flattened and sewn or wrapped onto hide or birchbark. Glass beadwork, like that on the Lenape bandolier bag (No. 163), largely replaced it once trade beads were plentiful.

quilt.def: A padded blanket made of layers of fabric stitched together, often with a top pieced from many patches. Faith Ringgold made painted ‘story quilts’ joining painting and Black women’s quilting traditions.
quilt.think: Think of a patchwork blanket that tells a story.

raﬀia.def: Fiber from the leaves of the raﬀia palm, used for weaving, cloth and the costumes that go with masks in Central and West Africa.
raﬀia.think: Think of the straw-like ribbon used for gift wrapping.

rank badge.def: An embroidered square on the chest and back of an oﬀicial’s robe in the Chinese and Korean courts, showing his rank with birds for civil oﬀicials and animals for military oﬀicers.

recycled materials.def: Discarded or reused materials, like bottle caps, tin cans or scrap metal, turned into art, often with comments on trade, waste and globalization.
recycled materials.think: Think of turning trash into treasure, with a message.
recycled materials.seen: No. 245 Old Man’s Cloth; No. 237 Pisupo Lua Afe.

red-figure.def: A Greek vase-painting technique where the background is painted black and the figures are left the red-orange color of the clay, with details drawn in with a brush. It allowed more lifelike detail than black-figure.
red-figure.think: Think of a photo negative of black-figure: red people on black.

reduction firing.def: Firing pottery with little oxygen so smoke changes the color of the clay or glaze. María Martínez’s pots turned black when the fire was smothered with powdered manure.

relief.def: Sculpture that projects from a flat background instead of standing free. It can be low (bas-relief), high, or sunken.
relief.think: Think of a design that pops up out of a wall.
relief.seen: No. 13 Palette of King Narmer; No. 19 Code of Hammurabi; No. 47 Ludovisi Battle Sarcophagus; No. 45 Forum of Trajan (Column).
relief.see: low relief, high relief, sunken relief, in the round.

repoussé.def: Shaping thin sheet metal by hammering it from the back to raise a design on the front.
repoussé.think: Think of pushing a spoon into tin foil from behind to make a bump.
repoussé.seen: No. 160 Maize cobs; No. 153 Chavín de Huántar (gold jewelry).

resin.def: A sticky material, natural (from trees) or synthetic (plastic), that hardens. Artists use it to cast shapes, stiffen fabric or coat surfaces.
resin.think: Think of epoxy glue that hardens clear.
resin.seen: No. 150 Lipstick (Ascending) on Caterpillar Tracks; No. 228 Androgyn III.

rivet.def: A metal pin hammered flat at both ends to fasten metal sheets together. Michel Tuffery built his bull from flattened corned-beef cans riveted together.

rock-cut.def: Carved directly out of a natural cliff or rock face, rather than built from separate blocks.
rock-cut.think: Think of sculpting a mountainside instead of stacking bricks.
rock-cut.seen: No. 181 Petra (Treasury); No. 182 Buddha (Bamiyan); No. 195 Longmen caves.

Roman copy.def: A marble copy made by Roman sculptors of a famous Greek statue, usually originally bronze. Many Greek originals are lost, so we know them only through copies. Marble copies often add a tree trunk or other strut to hold up the heavy stone.
Roman copy.think: Think of a cover version of a lost hit song.

sacrum.def: The large triangular bone at the base of the spine; the name is Latin for ‘sacred bone’. The Tequixquiac sacrum, from an extinct camelid, was carved so it looks like the head of a dog or coyote.
sacrum.seen: No. 3 Camelid sacrum in the shape of a canine.

sandstone.def: A stone made of sand grains pressed together over time, usually tan, red or yellow. Easy to carve, good for relief and buildings.
sandstone.think: Think of the rock in red desert canyons.
sandstone.seen: No. 6 Anthropomorphic stele; No. 200 Lakshmana Temple; No. 192 Great Stupa at Sanchi.

sarcophagus.def: A stone or clay coffin, often carved with figures or scenes. Plural: sarcophagi. Greek for ‘flesh-eater’.
sarcophagus.think: Think of a decorated stone coﬀin.
sarcophagus.seen: No. 29 Sarcophagus of the Spouses; No. 47 Ludovisi Battle Sarcophagus.

sarsen.def: A hard sandstone found in southern England. Stonehenge’s huge outer circle and trilithons are sarsens; the smaller ‘bluestones’ came from Wales.

sheet metal.def: Metal hammered or rolled into thin, flat sheets that can be cut, bent and joined. The Inka maize cobs are made of thin sheets of gold and silver alloys.

shell.def: Seashell and turtle shell used as a material for inlay, ornament, beads and, in the Pacific, even whole masks.
shell.think: Think of beach shells used like precious stones.
shell.seen: No. 16 Standard of Ur; No. 218 Buk (mask); No. 222 Malagan display and mask.

sherd.def: A broken piece of pottery, also called a potsherd. Archaeologists use sherds to date sites and identify cultures, because fired clay survives well.

silk.def: A fine, smooth, strong thread spun by silkworms, woven into cloth. In China, Korea and Japan it was also a support for painting and writing.
silk.think: Think of the softest, shiniest fabric you know.
silk.seen: No. 194 Funeral banner of Lady Dai; No. 201 Travelers among Mountains and Streams; No. 191 Ardabil Carpet.

site-specific.def: Art made for one particular place, so that its meaning depends on that location. Moving it would change or destroy the work.
site-specific.think: Think of a song written for one stadium that wouldn’t make sense anywhere else.
site-specific.seen: No. 151 Spiral Jetty; No. 248 Shibboleth; No. 224 The Gates.

slip.def: Clay mixed with water to make a creamy liquid, used to coat or paint pottery and to join clay pieces. Greek painters used a fine slip that turned black in firing.
slip.seen: No. 33 Niobides Krater; No. 166 Black-on-black ceramic vessel.

soft sculpture.def: Sculpture made from soft materials like vinyl, cloth or foam, often making hard everyday things floppy. Claes Oldenburg is its best-known maker; Lipstick (Ascending) first had a soft vinyl tip that was pumped up with air.

sowei.def: A helmet mask of the Sande society of the Mende (Sierra Leone), worn by women leaders when initiating girls into adulthood, one of the few African masks danced by women. Its neck rolls signal health and beauty. Also called a Bundu mask.
sowei.think: Think of a mask that shows the ideal grown woman, worn by women.

spangle.def: A small, thin, shiny disk sewn or hung on clothing or ornaments to catch the light. Gold spangles hang from the Silla crown on wires, so they trembled as the wearer moved.

sphinx.def: A creature with a lion’s body and a human head, in Egypt usually the king’s head, symbolizing royal power and protection.
sphinx.think: Think of a lion with a king’s face guarding the tombs.

staff god.def: A carved wooden figure from Rarotonga (Cook Islands) with a god’s head at the top, wrapped in a huge roll of tapa cloth. Christian missionaries removed and destroyed many wrappings.
staff god.think: Think of a sacred carved pole swaddled in bark cloth.

stele.def: An upright stone slab carved with images or writing, used as a marker, monument, law code or gravestone. Plural: stelae.
stele.think: Think of a giant stone sign or tombstone.
stele.seen: No. 6 Anthropomorphic stele; No. 19 Code of Hammurabi; No. 36 Grave stele of Hegeso.

stem stitch.def: An embroidery stitch of overlapping slanted stitches that makes a fine, rope-like line, used in the Bayeux Tapestry for outlines and lettering.

stick chart.def: A navigation chart from the Marshall Islands made of sticks tied with fiber and dotted with shells. The curved and straight sticks show ocean swells and currents; the shells show islands. Studied before voyages, not carried on board.
stick chart.think: Think of a 3D map of ocean waves.

stoneware.def: Pottery fired at a high temperature until it becomes very hard, dense and waterproof even without glaze. Between earthenware and porcelain in strength.
stoneware.think: Think of a heavy, sturdy mug.

story quilt.def: A quilt whose painted or sewn images and handwritten text tell a story. Faith Ringgold invented painted story quilts, joining African American quilting traditions to painting.

stucco.def: A plaster that can be molded into decorations or smoothed over walls. Used for decorative ceilings and carved patterns.
stucco.think: Think of cake frosting that hardens into stone.
stucco.seen: No. 65 Alhambra; No. 82 Il Gesù; No. 88 San Carlo alle Quattro Fontane.

subtractive.def: Making a sculpture by removing material, carving or cutting it away from a block. The opposite of additive.
subtractive.think: Think of Michelangelo’s idea of freeing a figure trapped inside the stone.
subtractive.seen: No. 37 Winged Victory of Samothrace; No. 129 The Kiss (Brancusi).

sunken relief.def: Relief where the figures are cut into the surface, so their highest points are level with (or below) the flat surface around them. Common in Egypt; it holds up well in bright sun.
sunken relief.think: Think of an engraved outline that sinks into the stone instead of popping out.
sunken relief.seen: No. 22 Akhenaton, Nefertiti, and three daughters.

tableau.def: A staged scene in which figures are arranged and frozen as if in a painting. Yinka Shonibare’s The Swing (after Fragonard) turns a painting into a three-dimensional tableau you can walk around.

tapestry.def: A heavy textile in which the picture is woven into the cloth itself, with colored weft threads. Careful: the Bayeux Tapestry is actually embroidery, stitched on top of linen, not woven.
tapestry.think: Think of a picture made entirely of woven threads.

tenon head.def: A stone head with a long peg (tenon) on the back so it can be set into a wall. At Chavín de Huántar they show a human face changing step by step into a snarling jaguar.

terracotta.def: Reddish-brown baked clay used for sculpture, pottery and roof tiles. Italian for ‘baked earth’.
terracotta.think: Think of a red clay flowerpot.
terracotta.seen: No. 29 Sarcophagus of the Spouses; No. 31 Temple of Minerva (Apollo of Veii); No. 193 Terra cotta warriors; No. 11 Terra cotta fragment (Lapita).

tesserae.def: The small cubes of stone, glass or tile used to make a mosaic. Singular: tessera. Glass tesserae backed with gold leaf make glittering gold backgrounds.
tesserae.think: Think of the individual pixels of a mosaic.
tesserae.seen: No. 40 Alexander Mosaic; No. 51 San Vitale.

textile.def: Any cloth or fabric made by weaving, knitting, knotting, felting or pressing fibers. In many cultures, like the Inka, fine textiles were worth more than gold.
textile.think: Think of everything from a T-shirt to a royal carpet.
textile.seen: No. 162 All-T’oqapu tunic; No. 191 Ardabil Carpet; No. 59 Bayeux Tapestry.

tie-dye.def: A resist-dye technique: cloth is tied, folded or bound so parts of it don’t take the dye, creating patterns. Faith Ringgold framed Dancing at the Louvre with tie-dyed fabric.

titanium.def: A light, strong, silvery metal that does not rust. Gehry covered the Guggenheim Bilbao in thin titanium panels that shimmer like fish scales.

tooling.def: Pressing or punching small patterns into a surface, such as gold leaf, leather or metal, with small tools. The gold backgrounds of the Golden Haggadah are tooled.

transformation mask.def: A mask of the Kwakwaka’wakw and other Northwest Coast peoples that opens with strings during a dance to reveal a second face inside, showing a being changing from animal to human or ancestor.
transformation mask.think: Think of a mask with a surprise face hidden inside.

truth to materials.def: The modernist belief that a material should look like itself: stone should feel like stone, and wood should show its grain. Brancusi’s direct carving follows it.

tufa.def: A soft, porous stone formed from volcanic ash (also called tuff), easy to carve or dig into.
tufa.think: Think of a lightweight, spongy rock.
tufa.seen: No. 32 Tomb of the Triclinium; No. 48 Catacomb of Priscilla; No. 214 Moai (volcanic tuff).

tuff.def: A soft, porous rock formed from compacted volcanic ash. Rapa Nui’s moai were carved from it. The volcanic stone of the Roman catacombs, often called tufa, is geologically tuff too.

ultramarine.def: A brilliant deep blue pigment made from ground lapis lazuli from Afghanistan. Before a synthetic version was invented in the 1820s it could cost more than gold; Vermeer used it lavishly.

undercutting.def: Carving deep behind the forms of a sculpture or relief so they stand away from the background and cast deep shadows.
undercutting.seen: No. 37 Winged Victory of Samothrace; No. 38 Great Altar of Zeus and Athena at Pergamon; No. 57 Pyxis of al-Mughira; No. 180 Veranda post (Opo Ogoga).

underglaze.def: Color painted onto pottery before the clear glaze is applied and fired, so the design is sealed under a glassy layer.
underglaze.think: Think of a drawing protected under clear nail polish.

veranda post.def: A carved wooden post that holds up the roof of a veranda (covered porch) of a palace. The Yoruba sculptor Olowe of Ise carved posts with figures that seem to carry the roof.
veranda post.think: Think of a support pillar that is also a sculpture.
veranda post.see: wood carving, architectural sculpture, hierarchical scale.

votive figure.def: A statue left at a shrine or temple as an offering or as a stand-in for a worshipper, so they could ‘keep praying’ when not there.
votive figure.think: Think of a stand-in that prays for you 24/7.

warp.def: On a loom, the threads stretched lengthwise and held tight. The weft threads are woven over and under them.
warp.think: Think of the strings on a guitar that you weave across.
warp.seen: No. 191 Ardabil Carpet; No. 162 All-T’oqapu tunic.

weaving.def: Making cloth by passing threads (weft) over and under a set of tightly stretched threads (warp), usually on a loom.
weaving.think: Think of a potholder loom from summer camp.
weaving.seen: No. 162 All-T’oqapu tunic; No. 191 Ardabil Carpet.

weft.def: The threads woven crosswise over and under the warp threads on a loom. In tapestry, colored wefts make the picture.
weft.think: Think of the thread that goes back and forth.
weft.seen: No. 162 All-T’oqapu tunic; No. 191 Ardabil Carpet.

wet drapery.def: A carving style in which thin cloth seems wet and clings to the body, revealing it while forming rippling folds. It began on the Parthenon sculptures and continued in Hellenistic works like the Winged Victory.
wet drapery.seen: No. 35 Acropolis (Parthenon); No. 36 Grave stele of Hegeso; No. 37 Winged Victory of Samothrace.

wood carving.def: Shaping wood with knives, adzes and chisels. Many of the 250 works from Africa and the Pacific are carved wood, often from a single piece.
wood carving.think: Think of whittling, at a master level.
wood carving.seen: No. 171 Ndop; No. 180 Veranda post (Opo Ogoga); No. 217 Female deity (Nukuoro); No. 62 Röttgen Pietà.
wood carving.see: carving, subtractive, polychromy. 5 Architecture Building parts and plans, from Greek columns to Gothic buttresses, mosque prayer niches, Buddhist stupas and steel skyscrapers. Architecture questions are usually about how a structural trick creates a particular space or effect.

acropolis.def: The high, fortified hilltop of a Greek city, where its most important temples stood. ‘The’ Acropolis usually means the one in Athens, with the Parthenon.
acropolis.think: ‘Akro’ means high and ‘polis’ means city: the ‘high city.’

adobe.def: Sun-dried brick made from clay, sand and straw, or the mud mortar and plaster made from the same mix. Used from Africa to the American Southwest.
adobe.think: Think of mud bricks baked by the sun, not an oven.
adobe.seen: No. 168 Great Mosque of Djenné; No. 154 Mesa Verde cliff dwellings.

aedicula.def: A small shrine-like frame made of columns or pilasters holding up a pediment, used to frame a statue, window, altar or doorway. Plural: aediculae.
aedicula.think: A mini temple front used as a picture frame.

agora.def: The open public square of a Greek city, used for markets, politics and daily social life, lined with stoas and civic buildings.
agora.think: downtown, the mall and city hall in one open space.

agricultural terrace.def: Flat strips of farmland cut into steep hillsides and held up by stone walls. They stop erosion and let people farm mountains, as at Machu Picchu.
agricultural terrace.think: Think of turning a mountainside into a staircase of fields.

ahu.def: A stone platform on Rapa Nui (Easter Island) on which moai figures stand in a row, usually facing inland. It served as a shrine and burial place for ancestors.
ahu.think: Think of a stage for giant ancestor statues.
ahu.seen: No. 214 Moai on ahu; No. 214 Moai on platform (ahu).

aisle.def: A long side passage that runs parallel to the nave of a church, separated from it by a row of columns or piers.
aisle.think: Think of the side lanes next to the main highway of the nave.
aisle.seen: No. 49 Santa Sabina; No. 60 Chartres Cathedral; No. 58 Sainte-Foy, Conques.

alcove.def: A small space set back into a wall or room. At Mesa Verde the word means the shallow, natural hollows in the cliff face where whole villages were built.
alcove.think: A nook. At Mesa Verde, a nook big enough for a village.

amalaka.def: A ribbed, disk-shaped stone that caps the shikhara of a north Indian temple, shaped like a segmented fruit.
amalaka.think: Think of a giant stone cogwheel on top of the tower.

ambulatory.def: A walkway that goes around something, such as the apse of a church or the central space of a round shrine. It let pilgrims circle relics without disturbing services. The Dome of the Rock has two ambulatories around its sacred rock.
ambulatory.think: From the Latin ‘to walk.’ Think of a loop path.
ambulatory.seen: No. 58 Sainte-Foy, Conques; No. 60 Chartres Cathedral; No. 51 San Vitale; No. 185 Dome of the Rock.
ambulatory.see: radiating chapels, apse, central plan, pradakshina patha.

amphitheater.def: A large round or oval open-air arena with seats rising all around, built by the Romans for gladiator fights and public shows.
amphitheater.think: Think of an ancient sports stadium.

anda.def: The solid, hemispherical dome of a stupa, which covers the relics and stands for the dome of heaven or the world mountain.

apadana.def: A great audience hall of the ancient Persian kings, a hypostyle hall where the king received visitors and gifts. The one at Persepolis stood on a raised platform reached by staircases carved with processions of tribute bearers.
apadana.think: Think of a royal throne room big enough to receive the whole empire.

applied ornament.def: Decoration attached to the surface of a building rather than growing out of its structure. In Postmodern architecture, like Venturi’s House in New Castle County, flat cut-out columns and arches are openly stuck on as signs.
applied ornament.think: Stickers on a laptop: they decorate, but they hold nothing up.
applied ornament.seen: No. 152 House in New Castle County.

apse.def: A semicircular space, usually covered by a half-dome, at the end of a basilica or church, where the altar or judge’s seat sits.
apse.think: Think of a rounded ‘stage’ at the far end of the hall.
apse.seen: No. 45 Forum of Trajan; No. 49 Santa Sabina; No. 51 San Vitale.

arabesque.def: A flowing, endlessly repeating pattern of curling vines, leaves and tendrils, common in Islamic art and architecture. It suggests the infinite and avoids pictures of people.
arabesque.think: Think of vine-like wallpaper with no beginning and no end.
arabesque.seen: No. 65 Alhambra; No. 185 Dome of the Rock; No. 186 Great Mosque of Isfahan; No. 191 Ardabil Carpet; No. 57 Pyxis of al-Mughira.

arcade.def: A row of arches held up by columns or piers.
arcade.think: Think of a colonnade that uses arches instead of flat beams.
arcade.seen: No. 44 Colosseum; No. 49 Santa Sabina; No. 56 Great Mosque of Córdoba; No. 60 Chartres Cathedral.

arch.def: A curved structure that spans an opening. Wedge-shaped stones (voussoirs) press against each other and pass the weight down to the sides. Arches can span wider gaps than a single beam.
arch.think: Think of people leaning shoulder to shoulder in a curve so no one falls.
arch.seen: No. 44 Colosseum; No. 56 Great Mosque of Córdoba; No. 60 Chartres Cathedral.
arch.see: voussoir, keystone, round arch, pointed arch.

architectural calligraphy.def: Beautiful writing used as decoration on a building, often Qur’an verses or poetry, carved in stone or stucco or laid in tile and mosaic. On the Taj Mahal the letters get larger near the top so they look the same size from the ground.
architectural calligraphy.think: Think of a building that literally speaks.
architectural calligraphy.seen: No. 185 Dome of the Rock; No. 209 Taj Mahal; No. 65 Alhambra; No. 84 Mosque of Selim II.

architectural drawing.def: A precise line drawing, such as a plan, elevation or section, used to design or record a building. Julie Mehretu layers drawings of stadiums and buildings into her paintings.

architrave.def: The lowest layer of the entablature: a plain horizontal beam resting directly on top of the columns.
architrave.think: the classical version of a lintel.

archivolt.def: One of the curved bands that frame the tympanum of a church doorway, often carved with small figures.
archivolt.think: Think of the rainbow-like stripes arching over a church door.

arcosolium.def: An arched niche cut into the wall of a catacomb, with a tomb below the arch. Wealthier families paid for them, and they were often painted. Plural: arcosolia.

ashlar masonry.def: Walls made of stone blocks cut and smoothed so precisely that they fit tightly without mortar. Inka ashlar is so exact that a knife blade cannot slip between the stones.
ashlar masonry.think: Think of a stone jigsaw puzzle with perfect pieces.
ashlar masonry.seen: No. 159 City of Cusco; No. 161 Machu Picchu.
ashlar masonry.see: dry-stone masonry, battered wall, trapezoidal doorway.

atrium.def: 1) The main entrance hall of a Roman house, with an opening in the roof. 2) The open courtyard in front of an Early Christian church. 3) Today, any tall, open central space inside a building.
atrium.think: Think of a room that opens up to the sky or to the full height of the building.
atrium.seen: No. 39 House of the Vettii; No. 240 Guggenheim Bilbao.

axial plan.def: A layout in which buildings and spaces line up along a straight central line (an axis), so you move through them in a set order toward the most important space.
axial plan.think: Like a runway leading to the main event.
axial plan.seen: No. 20 Temple of AmunRe, Karnak; No. 93 Palace at Versailles; No. 206 Forbidden City.

ballcourt.def: A long, narrow court with sloping or vertical walls where Mesoamericans played a ritual ballgame with a heavy rubber ball. The game was tied to cosmic battles, politics and sometimes sacrifice.
ballcourt.think: Think of an ancient sports arena that was also a temple.

banco.def: The fermented mud mixture used to build and plaster mosques and houses in Mali. At Djenné it is re-applied every year.
banco.think: Think of a mud plaster that is the building’s protective skin.

barrel vault.def: A ceiling made by extending a round arch in a straight line, like a tunnel. Also called a tunnel vault. It is heavy and pushes outward along its whole length, so the walls below must be thick.
barrel vault.think: Think of half of a tin can lying on its side.
barrel vault.seen: No. 44 Colosseum; No. 58 Sainte-Foy, Conques; No. 63 Arena (Scrovegni) Chapel; No. 82 Il Gesù.

basilica.def: Originally a long Roman public hall used for law courts and business, with a central nave, side aisles and an apse at the end. Early Christians copied this plan for their churches.
basilica.think: Think of a long hall built to hold a crowd and point everyone toward one end.
basilica.seen: No. 45 Forum of Trajan; No. 49 Santa Sabina; No. 52 Hagia Sophia; No. 60 Chartres Cathedral.

battered wall.def: A wall that leans slightly inward as it rises, so it is thicker at the bottom than at the top. This makes it very stable, which is why the Inka used it in earthquake country.
battered wall.think: Think of how you widen your stance to keep your balance.
battered wall.seen: No. 12 White Temple and ziggurat; No. 159 City of Cusco.

bay.def: One repeated section of a building, marked off by columns, piers, or vault ribs. A Gothic nave is a row of identical bays.
bay.think: Think of one slice of a loaf of bread.

bent-axis approach.def: A path into a holy building that forces you to turn corners instead of walking straight in. It slows visitors down and makes reaching the shrine feel like a journey.
bent-axis approach.think: The opposite of a straight hallway: you can never see the goal from the start.

Bilbao effect.def: The idea that one spectacular building by a famous architect can revive a struggling city by attracting tourists and money, as Gehry’s Guggenheim did for Bilbao, Spain.
Bilbao effect.think: Think of a building used as a city’s advertisement.

borrowed scenery.def: A garden-design idea, called shakkei in Japanese, of framing hills, trees or buildings outside the garden so they seem to be part of the view.
borrowed scenery.think: Like a cafe on the beach that makes the ocean part of its decor.

bouleuterion.def: A council house in a Greek city, where the elected council met to plan government business.
bouleuterion.think: Think of a city council chamber.

bracket system.def: In Chinese and Japanese wooden buildings, interlocking wooden blocks and arms (called dougong in Chinese) that sit on top of the columns and carry the heavy, overhanging tile roof. The more elaborate the brackets, the higher the building’s rank.
bracket system.think: Think of a wooden LEGO tower that spreads the roof’s weight onto the columns.

broken pediment.def: A pediment with a gap in it, either at the top point or along the bottom, so the triangle is not closed. Used for drama in Roman-era and Baroque buildings and for wit in Postmodern ones.
broken pediment.think: Think of a triangle with a bite taken out of it.
broken pediment.seen: No. 181 Petra Treasury; No. 152 House in New Castle County.

buttress.def: A mass of masonry built against a wall to brace it and resist the outward push of arches, vaults or domes.
buttress.think: Think of propping your hand against a wall to keep it from falling over.
buttress.seen: No. 52 Hagia Sophia; No. 60 Chartres Cathedral.

cantilever.def: A beam or floor that sticks out into the air, supported at only one end. Fallingwater’s terraces cantilever out over a waterfall.

capital.def: The decorated top of a column, which spreads out to support the beam above. The shape of the capital is the easiest way to tell the Greek orders apart: plain cushion (Doric), scrolls (Ionic), or leaves (Corinthian).
capital.think: Think of the column’s hat. Do not confuse it with ‘capitol’, a government building.
capital.seen: No. 35 Acropolis (Parthenon); No. 46 Pantheon; No. 20 Temple of Amun-Re, Karnak; No. 30 Apadana, Persepolis.
capital.see: Doric order, Ionic order, Corinthian order, column.

caryatid.def: A statue of a woman used as a column to hold up a roof. The Erechtheion on the Athenian Acropolis has a famous porch of six.
caryatid.think: Think of a column that is also a person balancing the building on her head.

cast iron.def: Iron melted and poured into molds. Strong and cheap in the 1800s, it was used for building frames and for intricate ornament, like the swirling decoration over the entrance of Sullivan’s Carson, Pirie, Scott store.

cathedral.def: The main church of a bishop’s district, holding the bishop’s throne (the ‘cathedra’). Medieval cathedrals were the biggest, most expensive buildings in their towns.
cathedral.think: Not every big church is a cathedral; it is about the bishop’s seat, not size.

causeway.def: A raised road or walkway. At Giza, a long causeway linked each pyramid’s valley temple near the Nile to its mortuary temple beside the pyramid.

cave temple.def: A shrine or temple carved into natural or artificial caves in a cliff, filled with sculpture. The Longmen caves in China hold thousands of Buddhist niches and statues.
cave temple.think: Think of a cliff turned into a vertical gallery of holy figures.
cave temple.seen: No. 195 Longmen caves; No. 182 Bamiyan Buddha.

cella.def: The inner room of a Greek or Roman temple, where the statue of the god stood. Ordinary worshippers usually stayed outside. The Greek word is ‘naos.’ Etruscan temples had a triple cella, three rooms side by side.
cella.think: the god’s private bedroom inside the temple.
cella.seen: No. 35 Acropolis (Parthenon); No. 31 Temple of Minerva, Veii.

cenotaph.def: A tomb-like monument that does not hold the body. In the Taj Mahal, the cenotaphs of Mumtaz Mahal and Shah Jahan sit in the main hall, while their real graves lie in a crypt below.

central plan.def: A building laid out around a central point, so all sides are equal or nearly so, such as a circle, square, octagon or Greek cross. It usually has a dome over the middle.
central plan.think: Think of a pizza (radiates from the center) versus a hot dog (long, like a basilica).
central plan.seen: No. 51 San Vitale; No. 185 Dome of the Rock; No. 84 Mosque of Selim II.
central plan.see: longitudinal plan, octagonal plan, dome, Greek cross plan.

chaitya.def: A Buddhist prayer hall, often cut into rock, with a long nave and a small stupa at the far rounded end so worshippers can walk around it.
chaitya.think: Think of a Buddhist basilica carved into a cliff.

chamber tomb.def: A tomb with one or more rooms built or cut underground, often decorated like a house for the dead. Etruscan families were buried in painted chamber tombs.

chapel.def: A small room or building for prayer, either standing alone or set inside a larger church.
chapel.seen: No. 63 Arena (Scrovegni) Chapel; No. 67 Pazzi Chapel; No. 89 Ecstasy of Saint Teresa.

chapter house.def: A meeting room attached to a monastery or cathedral, where monks or clergy gathered to discuss business and hear readings.
chapter house.think: Think of a monastery’s conference room.

charbagh.def: A Persian-style garden divided into four parts by water channels or paths, often seen as an image of paradise, which the Qur’an describes as having four rivers.

chattra.def: The umbrella-shaped disks stacked on a mast at the top of a stupa. Umbrellas were marks of royalty and honor; at Sanchi there are three, often read as the Three Jewels of Buddhism.
chattra.think: Think of stone parasols shading the Buddha’s relics.

chevron pattern.def: A zigzag or Vshaped pattern. At Great Zimbabwe, a chevron band runs along the top of the Great Enclosure wall.
chevron pattern.think: Think of the stripes on a sergeant’s sleeve.

chhatri.def: A small, open, dome-topped pavilion held up by columns, used on rooftops and corners in Indian and Mughal architecture. The Taj Mahal has four around its main dome.

Chicago School.def: Architects working in Chicago in the 1880s and 1890s, such as Louis Sullivan, who designed early steel-framed skyscrapers with large windows and clear structure.
Chicago School.think: Think of the birthplace of the skyscraper.
Chicago School.see: skyscraper, form follows function, Chicago window.

Chicago window.def: A wide window with a large fixed glass pane in the middle and a narrow window on each side that can open. A steel frame made it possible.
Chicago window.think: Think of a picture window flanked by two vents.

choir.def: The part of a church near the altar, beyond the crossing, where the clergy and singers sat during services.
choir.think: Think of the VIP section closest to the altar.

circulation.def: How people move through a building: the routes, ramps, stairs and corridors that connect its spaces. At MAXXI, Zaha Hadid made circulation the main idea of the design.

citadel.def: A fortified stronghold, often on high ground, protecting a city’s palace and temples. Sargon II’s palace at Dur Sharrukin stood within a walled citadel guarded by lamassu.

cladding.def: An outer covering or skin attached to a building’s frame, such as terra cotta, glass, stone or titanium.
cladding.seen: No. 124 Carson, Pirie, Scott Building; No. 146 Seagram Building; No. 240 Guggenheim Bilbao.

clerestory.def: A row of windows high up in a wall, above the roofs of the side aisles, that lets light into the center of a large hall or church.
clerestory.think: Pronounced like ‘clear story’: the clear, windowed story at the top.
clerestory.seen: No. 20 Temple of Amun-Re, Karnak; No. 49 Santa Sabina; No. 60 Chartres Cathedral.

cliff dwelling.def: A building or village tucked into a natural rock overhang in a canyon cliff. Ancestral Puebloans at Mesa Verde built multistory sandstone houses this way, protected from weather and enemies.
cliff dwelling.think: Think of an apartment complex built under a rocky ledge.

cloister.def: An enclosed garden courtyard surrounded by a covered walkway, part of a monastery or convent. The Spanish built a convent with a cloister on top of the Inka sun temple in Cusco.
cloister.think: Think of a quiet, walled garden with a covered path all around.

coffer.def: A sunken square or other shaped panel set into a ceiling or dome. Coffers make a dome lighter and decorate it with a grid pattern.
coffer.think: Think of the dimpled pattern of a waffle.
coffer.seen: No. 46 Pantheon; No. 88 San Carlo alle Quattro Fontane.

colonnade.def: A long row of columns spaced at regular intervals, usually holding up a roof or entablature.
colonnade.think: Think of a parade of columns marching in line.
colonnade.seen: No. 21 Mortuary temple of Hatshepsut; No. 35 Acropolis (Parthenon); No. 49 Santa Sabina.

column.def: An upright post, usually round, that holds up a roof or beam. A classical column has three parts: a base at the bottom, a long shaft, and a decorated capital on top.
column.think: Think of a tree trunk turned into stone, with feet and a hat.
column.seen: No. 35 Acropolis (Parthenon); No. 20 Temple of Amun-Re, Karnak; No. 46 Pantheon.

commemorative column.def: A single, tall freestanding column built to celebrate a person or event. Trajan’s Column is wrapped in a spiraling relief that tells the story of his wars like a scroll.
commemorative column.think: Think of a giant stone trophy with a comic strip wound around it.

Composite order.def: A Roman order that combines the scrolls of the Ionic capital with the leaves of the Corinthian capital. It is the showiest order of all.
Composite order.think: Think of an Ionic and a Corinthian capital mashed together.

compound pier.def: A pier with several thinner shafts attached to it. Each shaft lines up with an arch or rib above, so the wall’s structure reads as a set of lines rising to the vault.
compound pier.think: Think of a bundle of stems tied together.

computer-aided design.def: Using computer software to design and engineer buildings. Frank Gehry used CATIA, an aerospace program, to calculate the curves of the Guggenheim Bilbao. Often shortened to CAD.
computer-aided design.think: Think of designing a building the way engineers design a jet.

concrete.def: A building material made by mixing lime, sand, water and rubble that hardens like stone. Romans used it to pour huge curved shapes like domes and vaults, which changed architecture forever.
concrete.think: liquid stone that can be poured into any shape.
concrete.seen: No. 44 Colosseum; No. 45 Forum of Trajan; No. 46 Pantheon.
