congregational mosque.def: A large mosque where a whole community gathers for the Friday noon prayer and sermon. Also called a Friday mosque or, in Persian, masjid-e jameh.
congregational mosque.think: Think of the main mosque of a town, as opposed to a small neighborhood one.
congregational mosque.seen: No. 56 Great Mosque of Córdoba; No. 84 Mosque of Selim II ; No. 168 Great Mosque of Djenné; No. 186 Great Mosque of Isfahan.

conical tower.def: A solid, cone-shaped stone tower. The one inside Great Zimbabwe’s Great Enclosure may stand for a granary, symbolizing the ruler’s generosity.
conical tower.think: Think of a giant stone traﬀic cone.

corbel.def: A stone that sticks out from a wall to support something above it. A corbeled vault or arch is made by stacking stones that each stick out a bit farther than the one below, until the two sides meet at the top. It is not a true arch.
corbel.think: Think of stacking books so each one hangs over the edge a little more than the last.

Corinthian order.def: The most decorative order. Its tall capital is shaped like a basket covered in carved acanthus leaves with small scrolls at the corners. The Romans loved it.
Corinthian order.think: The fanciest order: a column wearing a leafy crown.
Corinthian order.seen: No. 46 Pantheon; No. 49 Santa Sabina; No. 181 Petra Treasury; No. 67 Pazzi Chapel.

cornice.def: The top, projecting layer of an entablature, or any strong ledge that sticks out along the top of a wall. It throws rainwater away from the wall and gives a building a firm ‘lid’.
cornice.think: Think of the brim on the top edge of a building.

coursed masonry.def: Stone or brick laid in neat, level horizontal rows (courses). Great Zimbabwe’s walls are coursed granite blocks laid without mortar.
coursed masonry.think: Think of stones stacked like rows of bricks in a wall.

courtyard.def: An open-air space enclosed by walls or buildings. Courtyards organize mosques, palaces, houses and temples across many cultures.
courtyard.think: Think of a private outdoor room with no ceiling.
courtyard.seen: No. 65 Alhambra; No. 186 Great Mosque of Isfahan; No. 206 Forbidden City; No. 39 House of the Vettii.

crépissage.def: The yearly festival in Djenné when the whole community re-plasters the Great Mosque with fresh mud before the rainy season.
crépissage.think: French for ‘plastering.’ Think of a town-wide repair party.

cromlech.def: An old Welsh and Breton word for a prehistoric stone circle, or for a few upright stones capped with a flat slab. Stonehenge is the most famous stone circle.

crossing.def: The spot in a church where the nave and the transept meet. It is often marked by a dome or tower above.
crossing.think: Think of the intersection of the two arms of the cross.
crossing.seen: No. 58 SainteFoy, Conques; No. 60 Chartres Cathedral; No. 82 Il Gesù.

cruciform.def: Shaped like a cross. At Chavín de Huántar the Lanzón stands where the passages of a cross-shaped gallery meet.
cruciform.see: Latin cross plan, Greek cross plan, Lanzón.

cubiculum.def: A small room cut into a catacomb wall for the burials of one family, often painted. Plural: cubicula.

cupola.def: A small dome, often on top of a roof or a larger dome, sometimes used as a lookout or to let in light.
cupola.think: Think of a mini-dome sitting on a building like a cherry on a sundae.

curtain wall.def: An outer wall, usually of glass and metal, that hangs on a building’s frame and carries no weight except its own. It lets buildings be wrapped in glass.
curtain wall.think: Think of a glass curtain draped over a steel skeleton.

Deconstructivism.def: An architecture style from the 1980s on that breaks buildings into fragmented, tilted, curving and colliding forms, rejecting the regular box. Computer design made its shapes buildable.
Deconstructivism.think: Think of a building that looks like it was taken apart and reassembled in motion.

decorated shed.def: Robert Venturi’s term for a plain, practical building with signs and ornament applied to it, like a roadside store with a big sign. He preferred it to the ‘duck’, a building shaped into a symbol of what it is.
decorated shed.think: A box with a billboard on it, proudly.
decorated shed.seen: No. 152 House in New Castle County.

dome.def: A rounded roof shaped like half a sphere (or taller, like an onion). A dome is basically an arch spun in a circle.
dome.think: Think of an upsidedown bowl over a room.
dome.seen: No. 46 Pantheon; No. 52 Hagia Sophia; No. 84 Mosque of Selim II ; No. 209 Taj Mahal.

domus.def: A private townhouse of a wealthy Roman family. It turned inward around an atrium and a peristyle garden, with few windows on the street.
domus.think: Think of a mansion whose best views face inward to its own courtyards.

Doric order.def: The plainest and sturdiest Greek order. Its columns have no base, a thick fluted shaft, and a simple cushion-shaped capital. The frieze above alternates triglyphs and metopes.
Doric order.think: The no-frills, muscular order. Think of a plain cushion on top.

drum.def: A round or many-sided wall that a dome sits on. It lifts the dome higher and often has windows.
drum.think: Think of a can that raises the dome, the way a pedestal raises a statue.
drum.seen: No. 102 Monticello; No. 185 Dome of the Rock.

dry landscape garden.def: A Japanese Zen garden (in Japanese, karesansui, said kah-ray-sahn-SOO-ee) made of raked gravel and carefully placed rocks, with little or no water or plants. The gravel suggests water and the rocks suggest islands or mountains. It is for looking at and meditating on, not walking through.
dry landscape garden.think: Think of an ocean drawn with gravel and a rake.

dry-stone masonry.def: Stone walls built without any mortar. The stones hold together through careful fitting and their own weight.
dry-stone masonry.think: Think of a stone puzzle where gravity is the glue.
dry-stone masonry.seen: No. 167 Great Zimbabwe; No. 213 Nan Madol.

earthen architecture.def: Buildings made mainly of earth, including mud brick, rammed earth and mud plaster. It stays cool in hot climates but must be repaired regularly.
earthen architecture.think: Think of buildings that are literally made of the ground they stand on.
earthen architecture.seen: No. 168 Great Mosque of Djenné; No. 12 White Temple and ziggurat.

earthwork.def: A structure or artwork made by moving and shaping earth, such as mounds, banks and ditches. It also names 1970s ‘land art’ made in the landscape.
earthwork.think: Think of sculpture made with a shovel or a bulldozer.
earthwork.seen: No. 156 Great Serpent Mound; No. 8 Stonehenge; No. 151 Spiral Jetty.

eﬀigy mound.def: A low earthen mound shaped like an animal or other figure, best seen from above. The Great Serpent Mound in Ohio is a quarter-mile-long snake.
eﬀigy mound.think: Think of a drawing made of earth on a giant scale.

elevation.def: 1) A drawing of one side of a building, seen straight on. 2) The layers of an inside wall, such as a Gothic nave’s arcade, triforium and clerestory.
elevation.think: Think of a ‘side view’, as opposed to a plan (the ‘top view’).

enclosure.def: A wall that surrounds and closes off an area. The Great Enclosure at Great Zimbabwe is the largest ancient structure in sub-Saharan Africa.
enclosure.think: Think of a giant stone fence that marks off a royal space.

engaged column.def: A column that is attached to a wall and sticks out from it, so it is decorative more than structural. The Colosseum’s arches are framed by engaged columns.
engaged column.think: Think of a column half-buried in the wall.

entablature.def: Everything that sits on top of the columns in a classical building and below the roof: the architrave, the frieze, and the cornice, stacked in that order.
entablature.think: Think of a three-layer sandwich resting on the columns.

entasis.def: A slight swelling in the middle of a column shaft. It makes columns look straight and strong rather than pinched, because perfectly straight columns can look thin in the middle from a distance.
entasis.think: Think of a column ‘flexing’ a little, like a muscle carrying weight.

exedra.def: A semicircular recess or niche opening off a larger space. San Vitale has curved exedrae between the piers of its central octagon. The plural is exedrae.

facade.def: The front or main face of a building, usually the most decorated side.
facade.think: Think of a building’s face, the side it shows the world.
facade.seen: No. 70 Palazzo Rucellai; No. 82 Il Gesù; No. 88 San Carlo alle Quattro Fontane; No. 181 Petra Treasury.

feng shui.def: A Chinese system for siting and arranging buildings in harmony with the land, water and cosmic forces. The Forbidden City faces south, with protective hills to the north.
feng shui.think: Literally ‘wind and water.’ Think of the cosmic rules of good placement.

Five Points of Architecture.def: Le Corbusier’s 1926 recipe for modern buildings: pilotis, a free plan, a free facade, horizontal ribbon windows and a roof garden. Villa Savoye shows all five.
Five Points of Architecture.think: Think of a five-item checklist for a modern house.
Five Points of Architecture.see: pilotis, free plan, free facade, ribbon windows.

fluting.def: Vertical grooves carved up and down a column’s shaft. They catch light and shadow and make the column look taller and slimmer.
fluting.think: Think of the ridges on a celery stalk.

flying buttress.def: An arch that ‘flies’ through the air from the upper wall of a church to a tall support standing outside it. It carries the outward push of the vaults away from the walls, so walls can be filled with huge stained-glass windows.
flying buttress.think: Think of a stone arm reaching out from the building to a crutch on the ground.
flying buttress.see: buttress, rib vault, stained glass, pinnacle.

form follows function.def: Louis Sullivan’s famous idea that a building’s shape should come from what it is used for. It became a motto of modern architecture.
form follows function.think: Think of a tool designed to do its job first and look pretty second.
form follows function.see: Chicago School, less is more, ornament.

formal garden.def: A garden laid out in strict geometric patterns, with straight paths, clipped hedges, pools and fountains arranged on an axis. Versailles’ gardens show the king controlling even nature.
formal garden.think: Think of nature given a haircut and organized with a ruler.

forum.def: The central public square of a Roman town, surrounded by temples, law courts, shops and government buildings. Emperors built grand forums to show off their power.
forum.think: The Roman version of the Greek agora.

four-iwan plan.def: A mosque or building layout with a central courtyard and an iwan in the middle of each of its four sides, facing one another. Introduced at the Great Mosque of Isfahan under the Seljuks, it became the standard Persian plan.
four-iwan plan.think: Think of a courtyard with a giant open-fronted hall on every side, like four stages facing one plaza.

free facade.def: An outside wall that can be designed freely, with windows placed anywhere, because it carries no weight. One of Le Corbusier’s Five Points.
free facade.think: Think of an outside wall that is just a skin.
free facade.see: Five Points of Architecture, curtain wall.

free plan.def: An interior layout in which walls can go anywhere, because columns, not walls, hold up the building. One of Le Corbusier’s Five Points.
free plan.think: Think of walls as movable room dividers rather than supports.
free plan.see: open plan, Five Points of Architecture, loadbearing wall.

frieze.def: 1) The middle band of the entablature, often decorated. 2) More generally, any long horizontal band of sculpture or painting. The Parthenon has a famous carved frieze of a procession; the Pergamon Altar has a frieze of gods fighting giants.
frieze.think: Think of a comic strip running around a building.
frieze.seen: No. 35 Acropolis (Parthenon); No. 38 Great Altar of Zeus at Pergamon; No. 70 Palazzo Rucellai; No. 35 Acropolis (Parthenon frieze); No. 38 Great Altar of Zeus and Athena at Pergamon.

gable.def: The triangular upper part of a wall at the end of a pitched roof. In classical buildings, a decorated gable is a pediment. Venturi’s House in New Castle County hides behind a big farmhouse gable.
gable.think: The triangle a kid draws on top of a house.
gable.seen: No. 152 House in New Castle County.

gallery.def: 1) An upper floor or balcony overlooking the nave of a church (in Byzantine churches, often where women stood). 2) A long covered corridor, like the dark stone passages at Chavín or the carved halls of Angkor Wat.
gallery.think: Think of a balcony or a long hallway.
gallery.seen: No. 51 San Vitale; No. 52 Hagia Sophia; No. 153 Chavín de Huántar; No. 199 Angkor Wat.

garbhagriha.def: The small, dark, innermost shrine of a Hindu temple, where the main image of the god is kept. Only priests may enter.
garbhagriha.think: Sanskrit for ‘womb chamber.’ Think of the temple’s hidden heart.

gatehouse.def: A building that forms the guarded entrance to a temple or palace compound. Todai-ji’s Great South Gate holds two giant guardian figures.
gatehouse.think: Think of a security checkpoint that is also a work of art.

glazed roof tile.def: Ceramic roof tiles coated with a shiny colored glaze. In the Forbidden City, yellowglazed tiles were reserved for the emperor.
glazed roof tile.think: Think of a roof color code that tells you who lives there.

glazed tile.def: Ceramic tiles covered in a shiny, colored glassy coat, used to cover walls and domes in bright patterns. Persian and Ottoman builders were masters of it.
glazed tile.think: Think of a building wrapped in shiny ceramic, like a bathroom wall turned into art.
glazed tile.seen: No. 186 Great Mosque of Isfahan; No. 84 Mosque of Selim II ; No. 185 Dome of the Rock; No. 186 Great Mosque (Isfahan).

gopura.def: A monumental entrance gateway tower in the outer walls of a Hindu temple complex, especially in south India and Cambodia.
gopura.think: Think of a gate that is also a skyscraper.

granary.def: A storehouse for grain. The Conical Tower at Great Zimbabwe may imitate a Shona granary, possibly as a symbol of the ruler’s generosity and wealth.

Greek cross plan.def: A church plan shaped like a cross with four arms of equal length, often with a dome at the center.

groin vault.def: A vault made where two barrel vaults cross each other at right angles. The weight is gathered at the four corners, so the walls between can have openings.
groin vault.think: Think of two tunnels crossing to make an X-shaped ceiling.

hall.def: In East Asian architecture, a large rectangular wooden building on a stone platform, used for worship or government. The Great Buddha Hall at Todai-ji and the Hall of Supreme Harmony in the Forbidden City are famous examples.
hall.think: Think of the main building of a temple or palace compound.
hall.see: bracket system, timber frame, hipped roof.

harmika.def: The small square railing on top of a stupa’s dome, surrounding the mast that holds the chattra. It marks the realm of the gods.
harmika.think: Think of a little fence on the roof.

header-and-stretcher.def: A way of stacking long building pieces in alternating layers: one layer laid lengthwise (stretchers), the next laid crosswise (headers). At Nan Madol, basalt columns are stacked this way, like a log cabin.
header-and-stretcher.think: Think of building a log cabin or playing Jenga.

henge.def: A prehistoric circular area surrounded by a ditch and a bank of earth, sometimes with stones or timber posts set inside. Stonehenge is the famous example.
henge.think: Think of a giant ring drawn on the landscape with a shovel.

hieroglyphic stairway.def: A Maya staircase whose steps are carved with writing (glyphs) and images that record a ruler’s history and deeds.
hieroglyphic stairway.think: Think of stairs you can read.

hipped roof.def: A roof that slopes down on all four sides. In China, a double-eaved hipped roof (two layers) was reserved for the most important imperial halls.
hipped roof.think: Think of a roof with no flat gable ends: every side is a slope.
hipped roof.see: glazed roof tile, bracket system, hall.

horseshoe arch.def: An arch that curves in past its widest point before meeting its supports, like a horseshoe. A hallmark of Islamic Spain.
horseshoe arch.think: Think of an arch that is a bit more than a half-circle.

hypogeum.def: An underground space. At the Colosseum, the hypogeum under the arena floor held tunnels, cages and lifts for animals and fighters.
hypogeum.think: Think of a stadium’s backstage basement.

hypostyle hall.def: A large hall whose roof is held up by many rows of columns. The word means ‘under columns.’ Ancient Egyptians, Persians and early Islamic mosque builders all used it.
hypostyle hall.think: Think of walking through a stone forest where every tree trunk is a column.
hypostyle hall.seen: No. 20 Temple of Amun-Re, Karnak; No. 30 Apadana, Persepolis; No. 56 Great Mosque of Córdoba.

hypostyle mosque.def: The earliest type of mosque: a large prayer hall filled with rows of columns, usually beside an open courtyard. It can be enlarged simply by adding more rows of columns.
hypostyle mosque.think: Think of a stone forest that can keep growing.

I-beam.def: A steel beam shaped like a capital letter I in cross-section, strong and light. On the Seagram Building, bronze I-beams run up the outside as decoration that shows off the structure.
I-beam.think: Think of a steel beam with a capital-I profile.

impluvium.def: A shallow basin in the floor of a Roman atrium that caught rainwater falling through the opening in the roof above.
impluvium.think: Think of an indoor rain-catching pool.

impost block.def: An extra block placed between a column’s capital and the arch above it, helping to carry the weight. Used in Byzantine churches like San Vitale.
impost block.think: Think of a stone cushion between the column and the arch.

International Style.def: A modern architecture style of the 1920s to 1960s, spread worldwide: boxy shapes, flat roofs, white walls or glass skins, steel and concrete frames, and no ornament.
International Style.think: Think of a clean glass-and-steel box that could stand in any city in the world.
International Style.seen: No. 135 Villa Savoye; No. 146 Seagram Building.
International Style.see: curtain wall, less is more, Bauhaus.

intihuatana.def: A carved stone outcrop at Inka sites, thought to be linked to the sun and the calendar. The name is often translated as ‘hitching post of the sun.’

Ionic order.def: A slimmer, more elegant Greek order. Its columns stand on a base and have a capital with two scrolls (volutes) like a rolled-up paper. Its frieze is one continuous band.
Ionic order.seen: No. 35 Acropolis (Parthenon); No. 44 Colosseum; No. 70 Palazzo Rucellai.

iwan.def: A large vaulted hall that is walled on three sides and completely open on the fourth, usually facing a courtyard. A standard feature of Persian and later Islamic architecture.
iwan.think: Think of a giant stone band shell or a room missing its front wall.
iwan.seen: No. 186 Great Mosque of Isfahan; No. 209 Taj Mahal.

Iznik tile.def: Brilliant ceramic tiles made in the Ottoman town of Iznik (Turkey), famous for vivid blue, turquoise and tomato-red flowers on white. Used inside Sinan’s mosques.
Iznik tile.think: Think of the Ottoman empire’s luxury tile brand.

jagati.def: The raised stone platform that a north Indian Hindu temple stands on. It lifts the temple above the world and provides a walkway around it.
jagati.think: Think of a stage the temple stands on.

jali.def: A carved stone screen with a pierced, lace-like pattern. It lets light and air through while keeping privacy. In the Taj Mahal a marble jali surrounds the tombs.
jali.think: Think of stone lace or a stone window screen.

jamb.def: The vertical side of a doorway or window. Gothic churches often carved tall statues, called jamb figures, into the jambs of their doorways.
jamb.think: Think of the side posts of a door frame.

keystone.def: The wedge-shaped stone at the very top center of an arch. It is the last stone put in, and it locks the others in place.
keystone.think: That is why ‘keystone’ means the most important piece of anything.

kiva.def: A round, partly underground room used by Puebloan peoples for ceremonies and meetings. A small hole in the floor (the sipapu) stands for the place where people emerged into this world.
kiva.think: Think of a sacred underground meeting room.

külliye.def: An Ottoman complex built around a mosque, which could also include schools, a hospital, a soup kitchen, baths and the founder’s tomb.
külliye.think: Think of a mosque with its own campus of public services.

lancet.def: A tall, narrow window with a pointed arch at the top.
lancet.think: Named after a lance (spear tip), which it resembles.
lancet.see: pointed arch, rose window, stained glass.

lantern.def: A small tower with windows on top of a dome that lets light into the space below and finishes the dome visually.
lantern.think: Think of a little glass crown on the top of a dome.
lantern.seen: No. 88 San Carlo alle Quattro Fontane.

Latin cross plan.def: A church plan shaped like a cross with one arm (the nave) much longer than the other three.
Latin cross plan.think: Think of a typical Christian cross lying on the ground.
Latin cross plan.seen: No. 58 SainteFoy, Conques; No. 60 Chartres Cathedral; No. 82 Il Gesù.

less is more.def: Mies van der Rohe’s motto: simple, stripped-down design with no extra ornament is more powerful. Robert Venturi later joked back, ‘less is a bore.’
less is more.think: Think of a minimalist apartment with only a few perfect objects.
less is more.see: International Style, form follows function, Postmodern architecture.

lintel.def: The horizontal beam that spans the top of a doorway or the space between two posts. At Yaxchilán the stone lintels over doorways are carved with scenes of rulers.
lintel.think: Think of the top bar of a door frame.
lintel.seen: No. 8 Stonehenge; No. 155 Yaxchilán; No. 60 Chartres Cathedral.

load-bearing wall.def: A wall that holds up the weight of the floors and roof above it. Because removing it would make the building fall, its openings must be small. Modern steel and concrete frames freed walls from this job.
load-bearing wall.think: Think of a wall doing the heavy lifting.
load-bearing wall.see: steel frame, curtain wall, free plan.

loculus.def: A long, shelf-like slot cut into a catacomb wall to hold a body, sealed with a slab or tiles. Plural: loculi.

loggia.def: A gallery or porch that is open on one or more sides, usually with columns or arches, and part of a larger building. It is an indoor-outdoor space for shade and air.
loggia.think: Think of a covered balcony or porch with arches.

longitudinal plan.def: A building that is longer than it is wide, leading you along a straight axis from the entrance to the altar, like a basilica.
longitudinal plan.think: Think of a long hallway pointing at a goal.
longitudinal plan.seen: No. 49 Santa Sabina; No. 60 Chartres Cathedral; No. 82 Il Gesù.

lunette.def: A half-moon-shaped wall area under an arch or vault, often filled with a painting or relief. The School of Athens fills one.

machine for living.def: Le Corbusier’s phrase for a modern house: an eﬀicient, functional object designed like a machine around how people actually live.
machine for living.think: Think of a house designed like a wellbuilt car.
machine for living.see: International Style, Five Points of Architecture.

madrasa.def: A school for Islamic religious learning, often attached to a mosque.

mandala plan.def: A building plan based on a mandala, a sacred diagram of the universe made of squares and circles arranged around a center. Walking through it is like moving toward enlightenment or the divine center.
mandala plan.think: Think of a floor plan that is also a cosmic map.
mandala plan.seen: No. 198 Borobudur; No. 199 Angkor Wat; No. 200 Lakshmana Temple.

mandapa.def: A hall or porch in a Hindu temple where worshippers gather before approaching the shrine. Larger temples have a series of them leading to the garbhagriha.
mandapa.think: Think of the temple’s waiting rooms.

maqsura.def: A screened-off area in a mosque near the mihrab, reserved for the ruler to pray in safety and in style.
maqsura.think: Think of a royal box at the front of the prayer hall.

martyrium.def: A church or shrine built over the grave of a martyr or at a site linked to Christ’s life, often with a central plan. San Vitale honors the martyr Saint Vitalis.

masonry.def: Building with stone, brick or mud-brick units stacked on one another, with or without mortar. The builders are called masons.
masonry.seen: No. 154 Mesa Verde cliff dwellings; No. 159 City of Cusco; No. 161 Machu Picchu.
masonry.see: ashlar masonry, dry-stone masonry, mortar, polygonal masonry.

mastaba.def: An early Egyptian tomb shaped like a flat-topped, low rectangular block with sloping sides, built over an underground burial chamber. Stacking mastabas of shrinking size led to the step pyramid and then the smooth pyramids at Giza.
mastaba.think: ‘Mastaba’ is Arabic for ‘bench’, which is what these tombs look like from a distance.

mausoleum.def: A large, grand building that serves as a tomb.
mausoleum.think: Named after King Mausolus, whose huge ancient tomb was one of the Seven Wonders.

megalith.def: A very large stone used to build a monument, usually without mortar. ‘Megalithic’ describes structures made of such stones, mostly from prehistoric times.
megalith.think: ‘Mega’ means big and ‘lith’ means stone: literally ‘big stone.’
megalith.seen: No. 8 Stonehenge; No. 213 Nan Madol; No. 214 Moai on ahu.

metope.def: One of the square panels in a Doric frieze, set between triglyphs. Metopes were often carved with relief sculpture, such as battles on the Parthenon.
metope.think: Think of picture frames lined up along the top of a temple.

mihrab.def: A niche, often richly decorated, set in the qibla wall of a mosque to show the direction of Mecca. It is not an altar and no one stands inside it to worship.
mihrab.think: Think of a decorated arrow in the wall saying ‘pray this way.’
mihrab.seen: No. 56 Great Mosque of Córdoba; No. 186 Great Mosque of Isfahan.

minaret.def: A tall, slender tower attached to a mosque, from which the call to prayer is given. Minarets also mark a mosque on the skyline. Djenné’s minarets rise from its qibla wall; Hagia Sophia’s were added when it became a mosque.
minaret.think: Think of a lighthouse for prayer.
minaret.seen: No. 84 Mosque of Selim II ; No. 209 Taj Mahal; No. 168 Great Mosque of Djenné; No. 52 Hagia Sophia.

minbar.def: A pulpit in a mosque: a staircase with a small platform at the top, set to the right of the mihrab, where the imam gives the Friday sermon.

moat.def: A wide water-filled ditch surrounding a building or city. At Angkor Wat, the moat stands for the cosmic ocean around Mount Meru; at the Forbidden City it protects the emperor.
moat.think: Think of a ring of water that both guards and symbolizes.
moat.seen: No. 199 Angkor Wat; No. 206 Forbidden City.

module.def: A standard unit of measurement repeated throughout a building to set its proportions. Brunelleschi based the Pazzi Chapel on such units for clear, harmonious geometry.

mortar.def: A paste, such as mud, lime or cement, spread between stones or bricks to bind them. Mesa Verde’s sandstone blocks sit in mud mortar; Inka builders famously used none, fitting stones so tightly they did not need it.

mortise-and-tenon joint.def: A way to lock two pieces together: a knob (tenon) on one fits into a hole (mortise) in the other. Stonehenge’s builders borrowed it from woodworking to keep lintels from sliding off the uprights.
mortise-and-tenon joint.think: Think of a LEGO stud clicking into a LEGO hole.

mortuary temple.def: An Egyptian temple built so priests could keep making offerings to a dead ruler forever. It was separate from, but connected to, the ruler’s tomb.

mud brick.def: Bricks made of mud (often mixed with straw) and dried in the sun instead of fired in a kiln. Cheap and easy where stone and wood are scarce, but it wears away and needs constant repair.
mud brick.think: the building block of places with lots of dirt and little stone, from Sumer to Mali.
mud brick.seen: No. 12 White Temple and ziggurat; No. 168 Great Mosque of Djenné.

mullion.def: A vertical bar that divides the panes of a window or the panels of a curtain wall.
mullion.think: Think of the stripes that separate the glass on a tall oﬀice tower.

multilobed arch.def: An arch whose inner edge is cut into a series of curves or ‘lobes’ like a scalloped edge. Used near the mihrab at Córdoba, sometimes in interlacing layers.
multilobed arch.think: Think of an arch with a clover-like scalloped edge.

muqarnas.def: Three-dimensional decoration made of many small, niche-like cells stacked in tiers, used to fill domes, vaults and squinches in Islamic buildings. It looks like a honeycomb or stalactites.
muqarnas.think: Think of a honeycomb hanging from the ceiling.
muqarnas.seen: No. 65 Alhambra; No. 186 Great Mosque of Isfahan.

Nagara style.def: The north Indian style of Hindu temple, with a curved, beehive-like shikhara rising over the sanctum, often surrounded by smaller towers, on a raised platform.
Nagara style.think: Think of a temple that looks like a mountain range.

naos.def: The Greek word for the inner chamber of a temple, which held the cult statue. Same as the Latin ‘cella.’

narthex.def: The entrance hall or porch across the front of a church, before you enter the nave.
narthex.seen: No. 51 San Vitale; No. 52 Hagia Sophia.

nave.def: The long central space of a church, running from the entrance toward the altar, where the congregation gathers.
nave.think: Think of the main aisle and seating area of a church. From the Latin word for ship.
nave.seen: No. 49 Santa Sabina; No. 60 Chartres Cathedral; No. 82 Il Gesù; No. 58 Sainte-Foy, Conques.

necropolis.def: Greek for ‘city of the dead’. A large ancient cemetery, often with tombs laid out like streets and houses.
necropolis.seen: No. 5 Beaker with ibex motifs; No. 29 Sarcophagus of the Spouses; No. 32 Tomb of the Triclinium.

niche.def: A shallow recess in a wall, often arched, made to hold a statue or object. The Bamiyan Buddhas stood in giant niches cut into a cliff.

obelisk.def: A tall, thin, four-sided stone pillar that narrows as it rises and ends in a small pyramid point. Egyptian pharaohs set them up in pairs at temple entrances to honor the sun god.
obelisk.think: Think of a giant stone needle. The Washington Monument copies the shape.

octagonal plan.def: A building laid out as an eightsided shape. San Vitale and the Dome of the Rock both use octagons, a shape halfway between a square (earth) and a circle (heaven).
octagonal plan.think: Think of a stop sign as a floor plan.
octagonal plan.seen: No. 51 San Vitale; No. 185 Dome of the Rock.

oculus.def: A round opening at the top of a dome that lets in light (and rain). The Pantheon’s oculus is about 30 feet wide and is the only light source inside.
oculus.think: a skylight shaped like an eye. ‘Oculus’ is Latin for eye.

onion dome.def: A dome that bulges out wider than its base and then rises to a point, like an onion.
onion dome.think: Think of a dome that has taken a deep breath.

open plan.def: An interior with few walls, where living spaces flow into each other instead of being divided into small closed rooms.
open plan.think: Think of a loft where the kitchen, dining and living areas all share one space.

optical refinements.def: Tiny, deliberate bends in a building that correct tricks of the eye. On the Parthenon the floor bulges up, the columns lean slightly inward, and the shafts swell, so the whole temple looks perfectly straight and alive.
optical refinements.think: Think of the Parthenon as ‘photoshopped in stone’ so it looks right to human eyes.

opus reticulatum.def: Latin for ‘net work’. Ancient Roman wall facing made of small square stones set diagonally in a diamond net pattern. Alberti imitated it at the base of the Palazzo Rucellai.

order.def: A classical order is a complete design ‘package’ for a column and the entablature above it, with set proportions and decoration. The main orders are Doric, Ionic, and Corinthian (Greek), plus Tuscan and Composite (Roman).
order.think: Think of an order as a matching outfit: if the column is Ionic, the beam above it should be Ionic too.
order.seen: No. 35 Acropolis (Parthenon); No. 44 Colosseum; No. 70 Palazzo Rucellai.
order.see: Doric order, Ionic order, Corinthian order, Tuscan order.

organic architecture.def: Frank Lloyd Wright’s idea that a building should grow out of its site and live in harmony with nature, using local materials and flowing spaces.
organic architecture.think: Think of a house that looks like it grew there.

ornament.def: Decoration added to a building, such as carving, molding, or patterns. Modernists like Mies tried to remove it; Sullivan and later the Postmodernists embraced it.
ornament.think: Think of the jewelry of a building.
ornament.seen: No. 124 Carson, Pirie, Scott Building; No. 152 House in New Castle County; No. 65 Alhambra.
ornament.see: form follows function, less is more, Postmodern architecture.

oval dome.def: A dome built over an oval rather than a circle, favored in the Baroque for its sense of movement and tension. Borromini’s San Carlo has one.
oval dome.seen: No. 88 San Carlo alle Quattro Fontane.

pagoda.def: A tall, many-storied tower with roofs at each level, found in Buddhist temples in China, Korea and Japan. It grew out of the Indian stupa and often holds relics. Todai-ji once had two huge pagodas, now lost.
pagoda.think: Think of a stupa stretched upward into a tower of stacked roofs.

palace.def: The grand home of a ruler or noble family, which also served as the seat of government and a stage for royal ceremonies.
palace.think: Think of the place where power lives, works and shows off.
palace.seen: No. 93 Palace at Versailles; No. 65 Alhambra; No. 206 Forbidden City.

palazzo.def: A large town house or palace of a wealthy family in Renaissance Italy, often built around an inner courtyard.
palazzo.think: Italian for ‘palace,’ but it can mean a rich family’s city mansion, not only a royal palace.

Palladian.def: In the style of Andrea Palladio, a 16th-century Italian architect who designed symmetrical villas with temple-like porticoes and pediments. His style spread to England and America, including Jefferson’s Monticello.
Palladian.think: Think of a house dressed as a Roman temple.

papyrus capital.def: The top of an Egyptian column carved to look like a bundle of papyrus plants, either open like a flower or closed like a bud. It turns a stone hall into a symbolic marsh, where Egyptians believed creation began.
papyrus capital.think: Think of columns dressed up as giant stalks of river reeds.

parametric design.def: Design in which computer formulas generate and adjust a building’s shapes. It is associated with the flowing, curving forms of Zaha Hadid.
parametric design.think: Think of a building shaped by an algorithm.

parterre.def: A formal garden of flat, level beds laid out in symmetrical patterns, often edged with low clipped hedges and gravel paths, as at Versailles.

pediment.def: The triangle at the end of a sloped roof, above the entablature, on a classical temple or a building copying one. Greek temples filled pediments with sculpture.
pediment.think: Think of the triangle on top of a house in a kid’s drawing.
pediment.seen: No. 35 Acropolis (Parthenon); No. 46 Pantheon; No. 102 Monticello; No. 181 Petra Treasury.

pendentive.def: A curved triangle of masonry that fills the corner between two arches and lets a round dome sit on a square base. Byzantine builders perfected it at Hagia Sophia.
pendentive.think: Think of four curved funnels that turn a square into a circle.
pendentive.seen: No. 52 Hagia Sophia; No. 67 Pazzi Chapel.

peristyle.def: A row of columns surrounding a building or a courtyard. A Greek temple like the Parthenon is wrapped in a peristyle; a Roman house has a peristyle garden, a courtyard ringed by columns.
peristyle.think: ‘Peri’ means around: columns all the way around.
peristyle.seen: No. 35 Acropolis (Parthenon); No. 39 House of the Vettii.

pier.def: A thick, solid upright support, usually square or rectangular, bigger and stronger than a column.
pier.think: Think of a column that has been working out.
pier.seen: No. 51 San Vitale; No. 60 Chartres Cathedral; No. 84 Mosque of Selim II.

pietra serena.def: A smooth gray sandstone from Florence, used by Brunelleschi for pilasters, columns and moldings set against white walls, so the building’s geometry reads clearly.
pietra serena.think: Italian for ‘serene stone.’ Think of a gray pencil outline on white paper.

pilaster.def: A flat, rectangular version of a column attached to a wall. It has a base and a capital but sticks out only slightly. It is decoration that makes a wall look organized and classical.
pilaster.think: Think of a column flattened against the wall like a sticker.
pilaster.seen: No. 44 Colosseum; No. 67 Pazzi Chapel; No. 70 Palazzo Rucellai; No. 82 Il Gesù.
pilaster.see: engaged column, pietra serena, superimposed orders.

pilgrimage church.def: A medieval church built to handle crowds of travelers visiting holy relics. It has wide aisles, an ambulatory, and radiating chapels so people can flow past the relics without disturbing Mass.
pilgrimage church.think: Think of a building designed for crowd control around a famous attraction.

pilotis.def: Slender columns that lift a building off the ground, leaving open space underneath. One of Le Corbusier’s Five Points.
pilotis.think: Think of a house standing on stilts.
pilotis.see: Five Points of Architecture, reinforced concrete.

pinnacle.def: A small pointed turret on top of a buttress or roof. It adds weight that helps hold the buttress steady, and it decorates the skyline.
pinnacle.think: Think of a stone party hat on top of each buttress.
pinnacle.seen: No. 60 Chartres Cathedral; No. 112 Houses of Parliament.

pishtaq.def: A tall rectangular frame around an iwan’s arched opening, which makes the entrance look bigger and grander. Persian and Mughal buildings use it; the Taj Mahal has one on each side.
pishtaq.think: Think of a huge picture frame around a doorway.

pit house.def: A dwelling dug partly into the ground and roofed with timber and earth. Ancestral Puebloans lived in pit houses before building cliff dwellings, and their kivas grew out of them.

plan.def: A drawing of a building as seen from directly above, as if the roof were removed, showing the layout of walls, rooms and columns.
plan.think: Think of a map of a building.

platform mound.def: A large, flat-topped earthen mound built to hold a temple, a chief’s house or a ritual space. The Mississippian culture built them at sites such as Cahokia.
platform mound.think: Think of a man-made hill with a flat roof for a building.

plaza.def: A large open public square in a town or ceremonial center, used for gatherings, markets or ritual.
plaza.think: Think of the outdoor living room of a city.
plaza.seen: No. 45 Forum of Trajan; No. 146 Seagram Building; No. 153 Chavín de Huántar; No. 161 Machu Picchu.

podium.def: A tall platform that an Etruscan or Roman temple stands on, with stairs only at the front. It makes the temple face one way, unlike a Greek temple you can approach from all sides.
podium.think: Think of a stage that tells you where the front door is.

pointed arch.def: An arch with a pointed top, formed by two curves meeting at an angle. It pushes weight down more steeply than a round arch, so Gothic builders could go taller and use thinner walls.
pointed arch.think: Think of the shape of praying hands.
pointed arch.seen: No. 60 Chartres Cathedral; No. 112 Houses of Parliament.

polygonal masonry.def: Stonework of many-sided blocks cut to fit together like a jigsaw puzzle, without mortar. The Inka walls of Cusco and Saqsaywaman are famous examples.

portal.def: A grand, elaborate doorway, especially the sculpted entrances of a medieval church.
portal.think: Think of a door that is also a billboard of sculpture.
portal.seen: No. 58 Sainte-Foy, Conques; No. 60 Chartres Cathedral.

portico.def: A porch with a roof held up by columns, usually at the main entrance, often topped by a pediment.
portico.think: Think of a columned front porch that announces ‘this building is important.’
portico.seen: No. 46 Pantheon; No. 102 Monticello; No. 67 Pazzi Chapel.

post-and-lintel.def: The simplest way to build an opening: two upright posts with a horizontal beam (the lintel) laid across their tops. Used from Stonehenge to the Parthenon.
post-and-lintel.think: Think of a doorway made of three sticks: two standing, one lying across.
post-and-lintel.seen: No. 8 Stonehenge; No. 20 Temple of AmunRe, Karnak; No. 35 Acropolis (Parthenon).

Postmodern architecture.def: Architecture from the 1970s on that reacted against plain modern boxes by bringing back color, ornament, historical references and humor, often in an ironic way.
Postmodern architecture.think: Think of a building that winks at you with a cartoon version of a classical column.
Postmodern architecture.seen: No. 152 House in New Castle County.
Postmodern architecture.see: broken pediment, less is more, Postmodernism.

pradakshina patha.def: The path for circumambulation, the ritual of walking clockwise around a holy object like a stupa or a temple’s sanctum. At Borobudur, pilgrims circle and climb through the terraces toward the top.
pradakshina patha.think: Think of walking laps around something sacred as a form of prayer.
pradakshina patha.seen: No. 192 Great Stupa at Sanchi; No. 198 Borobudur.

Prairie style.def: Frank Lloyd Wright’s early-1900s house style for the American Midwest: low, long and horizontal, with wide overhanging roofs and open interiors that echo the flat prairie. Fallingwater’s stacked horizontal terraces grow out of it.
Prairie style.think: Think of a house that lies low, hugging the ground like the prairie.

prang.def: A tall, rounded, finger-like tower of a Thai or Khmer-style temple, descended from Khmer prasats like those at Angkor Wat.
prang.think: Think of a corncob-shaped temple tower.

prasat.def: A Khmer temple tower, often shaped like a lotus bud or corncob, rising over a shrine. Angkor Wat has five arranged in a quincunx. The Thai version is called a prang.
prasat.think: Think of a tall, rounded stone tower standing in for a mountain peak.

propylaia.def: A grand gateway building marking the entrance to a sacred area. The Propylaia on the Athenian Acropolis is the most famous.
propylaia.think: the ticket gate to a holy site.

proto-doric.def: Columns that look like early versions of the Greek Doric column: plain, fluted and manysided. Hatshepsut’s mortuary temple has them, about a thousand years before the first Greek Doric temples.

protome capital.def: A column top carved with the front halves of two animals (such as bulls) back to back. Their shared back forms a saddle where a roof beam rests.
protome capital.think: Think of two bulls stuck together at the hips, holding up the ceiling with their backs.

pylon.def: A massive gateway to an Egyptian temple: two tall, slanted towers with a doorway between them. Pylons were covered in carved scenes of the pharaoh’s power.
pylon.think: a fortresslike front door that says ‘only the worthy go further.’

pyramid.def: A huge structure with a square base and four sloping sides that meet at a point (or, in the Americas, a flat top for a temple). Egyptian pyramids were royal tombs; Mesoamerican stepped pyramids were platforms for temples.
pyramid.think: Same basic shape on two continents, very different jobs: a tomb in Egypt, a stage for ritual in Mexico.
pyramid.seen: No. 17 Great Pyramids of Giza; No. 157 Templo Mayor; No. 155 Yaxchilán.

qibla.def: The direction of Mecca, which Muslims face when they pray. The qibla wall of a mosque faces Mecca and holds the mihrab.
qibla.think: Think of a compass needle that points every mosque toward Mecca.
qibla.seen: No. 56 Great Mosque of Córdoba; No. 168 Great Mosque of Djenné; No. 186 Great Mosque of Isfahan.

quincunx.def: An arrangement of five things: four at the corners of a square and one in the middle, like the five dots on dice. Angkor Wat’s five towers form one, standing for the five peaks of Mount Meru.
quincunx.think: Think of the five-dot face of a die.

radiating chapels.def: Small chapels that branch outward from the ambulatory around the apse of a church, like the spokes of a wheel. Each could hold relics or an altar for pilgrims.
radiating chapels.think: Think of petals around the end of the church.
radiating chapels.seen: No. 58 Sainte-Foy, Conques; No. 60 Chartres Cathedral.

refectory.def: The dining hall of a monastery or convent. Leonardo painted the Last Supper on the refectory wall of Santa Maria delle Grazie, so the friars ate with Christ and the apostles.

reinforced concrete.def: Concrete with steel bars or mesh embedded in it. The concrete resists squeezing and the steel resists pulling, so it can span long distances and form daring shapes. Also called ferroconcrete.
reinforced concrete.think: Think of concrete with a steel skeleton inside.
reinforced concrete.seen: No. 135 Villa Savoye; No. 139 Fallingwater; No. 249 MAXXI.

rib vault.def: A vault supported by a framework of thin stone arches (ribs) that cross diagonally. The ribs carry the weight to specific points, so the panels between them can be thinner and lighter.
rib vault.think: Think of an umbrella: the ribs do the work and the fabric just fills in.
rib vault.see: vault, groin vault, pointed arch, bay.

ribbed dome.def: A dome built on a framework of crossing arches or ribs, which often form a star pattern. The dome in front of Córdoba’s mihrab is a famous early example.
ribbed dome.think: Think of a dome with its skeleton showing.

ribbon windows.def: Long horizontal bands of windows that stretch across a building’s facade. One of Le Corbusier’s Five Points.
ribbon windows.think: Think of a strip of glass wrapped around a building like a ribbon.
ribbon windows.see: Five Points of Architecture, free facade.

rock-cut architecture.def: Buildings or shrines carved directly out of a cliff or rock face instead of being built up from blocks. The builders remove stone rather than add it.
rock-cut architecture.seen: No. 181 Petra Treasury; No. 21 Mortuary temple of Hatshepsut; No. 195 Longmen caves; No. 182 Bamiyan Buddha.

roof comb.def: A tall, often lacy stone crest built on the roof of a Maya temple to make it look taller and to display painted or sculpted images.
roof comb.think: Think of a decorative mohawk on top of the temple.

roof garden.def: A flat roof used as a garden or terrace, giving back the green space a building takes from the ground. One of Le Corbusier’s Five Points.
roof garden.think: Think of a backyard moved to the roof.

rose window.def: A large, circular window filled with stained glass and tracery that radiates from the center like the petals of a flower. Found on the facades and transept ends of Gothic churches.
rose window.think: Think of a kaleidoscope set into a wall.

rotunda.def: A round building or round room, usually covered by a dome.
rotunda.think: Think of a giant round room under a bowl-shaped roof.

round arch.def: An arch shaped like a half-circle. It was the standard Roman arch and was used again in Romanesque and Renaissance buildings.
round arch.seen: No. 44 Colosseum; No. 58 Sainte-Foy, Conques; No. 70 Palazzo Rucellai.
round arch.see: arch, pointed arch, horseshoe arch, barrel vault.

rustication.def: Stone blocks left rough or cut with deep grooves around their edges, so each block stands out. Used on lower stories of Renaissance palaces to look strong and solid.
rustication.think: Think of a building wearing chunky, rugged armor at street level.

sahn.def: The open courtyard of a mosque, usually surrounded by arcades and often holding a fountain for washing before prayer.
sahn.think: Think of an outdoor waiting room and wash area before the prayer hall.
sahn.seen: No. 56 Great Mosque of Córdoba; No. 186 Great Mosque of Isfahan.

semidome.def: A half-dome, usually covering an apse or a curved niche. At Hagia Sophia, semidomes on either side help hold up the main dome and make the space flow.
semidome.think: Think of a dome sliced in half like an orange.

serdab.def: A sealed room in an Egyptian tomb holding a statue of the dead person for their ka (life force), sometimes with a small slit so the statue could ‘see’ offerings. The Seated Scribe probably stood in a tomb chapel or serdab.

shaft.def: The long, tall middle part of a column, between the base and the capital. Greek shafts were often fluted (carved with vertical grooves).
shaft.think: The body of the column, between its feet and its head.

shikhara.def: The tall, curving tower that rises over the garbhagriha of a north Indian Hindu temple. Clusters of smaller towers climb toward it like a mountain range, evoking Mount Meru, home of the gods.

skyscraper.def: A very tall building made possible by steel frames and elevators. It started in Chicago and New York in the late 1800s.
skyscraper.think: Think of stacking floors on a steel skeleton instead of on thick walls.
skyscraper.seen: No. 124 Carson, Pirie, Scott Building; No. 146 Seagram Building.
skyscraper.see: steel frame, Chicago School, curtain wall.

spire.def: A tall, pointed, cone- or pyramid-shaped structure on top of a tower, especially on a church.
spire.think: Think of the church’s finger pointing to heaven.

spolia.def: Pieces taken from older buildings and reused in new ones, such as columns, capitals or carvings. It saves work and can also show victory over, or connection to, the past.
spolia.think: Latin for ‘spoils.’ Think of architectural recycling.
spolia.seen: No. 49 Santa Sabina; No. 56 Great Mosque of Córdoba.

squinch.def: An arch or small half-cone built across the corner of a square room, turning the square into an octagon so a dome can sit on top. Islamic builders often filled squinches with muqarnas.
squinch.think: Think of a little shelf bridging each corner of a box.
squinch.seen: No. 51 San Vitale; No. 186 Great Mosque of Isfahan.

stained glass.def: Pieces of colored glass held together by strips of lead to form pictures in a window. In Gothic churches the colored light was meant to feel like heavenly light.
stained glass.think: Think of a glowing comic book made of glass.

steel frame.def: A skeleton of steel beams and columns that carries a building’s whole weight, so walls do not have to. It made skyscrapers possible in the late 1800s.
steel frame.think: Think of a building’s steel skeleton, with the walls just hung on like skin.
steel frame.seen: No. 124 Carson, Pirie, Scott Building; No. 146 Seagram Building.
steel frame.see: skyscraper, curtain wall, I-beam, load-bearing wall.

stoa.def: A long, covered walkway in a Greek city, with a wall at the back and a colonnade in front. People met, shopped, and talked philosophy there.
stoa.think: Think of an ancient covered strip mall.

stupa.def: A Buddhist monument shaped like a solid dome or mound that holds relics of the Buddha or a holy teacher. You cannot go inside; instead, worshippers walk around it clockwise.
stupa.think: Think of a giant stone mound that is a reliquary you walk around, not into.
stupa.seen: No. 192 Great Stupa at Sanchi; No. 198 Borobudur.

stylobate.def: The top step of a Greek temple’s platform, the floor that the columns stand on.
stylobate.think: Think of the stage floor the columns stand on.

Sudano-Sahelian architecture.def: A building style of the West African Sahel (Mali, Niger, Burkina Faso) using sun-dried mud brick coated in mud plaster, with tapering towers, rounded pinnacles and wooden beams sticking out of the walls.
Sudano-Sahelian architecture.think: Think of sculpted mud skyscrapers with built-in scaffolding.

sunken plaza.def: An open courtyard set lower than the ground around it, entered by steps. At Chavín de Huántar it was the stage for rituals before pilgrims entered dark galleries.
sunken plaza.think: Think of an outdoor amphitheater dug into the ground.

superimposed orders.def: Stacking different column orders on different floors of a building, usually the sturdiest at the bottom and the most delicate at the top (Tuscan or Doric, then Ionic, then Corinthian).
superimposed orders.think: Think of a building that gets fancier as it gets taller.

talud-tablero.def: A Mesoamerican way of building stepped pyramids: each level has a sloping wall (talud) topped by a vertical, framed panel (tablero). It began at Teotihuacan and spread across Mexico.
talud-tablero.think: Think of a staircase of alternating ramps and boxes.

temenos.def: A sacred area set apart for a god, often walled, that contains temples, altars and offerings.
temenos.think: Think of the holy ‘campus’ around a Greek temple.

temple-mountain.def: A temple designed as a model of a sacred mountain, usually Mount Meru, the center of the universe in Hindu and Buddhist belief, with towers or terraces rising to a high center.
temple-mountain.think: Think of a building that is also a map of the cosmos.
temple-mountain.seen: No. 199 Angkor Wat; No. 198 Borobudur; No. 200 Lakshmana Temple.

terrace.def: A flat, level step cut into a slope or built up as a platform. Inka farmers carved mountains into terraces; Hatshepsut’s temple and Borobudur rise in terraces.
terrace.think: Think of a giant staircase where each step is a garden or a floor.
terrace.seen: No. 161 Machu Picchu; No. 21 Mortuary temple of Hatshepsut; No. 198 Borobudur; No. 30 Apadana, Persepolis.

tholos.def: A round building, often with a ring of columns and a cone-shaped or domed roof. Athens’ agora had a tholos where oﬀicials ate and slept; Petra’s Treasury carves one into its facade.
tholos.seen: No. 26 Athenian agora; No. 181 Petra Treasury.

timber frame.def: A building structure made of a wooden skeleton of posts and beams, with the walls only filling the gaps. Traditional Chinese and Japanese temples and palaces use it.
timber frame.think: Think of a wooden skeleton with a tiled hat.

torana.def: An ornamental gateway at the entrance to a stupa enclosure, made of posts and crossbars covered in carved scenes. Sanchi has four, one at each compass point.
torana.think: Think of a carved picture-book gate.

toron.def: Bundles of palm wood that stick out from the walls of West African mud buildings. They act as built-in scaffolding for the yearly replastering and also decorate the walls.
toron.think: Think of a building with permanent ladder rungs poking out of it.

tracery.def: Decorative stone ribs that divide a Gothic window into sections and patterns, or similar patterns carved on walls.
tracery.think: Think of stone lace holding the glass.
tracery.seen: No. 60 Chartres Cathedral; No. 112 Houses of Parliament.

transept.def: The part of a church that crosses the nave at right angles, near the altar end, giving the building a cross-shaped plan.
transept.think: Think of the crossbar of a cross.
transept.seen: No. 58 Sainte-Foy, Conques; No. 60 Chartres Cathedral; No. 82 Il Gesù.

trapezoidal doorway.def: A door, window or niche that is narrower at the top than at the bottom. The Inka used it because it is very stable in earthquakes.
trapezoidal doorway.think: Think of a doorway shaped like a slice of pizza with the tip cut off.
trapezoidal doorway.seen: No. 159 City of Cusco; No. 161 Machu Picchu.

trefoil.def: A three-lobed shape like a clover leaf, common in Gothic arches and tracery. The Bible moralisée dedication page sets its figures under trefoil arches.

triclinium.def: The dining room of a Roman house, named for its three couches, arranged in a U, where diners reclined. The Etruscan Tomb of the Triclinium is named for its painted banquet scenes.

triforium.def: A narrow arcaded passage in the wall of a Gothic church, between the ground-level arcade and the high clerestory windows.
triforium.think: Think of the dark middle stripe in a three-layer cake of arcade, triforium, clerestory.

triglyph.def: A block with three vertical grooves that alternates with metopes in a Doric frieze. It probably recalls the ends of wooden beams in earlier wooden temples.
triglyph.think: ‘Tri’ means three and ‘glyph’ means carving: three carved bars.

trilithon.def: A post-and-lintel unit of three huge stones: two uprights with one laid across the top. Stonehenge’s inner horseshoe has five of them.

trumeau.def: The central post that divides a large church doorway into two openings and holds up the lintel, often carved with a figure.
trumeau.think: Think of a pillar standing in the middle of a double door.

tumulus.def: A large mound of earth and stones heaped over a grave. The gold crowns of Silla Korea were found in royal tumuli. Plural: tumuli.

Tuscan order.def: A simple Etruscan and Roman order, like Doric but with a smooth (unfluted) shaft and a base. It is often used on the ground floor of buildings with stacked orders.
Tuscan order.think: Think of a stripped-down Doric column.
Tuscan order.seen: No. 31 Temple of Minerva, Veii; No. 44 Colosseum; No. 70 Palazzo Rucellai.

twin-temple pyramid.def: A stepped pyramid with two staircases and two shrines on top, side by side. Aztec Templo Mayor honored Huitzilopochtli (war and sun) and Tlaloc (rain).
twin-temple pyramid.think: Think of a double-decker temple for two gods.

tympanum.def: The half-moon-shaped space above a church doorway, framed by the lintel and the arch, often filled with relief sculpture. Romanesque tympana frequently show the Last Judgment.
tympanum.think: Think of a stone billboard over the door telling you what is at stake.
tympanum.seen: No. 58 Sainte-Foy, Conques; No. 60 Chartres Cathedral.

U-shaped temple.def: An Andean temple layout in which platform mounds form three sides of a U around a plaza, opening in one direction, often east toward sunrise.
U-shaped temple.think: Think of arms reaching around to embrace a courtyard.

undulating facade.def: A building front that curves in and out in waves instead of being flat. Borromini’s San Carlo is the classic Baroque example.
undulating facade.think: Think of a wall that ripples like a flag or a stage curtain.
undulating facade.seen: No. 88 San Carlo alle Quattro Fontane.

valley temple.def: A temple at the edge of the Nile floodplain where a pharaoh’s funeral began, linked by a causeway to the mortuary temple beside his pyramid.

vault.def: An arched ceiling or roof made of stone, brick or concrete. There are many types: barrel, groin, rib, and corbeled.
vault.think: Think of a ceiling that is an arch stretched out.
vault.seen: No. 44 Colosseum; No. 58 Sainte-Foy, Conques; No. 60 Chartres Cathedral.
vault.see: barrel vault, groin vault, rib vault, corbel.

vedika.def: The stone railing that surrounds a stupa and encloses the path for walking around it, separating holy space from everyday space.
vedika.think: Think of a fence marking the sacred zone.

vernacular.def: Ordinary, local building styles and everyday forms made without architects, like farmhouses, barns and roadside stores.
vernacular.think: In language, vernacular means everyday speech; in buildings, everyday construction.
vernacular.seen: No. 152 House in New Castle County.

vihara.def: A Buddhist monastery, a place where monks live, often with small cells arranged around a courtyard and sometimes carved into rock.

volute.def: A spiral scroll shape. It forms the corners of an Ionic capital, and in Baroque church facades large volutes link a wide lower story to a narrower upper story.
volute.think: Think of a curl of paper or the shape of a snail shell.

voussoir.def: One of the wedge-shaped stones that make up an arch. At Córdoba the voussoirs alternate red brick and white stone, giving the arches their candy-stripe look.
voussoir.think: Think of the wedge-shaped slices of a pie arranged in a curve.
voussoir.seen: No. 56 Great Mosque of Córdoba; No. 44 Colosseum.

westwork.def: A massive, tower-flanked front block at the west end of Carolingian and Ottonian churches, holding an entrance, chapels and an upper gallery.
westwork.think: Think of a fortress-like front entrance to a church.

ziggurat.def: A huge stepped platform of mud brick built in ancient Mesopotamia (modern Iraq), with a temple on top. Raising the temple high lifted it closer to the gods and made it visible across the flat plain.
ziggurat.think: a giant layered wedding cake with a shrine on the top tier.
ziggurat.see: mud brick, bentaxis approach, battered wall, pyramid. 6 Styles, periods and movements The labels for when and how something was made. If you can name the style, you can usually answer the attribution question.

Abbasid.def: The Islamic dynasty that overthrew the Umayyads and ruled from Baghdad, 750 to 1258 C.E. Its age was a golden age of learning, and Qur’an manuscripts were written in bold, angular Kufic script.
Abbasid.think: Think of Baghdad as the world’s center of books and science.

Abstract Expressionism.def: The first major American art movement, centered in New York in the 1940s and 1950s. Large abstract canvases express emotion through gesture (action painting) or fields of color (color field painting).
Abstract Expressionism.think: Think of huge canvases where the act of painting is the subject.
Abstract Expressionism.seen: No. 145 Woman, I ; No. 149 The Bay.
Abstract Expressionism.see: action painting, color field painting, Expressionism.

Academic art.def: Art made by the rules of oﬀicial art schools (academies), like the French Academy, from the 1600s to the 1800s: polished finish, perfect drawing and serious historical or mythological subjects. Shown at the yearly Salon in Paris.
Academic art.think: Think of the art establishment that later rebels rebelled against.
Academic art.seen: No. 103 Oath of the Horatii; No. 107 La Grande Odalisque.

Achaemenid.def: The first Persian empire, about 550 to 330 B.C.E., stretching from Egypt to India. Its art, best seen at Persepolis, shows orderly processions of subject peoples bringing gifts to the king, in a polished, calm style mixing many cultures.
Achaemenid.think: Think of an empire showing itself as peaceful and orderly rather than violent.

Afrofuturism.def: An art and culture movement that mixes African and African diaspora history and myth with science fiction, technology and imagined futures, to picture Black life beyond the limits of the past and present.
Afrofuturism.think: Think of Wakanda in Black Panther: African tradition plus a high-tech future.

Amarna period.def: A short, radical period during Akhenaton’s reign (about 1353 to 1336 B.C.E.), when he worshipped one sun god, the Aten, and moved the capital to Amarna. Art became more relaxed and intimate, with long faces, swelling hips and tender family scenes.
Amarna period.think: Think of Egyptian art’s brief rebellion against its own rules.

Analytic Cubism.def: The first main phase of Cubism (about 1909 to 1912). Objects are broken into many small, overlapping facets in a narrow range of browns and grays, so the subject is hard to read.
Analytic Cubism.think: Think of a still life shattered into shards.

animal style.def: An art tradition of the nomads of the Eurasian steppes and of early medieval northern Europe in which animals, such as birds of prey, beasts and fish, are twisted, stretched and woven into patterns on small, portable metal objects.
animal style.think: Animals turned into decoration on jewelry and gear you could carry on horseback.

anti-art.def: Art and attitudes that attack the very idea of art: its skill, beauty, museums and market. Dada artists, above all Marcel Duchamp with his readymades, made anti-art to question what counts as art at all.
anti-art.think: Like a prank on the art world that ended up changing it.

Archaic Greek.def: Greek art of about 600 to 480 B.C.E. Statues stand stiff and frontal with one foot forward, show patterned hair and wear a slight ‘Archaic smile.’ Influenced by Egypt.
Archaic Greek.think: Think of Greek sculpture before it learned to relax.
Archaic Greek.seen: No. 27 Anavysos Kouros; No. 28 Peplos Kore.

Art Nouveau.def: A decorative style of about 1890 to 1910 in architecture, design and art, based on flowing, curving lines inspired by plants. It appeared in ironwork, posters, jewelry and buildings.
Art Nouveau.think: French for ‘new art.’ Think of whiplash curves and vines on everything.
Art Nouveau.seen: No. 124 Carson, Pirie, Scott Building; No. 128 Klimt’s The Kiss.

avant-garde.def: Artists who push new, experimental ideas ahead of public taste and challenge tradition. Manet is often seen as an early avant-garde painter.
avant-garde.think: French for ‘advance guard,’ the soldiers who go first.
avant-garde.seen: No. 115 Olympia; No. 126 Les Demoiselles d’Avignon.

Aztec (Mexica).def: The people who built the empire centered on Tenochtitlan (modern Mexico City), about 1325 to 1521, when it fell to the Spanish. They called themselves Mexica. Known for the twin-temple Templo Mayor, monumental stone sculpture and featherwork.
Aztec (Mexica).seen: No. 157 Templo Mayor; No. 158 Feather headdress of Motecuhzoma.

Babylonian.def: Art of Babylon in Mesopotamia. The Old Babylonian period (about 1900 to 1600 B.C.E.) under King Hammurabi produced the famous carved law code; a later NeoBabylonian empire flourished in the 600s B.C.E.
Babylonian.think: Think of the empire of the first great written law code.

Baroque.def: European art of about 1600 to 1750: dramatic, emotional and full of movement, with strong contrasts of light and dark, swirling compositions and theatrical effects that pull the viewer in. Used by the Catholic Church and absolute monarchs alike.
Baroque.think: Think of art as a blockbuster movie: big, dramatic and in your face.
Baroque.seen: No. 85 Calling of Saint Matthew; No. 86 Marie de’ Medici Cycle; No. 88 San Carlo alle Quattro Fontane; No. 89 Ecstasy of Saint Teresa.

Bauhaus.def: A German art and design school (1919 to 1933) that joined art, craft and industry. It taught clean, functional, geometric design and shaped modern architecture and furniture. Mies van der Rohe was its last director.
Bauhaus.think: Think of where modern design was taught as a system.
Bauhaus.see: International Style, De Stijl, less is more.

Byzantine.def: Art of the Eastern Roman Empire, centered on Constantinople (now Istanbul), from 330 to 1453 C.E. It features gold-background mosaics, flat, floating, front-facing holy figures, icons and domed churches like Hagia Sophia.
Byzantine.think: Think of glowing gold walls and saints who stare straight at you.
Byzantine.seen: No. 50 Vienna Genesis; No. 51 San Vitale; No. 52 Hagia Sophia; No. 54 Theotokos icon.

caravaggisti.def: The many painters across Europe in the early 1600s who copied Caravaggio’s style: harsh light against deep darkness, ordinary-looking people and close-up, real-life drama. Caravaggio’s Calling of Saint Matthew (No. 85) shows the model they followed.

Carolingian.def: Art under Charlemagne and his heirs, about 768 to 900 C.E., in France and Germany. It deliberately revived Roman and Early Christian models in manuscripts, metalwork and churches with westworks.
Carolingian.think: Think of Charlemagne trying to reboot the Roman Empire.

Chandella.def: A Hindu dynasty of central India, 9th to 13th centuries C.E., which built the temples of Khajuraho with their towering shikharas and dense, sensual sculpture.

Chavín.def: An Andean culture in Peru, about 900 to 200 B.C.E., centered on the pilgrimage temple at Chavín de Huántar. Its art shows fanged, composite gods mixing jaguars, snakes and birds.

Chola.def: A south Indian Hindu dynasty, strongest from about 850 to 1279 C.E., famous for bronze statues of gods, especially Shiva as Lord of the Dance, made by the lost-wax method.
Chola.seen: No. 202 Shiva as Lord of Dance.

Classical Greek.def: Greek art of about 480 to 323 B.C.E., centered on Athens. It aims for ideal balance and calm: perfect human bodies in natural poses (contrapposto), harmonious proportions and the Parthenon.
Classical Greek.think: Think of the ‘golden age’ that later artists kept trying to copy.
Classical Greek.seen: No. 33 Niobides Krater; No. 34 Doryphoros; No. 35 Acropolis (Parthenon); No. 36 Grave stele of Hegeso.

color field painting.def: A type of Abstract Expressionism using large areas of flat or stained color to create calm, immersive, spiritual effects. Frankenthaler poured thinned paint into raw canvas.
color field painting.think: Think of a canvas you sink into like a pool of color.

community-based art.def: Art made with and for a particular community, often through conversations, workshops and shared stories, and shown in that neighborhood rather than only in museums.
community-based art.seen: No. 236 No Crying Allowed in the Barbershop.

Conceptual art.def: Art, especially from the 1960s on, in which the idea matters more than the finished object or the artist’s skill. Duchamp’s readymades were its forerunners.
Conceptual art.think: Think of art as a thought experiment.
Conceptual art.seen: No. 144 Fountain; No. 229 A Book from the Sky.

Constructivism.def: A Russian movement of about 1915 to the 1930s that wanted art to serve the new Soviet society, using geometric forms, industrial materials, graphic design and photomontage.
Constructivism.think: Think of art as a tool for building a new society.
Constructivism.seen: No. 137 Results of the First Five-Year Plan.

Contemporary art.def: Art of the recent past and present, roughly 1980 to now, made by artists around the world in every medium. It often deals with globalization, identity, politics and memory.
Contemporary art.think: Think of the art of your own lifetime.
Contemporary art.seen: No. 245 Old Man’s Cloth; No. 246 Stadia II ; No. 248 Shibboleth; No. 250 Sunflower Seeds.

Cubism.def: A revolutionary movement started in Paris around 1907 by Picasso and Braque. It breaks objects into flat, geometric pieces and shows them from several angles at once, abandoning single-point perspective.
Cubism.think: Think of looking at something from all sides at once and gluing the views together.
Cubism.seen: No. 126 Les Demoiselles d’Avignon; No. 130 The Portuguese.

Cultural Revolution.def: Mao Zedong’s political campaign in China, 1966 to 1976, which attacked traditional culture and required art to glorify Mao and Communist ideals in a Socialist Realist style.
Cultural Revolution.seen: No. 212 Chairman Mao en Route to Anyuan.

Dada.def: An anti-art movement started in Zurich in 1916 during World War I. Artists used absurdity, chance and everyday objects (readymades) to mock the reason and values they blamed for the war.
Dada.think: Think of art as a protest prank.

De Stijl.def: A Dutch movement of 1917 to 1931 (Piet Mondrian, among others) that reduced art to horizontal and vertical lines and the primary colors plus black, white and gray, seeking universal harmony.
De Stijl.think: Dutch for ‘The Style.’ Think of a grid with red, yellow and blue squares.
De Stijl.seen: No. 136 Composition with Red, Blue and Yellow.

Der Blaue Reiter.def: ‘The Blue Rider,’ a German Expressionist group founded in Munich in 1911 by Kandinsky and Franz Marc, which moved toward spiritual abstraction using color like music.

Die Brücke.def: ‘The Bridge,’ a German Expressionist group founded in Dresden in 1905 (Kirchner, among others), known for harsh colors, jagged forms and woodcuts.

Dutch Golden Age.def: The 1600s in the Dutch Republic, a rich Protestant trading nation. Artists sold to middle-class buyers on an open market, painting portraits, still lifes, landscapes and everyday scenes in exquisite detail.
Dutch Golden Age.think: Think of art for merchants’ living rooms rather than churches or palaces.
Dutch Golden Age.seen: No. 87 Self-Portrait with Saskia; No. 92 Woman Holding a Balance; No. 96 Fruit and Insects.

Early Christian.def: Christian art from about 200 to 500 C.E. At first hidden in catacomb paintings with simple symbols, it became public after Christianity was legalized in 313, when churches were built on the basilica plan.
Early Christian.think: Think of Christianity’s first art: from underground walls to grand churches.
Early Christian.seen: No. 48 Catacomb of Priscilla; No. 49 Santa Sabina.

Early Medieval.def: European art of about 500 to 1000 C.E., after the fall of Rome, made by peoples such as the Franks, Anglo-Saxons and Irish. Much of it is portable metalwork and illuminated manuscripts with dense interlaced patterns.
Early Medieval.think: Think of art made by migrating peoples who carried their wealth with them.
Early Medieval.seen: No. 53 Merovingian looped fibulae; No. 55 Lindisfarne Gospels.

Early Renaissance.def: Italian art of about 1400 to 1495, centered in Florence. Artists revived classical forms, invented linear perspective and studied anatomy and proportion. Key names: Brunelleschi, Donatello, Alberti, Botticelli.
Early Renaissance.think: Think of Florence rediscovering ancient Rome and math at the same time.
Early Renaissance.seen: No. 67 Pazzi Chapel; No. 69 Donatello’s David; No. 70 Palazzo Rucellai; No. 72 Birth of Venus.

Eastern Woodlands.def: The Native American culture region east of the Mississippi River, from the Great Lakes to the Atlantic. Its peoples made mound earthworks in ancient times and later beadwork such as bandolier bags.
Eastern Woodlands.seen: No. 163 Bandolier bag; No. 156 Great Serpent Mound.

Edo period.def: Japan’s period from 1615 to 1868, under the Tokugawa shoguns in Edo (Tokyo), when the country was largely closed to the outside world. A wealthy merchant class enjoyed Rinpa painting and ukiyo-e woodblock prints.
Edo period.seen: No. 210 White and Red Plum Blossoms; No. 211 Great Wave.

Enlightenment.def: The 18th-century movement that valued reason, science and individual rights over tradition and royal power. Its art shows scientific demonstrations, moral lessons and, later, the ideals of new republics.
Enlightenment.seen: No. 100 Philosopher Lecturing on the Orrery; No. 102 Monticello.

environmental art.def: Art that fills or changes a real outdoor environment, often on a huge scale, so that viewers walk through it rather than look at it. Christo and Jeanne-Claude’s The Gates wound through Central Park.

Etruscan.def: Art of the Etruscans, who lived in central Italy (Tuscany) from about 700 to 100 B.C.E. before Rome absorbed them. Known for lively terra cotta sculpture, painted tombs, joyful banquet scenes and temples on high podiums.
Etruscan.think: Think of Rome’s fun-loving neighbors and teachers.
Etruscan.seen: No. 29 Sarcophagus of the Spouses; No. 31 Temple of Minerva, Veii; No. 32 Tomb of the Triclinium.

Expressionism.def: Art, especially in Germany around 1905 to 1925, that distorts form and color to express strong inner emotions such as anxiety, anger or spiritual feeling, rather than show the world accurately.
Expressionism.think: Think of a painting that screams how it feels.
Expressionism.seen: No. 122 The Scream; No. 133 SelfPortrait as a Soldier; No. 134 Memorial Sheet for Karl Liebknecht.
Expressionism.see: Die Brücke, Der Blaue Reiter, Fauvism, Abstract Expressionism.

Fauvism.def: A short movement in France (about 1905 to 1908), led by Henri Matisse, using wild, bright, unnatural colors and loose brushwork to express feeling.
Fauvism.think: Critics called them ‘fauves,’ French for ‘wild beasts,’ because of their colors.

Feminist art.def: Art since the 1970s that challenges how women have been represented and excluded in art history and society, often using craft, the body and stereotypes as subjects.
Feminist art.think: Think of artists talking back to centuries of male-made images of women.
Feminist art.seen: No. 231 Cindy Sherman, Untitled (228); No. 232 Dancing at the Louvre.

fête galante.def: French for ‘courtly party’. A Rococo type of painting showing elegant aristocrats flirting and amusing themselves in dreamy parks and gardens.
fête galante.think: A fancy garden party with secret romance.

Fluxus.def: An international art network of the 1960s that mixed music, performance, everyday actions and humor to blur the line between art and life. Nam June Paik, maker of Electronic Superhighway (No. 238), began as a Fluxus artist.

Formative period.def: The early era of Mesoamerican history, roughly 2000 B.C.E. to 250 C.E., when farming villages, pottery and the first complex societies, such as the Olmec, developed. Also called the Preclassic.

Futurism.def: An Italian movement founded in 1909 that celebrated speed, machines, cities, technology and even war, showing motion with repeated forms and fractured lines.
Futurism.think: Think of art obsessed with fast cars.

Gandharan.def: Buddhist art of Gandhara (today’s Pakistan and Afghanistan), about the first to eighth centuries C.E., which blended Indian Buddhism with Greek and Roman sculpture, giving the Buddha wavy hair and toga-like robes.
Gandharan.think: Think of the Buddha carved by sculptors trained in Greek styles.

geometric abstraction.def: Abstract art built from geometric shapes, such as squares, rectangles, circles and straight lines, usually in flat color. Mondrian’s grids are a classic example.
geometric abstraction.seen: No. 136 Composition with Red, Blue and Yellow.

Gothic.def: European art and architecture of about 1140 to 1500 C.E., starting in France. Cathedrals soar upward on pointed arches, rib vaults and flying buttresses, with walls of stained glass. Sculpture and painting become more natural and graceful.
Gothic.think: Think of buildings that reach for heaven and fill with colored light.
Gothic.seen: No. 60 Chartres Cathedral; No. 61 Bible moralisée dedication page; No. 62 Röttgen Pietà.
Gothic.see: Romanesque, pointed arch, flying buttress, Gothic Revival.

Gothic Revival.def: A 1700s to 1800s movement that brought back medieval Gothic architecture, with pointed arches, spires and tracery. In Britain it was promoted as a Christian and national style.
Gothic Revival.think: Think of new buildings dressed in medieval costume.

Gupta.def: An Indian dynasty of about 320 to 550 C.E., a classical golden age whose calm, graceful Buddha images became the model across Asia.

Han dynasty.def: A long Chinese dynasty, 206 B.C.E. to 220 C.E., that set up Confucian government and the Silk Road. Its tombs held painted silk banners, lacquer and jade showing belief in the afterlife.
Han dynasty.seen: No. 194 Funeral banner of Lady Dai.

Harlem Renaissance.def: A flowering of African American art, music and literature centered in Harlem, New York, in the 1920s and 1930s, celebrating Black identity, history and culture. Jacob Lawrence grew up in its world.
Harlem Renaissance.think: Think of a cultural awakening led by Black artists in New York.
Harlem Renaissance.seen: No. 141 Migration of the Negro, Panel 49.

Heian period.def: Japan’s period from 794 to 1185 C.E., when the court in Heian (Kyoto) produced refined literature and painting. It ended in civil wars between the Taira and Minamoto clans, the war shown in the later Night Attack scroll.

Hellenistic.def: Greek art after Alexander the Great, 323 to 31 B.C.E., spread across a huge territory from Egypt to Asia. It is dramatic and emotional, shows twisting motion, and includes real people: the old, the poor and the suffering.
Hellenistic.think: Think of Classical Greek art turned up to maximum drama.
