Hellenistic.seen: No. 37 Winged Victory of Samothrace; No. 38 Great Altar of Zeus at Pergamon; No. 41 Seated boxer.

Hiberno-Saxon.def: Art of the monasteries of Ireland and Britain, about 600 to 900 C.E., also called Insular art. It mixes Celtic and Anglo-Saxon interlaced patterns with Christian themes in illuminated manuscripts like the Lindisfarne Gospels.
Hiberno-Saxon.think: ‘Hibernia’ is Latin for Ireland. Think of pages woven like Celtic knots.

High Renaissance.def: The peak of the Italian Renaissance, about 1495 to 1520 (longer in Venice). Leonardo, Michelangelo, Raphael and Titian created balanced, monumental, idealized works.
High Renaissance.think: Think of the Renaissance’s greatest-hits album.
High Renaissance.seen: No. 73 Last Supper; No. 75 Sistine Chapel; No. 76 School of Athens; No. 80 Venus of Urbino.

horizon.def: Besides its everyday meaning, in Andean archaeology a ‘horizon’ is a period when one art style spreads over a huge area. The Chavín style defines the Early Horizon.

Hudson River School.def: American landscape painters of about 1825 to 1875, led by Thomas Cole, who painted grand views of the American wilderness, often with a message about nature, nation and progress.
Hudson River School.think: Think of Romanticism with American mountains.

Iberian sculpture.def: Stone carvings by the ancient Iberians, the pre-Roman peoples of Spain, with simplified faces, large almond eyes and heavy features. Picasso borrowed their look for the faces of the women on the left of Les Demoiselles d’Avignon.

Il-Khanid.def: The Mongol dynasty that ruled Iran from 1256 to 1353 after converting to Islam. It produced illustrated manuscripts such as the Great Mongol Shahnama and fine stucco work like Oljeitu’s mihrab in Isfahan.
Il-Khanid.think: Think of Mongol conquerors who became great patrons of Persian art.
Il-Khanid.seen: No. 189 Bahram Gur Fights the Karg; No. 186 Great Mosque of Isfahan.

Imperial Roman.def: Roman art under the emperors, starting with Augustus in 27 B.C.E. It mixes idealized Greek-style portraits of rulers with huge engineering projects in concrete, like the Colosseum and Pantheon, all promoting the emperor’s power.
Imperial Roman.think: Think of art and buildings as the emperor’s advertising campaign.
Imperial Roman.seen: No. 43 Augustus of Prima Porta; No. 44 Colosseum; No. 45 Forum of Trajan; No. 46 Pantheon.

Impressionism.def: A movement in France of about 1867 to 1886 (Monet, Renoir, Degas, Cassatt) that captured quick impressions of light, color and modern life with visible, broken brushstrokes, often painting outdoors.
Impressionism.think: Think of a snapshot of a fleeting moment, made in paint.
Impressionism.seen: No. 116 Saint-Lazare Station; No. 121 The Coiffure.

Inka.def: The largest empire of the Americas, based in Cusco, Peru, about 1400 to 1533. Known for precise mortarless stonework, mountain sites like Machu Picchu, fine textiles and gold and silver objects.
Inka.seen: No. 159 City of Cusco; No. 161 Machu Picchu; No. 162 All-T’oqapu tunic; No. 160 Inka maize cobs.

installation art.def: Large artworks, from the 1960s on, that fill or transform a whole room or site, so viewers walk into and experience them.
installation art.think: Think of art you step inside.
installation art.seen: No. 236 No Crying Allowed in the Barbershop; No. 238 Electronic Superhighway; No. 248 Shibboleth; No. 229 A Book from the Sky.

Japonisme.def: The craze in late1800s Europe for Japanese art, especially woodblock prints. It inspired flat color, bold outlines, unusual viewpoints and cropped compositions.
Japonisme.think: Think of Paris falling in love with Japanese prints.

Joseon.def: Korea’s longest dynasty, 1392 to 1910, guided by Confucian ideals. Oﬀicial portraits of scholars and oﬀicials show them formally and soberly in court dress.

Kamakura period.def: Japan’s period from 1185 to 1333, when samurai warlords (shoguns) took power. Art became more realistic and energetic, from narrative war scrolls to muscular guardian sculptures.
Kamakura period.seen: No. 203 Night Attack on the Sanjô Palace; No. 197 Todai-ji.

Khmer.def: The empire that ruled Cambodia and much of Southeast Asia from about 802 to 1431 C.E. from its capital at Angkor. It built huge stone temple-mountains, first Hindu (Angkor Wat), then Buddhist (Angkor Thom).

Kingdom of Benin.def: A powerful West African kingdom of the Edo people in what is now southern Nigeria, about 1200 to 1897, when British troops looted its palace. Royal artists cast brass plaques and heads honoring the Oba (king).

Land art.def: Art made from 1960s onward in and from the landscape, using earth, rocks, water and natural sites, often huge and far from museums. Also called earthworks.
Land art.think: Think of sculpture made with bulldozers in the desert.
Land art.seen: No. 151 Spiral Jetty; No. 224 The Gates.

Lapita.def: The seafaring culture, about 1500 to 500 B.C.E., that first settled the islands of the western Pacific. It is known for pottery decorated with stamped and incised patterns, many later found in Polynesian tattoo and tapa designs.
Lapita.think: Think of the ancestors of the Polynesians, traceable by their pottery patterns.

Late Antique.def: The period from about 200 to 600 C.E., when the Roman world was turning Christian. Art becomes less naturalistic and more symbolic, with crowded or flattened figures, and Christian art begins in catacombs and basilicas.
Late Antique.think: Think of the bridge between ancient Rome and the Middle Ages.
Late Antique.seen: No. 47 Ludovisi Battle Sarcophagus; No. 48 Catacomb of Priscilla; No. 49 Santa Sabina.

Liangzhu culture.def: A Neolithic culture in the Yangtze River delta of China, about 3300 to 2200 B.C.E., known for finely carved jade objects such as the cong, a square tube with a round hole.
Liangzhu culture.think: Think of China’s earliest jade masters, working without metal tools.

Mamluk.def: A dynasty of former slavesoldiers that ruled Egypt and Syria from 1250 to 1517, famous for luxury metalwork, glass and grand mosques in Cairo.

Mannerism.def: Italian art of about 1520 to 1600, after the High Renaissance. Figures are stretched and twisted, colors are strange, space is crowded or unclear, and the mood is tense: elegance and artificiality over balance.
Mannerism.think: Think of the Renaissance rules being bent on purpose.

Maurya.def: The first great empire of India, about 322 to 185 B.C.E. Its emperor Ashoka converted to Buddhism, spread it widely and began the Great Stupa at Sanchi. The Sunga dynasty that followed added its famous gateways.

Maya.def: A Mesoamerican civilization of southern Mexico and Central America, at its height about 250 to 900 C.E. Maya city-states built pyramid temples with roof combs and carved stone reliefs with hieroglyphic writing recording rulers’ histories.

Merovingian.def: Art of the Franks under the Merovingian kings (about 481 to 751 C.E.) in what is now France and Germany, known for jeweled metalwork such as brooches (fibulae) with garnets and animal shapes.
Merovingian.think: Think of bling for early medieval warriors.

Middle Kingdom.def: Egypt’s second great period, about 2040 to 1650 B.C.E. Royal portraits often look tired and careworn, and nobles were buried in rockcut tombs instead of pyramids.
Middle Kingdom.think: Think of the age between the pyramid builders and the empire builders.

Migration Period.def: The era of about 300 to 700 C.E. when Germanic peoples such as the Goths, Franks and Anglo-Saxons moved across Europe as the Western Roman Empire collapsed. Its art focused on portable metalwork and jewelry.

Ming dynasty.def: A Chinese dynasty, 1368 to 1644, that restored native Chinese rule, built the Forbidden City and the Great Wall as we know it, and made famous blue-and-white porcelain.

Minimalism.def: A 1960s movement of art reduced to simple geometric forms, often industrial materials and repeated units, with no personal expression. It focuses attention on the object and the viewer’s experience of the space.
Minimalism.think: Think of art stripped down to the bare minimum.

Modernism.def: The broad movement, from roughly the 1860s to the 1970s, of artists rejecting tradition to invent new forms suited to modern life. It includes Impressionism through Abstract Expressionism and the International Style.
Modernism.think: Think of ‘make it new’ as a century-long motto.
Modernism.seen: No. 115 Olympia; No. 126 Les Demoiselles d’Avignon; No. 135 Villa Savoye.

Momoyama period.def: Japan’s short period from 1573 to 1615 when warlords reunified the country and built castles decorated with bold, gold-leaf folding screens.

Mughal.def: The Muslim dynasty that ruled most of South Asia from 1526 to 1857, mixing Persian, Indian and Islamic traditions. Known for the Taj Mahal and refined, detailed miniature paintings.
Mughal.seen: No. 208 Jahangir Preferring a Sufi Shaikh; No. 209 Taj Mahal.

Muromachi period.def: Japan’s period from 1336 to 1573, when Zen Buddhism shaped the arts, producing ink painting, the tea ceremony and dry rock gardens.
Muromachi period.see: Kamakura period, Momoyama period, dry landscape garden.

Nabataean.def: Art of the Nabataeans, Arab traders who controlled desert caravan routes and built the city of Petra (Jordan), about 400 B.C.E. to 106 C.E. They carved huge tomb facades into cliffs, mixing Greek and Roman forms with local taste.
Nabataean.think: Think of desert merchants who carved Greek-style temples into mountains.

Nara period.def: Japan’s period from 710 to 794 C.E., when the capital was at Nara and emperors sponsored Buddhism as a state religion, building Todai-ji.

Nasrid.def: The last Muslim dynasty in Spain, ruling Granada from 1232 until 1492, when it fell to Ferdinand and Isabella. It built the Alhambra palace.

Neo-Assyrian.def: Art of the Assyrian empire in northern Mesopotamia, about 911 to 612 B.C.E. Its palaces had giant human-headed winged bulls (lamassu) at the gates and stone reliefs of kings hunting lions and winning wars.
Neo-Assyrian.think: Think of art as royal muscle-flexing.

Neo-Expressionism.def: A 1980s return to expressive, rough, large-scale painting of figures and symbols, after years of Minimalism and Conceptual art. Basquiat is a leading figure.
Neo-Expressionism.think: Think of messy, raw painting making a comeback.

Neoclassicism.def: A style of about 1750 to 1830 that revived ancient Greek and Roman art after the excavation of Pompeii. Crisp lines, calm compositions and heroic, moral subjects; it became the style of revolutions and new republics.
Neoclassicism.think: Think of the anti-Rococo: serious, clean and patriotic.
Neoclassicism.seen: No. 102 Monticello; No. 103 Oath of the Horatii; No. 104 Houdon’s George Washington.

Neolithic.def: The New Stone Age, beginning around 10,000 to 8000 B.C.E. in the Near East and later elsewhere, when people started farming, raising animals and living in villages. It brought pottery, polished stone tools and huge stone monuments.
Neolithic.think: Think of the moment people settled down and started building to last.

Neoplasticism.def: Piet Mondrian’s name for his pure abstract style: only straight horizontal and vertical lines, the three primary colors, and black, white and gray. He hoped it would express universal harmony.
Neoplasticism.seen: No. 136 Composition with Red, Blue and Yellow.
Neoplasticism.see: De Stijl, geometric abstraction, primary colors.

New Kingdom.def: Egypt’s empire period, about 1550 to 1070 B.C.E., the age of Hatshepsut, Akhenaton, Tutankhamun and Ramses II. Pharaohs built huge temples like Karnak and were buried in hidden tombs in the Valley of the Kings.
New Kingdom.think: Think of Egypt at its richest and most powerful.
New Kingdom.seen: No. 20 Temple of Amun-Re, Karnak; No. 21 Mortuary temple of Hatshepsut; No. 23 Tutankhamun’s coﬀin; No. 24 Last judgment of Hu-Nefer.
New Kingdom.see: Amarna period, Old Kingdom, hypostyle hall.

New York School.def: The Abstract Expressionist artists active in New York City in the 1940s and 1950s, such as Pollock, de Kooning and Rothko, who made New York the center of the art world.
New York School.see: Abstract Expressionism, action painting, color field painting.

Northern Renaissance.def: Art of about 1400 to 1600 in Flanders, the Netherlands and Germany. Artists pioneered oil paint to show tiny details, textures and hidden symbols, and Dürer spread printmaking.
Northern Renaissance.think: Think of microscope-level detail, where every object means something.
Northern Renaissance.seen: No. 66 Merode Altarpiece; No. 68 Arnolfini Portrait; No. 74 Dürer’s Adam and Eve; No. 83 Hunters in the Snow.

Northwest Coast.def: The Native American culture region along the Pacific coast of Canada and Alaska, home to peoples like the Kwakwaka’wakw, known for carved masks, totem poles and potlatch ceremonies.

Old Kingdom.def: The first great age of Egypt, about 2575 to 2150 B.C.E., when pharaohs built the pyramids at Giza. Its statues are blocky, calm and idealized, made to last forever as homes for the spirit (ka).
Old Kingdom.seen: No. 15 Seated scribe; No. 17 Great Pyramids of Giza; No. 18 King Menkaura and queen.

Olmec.def: The first major civilization of Mesoamerica, on Mexico’s Gulf Coast, about 1200 to 400 B.C.E. Known for colossal stone heads and fine jade carvings; later cultures like the Aztecs treasured Olmec objects as heirlooms.
Olmec.think: Think of the ‘mother culture’ of Mesoamerica.
Olmec.seen: No. 157 Templo Mayor (offering with an Olmec mask).

Orientalism.def: Western art of the 1800s that showed North Africa, the Middle East and Asia as exotic, sensual or dangerous. It reflects European fantasies and colonial power more than the real places.
Orientalism.think: Think of a fantasy postcard of ‘the East’ made by outsiders.

Ottoman.def: The Turkish empire that ruled from about 1299 to 1922, capturing Constantinople in 1453. Its architect Sinan built huge domed mosques inspired by Hagia Sophia, with slender pencil-shaped minarets and Iznik tiles.

Ottonian.def: Art of the German emperors named Otto and their successors, about 919 to 1024 C.E. It produced massive churches, bronze doors and solemn manuscripts that bridge Carolingian and Romanesque art.
Ottonian.think: Think of the Carolingian revival’s sequel in Germany.

Paleolithic.def: The Old Stone Age, from about 2.5 million years ago to about 10,000 B.C.E., when people lived as hunter-gatherers using stone tools. Its art, mostly from after 40,000 B.C.E., includes cave paintings of animals and small carved or portable objects.
Paleolithic.think: Think of art by people who had no farms, no metal and no writing.
Paleolithic.seen: No. 1 Apollo 11 Stones; No. 2 Great Hall of the Bulls, Lascaux; No. 3 Camelid sacrum.

performance art.def: Art in which the work is a live action by the artist, sometimes with the audience, rather than an object. It became a major form from the 1960s on.
performance art.think: Think of art that happens rather than art that hangs.
performance art.seen: No. 148 Narcissus Garden; No. 223 Presentation of Fijian mats and tapa.

Perpendicular Gothic.def: The last phase of English Gothic architecture, about 1350 to 1550, with strong vertical lines, huge windows and grid-like panels of tracery. The Houses of Parliament revived it.

Pictorialism.def: A photography movement of about 1885 to 1915 that tried to make photographs look like paintings, with soft focus, special printing and artistic subjects. Stieglitz, maker of The Steerage (No. 127), started as a Pictorialist before championing sharp ‘straight’ photography.

picturesque.def: A 1700s British idea of scenery that is pleasingly rough, irregular and varied, as if made for a painting, between the calm ‘beautiful’ and the terrifying ‘sublime’. It shaped landscape painting, gardens and Gothic Revival buildings.
picturesque.seen: No. 109 The Oxbow; No. 112 Houses of Parliament.

Pop Art.def: A movement of the late 1950s and 1960s, in Britain and the U.S., that used images from mass culture, such as ads, comics, celebrities and consumer products, often with commercial techniques like silkscreen.
Pop Art.think: Think of a soup can or a movie star treated as fine art.

Post-Impressionism.def: Art of about 1886 to 1905 by painters who began with Impressionism but went further in their own directions: Van Gogh (emotional color), Gauguin (flat symbolic color), Cézanne (solid geometric structure), Seurat (dots of color).
Post-Impressionism.seen: No. 120 The Starry Night; No. 123 Where Do We Come From?; No. 125 Mont Sainte-Victoire.

Postmodernism.def: A movement from the 1970s on that rejects Modernism’s belief in purity and progress. It mixes styles, quotes the past, uses irony and questions ideas of originality and identity.
Postmodernism.think: Think of art and buildings that remix everything with a wink.
Postmodernism.seen: No. 152 House in New Castle County; No. 230 Pink Panther; No. 231 Cindy Sherman, Untitled (228).

Predynastic Egypt.def: Egypt before and around the time its first kings united Upper and Lower Egypt, about 3000 B.C.E. The Narmer Palette already shows the conventions Egyptian art kept for 3,000 years.
Predynastic Egypt.think: Think of the moment Egyptian art’s rules were first written down in stone.

Primitivism.def: The interest of European modern artists, around 1890 to 1940, in art from Africa, Oceania and other non-Western cultures, which they wrongly saw as ‘primitive’ and pure. It shaped Gauguin and Picasso but relied on colonial stereotypes.
Primitivism.think: Think of borrowing from cultures without understanding them.
Primitivism.seen: No. 123 Where Do We Come From?; No. 126 Les Demoiselles d’Avignon.

proto-cubism.def: Work leading up to Cubism, especially Picasso’s Les Demoiselles d’Avignon (1907), which broke figures into flat, angular planes before Cubism was fully developed.

Proto-Renaissance.def: Italian art of about 1280 to 1400 that started to move toward the Renaissance, especially in Giotto’s frescoes, which give figures real weight, space around them and human emotion.
Proto-Renaissance.think: Think of the warm-up act before the Renaissance.

Qin dynasty.def: The dynasty that first unified China, 221 to 206 B.C.E., under the first emperor, who standardized writing and coins and was buried with thousands of terra cotta warriors.
Qin dynasty.think: China’s English name may come from ‘Qin.’

Qing dynasty.def: The last imperial dynasty of China, 1644 to 1912, ruled by the Manchus, who kept and expanded the Forbidden City.

Rajput.def: Hindu kingdoms in Rajasthan and the Himalayan foothills of India, about 1500 to 1900, whose court painters made bold, colorful miniature paintings of Hindu epics, poetry and princely life, sometimes borrowing Mughal techniques.

Republican Roman.def: Roman art from 509 to 27 B.C.E., when Rome was a republic governed by elected oﬀicials. Portraits of older men are ‘veristic’: brutally realistic, showing wrinkles to signal wisdom and service.
Republican Roman.think: Think of politicians proud of every wrinkle.
Republican Roman.seen: No. 40 Alexander Mosaic; No. 42 Head of a Roman patrician.

Rinpa.def: A Japanese painting school of the Edo period, named after Ogata Korin, known for bold, decorative designs, gold and silver backgrounds and stylized natural forms.
Rinpa.seen: No. 210 White and Red Plum Blossoms.

Rococo.def: A light, playful style of about 1720 to 1780, mostly in France. Pastel colors, curving lines, frothy decoration and flirty scenes of aristocrats at leisure.
Rococo.think: Think of Baroque in a pastel party dress.

Romanesque.def: European art and architecture of about 1000 to 1150 C.E. Churches have thick walls, round arches, barrel vaults, small windows and sculpted portals, often built along pilgrimage roads.
Romanesque.think: ‘Roman-esque’ because it reuses Roman round arches and vaults. Think heavy, solid and fortress-like.
Romanesque.seen: No. 58 Sainte-Foy, Conques; No. 59 Bayeux Tapestry.
Romanesque.see: Gothic, round arch, barrel vault, pilgrimage church.

Romanticism.def: A movement of about 1790 to 1850 that valued emotion, imagination and the power of nature over reason. Expect stormy skies, exotic places, heroic struggles, loose brushwork and strong color.
Romanticism.seen: No. 106 Goya, Y no hai remedio; No. 108 Liberty Leading the People; No. 109 The Oxbow; No. 111 Slave Ship.

Safavid.def: The dynasty that ruled Iran from 1501 to 1736 and made Shia Islam the state religion. Its court produced dazzling illustrated manuscripts, carpets and tiled buildings.
Safavid.seen: No. 190 The Court of Gayumars; No. 191 Ardabil Carpet; No. 186 Great Mosque of Isfahan.

Sailendra.def: A Buddhist dynasty in Java, Indonesia, in the 8th and 9th centuries C.E., which built Borobudur.

Salon.def: The oﬀicial yearly (later every two years) art exhibition in Paris, run by the Academy. Getting in made an artist’s career; rejected artists eventually staged their own shows, such as the Salon des Refusés of 1863.
Salon.think: Think of the art world’s main awards show.
Salon.seen: No. 103 Oath of the Horatii; No. 113 The Stone Breakers; No. 115 Olympia.

Saudeleur dynasty.def: Rulers who unified the Micronesian island of Pohnpei from about 1100 to the early 1600s and built Nan Madol, a royal and ritual center on artificial islets.

Seljuk.def: A Turkish dynasty ruling Iran and much of the Middle East in the 11th and 12th centuries. At the Great Mosque of Isfahan they introduced the four-iwan plan that became standard in Iran.

Silla.def: One of the Three Kingdoms of ancient Korea (57 B.C.E. to 935 C.E.), later ruling a unified Korea. Its royal tombs held spectacular gold crowns shaped like trees and antlers.
Silla.seen: No. 196 Silla gold and jade crown.

Socialist Realism.def: The oﬀicial art style of the Soviet Union and Communist China: realistic, heroic, optimistic images glorifying workers, leaders and the state.
Socialist Realism.think: Think of propaganda posters painted in a realistic style.
Socialist Realism.seen: No. 212 Chairman Mao en Route to Anyuan.

Song dynasty.def: A Chinese dynasty, 960 to 1279 C.E., known for monumental ink landscape paintings, refined ceramics and scholar culture.
Song dynasty.seen: No. 201 Travelers among Mountains and Streams.

straight photography.def: Photography from the early 1900s that used the camera’s sharp focus and real subjects instead of imitating painting with soft focus and staged scenes.
straight photography.think: Think of a photo proud to be a photo.

Sumerian.def: Art of Sumer, the world’s first civilization of cities, in southern Mesopotamia (modern Iraq), about 3500 to 2000 B.C.E. It includes ziggurats, wide-eyed praying statues and inlaid objects, and it invented writing (cuneiform).
Sumerian.think: Think of the inventors of the city, writing and the wheel.
Sumerian.seen: No. 12 White Temple and ziggurat; No. 14 Votive figures, Eshnunna; No. 16 Standard of Ur.

Surrealism.def: A movement launched in 1924 that explored dreams, the unconscious mind and strange combinations of images, inspired by Freud’s ideas.
Surrealism.think: Think of a dream painted with convincing detail.
Surrealism.seen: No. 138 Object (fur teacup); No. 140 The Two Fridas; No. 142 The Jungle.

Symbolism.def: A late-1800s movement (about 1880 to 1910) that rejected plain realism to express dreams, moods, spirituality and inner life through suggestive images and symbols.
Symbolism.think: Think of art that paints the inside of your head.
Symbolism.seen: No. 122 The Scream; No. 123 Where Do We Come From?; No. 128 Klimt’s The Kiss.

Synthetic Cubism.def: The second phase of Cubism (from about 1912). Instead of breaking objects down, artists built pictures up from flat, simpler shapes, brighter colors, and real materials glued on (collage).
Synthetic Cubism.think: Think of building a picture from cutout pieces.

synthetism.def: The approach Gauguin and his circle developed in the late 1880s: flat areas of bold color, strong outlines and simplified forms that combine what the artist saw with memory, feeling and symbols.
synthetism.seen: No. 123 Where Do We Come From?.

Tang dynasty.def: A Chinese dynasty, 618 to 907 C.E., often called a golden age, cosmopolitan and Buddhist. Its emperors sponsored colossal Buddhist sculpture like the Vairocana Buddha at Longmen.
Tang dynasty.see: Han dynasty, Song dynasty, cave temple.

Timurid.def: The dynasty founded by the conqueror Timur (Tamerlane), ruling Central Asia and Iran from 1370 to 1507, famous for tiled domed buildings and book painting. It added to the Great Mosque of Isfahan.

ukiyo-e.def: Japanese woodblock prints and paintings of the Edo period showing the ‘floating world’ of entertainment, actors, beauties and later landscapes. Cheap and popular, they deeply influenced European artists.
ukiyo-e.think: Think of Edo Japan’s pop art.

Umayyad.def: The first hereditary Islamic dynasty, ruling from Damascus 661 to 750 C.E.; a surviving branch ruled Spain (al-Andalus) from Córdoba, 756 to 1031. It built the Dome of the Rock and the Great Mosque of Córdoba.
Umayyad.think: Think of the founders of Islamic architecture.
Umayyad.seen: No. 185 Dome of the Rock; No. 56 Great Mosque of Córdoba; No. 57 Pyxis of al-Mughira.

Venetian school.def: Renaissance painting in Venice, led by artists like Titian, which stressed rich color, soft light and the texture of oil paint more than precise drawing.
Venetian school.think: Think of Florence focusing on drawing and Venice focusing on color.

Viceregal art.def: Art made in Spain’s American colonies (the viceroyalties of New Spain and Peru) from the 1500s to the early 1800s. It blends European styles with Indigenous materials, ideas and artists, from feather and shell inlay to casta paintings.
Viceregal art.think: Think of European Baroque translated by the Americas.
Viceregal art.seen: No. 81 Codex Mendoza; No. 90 Angel with Arquebus; No. 95 Virgin of Guadalupe; No. 97 Spaniard and Indian Produce a Mestizo.

video art.def: Art made with video and television technology, which began in the 1960s. Nam June Paik and Bill Viola are major names.
video art.think: Think of TV used as a paintbrush.
video art.seen: No. 238 Electronic Superhighway; No. 239 The Crossing.

Vienna Secession.def: A group of artists in Vienna, led by Gustav Klimt, who broke away (seceded) from the oﬀicial academy in 1897 to make modern art, including richly decorated, goldfilled paintings.
Vienna Secession.think: Think of Vienna’s version of Art Nouveau.

yamato-e.def: Japanese for ‘Japanese-style painting’. A style that grew up in the Heian period, with bright colors, high angled views, roofs left off to show interiors, and Japanese stories and places, in contrast to Chinese-style painting.
yamato-e.seen: No. 203 Night Attack on the Sanjô Palace.

Yarlung dynasty.def: The early Tibetan kingdom (7th to 9th centuries C.E.) that brought Buddhism to Tibet. Its king Songtsen Gampo is linked to the arrival of the Jowo Rinpoche statue in Lhasa.

Yuan dynasty.def: The Mongol dynasty that ruled China from 1271 to 1368, founded by Kublai Khan. Blue-and-white porcelain was developed for trade with the Islamic world.
Yuan dynasty.see: Song dynasty, Ming dynasty. 7 Religion, myth and symbols Most art before 1800 is religious. These are the stories, figures and symbols you need to read the works: Christian, Jewish, Islamic, Buddhist, Hindu, ancient Egyptian, Greek and Roman, Mesoamerican, African and Pacific.

abhaya mudra.def: The ‘do not fear’ gesture: right hand raised, palm facing out. It means protection and reassurance.
abhaya mudra.think: Like a crossing guard’s ‘stop, you’re safe’ hand.
abhaya mudra.seen: No. 202 Shiva as Lord of Dance; No. 197 Todai-ji Great Buddha.

Abraham.def: The founding father of Judaism, Christianity and Islam. God tested him by asking him to sacrifice his son (Isaac in the Bible, Ishmael in Muslim tradition). Muslims believe he and Ishmael built the Kaaba.
Abraham.seen: No. 51 San Vitale (lunettes); No. 183 The Kaaba; No. 185 Dome of the Rock.

afterlife.def: Life after death. Belief in an afterlife drove huge amounts of art: tombs, coﬀins, grave goods and guardian figures meant to help or protect the dead.
afterlife.seen: No. 17 Great Pyramids; No. 24 Last judgment of Hu-Nefer; No. 193 Terra cotta warriors; No. 194 Funeral banner of Lady Dai.

Ahura Mazda.def: The supreme god of Zoroastrianism, the religion of ancient Persia’s kings, sometimes symbolized by a winged disk.

Allah.def: The Arabic word for God, used by Muslims and also by Arabic-speaking Christians and Jews.

allegory.def: A work in which characters and events stand for bigger ideas, so the whole thing carries a second, hidden meaning.
allegory.seen: No. 79 Allegory of Law and Grace; No. 108 Liberty Leading the People; No. 38 Great Altar at Pergamon.

Amida.def: The Buddha of Infinite Light (Amitabha in Sanskrit), who rules a Western Paradise called the Pure Land. Believers who call his name hope to be reborn there.

Ammit.def: The ‘Devourer of the Dead’, a monster that is part crocodile, part lion, part hippo. It eats the heart of anyone who fails the weighing of the heart.
Ammit.see: weighing of the heart, composite creature.

Amun.def: ‘The Hidden One’: Egyptian god of Thebes who merged with the sun god as Amun-Re, king of the gods in the New Kingdom.
Amun.seen: No. 20 Temple of Amun-Re and Hypostyle Hall; No. 21 Mortuary temple of Hatshepsut.

ancestor figure.def: A carved figure that stands for or houses the spirit of a family or clan ancestor. It may be given offerings, kept in a shrine, or used to guard remains.
ancestor figure.seen: No. 179 Reliquary figure (byeri); No. 214 Moai; No. 171 Ndop.

ancestor veneration.def: Honoring dead family members as spirits who still protect and guide the living. Many works are made to house, remember or honor ancestors.
ancestor veneration.seen: No. 171 Ndop of King Mishe miShyaang maMbul; No. 179 Reliquary figure (byeri); No. 214 Moai on platform; No. 205 Portrait of Sin Sukju.

Andachtsbild.def: German for ‘devotional image’. A late medieval image made for private prayer and emotional meditation, often showing Christ’s suffering up close.
Andachtsbild.think: Made to make you feel, not to tell a story.

angel.def: A heavenly messenger or servant of God, usually shown as a winged human. Angels announce news, guard, fight and sing.
angel.think: ‘Angel’ comes from the Greek word for ‘messenger’.
angel.seen: No. 66 Merode Altarpiece (Gabriel); No. 89 Ecstasy of Saint Teresa; No. 90 Angel with Arquebus; No. 54 Theotokos icon.

aniconism.def: Avoiding pictures of people, animals or God, especially in religious settings. Islamic religious art uses words, geometry and plant patterns instead. Early Buddhist art also avoided showing the Buddha’s body.
aniconism.seen: No. 187 Folio from a Qur’an; No. 185 Dome of the Rock; No. 56 Great Mosque of Córdoba; No. 192 Great Stupa at Sanchi (Buddha shown by symbols).

ankh.def: An Egyptian symbol shaped like a cross with a loop on top, meaning ‘life’. Gods hold it to give life to the king.
ankh.seen: No. 22 Akhenaton, Nefertiti, and three daughters.

Annunciation.def: The Bible scene in which the angel Gabriel tells Mary she will give birth to Jesus. Artists often add a lily for purity and a dove or rays of light for God’s spirit.
Annunciation.seen: No. 66 Merode Altarpiece; No. 77 Isenheim altarpiece (first opening).

Anu.def: The Sumerian sky god, father of the gods. The White Temple at Uruk was most likely built for him.
Anu.seen: No. 12 White Temple and its ziggurat.

Anubis.def: Jackal-headed Egyptian god of mummification who guides the dead to judgment and weighs the heart.
Anubis.see: weighing of the heart, Book of the Dead.

apasmara.def: The dwarf of ignorance that Shiva Nataraja crushes under his foot while dancing.
apasmara.seen: No. 202 Shiva as Lord of Dance.

Aphrodite.def: Greek goddess of love and beauty, called Venus by the Romans. She was born from sea foam, and Julius Caesar’s family (including Augustus) claimed to descend from her.
Aphrodite.seen: No. 72 Birth of Venus; No. 80 Venus of Urbino; No. 43 Augustus of Prima Porta (Cupid points to Venus).

Apocalypse.def: The end of the world as described in the Book of Revelation, the last book of the Bible, full of visions of beasts, angels and Christ’s final victory.
Apocalypse.think: Today it means any disaster; in art history it means this Bible book.
Apocalypse.seen: No. 61 Bible moralisée (Scenes from the Apocalypse).

Apollo.def: Greek and Roman god of the sun, light, music, poetry and prophecy, always shown young and handsome. Twin brother of Artemis.
Apollo.seen: No. 31 Temple of Minerva and sculpture of Apollo; No. 33 Niobides Krater.

apostle.def: One of the twelve chosen followers of Jesus, such as Peter, John, Matthew and Judas. The word means ‘one who is sent out’.
apostle.seen: No. 73 Last Supper; No. 85 Calling of Saint Matthew.

apotheosis.def: The raising of a person to the status of a god, often shown as being carried up into heaven.

apsara.def: A heavenly female dancer or nymph in Hindu and Buddhist belief. Hundreds of carved apsaras decorate the walls of Angkor Wat.

apu.def: A sacred mountain spirit in Andean belief. Inka sites were laid out to frame views of these holy peaks.

archangel.def: A high-ranking angel, such as Gabriel (the messenger of the Annunciation) or Michael (the warrior who weighs souls and fights Satan).

Artemis.def: Greek goddess of the hunt, wild animals and the moon, twin of Apollo. The Romans called her Diana. She carries a bow.

ase.def: A Yoruba idea of life force or the power to make things happen, held by gods, kings, elders and some women. Also spelled àṣẹ.

Aten.def: The sun disk, worshipped by the pharaoh Akhenaten as the one true god. It is shown as a disk with rays ending in little hands.
Aten.seen: No. 22 Akhenaton, Nefertiti, and three daughters.

Athena.def: Greek goddess of wisdom, war strategy and crafts, and protector of Athens. The Romans called her Minerva. She wears a helmet and carries a shield and spear.
Athena.seen: No. 35 Acropolis (Parthenon); No. 38 Great Altar of Zeus and Athena at Pergamon; No. 31 Temple of Minerva.

attribute.def: An object or feature that identifies a figure, like Zeus’s thunderbolt, a saint’s tool of martyrdom, or Shiva’s drum and flame.
attribute.seen: No. 43 Augustus of Prima Porta (bare feet); No. 202 Shiva as Lord of Dance; No. 99 Portrait of Sor Juana (books).

atua.def: A Polynesian word for a god or powerful ancestral spirit.

avatar.def: In Hinduism, a form a god takes when coming down to earth, especially the ten avatars of Vishnu (such as the boar, Rama and Krishna).
avatar.think: The gaming meaning (your character in a game) comes from this.

axis mundi.def: Latin for ‘axis of the world’: an imagined central pole connecting earth with heaven and the underworld. A mountain, tree, pillar or temple can play this role.
axis mundi.seen: No. 192 Great Stupa at Sanchi (mast); No. 199 Angkor Wat; No. 157 Templo Mayor.

ba.def: In Egyptian belief, a person’s personality or soul, shown as a bird with a human head. It could fly out of the tomb by day and return at night.

Bahram Gur.def: A Persian king of legend, famous as a hunter and hero, whose adventures appear in the Shahnama.
Bahram Gur.seen: No. 189 Bahram Gur Fights the Karg.

baptism.def: The Christian ritual of washing or dipping in water to welcome a person into the faith and wash away sin.

bhumisparsha mudra.def: The ‘earth-touching’ gesture: the right hand reaches down to touch the ground. It recalls the moment the Buddha called the earth to witness his enlightenment.

Bible.def: The holy book of Christianity. It has two parts: the Old Testament (the Hebrew scriptures, shared with Judaism) and the New Testament (about Jesus and his followers). Most Christian art illustrates a Bible story.
Bible.think: When a work is a ‘scene’, ask: which Bible story is this?
Bible.seen: No. 50 Vienna Genesis; No. 61 Bible moralisée; No. 75 Sistine Chapel ceiling.

Bible moralisée.def: French for ‘moralized Bible’. A luxury illustrated Bible made for French royalty, pairing each Bible scene with a second image explaining its moral or Christian lesson, in stacked roundels.
Bible moralisée.think: A Bible with a built-in study guide.

bloodletting.def: A Maya ritual in which rulers and nobles drew their own blood, for example through the tongue, as an offering to gods and to call up ancestors in visions.

Bodhi tree.def: The fig tree under which the Buddha meditated and reached enlightenment. In early Buddhist art a tree can stand in for the Buddha himself.

bodhisattva.def: In Mahayana Buddhism, a being who has reached enlightenment but chooses to stay in the world to help others. Bodhisattvas are often shown as richly dressed princes, unlike the plain-robed Buddha.
bodhisattva.think: A spiritual helper who holds the door open for everyone else.
bodhisattva.seen: No. 195 Longmen caves (flanking the Vairocana Buddha).

Book of the Dead.def: An Egyptian collection of spells and pictures, written on papyrus and buried with the dead to guide them safely through the underworld to the afterlife.
Book of the Dead.think: A travel guide and insurance policy for the afterlife.

Brahma.def: The Hindu creator god, usually shown with four faces. With Vishnu and Shiva he forms the trimurti (the ‘three forms’), though he is rarely worshipped on his own.

Buddha.def: ‘The Awakened One’: a being who has reached enlightenment. Usually it means Siddhartha Gautama (Shakyamuni), the historical founder of Buddhism, but there are other Buddhas too, such as Amida and Vairocana. Buddha images share fixed features: ushnisha, urna, long earlobes, calm face.
Buddha.seen: No. 182 Bamiyan Buddhas; No. 184 Jowo Rinpoche; No. 195 Longmen caves; No. 197 Todai-ji (Great Buddha).

Buddhism.def: A religion founded in India around 500 B.C.E. by Siddhartha Gautama, the Buddha. It teaches that life is full of suffering caused by desire, and that one can escape the cycle of rebirth by reaching enlightenment. It spread across Asia along trade routes.
Buddhism.seen: No. 192 Great Stupa at Sanchi; No. 195 Longmen caves; No. 197 Todai-ji; No. 198 Borobudur.

calavera.def: Spanish for ‘skull’. In Mexico, a skeleton or skull figure, often dressed up and joking, used in prints and Day of the Dead celebrations to mock vanity and remind everyone that death comes to all.
calavera.seen: No. 143 Dream of a Sunday Afternoon.
calavera.see: Calavera Catrina, memento mori, Mexican muralism.

Calavera Catrina.def: An elegant, fashionably dressed female skeleton, created by the printmaker José Guadalupe Posada to mock upper-class pretension. It became a symbol of Mexico’s Day of the Dead.
Calavera Catrina.seen: No. 143 Dream of a Sunday Afternoon in the Alameda Park.

calligraphy.def: The art of beautiful handwriting. In Islam it is the most honored art form because it records God’s words. Chinese and Japanese calligraphy is also a high art, done with brush and ink.
calligraphy.think: Handwriting raised to the level of painting.
calligraphy.seen: No. 187 Folio from a Qur’an; No. 185 Dome of the Rock; No. 209 Taj Mahal; No. 65 Alhambra; No. 183 The Kaaba (kiswa); No. 235 Rebellious Silence.

canopic jars.def: Four jars that held a mummy’s removed organs (liver, lungs, stomach, intestines), each lid often shaped as the head of a protective god.

catacomb.def: An underground cemetery of tunnels with burial shelves cut into the walls. Early Christians in Rome buried their dead in catacombs and painted their small chambers.

ceque.def: Imaginary lines radiating out from the Qorikancha, the sun temple in Cusco, linking hundreds of shrines (huacas) across the Inka landscape. They organized worship, water rights and family groups.
ceque.think: Like spokes of a sacred wheel with Cusco as the hub.

chador.def: A full-length cloak, usually black, worn by many women in Iran that covers the head and body but leaves the face open. Shirin Neshat’s Women of Allah photographs use it to explore Iranian women’s identity.

Christ.def: The title Christians give Jesus. It comes from the Greek word for ‘anointed one’ (the same meaning as the Hebrew ‘messiah’). In art he is usually the central figure, often with a cross-shaped halo.
Christ.think: ‘Christ’ is a title, like ‘King’, not a last name.
Christ.seen: No. 73 Last Supper; No. 77 Isenheim altarpiece; No. 85 Calling of Saint Matthew; No. 63 Arena Chapel.

Christ in Majesty.def: Christ shown enthroned as ruler of heaven, usually facing straight out, often inside a mandorla and surrounded by the four evangelist symbols. It is a common subject over church doorways.
Christ in Majesty.think: Jesus as king on his throne, not as a baby or a suffering man.

Christianity.def: The religion built around Jesus of Nazareth, whom Christians believe is the Son of God who died and rose again to save people from sin. It became the main religion of Europe, so most European art from about 300 to 1700 C.E. is Christian art.
Christianity.think: If a European painting before 1700 has a halo in it, the story almost certainly comes from the Bible or the lives of saints.
Christianity.seen: No. 48 Catacomb of Priscilla; No. 51 San Vitale; No. 60 Chartres Cathedral; No. 75 Sistine Chapel.

church (institution).def: Lower-case ‘church’ can mean a building for Christian worship; capital-C ‘the Church’ means the organization of Christianity itself, with its leaders (popes, bishops, priests). The Church was the biggest art patron in Europe for over a thousand years.
church (institution).think: Think of ‘the Church’ as a huge company that ordered most of Europe’s art.
church (institution).seen: No. 49 Santa Sabina; No. 58 Sainte-Foy; No. 82 Il Gesù.

Churning of the Ocean of Milk.term: Churning of the Ocean of Milk
Churning of the Ocean of Milk.def: A Hindu creation myth in which gods and demons pull a giant serpent wrapped around a mountain, like a tug-ofwar, to churn the cosmic sea and release the nectar of immortality. Vishnu directs the churning.

circumambulation.def: Walking around a sacred object or building as an act of worship. Buddhists and Hindus circle clockwise; Muslims circle the Kaaba counterclockwise.
circumambulation.seen: No. 192 Great Stupa at Sanchi; No. 198 Borobudur; No. 183 The Kaaba; No. 185 Dome of the Rock.

Coatepec.def: ‘Serpent Mountain’: the mythical mountain where Huitzilopochtli was born and defeated Coyolxauhqui. The Templo Mayor’s Huitzilopochtli side was built as Coatepec.

Coatlicue.def: ‘Serpent Skirt’: the Aztec earth goddess, mother of the war god Huitzilopochtli. In the myth, she gave birth to him on Serpent Mountain (Coatepec) as her daughter Coyolxauhqui attacked her. The Templo Mayor re-creates that mountain.

codex.def: A handmade book. In Mesoamerica, a folding screen book of painted pictures and symbols recording history, calendars and rituals; in Europe, a bound manuscript. The plural is codices.
codex.seen: No. 81 Codex Mendoza; No. 64 Golden Haggadah; No. 50 Vienna Genesis; No. 55 Lindisfarne Gospels.

composite creature.def: An imaginary beast made of parts of different animals (and sometimes humans), usually with supernatural power.
composite creature.seen: No. 25 Lamassu; No. 24 Last judgment of Hu-Nefer (Ammit); No. 153 Chavín de Huántar.

conclave.def: The closed meeting in which the Catholic cardinals elect a new pope. Today it is held in the Sistine Chapel.
conclave.think: From the Latin for ‘with a key’: the cardinals are locked in until they decide.

Confucianism.def: A Chinese philosophy based on the teachings of Confucius (551 to 479 B.C.E.), stressing proper behavior, respect for elders and ancestors, loyalty to rulers, and education. It shaped government and family life in China and Korea.
Confucianism.think: A rulebook for being a good son, oﬀicial and citizen.
Confucianism.seen: No. 205 Portrait of Sin Sukju; No. 201 Travelers among Mountains and Streams (Neo-Confucian ideas).

consecration.def: A ceremony that makes a building or object sacred, setting it apart for religious use. Todai-ji’s Great Buddha was consecrated in 752 with an ‘eye-opening’ ceremony.

cosmology.def: A people’s picture of how the universe is arranged: heaven, earth, underworld, and how they connect. Many buildings and objects are maps of a cosmology.
cosmology.seen: No. 194 Funeral banner of Lady Dai; No. 198 Borobudur; No. 199 Angkor Wat; No. 7 Jade cong.

Counter-Reformation.def: The Catholic Church’s response to the Reformation, set out at the Council of Trent (1545 to 1563). It wanted art that was clear, emotional and dramatic to pull believers back to Catholicism. This fueled Baroque art.
Counter-Reformation.think: Also called the Catholic Reformation. The Church fighting back with spectacular art.
Counter-Reformation.seen: No. 82 Il Gesù; No. 85 Calling of Saint Matthew; No. 89 Ecstasy of Saint Teresa.

Coyolxauhqui.def: Aztec moon goddess who led an attack on her mother Coatlicue and was killed and cut apart by her brother Huitzilopochtli. A stone disk of her broken body lay at the foot of the Templo Mayor.

creation story.def: A myth explaining how the world, people or a clan came to be.
creation story.seen: No. 75 Sistine Chapel ceiling (Genesis); No. 164 Transformation mask; No. 234 Earth’s Creation.

crest.def: An inherited animal or ancestor emblem owned by a family or clan, shown on masks, poles and blankets, especially on the Northwest Coast. Only the owners may use it.
crest.think: Like a family coat of arms.

crook and flail.def: A shepherd’s hooked staff and a whip-like rod held crossed over the chest by Egyptian kings and by Osiris. They stand for royal power to guide and to punish.

cross.def: The chief symbol of Christianity, recalling the Crucifixion. It may be hidden in decoration, as on the Lindisfarne cross-carpet page.
cross.seen: No. 55 Lindisfarne Gospels (cross-carpet page); No. 79 Allegory of Law and Grace.

Crucifixion.def: The execution of Jesus by nailing him to a wooden cross, the central event of Christianity. Images range from calm and triumphant to bloody and painful.
Crucifixion.seen: No. 77 Isenheim altarpiece; No. 79 Allegory of Law and Grace; No. 63 Arena Chapel.

cult.def: In art history, simply the worship and rituals given to a particular god, saint or image, as in ‘cult statue’. It does not mean a strange sect.
cult.seen: No. 217 Female deity (kept in a cult house); No. 31 Temple of Minerva.

cypress.def: A tall, dark, flame-shaped evergreen tree. Around the Mediterranean it is planted in cemeteries and linked with death and eternity. Van Gogh’s cypress rises like a dark flame in The Starry Night.

Daoism.def: A Chinese philosophy and religion based on the Dao (‘the Way’), the natural flow of the universe. It values simplicity, harmony with nature and long life; Chinese landscape painting often expresses its ideas. Also spelled Taoism.
Daoism.think: Go with the flow of nature.
Daoism.seen: No. 201 Travelers among Mountains and Streams; No. 204 The David Vases (made for a Daoist temple).

darshan.def: In Hinduism, seeing and being seen by a god through its sacred image. The exchange of looks is itself a blessing, which is why images have large, open eyes and are paraded in processions.
darshan.seen: No. 200 Lakshmana Temple; No. 202 Shiva as Lord of Dance (carried in processions).

deity.seen: No. 202 Shiva as Lord of Dance; No. 216 Staff god; No. 217 Female deity.

devaraja.def: Sanskrit for ‘god-king’. A royal cult in the Khmer Empire that linked the king with a Hindu god, usually Shiva or Vishnu, so that royal temples were also the god’s palaces.

Devi.def: ‘The Goddess’: the great Hindu mother goddess, worshipped in many forms, gentle (Parvati, Lakshmi) or fierce (Durga, Kali).

dharma.def: In Buddhism, the Buddha’s teaching; in Hinduism, duty and the right order of the universe. In Buddhist art the dharma is shown as a wheel.
dharma.seen: No. 192 Great Stupa at Sanchi (wheel symbol).

dharma wheel.def: A wheel (dharmachakra) standing for the Buddha’s teaching, which he ‘set in motion’ with his first sermon. Early Buddhist art used it instead of showing the Buddha.

dharmachakra mudra.def: The ‘turning the wheel of the law’ gesture, with both hands at the chest forming circles with the fingers. It stands for the Buddha’s first sermon.

dhyana mudra.def: The meditation gesture: both hands rest in the lap, palms up, one on top of the other.

Dionysus.def: Greek god of wine, theater and wild celebration, called Bacchus by the Romans. His followers included frenzied women (maenads) and satyrs.
Dionysus.seen: No. 39 House of the Vettii (Death of Pentheus).

divination.def: Finding hidden knowledge or the future by ritual means, such as reading objects, casting lots or consulting spirits.
divination.think: Fortune-telling, but as a serious community practice.

divine kingship.def: The belief that a ruler is a god, descends from gods, or rules by a god’s choice. It explains why rulers are shown huge, calm, ageless and surrounded by sacred symbols.
divine kingship.seen: No. 13 Palette of King Narmer; No. 23 Tutankhamun’s coffin; No. 169 Wall plaque from Oba’s palace; No. 208 Jahangir Preferring a Sufi Shaikh to Kings.

dragon (Chinese).def: In China, a powerful and lucky creature linked to water, rain and the emperor, not an evil monster as in Europe.
dragon (Chinese).seen: No. 194 Funeral banner of Lady Dai; No. 204 The David Vases.

Dreaming.def: In Aboriginal Australian belief, the time and ongoing reality in which ancestral beings created the land, laws and living things. Aboriginal art often maps a person’s Dreaming and country.

duality.def: In Mesoamerican and many other beliefs, the idea that opposites (life and death, male and female, human and spirit) are linked halves of one whole.
duality.seen: No. 10 Tlatilco female figurine; No. 179 Reliquary figure (byeri).

eagle on a cactus.def: The founding sign of the Aztec capital: the god Huitzilopochtli told the Mexica to settle where they saw an eagle perched on a cactus. It is on the flag of Mexico today.
eagle on a cactus.seen: No. 81 Frontispiece of the Codex Mendoza.

enlightenment (Buddhist).def: In Buddhism, the moment of fully understanding the truth about life and being freed from desire and suffering. The Buddha reached it while meditating under the Bodhi tree.
enlightenment (Buddhist).think: Not the same as the European ‘Enlightenment’ of the 1700s.
enlightenment (Buddhist).seen: No. 184 Jowo Rinpoche (earth-touching gesture); No. 192 Great Stupa at Sanchi.

Entombment.def: The scene of Jesus’ body being carried to and laid in his tomb after the Crucifixion.

Eros.def: Greek god of desire, called Cupid by the Romans: a winged boy with a bow whose arrows make people fall in love.
Eros.seen: No. 43 Augustus of Prima Porta; No. 86 Henri IV Receives the Portrait; No. 101 The Swing (statue of Cupid).

Eucharist.def: The Christian ritual of sharing bread and wine in memory of the Last Supper. Catholics believe the bread and wine become Christ’s body and blood. Also called Holy Communion or the Mass.
Eucharist.seen: No. 51 San Vitale (Justinian holds the bread, Theodora the chalice); No. 73 Last Supper.

evangelist.def: One of the four writers of the Gospels: Matthew, Mark, Luke and John. Gospel books often begin each Gospel with a full-page ‘portrait’ of its evangelist writing.
evangelist.think: Today ‘evangelist’ can mean a preacher; in art history it almost always means one of these four men.
evangelist.seen: No. 55 Lindisfarne Gospels (St. Matthew, St. Luke).

evangelist symbols.def: Four creatures that stand for the four Gospel writers: a winged man or angel for Matthew, a lion for Mark, an ox or calf for Luke, and an eagle for John. They often surround Christ or appear next to each writer.
evangelist symbols.think: Memory trick: Man, Lion, Ox, Eagle go in Gospel order (Matthew, Mark, Luke, John).
evangelist symbols.seen: No. 55 Lindisfarne Gospels (St. Luke with his calf); No. 60 Chartres Cathedral (Royal Portal).

Exodus.def: The Bible story of the Israelites escaping slavery in Egypt, with the ten plagues and the parting of the Red Sea. Also the name of the second book of the Bible.
Exodus.seen: No. 64 Golden Haggadah (Plagues of Egypt, Scenes of Liberation).

fasces.def: A bundle of rods tied around an axe, carried in front of ancient Roman oﬀicials as a sign of their power. Houdon’s George Washington rests his hand on a fasces of 13 rods, one for each original state.

filial piety.def: The Confucian duty of children to respect, obey and care for their parents and honor their ancestors.
filial piety.seen: No. 205 Portrait of Sin Sukju (used in ancestral rites).

Five Pillars.def: The five basic duties of Islam: declaring faith in one God and Muhammad as his prophet, praying five times a day, giving to the poor, fasting in Ramadan, and making the hajj if possible.

frigate bird.def: A large seabird that appears on Torres Strait masks and other Pacific art, linked to clans, ancestors and seafaring.

Gaia.def: The Greek goddess who is the Earth itself, mother of the Giants.
Gaia.seen: No. 38 Great Altar of Zeus and Athena at Pergamon.

Gayumars.def: In the Shahnama, the first king of the world, who ruled from a mountaintop when people wore leopard skins and had not yet learned cooking or clothing.

Genesis.def: The first book of the Bible, with the creation of the world, Adam and Eve, Noah’s flood, and stories of Abraham, Isaac, Jacob and Rebecca.
Genesis.seen: No. 50 Vienna Genesis; No. 74 Adam and Eve; No. 75 Sistine Chapel ceiling.

Gigantomachy.def: The mythical battle between the Greek gods and the Giants. Greeks used it as a symbol of civilization (or their own side) defeating chaos and barbarians.
Gigantomachy.seen: No. 38 Great Altar of Zeus and Athena at Pergamon.

Good Shepherd.def: An early image of Jesus as a young shepherd carrying a sheep on his shoulders, based on his saying ‘I am the good shepherd’. Early Christians borrowed it from pagan Roman art.
Good Shepherd.think: It let early Christians show Christ without showing the Crucifixion.

Gospels.def: The four books of the New Testament (Matthew, Mark, Luke and John) that tell the life of Jesus. A ‘Gospel book’ is a hand-made copy of just these four books, often richly decorated.

grave good.def: An object buried with a dead person, such as pottery, weapons, jewelry or food, for use in the afterlife or to show the person’s status. Plural: grave goods.
grave good.seen: No. 5 Beaker with ibex motifs; No. 7 Jade cong; No. 53 Merovingian looped fibulae.

guardian figure.def: A fierce statue placed at a gate or around a sacred object to protect it. Examples range from Assyrian lamassu to Buddhist temple guardians to Fang byeri figures.
guardian figure.seen: No. 25 Lamassu; No. 197 Todai-ji (Nio guardians); No. 195 Longmen caves (guardians); No. 179 Reliquary figure (byeri).

hadith.def: Reports of what the Prophet Muhammad said and did, collected after his death. Some hadith warn against making images of living beings, which shaped Islamic religious art.

Haggadah.def: The book read aloud at the Passover seder meal, telling the story of the Exodus. Rich families commissioned illustrated copies.

hajj.def: The pilgrimage to Mecca that every Muslim who is able should make once in life. Pilgrims circle the Kaaba seven times counterclockwise.

halo.def: A ring or disc of light around a holy person’s head, showing their holiness or (for rulers) their godgiven power. Also called a nimbus. Christ’s halo often has a cross in it.
halo.think: A holy ‘glow’ drawn as a gold circle.
halo.seen: No. 51 San Vitale (Justinian and Theodora); No. 54 Theotokos icon; No. 63 Arena Chapel; No. 208 Jahangir Preferring a Sufi Shaikh to Kings.

hand of God.def: A hand reaching from the sky or a cloud, used to show God’s presence without showing God’s whole body.

Hathor.def: Egyptian goddess of love, music and motherhood, shown as a cow or a woman with cow ears or horns.

Hebrew Bible.def: The Jewish scriptures (the Tanakh), written mostly in Hebrew. Christians call it the Old Testament. Hebrew is read right to left, so Jewish manuscripts read right to left too.

Hera.def: Queen of the Greek gods, wife of Zeus, goddess of marriage. The Romans called her Juno; her symbol is the peacock.
Hera.seen: No. 86 Henri IV Receives the Portrait (as Juno).

Herakles.def: The greatest Greek hero, son of Zeus, famous for his strength and his twelve labors. The Romans called him Hercules; he wears a lion skin and carries a club.

Hinduism.def: The major religion of India, with many gods who are often seen as forms of one ultimate reality (Brahman). Key ideas include dharma, karma, rebirth, and devotion to a chosen god.
Hinduism.seen: No. 199 Angkor Wat; No. 200 Lakshmana Temple; No. 202 Shiva as Lord of Dance.

horned crown.def: A crown with stacked pairs of horns, worn only by gods in Mesopotamian art. It tells you the figure is divine, like Shamash on the Code of Hammurabi.

Horus.def: Egyptian sky god with a falcon head, son of Osiris. The living pharaoh was seen as Horus on earth.
Horus.seen: No. 13 Palette of King Narmer; No. 24 Last judgment of Hu-Nefer.

house altar.def: A small shrine or carved image set up in a private home for family worship. The relief of Akhenaton, Nefertiti and their daughters was a house altar honoring the royal family and the sun god Aten.
house altar.seen: No. 22 Akhenaton, Nefertiti, and three daughters.

huaca.def: In Andean belief, any sacred place or thing: a mountain, a spring, a carved rock, a mummy or a shrine full of spiritual power.
huaca.seen: No. 159 City of Cusco; No. 161 City of Machu Picchu.

hubris.def: Excessive pride that challenges the gods; in Greek myth it is always punished.

Huitzilopochtli.def: Aztec god of war and the sun and patron of the Mexica people. One of the two shrines on top of the Templo Mayor was his.

human sacrifice.def: Killing people as an offering to the gods. For the Mexica (Aztecs), sacrifice repaid the gods, who had sacrificed themselves to create the world, and kept the sun moving and the rains coming. The Templo Mayor was its center.

Hymen.def: The Greek and Roman god of marriage, shown as a winged young man with a torch.
Hymen.seen: No. 86 Henri IV Receives the Portrait of Marie de’ Medici.

icon.def: In Byzantine and Orthodox Christianity, a holy image of Christ, Mary or a saint, usually painted on a wooden panel. Believers pray before icons, believing the image is a window to the holy person.
icon.think: Today an ‘icon’ is a little picture on your phone; the original meaning is a sacred portrait.
icon.seen: No. 54 Virgin (Theotokos) and Child; No. 54 Theotokos and Child.

iconoclasm.def: The destruction of religious images, or a belief that such images are wrong. The Byzantine Empire banned and destroyed icons in 726 to 843 C.E.; Protestants smashed church images in the 1500s; the Taliban blew up the Bamiyan Buddhas in 2001.
iconoclasm.think: Literally ‘imagebreaking’. Someone who does it is an iconoclast.
iconoclasm.seen: No. 54 Theotokos icon (survived iconoclasm); No. 182 Bamiyan Buddha (destroyed 2001).

iconography.def: The meaning of the images and symbols in a work: who is shown, what the objects stand for, and what story is told. Also, the study of that meaning.
iconography.think: Decoding the picture’s symbols, like reading emoji.
iconography.seen: No. 66 Merode Altarpiece; No. 202 Shiva as Lord of Dance; No. 24 Last judgment of Hu-Nefer.

idol.def: A statue worshipped as a god. The word is often used as an insult by outsiders, so scholars usually prefer ‘cult image’ or ‘sacred image’.
idol.seen: No. 183 The Kaaba (cleared of idols); No. 123 Where Do We Come From? (blue idol).

increase ceremony.def: A ritual meant to make crops, animals or fish multiply and the community prosper.

inhumation.def: Burying a whole body, as opposed to cremating (burning) it. Romans shifted from cremation to inhumation in the 100s C.E., which created demand for carved sarcophagi.

initiation.def: A ritual that moves a person into a new stage of life or into a group, such as boys or girls becoming adults. Masks and ceremonies often mark it.
initiation.think: A graduation ceremony for life stages.
initiation.seen: No. 173 Female (Pwo) mask; No. 175 Bundu mask; No. 218 Buk mask.

intercessor.def: Someone who pleads with God on behalf of others. Christians pray to the Virgin Mary and the saints as intercessors.
intercessor.think: Like a friend who puts in a good word for you with the boss.

Inti.def: The Inka sun god, ancestor of the Inka ruler. His main temple was the Qorikancha in Cusco.
Inti.seen: No. 159 City of Cusco (Qorikancha); No. 161 City of Machu Picchu (Intihuatana).

Islam.def: The religion founded in Arabia in the 600s C.E. by the Prophet Muhammad, who Muslims believe received God’s final message, the Qur’an. A follower is a Muslim. Islam spread quickly from Spain to India.
Islam.seen: No. 183 The Kaaba; No. 185 Dome of the Rock; No. 187 Folio from a Qur’an.

Jataka tales.def: Stories of the Buddha’s earlier lives, before he became the Buddha, often as an animal or a generous prince. They teach Buddhist values and are carved on stupas.
Jataka tales.think: Fables with a moral, starring the Buddha in past lives.
Jataka tales.seen: No. 192 Great Stupa at Sanchi; No. 198 Borobudur.

Jesuits.def: The Society of Jesus, a Catholic religious order founded in 1540 by Ignatius of Loyola. Jesuits led the Counter-Reformation as teachers and missionaries around the world.
Jesuits.seen: No. 82 Il Gesù (the Jesuits’ main church).

Judaism.def: The religion of the Jewish people, based on the Hebrew Bible and God’s covenant with Abraham and Moses. Christianity and Islam both grew out of it.

Judith and Holofernes.def: A story from the Book of Judith: a Jewish widow saves her city by beheading the enemy general Holofernes. Old Master painters loved the subject.

ka.def: In Egyptian belief, a person’s life force or spiritual double, which lived on after death and needed a body or a statue to live in and food offerings to survive.
ka.think: A spiritual twin that needs a ‘home’ after you die.
ka.seen: No. 15 Seated scribe; No. 18 King Menkaura and queen; No. 17 Great Pyramids.

Kaaba.def: The cube-shaped shrine in Mecca, the holiest site in Islam. Muslims everywhere face it when they pray, and pilgrims walk around it seven times during the hajj. It is covered by a black cloth, the kiswa.

karesansui.def: A Japanese dry landscape garden made of rocks and raked gravel or sand, with little or no water or plants, used for Zen meditation.
karesansui.think: A garden that is meant to be looked at and thought about, not walked through.

karma.def: In Hinduism and Buddhism, the idea that your actions decide what happens to you in future lives. Good deeds bring a better rebirth.
karma.think: What goes around comes around, across lifetimes.

katsina.def: A spirit being of the Hopi and other Pueblo peoples who brings rain and blessings. Masked dancers embody katsinas, and carved katsina dolls teach children about them. Also spelled kachina.

lakshana.def: One of the special body marks that identify a Buddha: the ushnisha, the urna, long earlobes (from the heavy earrings he wore as a prince), and others.
lakshana.seen: No. 195 Longmen caves; No. 197 Todai-ji Great Buddha.

Lamb of God.def: A title for Jesus, who Christians say was sacrificed like a lamb to take away sins. In art a lamb, sometimes with a cross or banner, stands for Christ.
Lamb of God.seen: No. 79 Allegory of Law and Grace.

Lamentation.def: The scene right after the Crucifixion in which Mary and Jesus’ followers weep over his dead body. Artists use it to show intense grief.
Lamentation.think: ‘Lament’ means to cry out in sorrow.
Lamentation.seen: No. 63 Arena Chapel (Lamentation); No. 134 Memorial Sheet for Karl Liebknecht (borrows the composition).

Lanzón.def: A 15-foot carved granite pillar shaped like a lance, standing in a dark underground chamber at Chavín de Huántar, carved with a fanged, snake-haired god.

lararium.def: A household shrine in a Roman house where the family honored its guardian spirits, the Lares, with prayers and small offerings. The House of the Vettii has a painted one.

Last Judgment.def: The Christian belief that at the end of time Christ will judge everyone: the saved go up to heaven on his right, the damned go down to hell on his left. Big Last Judgment scenes often go over church doors or on the end wall, as a warning.
Last Judgment.think: Ancient Egypt had its own version: the weighing of the heart.
Last Judgment.seen: No. 58 SainteFoy (tympanum); No. 63 Arena Chapel (west wall); No. 75 Sistine Chapel (altar wall); No. 92 Woman Holding a Balance (painting on back wall).
Last Judgment.see: Apocalypse, weighing of the heart, Christ in Majesty.

Last Supper.def: Jesus’ final meal with his twelve apostles before his arrest. He announces that one of them (Judas) will betray him, and he shares bread and wine, which became the Christian rite of the Eucharist.

lily.def: A white flower that stands for purity in Christian art, especially Mary’s. It often appears in Annunciation scenes.

lingam.def: An upright, rounded pillar that stands for Shiva’s creative energy. It is the main object of worship in most Shiva temples.

lotus.def: A water flower that grows out of mud yet blooms clean, so in Buddhism and Hinduism it stands for purity and enlightenment. Buddhas and gods often sit or stand on lotus thrones.

Ma’at.def: The Egyptian idea of truth, justice and cosmic order, also a goddess with an ostrich feather on her head. The dead person’s heart is weighed against her feather.

Madonna.def: Italian for ‘my lady’. A name for the Virgin Mary, and for any painting or statue of her, usually holding the baby Jesus.
Madonna.seen: No. 71 Madonna and Child with Two Angels.

Mahayana.def: The ‘Great Vehicle’: the branch of Buddhism common in China, Korea, Japan and Tibet. It honors many Buddhas and bodhisattvas who help all beings toward enlightenment.

mana.def: In Polynesian belief, sacred power and prestige that can live in people (especially chiefs), objects and places. It can grow or be lost.
mana.think: Spiritual charge, like a battery of holiness and status.
mana.seen: No. 215 ʻAhu ʻula (feather cape); No. 214 Moai; No. 216 Staff god.

mandala.def: A diagram of the universe, usually a circle inside a square, used in Hindu and Buddhist meditation. Some temples are built as 3-D mandalas.
mandala.think: A map of the cosmos you meditate with.

Mandate of Heaven.def: The Chinese belief that heaven grants a ruler the right to rule as long as he rules justly; disasters and rebellion showed that the mandate was lost.

mandorla.def: An almond-shaped frame of light around the whole body of a holy figure, usually Christ or Mary. It is like a full-body halo.
mandorla.seen: No. 58 Sainte-Foy (tympanum); No. 60 Chartres Cathedral (Royal Portal); No. 95 Virgin of Guadalupe.

martyr.def: Someone killed for refusing to give up their faith. Early Christian martyrs became saints, and their bones became valued relics.

masquerade.def: A performance with masks, full costumes, music and dance, in which the masker becomes a spirit or character. The mask is only one part of the work.
masquerade.think: To understand an African mask, imagine it moving at night with drums, not hanging in a museum.
masquerade.seen: No. 173 Pwo mask; No. 174 Mblo; No. 175 Bundu mask; No. 178 Aka elephant mask.

Mass.def: The main Catholic worship service, centered on the Eucharist. Altarpieces stood behind the altar where the Mass was performed.
Mass.seen: No. 73 Last Supper; No. 51 San Vitale; No. 18 King Menkaura and queen; No. 129 The Kiss (Brancusi); No. 214 Moai on platform.

mater dolorosa.def: Latin for ‘sorrowful mother’. The Virgin Mary grieving over Christ’s suffering and death, a favorite late medieval devotional subject.

Mecca.def: The city in western Saudi Arabia where Muhammad was born and where the Kaaba stands. It is Islam’s holiest city.

meditation.def: Focusing and quieting the mind, a central practice in Buddhism and especially in Zen, which seeks enlightenment through direct experience. Zen gardens like Ryoan-ji are aids to quiet contemplation.
meditation.see: Zen, dhyana mudra, dry landscape garden.

memento mori.def: Latin for ‘remember that you will die’. An object or image, like a skull or rotting fruit, that reminds viewers that life is short.

menorah.def: A seven-branched lamp that stood in the ancient Temple in Jerusalem, a lasting symbol of Judaism. (A nine-branched version is used at Hanukkah.)

merit.def: In Buddhism, spiritual credit earned by good acts like paying for a temple or image. Rulers and donors sponsored Buddhist art partly to gain merit.
merit.seen: No. 195 Longmen caves; No. 184 Jowo Rinpoche (covered in donated gifts).

miracle.def: An event believed to be caused directly by God or a holy person, beyond nature’s laws.
miracle.seen: No. 95 Virgin of Guadalupe; No. 85 Calling of Saint Matthew.

missionary.def: A person sent to spread their religion to other peoples. Christian missionaries in the Americas, Africa and the Pacific changed local art, often destroying or hiding ‘pagan’ objects.
missionary.seen: No. 90 Angel with Arquebus; No. 216 Staff god; No. 218 Buk mask.

mithuna.def: An embracing, often erotic couple carved on Hindu temples, a sign of good fortune and of the union of the soul with the divine.

moksha.def: In Hinduism, final release from the cycle of rebirth.
moksha.seen: No. 202 Shiva as Lord of Dance (raised foot signals release).

monastery.def: A community where monks (or nuns, in a convent) live apart from the world to pray and work under strict rules. Medieval monasteries copied and decorated most books in Europe.
monastery.seen: No. 55 Lindisfarne Gospels; No. 54 Theotokos icon (Monastery of St. Catherine, Sinai); No. 99 Sor Juana (a nun in a convent).

monk.def: A man who has given up ordinary life to live in a religious community under vows of prayer, poverty and obedience. Christian, Buddhist and other religions all have monks.
monk.seen: No. 55 Lindisfarne Gospels; No. 61 Bible moralisée (monk dictating); No. 182 Bamiyan Buddha (monks’ caves).

monotheism.def: Belief in only one god, as in Judaism, Christianity and Islam, and briefly in Akhenaten’s Egypt.
monotheism.seen: No. 22 Akhenaton, Nefertiti, and three daughters; No. 185 Dome of the Rock.

Moses.def: The Hebrew prophet who led the Israelites out of Egypt and received the Ten Commandments (God’s law) on Mount Sinai.
Moses.think: In Christian art he stands for the Old Law.
Moses.seen: No. 64 Golden Haggadah; No. 79 Allegory of Law and Grace.

mosque.def: A Muslim building for communal prayer. Key parts: a wall facing Mecca (qibla) with a niche (mihrab), a pulpit (minbar), often a courtyard, and towers (minarets). ‘Masjid’ is the Arabic word.
mosque.seen: No. 56 Great Mosque of Córdoba; No. 84 Mosque of Selim II ; No. 168 Great Mosque of Djenné; No. 186 Great Mosque, Isfahan; No. 186 Great Mosque of Isfahan.

mosque lamp.def: A glass or metal hanging lamp used in mosques and shrines. It echoes a famous Qur’an verse comparing God’s light to a lamp.
mosque lamp.seen: No. 191 Ardabil Carpet (two lamps woven in).

Mount Meru.def: The sacred mountain at the center of the universe in Hindu and Buddhist belief. Temple towers in India and Southeast Asia are built to look like it.

mudra.def: A symbolic hand gesture in Buddhist and Hindu art. Each has a fixed meaning, so you can tell what a figure is ‘saying’ by its hands.
mudra.seen: No. 184 Jowo Rinpoche (earth-touching); No. 197 Todai-ji Great Buddha; No. 202 Shiva as Lord of Dance (do not fear).
mudra.see: abhaya mudra, bhumisparsha mudra, dhyana mudra, varada mudra.

muezzin.def: The person who calls Muslims to prayer five times a day, traditionally from a minaret.

Muhammad.def: The Prophet of Islam (c. 570 to 632 C.E.), born in Mecca. Muslims believe God revealed the Qur’an to him. He is usually not pictured in religious settings.
Muhammad.seen: No. 183 The Kaaba; No. 185 Dome of the Rock.

mummy.def: A dead body preserved by drying and wrapping, as the Egyptians did so the ka would have a body to return to.

mystery cult.def: An ancient religious group with secret rites revealed only to initiates, who were promised protection or a better afterlife. The Sanctuary of the Great Gods on Samothrace, where the Winged Victory stood, was the center of one.

mysticism.def: The pursuit of direct, personal union with God through prayer, vision or trance, beyond ordinary thinking.
mysticism.seen: No. 89 Ecstasy of Saint Teresa; No. 208 Jahangir Preferring a Sufi Shaikh to Kings; No. 239 The Crossing.

myth.def: A traditional story about gods, heroes or the origins of the world that explains how things came to be or what a people believes.
myth.seen: No. 72 Birth of Venus; No. 190 The Court of Gayumars; No. 157 Templo Mayor.

naga.def: A divine serpent in Hindu and Buddhist myth, often many-headed, linked to water and protection.
naga.seen: No. 199 Angkor (naga railings and the churning myth).
naga.see: serpent, Churning of the Ocean of Milk.

Narcissus.def: A beautiful youth in Greek myth who fell in love with his own reflection in a pool and wasted away. The source of the word ‘narcissism’.

naskh.def: A rounded, flowing, easy-to-read Arabic script that became the standard for copying the Qur’an and books from about the 900s on.
naskh.think: Kufic is blocky; naskh is cursive and readable.

Nataraja.def: ‘Lord of Dance’: Shiva dancing inside a ring of fire to destroy and re-create the universe. He holds a drum (creation) and a flame (destruction), raises a hand in ‘do not fear’, and steps on a dwarf of ignorance.
Nataraja.seen: No. 202 Shiva as Lord of Dance (Nataraja).

Nativity.def: The birth of Jesus in Bethlehem, usually shown with Mary, Joseph and the baby in a stable or cave, sometimes with shepherds or angels.

Nekhbet and Wadjet.def: The vulture goddess of Upper Egypt and the cobra goddess of Lower Egypt, protectors of the king. Together they stand for the united land.

nemes.def: The striped cloth headdress with side flaps worn by Egyptian kings.
nemes.seen: No. 17 Great Sphinx; No. 18 King Menkaura and queen; No. 23 Tutankhamun’s coﬀin.

Neo-Confucianism.def: A revived form of Confucianism from the Song dynasty onward that blended in ideas from Daoism and Buddhism about the order of the universe. It became the oﬀicial philosophy of Joseon Korea.
Neo-Confucianism.seen: No. 201 Travelers among Mountains and Streams; No. 205 Portrait of Sin Sukju.

New Testament.def: The second part of the Christian Bible: the four Gospels about Jesus’ life, letters by early followers, and the Book of Revelation about the end of the world.
New Testament.seen: No. 73 Last Supper; No. 85 Calling of Saint Matthew; No. 61 Bible moralisée.

Night Journey.def: Muslim belief that Muhammad was carried in one night from Mecca to Jerusalem, then rose to heaven from a rock there. The Dome of the Rock stands over that rock.
Night Journey.think: Also called the Isra and Mi’raj.

Nike.def: Greek goddess of victory, shown as a winged woman. (The sports brand is named after her.)
Nike.seen: No. 37 Winged Victory of Samothrace; No. 35 Acropolis (Temple of Athena Nike).

nimbus.def: Another word for halo: the circle of light behind a sacred person’s head.
nimbus.seen: No. 51 San Vitale; No. 54 Theotokos icon.

Nio.def: A pair of muscular, angry guardian kings who stand at the gates of Japanese Buddhist temples to frighten away evil. One has an open mouth, the other closed.
Nio.seen: No. 197 Todaiji (Great South Gate, by Unkei and Kaikei).

Niobe.def: A Greek queen who bragged that she had more children than the goddess Leto, so Leto’s twins, Apollo and Artemis, killed her children with arrows. A warning against pride.

nirvana.def: In Buddhism, the final state of peace in which desire and suffering are blown out and the cycle of rebirth ends. The Buddha’s death is called his parinirvana (‘complete nirvana’).

nkisi.def: Among the Kongo peoples, any object filled with spiritual power and medicines by a ritual specialist (nganga). The nkisi n’kondi is one powerful type. Plural: minkisi.
nkisi.see: nkisi n’kondi, nganga, power figure, bilongo.

offering.def: A gift given to a god, spirit or ancestor, such as food, flowers, precious objects or a statue.
offering.seen: No. 14 Votive figures from Eshnunna; No. 157 Templo Mayor (buried offerings); No. 184 Jowo Rinpoche.

Old Testament.def: The first, older part of the Christian Bible: the Hebrew scriptures, with stories like Adam and Eve, Noah, Abraham and Moses. Jews call these books the Tanakh or Hebrew Bible.
Old Testament.think: The ‘prequel’ to the Jesus story, from the Christian point of view.
Old Testament.seen: No. 50 Vienna Genesis; No. 64 Golden Haggadah; No. 75 Sistine Chapel ceiling.

Olokun.def: In Benin and Yoruba belief, the god of the sea and wealth. The Oba is linked to him through coral beads and river-leaf patterns.
Olokun.seen: No. 169 Wall plaque from Oba’s palace.

Olympian gods.def: The twelve major gods of ancient Greece, believed to live on Mount Olympus. The Romans adopted them under Latin names (Zeus became Jupiter, Athena became Minerva, and so on).
Olympian gods.seen: No. 35 Acropolis; No. 38 Great Altar of Zeus and Athena at Pergamon; No. 46 Pantheon.

oracle.def: A priest or priestess through whom a god was believed to answer questions about the future, or the sacred place where this happened. Chavín de Huántar may have housed an oracle at the Lanzón.

orant.def: A figure standing with both arms raised in prayer. It is common in early Christian catacomb paintings and stands for the praying soul.
orant.think: Picture someone with hands up as if shouting ‘hallelujah’.

orisha.def: A Yoruba god or spirit, such as Shango (thunder) or Ogun (iron). The orishas traveled with enslaved Africans to the Americas and live on in Santería and Candomblé.

Osiris.def: Egyptian god of the dead and the afterlife, who was killed and brought back to life. He is shown as a mummy wearing a tall white crown and holding the crook and flail. Dead kings became Osiris.
Osiris.seen: No. 23 Tutankhamun’s coﬀin; No. 24 Last judgment of Hu-Nefer.

Pachamama.def: ‘Mother Earth’ in Andean belief, goddess of the earth and fertility, still honored today.

Panathenaic Festival.def: A big religious festival in ancient Athens honoring Athena, with a procession up to the Acropolis to give her a new robe (peplos).
Panathenaic Festival.seen: No. 35 Acropolis (Parthenon frieze); No. 26 Athenian agora (procession route).

Pantocrator.def: Greek for ‘ruler of all’. A Byzantine image of Christ as stern ruler of the universe, seen from the chest up, holding a book and blessing with his right hand. It usually fills the central dome of a Byzantine church.
Pantocrator.think: the ‘boss’ portrait of Christ, looking down from the highest point of the church.

paradise garden.def: A garden divided into four parts by water channels, picturing the Qur’an’s description of paradise with its four rivers. The Persian name is charbagh (‘four gardens’).

Passion.def: The suffering of Jesus in his last days: his arrest, beating, crucifixion and death. ‘Passion’ here comes from the Latin for ‘suffering’, not ‘love’.
Passion.think: Passion scenes ask the viewer to feel Christ’s pain.
Passion.seen: No. 62 Röttgen Pietà; No. 77 Isenheim altarpiece; No. 78 Entombment of Christ.

Passover.def: A Jewish holiday remembering how God freed the Israelites from slavery in Egypt, led by Moses. Families retell the story at a ritual meal called the seder.
