personification.def: Showing an idea, place or quality as a person, such as Liberty as a woman or France as a woman in armor.
personification.think: Turning a concept into a character.
personification.seen: No. 108 Liberty Leading the People; No. 86 Henri IV Receives the Portrait (France); No. 63 Arena Chapel (virtues and vices); No. 37 Winged Victory of Samothrace.

pharaoh.def: The king of ancient Egypt, believed to be a living god, the earthly form of Horus. Pharaohs are shown idealized, calm and young forever.
pharaoh.seen: No. 13 Palette of King Narmer; No. 18 King Menkaura and queen; No. 22 Akhenaton, Nefertiti, and three daughters; No. 23 Tutankhamun’s coﬀin.

phoenix.def: A mythical bird. In China it is a sign of peace, virtue and the empress, often paired with the dragon; in the West it is reborn from its own ashes.

Phrygian cap.def: A soft, floppy cap with the tip bent forward, worn by freed slaves in ancient Rome. It became the symbol of liberty in the French and American Revolutions.

Pietà.def: Italian for ‘pity’. An image of the Virgin Mary alone holding the dead body of Jesus across her lap. It is a close-up, private version of the Lamentation.

pilgrimage.def: A journey to a holy place for religious reasons. Christian pilgrims walked to churches with famous relics; Muslims make the hajj to Mecca; Buddhists travel to stupas and sacred images.
pilgrimage.seen: No. 58 Sainte-Foy; No. 60 Chartres Cathedral; No. 183 The Kaaba; No. 192 Great Stupa at Sanchi.

polytheism.def: Belief in many gods, as in ancient Egypt, Greece, Rome, the Aztec Empire and Hinduism.
polytheism.seen: No. 20 Temple of Amun-Re; No. 46 Pantheon; No. 157 Templo Mayor.

power figure.def: A figure that holds spiritual power gathered by a ritual specialist, used to protect, heal, seal oaths or punish wrongdoers. The Kongo nkisi n’kondi is the best-known example.

prophet.def: A person believed to speak for God and to foretell the future. Hebrew prophets like Isaiah appear in Christian art; Muslims call Muhammad the final prophet.
prophet.seen: No. 75 Sistine Chapel ceiling; No. 185 Dome of the Rock.

Protestant.def: A Christian who belongs to a church that came out of the Reformation, such as Lutherans and Calvinists. Protestant regions like the Dutch Republic made fewer church paintings and more portraits, landscapes and still lifes for homes.
Protestant.seen: No. 79 Allegory of Law and Grace (Lutheran); No. 92 Woman Holding a Balance; No. 96 Fruit and Insects.

puja.def: Hindu worship: offering a god’s image flowers, food, incense, light and prayer, treating it as an honored guest.
puja.seen: No. 200 Lakshmana Temple; No. 202 Shiva as Lord of Dance.

Pure Land.def: A Buddhist paradise, especially Amida Buddha’s Western Paradise. Pure Land Buddhism, very popular in Japan, teaches that faith in Amida brings rebirth there.

putto.def: A chubby, naked baby boy, often with wings, in European art. The plural is putti. They can be cupids or baby angels.
putto.seen: No. 208 Jahangir Preferring a Sufi Shaikh to Kings; No. 101 The Swing.

quetzal.def: A Central American bird with long, shimmering green tail feathers, which were more precious than gold to the Aztecs and signaled rank and divinity.

Quetzalcoatl.def: ‘Feathered Serpent’: a major Mesoamerican god of wind, learning and priests, worshipped from Teotihuacan to the Aztecs.

Qur’an.def: The holy book of Islam, believed by Muslims to be the exact words of God given to Muhammad in Arabic. Because the words are sacred, writing them beautifully (calligraphy) became the highest Islamic art. Also spelled Koran.
Qur’an.seen: No. 187 Folio from a Qur’an; No. 185 Dome of the Rock (inscriptions); No. 209 Taj Mahal (inscriptions); No. 183 Kaaba (kiswa).

Ra.def: Egyptian sun god, also spelled Re, who sails across the sky by day. He merged with other gods, as in Amun-Re.

Reformation.def: The 1500s movement, started by Martin Luther in 1517, that broke away from the Catholic Church and created Protestant churches. Protestants stressed the Bible and faith over images, saints and relics, so many churches were stripped of art.
Reformation.think: A split in Western Christianity that changed what art was made in the north.
Reformation.seen: No. 79 Allegory of Law and Grace.

relic.def: A holy object: part of a saint’s body (bones, hair) or something they touched (clothing). People believed relics could heal and protect, so churches that owned them drew crowds of pilgrims. Buddhists also honor relics of the Buddha.
relic.think: Like a celebrity’s belongings, but believed to have miraculous power.
relic.seen: No. 58 SainteFoy; No. 60 Chartres Cathedral (the Virgin’s tunic); No. 192 Great Stupa at Sanchi.

reliquary.def: A container made to hold relics, often of gold and jewels, sometimes shaped like the body part or person inside. Fang byeri figures guard boxes of ancestors’ bones in a similar way.
reliquary.think: A treasure box for holy remains.
reliquary.seen: No. 58 Reliquary statue of SainteFoy; No. 179 Reliquary figure (byeri); No. 58 Reliquary of Sainte-Foy.

Resurrection.def: Christianity’s belief that Jesus rose from the dead three days after he died. In art he often bursts from the tomb surrounded by light.
Resurrection.think: Easter is the holiday that celebrates it.

sacrament.def: A holy ritual of the Church that Christians believe gives God’s grace, such as baptism, the Eucharist and marriage. Catholics count seven sacraments; most Protestants count two.
sacrament.seen: No. 51 San Vitale; No. 188 Basin (Baptistère de St. Louis), later used for royal baptisms.

sacred mountain.def: A mountain believed to be holy or to connect earth and heaven. Pyramids, ziggurats, stupas and temple towers often imitate one.
sacred mountain.seen: No. 157 Templo Mayor; No. 161 City of Machu Picchu; No. 199 Angkor Wat.
sacred mountain.see: Mount Meru, temple mountain, axis mundi.

sacrifice.def: Offering something valuable, such as an animal, food, one’s own blood or even a human life, to a god. Mesoamerican religions held that the gods needed blood to keep the universe running.
sacrifice.seen: No. 155 Yaxchilán; No. 157 Templo Mayor; No. 193 Terra cotta warriors (replaced human sacrifice).

saint.def: A person the Church honors as especially holy, usually because of a holy life or death as a martyr. Saints are shown with halos and with objects (attributes) that identify them.
saint.think: Think of saints as Christianity’s heroes, each with a signature prop.
saint.seen: No. 54 Saints Theodore and George; No. 58 Sainte-Foy; No. 89 Ecstasy of Saint Teresa; No. 85 Calling of Saint Matthew.

salat.def: The ritual prayer Muslims perform five times a day, facing Mecca. Mosques are designed around it.
salat.seen: No. 56 Great Mosque of Córdoba; No. 186 Great Mosque, Isfahan.

samsara.def: In Hinduism and Buddhism, the endless cycle of birth, death and rebirth that a soul is trapped in until it is released.
samsara.think: A loop you are trying to get out of.
samsara.seen: No. 198 Borobudur; No. 202 Shiva as Lord of Dance.

Santería.def: An Afro-Cuban religion blending Yoruba orisha worship with Catholic saints, created by enslaved Africans in Cuba.

scriptorium.def: The room in a monastery where monks copied and decorated books by hand.
scriptorium.think: A medieval copy shop and design studio.
scriptorium.seen: No. 55 Lindisfarne Gospels; No. 61 Bible moralisée (scribe at work).

seder.def: The Jewish ritual meal held on the first night (or two) of Passover, during which the Haggadah is read to retell the Exodus from Egypt.

serpent.def: A snake, which carries many meanings across cultures: danger and sin (Eden), rebirth (it sheds its skin), water, or a link between worlds.
serpent.seen: No. 156 Great Serpent Mound; No. 155 Yaxchilán; No. 74 Adam and Eve; No. 199 Angkor (naga).

serpopard.def: A modern name for the creature on the Narmer Palette that is part serpent (a long snaky neck) and part leopard (the body). Two with intertwined necks form the circle in the palette’s center.

Shahnama.def: The ‘Book of Kings’, the national epic poem of Persia, written by Ferdowsi around 1010 C.E. It tells the myths and history of Persian kings, and rulers commissioned lavish illustrated copies to claim Persian kingship.
Shahnama.think: Persia’s version of a national legend book, like the Iliad for Greece.
Shahnama.seen: No. 189 Bahram Gur Fights the Karg; No. 190 The Court of Gayumars.

Shakyamuni.def: ‘Sage of the Shakya clan’: a name for the historical Buddha, Siddhartha Gautama, a prince who gave up his palace life to seek the end of suffering.

shaman.def: A religious specialist who enters a trance to travel to the spirit world, heal, or talk with spirits, sometimes taking on animal form. Shamanism is linked to many prehistoric and Indigenous works.
shaman.seen: No. 1 Apollo 11 Stones; No. 153 Chavín de Huántar; No. 196 Gold and jade crown; No. 10 Tlatilco female figurine.

Shamash.def: The Mesopotamian sun god and god of justice. On the stele of Hammurabi’s laws, the king receives authority from him.

shaykh.def: An Arabic title for a respected elder, religious scholar or Sufi master. Also spelled sheikh or shaikh.
shaykh.seen: No. 208 Jahangir Preferring a Sufi Shaikh to Kings; No. 191 Ardabil Carpet (shrine of Shaykh Safi al-Din).

Shinto.def: Japan’s native religion, honoring kami: spirits found in nature, places and ancestors. It coexists with Buddhism in Japan.

Shiva.def: One of the main Hindu gods, the destroyer and re-creator of the universe. He is often shown with a third eye, matted hair, a snake and a trident, and is worshipped as the lingam.
Shiva.seen: No. 202 Shiva as Lord of Dance (Nataraja).

shrine.def: A holy place or container for a god, saint, relic or sacred image, from a tiny household altar to a whole building.
shrine.seen: No. 176 Ikenga; No. 185 Dome of the Rock; No. 191 Ardabil Carpet (for a shrine); No. 22 Akhenaton household altar.

sibyl.def: A female prophet of ancient Greece and Rome. Christians believed some sibyls predicted Christ’s coming, so they appear beside Hebrew prophets in Christian art.

sipapu.def: A small hole in the floor of a kiva marking the place where Pueblo ancestors emerged into this world.

solstice.def: The longest or shortest day of the year. Many ancient monuments line up with the solstice sunrise or sunset.
solstice.seen: No. 8 Stonehenge; No. 156 Great Serpent Mound; No. 161 Machu Picchu.

Son of Heaven.def: The title of the Chinese emperor, who was believed to rule by the Mandate of Heaven as the link between heaven and earth. Imperial palaces placed him at the symbolic center of the world.

spirit spouse.def: In Baule belief, a spirit husband or wife from the other world who can cause trouble in one’s life. A diviner may advise carving a figure of the spirit spouse and caring for it.

spiritual double.def: An object believed to share a person’s spirit, so that it can stand in for them. The Kuba ndop figure was a king’s spiritual double.
spiritual double.seen: No. 171 Ndop of King Mishe miShyaang maMbul.

Sufism.def: The mystical side of Islam, seeking a direct, loving experience of God through poetry, music, dance and meditation. A Sufi master is called a shaykh. The Safavid dynasty began as a Sufi order.
Sufism.seen: No. 208 Jahangir Preferring a Sufi Shaikh to Kings; No. 191 Ardabil Carpet (for a Sufi shrine).

Sun Dance.def: A major summer ceremony of many Plains peoples involving fasting, dance and sacrifice for the renewal of the community. The U.S. government banned it in the late 1800s.

sun (symbol).def: Across cultures the sun stands for life, kingship and the divine: the Aten, Inti, the Mughal emperor’s halo, Mao as the ‘sun’ of China.
sun (symbol).seen: No. 22 Akhenaton household altar; No. 159 City of Cusco; No. 208 Jahangir Preferring a Sufi Shaikh to Kings; No. 250 Sunflower Seeds.

sutra.def: A sacred text recording the teachings of the Buddha (or, in Hinduism, short teachings). Copying sutras was a way to earn merit.

symbol.def: A thing that stands for something else, such as a lily for purity or a crown for kingship.
symbol.seen: No. 66 Merode Altarpiece; No. 68 The Arnolfini Portrait.

synagogue.def: A Jewish house of prayer and study. Its focus is the ark holding the Torah scrolls.

taotie.def: A Chinese mask-like monster face, with big eyes and seen straight on, found on Shang dynasty bronzes. Its meaning is uncertain. Some scholars see the faces on Liangzhu jade cong as its ancestor.

tapu.def: In Polynesian belief, sacred and restricted: things or people with strong mana that must not be touched or approached casually. The English word ‘taboo’ comes from it.

tawaf.def: The ritual of walking seven times counterclockwise around the Kaaba during the hajj and other pilgrimages to Mecca.

Temple Mount.def: The hill in Jerusalem where the ancient Jewish Temple stood. Muslims call it the Noble Sanctuary and built the Dome of the Rock on it, over the rock linked to Abraham and Muhammad’s Night Journey.
Temple Mount.think: One of the most contested pieces of land on Earth.

the Fall.def: The Bible story in which Adam and Eve disobey God by eating the forbidden fruit and are thrown out of the Garden of Eden. Christians call this the origin of sin and death.
the Fall.seen: No. 74 Adam and Eve (Dürer); No. 75 Sistine Chapel ceiling; No. 79 Allegory of Law and Grace.

Theosophy.def: A spiritual movement founded in 1875 that mixed Eastern and Western religions and taught that a hidden spiritual reality lies behind the physical world. It inspired Kandinsky’s and Mondrian’s move into abstraction.

Theotokos.def: Greek for ‘Godbearer’ or ‘Mother of God’. The Byzantine title for the Virgin Mary, used for icons of her with the Christ child.
Theotokos.seen: No. 54 Virgin (Theotokos) and Child between Saints Theodore and George.

Theravada.def: ‘Way of the Elders’: the older branch of Buddhism, common in Sri Lanka, Thailand and Myanmar, focused on the historical Buddha and on monks seeking their own enlightenment.

therianthrope.def: A being that is part human and part animal, often a shaman in transformation or a god.
therianthrope.seen: No. 1 Apollo 11 Stones; No. 4 Running horned woman; No. 24 Last judgment of Hu-Nefer (animal-headed gods).

theriomorphic.def: Having the form of an animal, especially for a god or spirit.
theriomorphic.seen: No. 3 Camelid sacrum in the shape of a canine; No. 9 The Ambum Stone.

Thoth.def: Ibis-headed Egyptian god of writing and wisdom, who records the result of the weighing of the heart.

thuluth.def: A large, elegant, curving Arabic script used for grand inscriptions on buildings.
thuluth.seen: No. 209 Taj Mahal (Qur’anic inscriptions around the arches).

tlacuilo.def: An Aztec painter-scribe who wrote by painting pictures in codices.

Tlaloc.def: Aztec god of rain, water and farming, shown with goggle eyes and fangs. He shared the top of the Templo Mayor with Huitzilopochtli.

Torah.def: The first five books of the Hebrew Bible, believed to be God’s law given to Moses. It is handwritten on a scroll and kept in an ark (cabinet) in the synagogue.
Torah.think: The most sacred object in a synagogue.

totem.def: An animal, plant or natural object that a clan or family claims as its spiritual ancestor or emblem.
totem.think: A family mascot with sacred meaning.

transformation.def: A change from one being into another, such as a human into an animal or ancestor, a common theme in shamanic and masking art.
transformation.seen: No. 164 Transformation mask; No. 153 Chavín de Huántar; No. 10 Tlatilco female figurine.

trimurti.def: The Hindu trio of Brahma the creator, Vishnu the preserver and Shiva the destroyer.

Trinity.def: The Christian belief that one God exists as three persons: the Father, the Son (Jesus) and the Holy Spirit (often shown as a dove).
Trinity.think: Three-in-one: like water, ice and steam being the same substance.
Trinity.seen: No. 88 San Carlo alle Quattro Fontane (built for the Trinitarian order).

trophy head.def: A head, or an image of one, taken from an enemy as proof of victory and power. Some Igbo ikenga figures hold one, symbolizing success.

typology.def: A way of reading the Bible in which an Old Testament event is seen as a preview of a New Testament event. For example, Abraham’s near-sacrifice of his son Isaac ‘foreshadows’ God’s sacrifice of Jesus.
typology.think: Like a movie that plants hints early that pay off later.
typology.seen: No. 51 San Vitale (Abraham and Melchizedek scenes near the altar); No. 61 Bible moralisée; No. 79 Allegory of Law and Grace.

underworld.def: The world of the dead, usually imagined below the earth.
underworld.seen: No. 194 Funeral banner of Lady Dai; No. 24 Last judgment of Hu-Nefer.

urna.def: A dot or curl of hair between the Buddha’s eyebrows, a sign of spiritual insight. It is one of the marks of a Buddha.

ushnisha.def: The bump on top of the Buddha’s head, a sign of his expanded wisdom. It is one of the fixed marks (lakshanas) of a Buddha.
ushnisha.seen: No. 195 Longmen caves (Vairocana); No. 197 Todai-ji Great Buddha.

Vairocana.def: The ‘Cosmic Buddha’, a Buddha of light who is the center of the universe in some Mahayana schools. Colossal Vairocana statues were made under imperial sponsorship.
Vairocana.seen: No. 195 Longmen caves (Fengxian Temple); No. 197 Todai-ji (Great Buddha).

Vajrayana.def: Tibetan or esoteric Buddhism, which adds rituals, chants, mandalas and many deities to reach enlightenment faster.

vanitas.def: A type of still life, popular in the Dutch Republic, whose objects (skulls, wilting flowers, decaying fruit, hourglasses) warn that earthly pleasures and life itself are brief.
vanitas.think: From the Bible: ‘vanity of vanities, all is vanity’.
vanitas.seen: No. 96 Fruit and Insects; No. 92 Woman Holding a Balance (related ideas).

varada mudra.def: The gift-giving gesture: hand lowered, palm facing out, offering blessings or wishes granted.

Venus pudica.def: ‘Modest Venus’: a pose in which the nude goddess covers herself with her hands. It comes from ancient Greek statues.

Virgin and Child.def: An image of Mary holding the baby Jesus. One of the most repeated subjects in Christian art, it stresses that God became a real human child.
Virgin and Child.seen: No. 48 Catacomb of Priscilla; No. 54 Virgin (Theotokos) and Child; No. 71 Madonna and Child with Two Angels.

Virgin Mary.def: The mother of Jesus, the most important woman in Christian art. Christians call her the Virgin because they believe she conceived Jesus miraculously. She is usually dressed in blue.
Virgin Mary.think: Also called Madonna, Our Lady, or Theotokos.
Virgin Mary.seen: No. 54 Virgin (Theotokos) and Child; No. 66 Merode Altarpiece; No. 62 Röttgen Pietà; No. 95 Virgin of Guadalupe.
Virgin Mary.see: Madonna, Theotokos, Virgin and Child, Annunciation.

Virgin of Guadalupe.def: A vision of the Virgin Mary that appeared to Juan Diego, an Indigenous man in Mexico, in 1531, leaving her image on his cloak. She became the patron of Mexico and a symbol of Mexican identity.
Virgin of Guadalupe.seen: No. 95 The Virgin of Guadalupe (Miguel González).

virtues and vices.def: Good qualities (like justice, hope, charity) and bad qualities (like envy, anger, despair) shown as people. Medieval artists often lined them up as opposites.
virtues and vices.seen: No. 63 Arena Chapel (grisaille figures on lower walls).

Vishnu.def: One of the main Hindu gods, the preserver who keeps the universe in order. He comes down to earth in different forms (avatars), such as Rama and Krishna, when the world needs saving.
Vishnu.seen: No. 199 Angkor Wat; No. 200 Lakshmana Temple.
Vishnu.see: avatar, Hinduism, Churning of the Ocean of Milk.

vision.def: A religious experience of seeing a sacred being or event, often shown in art as rays of light, clouds or a figure appearing.
vision.seen: No. 89 Ecstasy of Saint Teresa; No. 155 Yaxchilán (vision serpent).

vision serpent.def: A giant snake in Maya art from whose mouth an ancestor or god appears, called up through bloodletting rituals.

weighing of the heart.def: The Egyptian judgment after death: the heart is weighed against the feather of Ma’at. A light heart (a good life) wins eternal life with Osiris; a heavy one is eaten by Ammit.

yakshi.def: A female nature spirit of fertility in Indian art, often shown as a curvy woman clinging to a tree. Yakshis decorate Buddhist and Hindu monuments.
yakshi.seen: No. 192 Great Stupa at Sanchi (torana brackets).

yin and yang.def: The Chinese idea that the universe is made of two opposite but connected forces: yin (dark, soft, female, cool) and yang (bright, hard, male, warm). Balance between them brings harmony.

Zen.def: A Japanese school of Buddhism (Chan in Chinese) that stresses meditation, simplicity and sudden insight over texts and rituals. Zen shaped Japanese gardens, ink painting and the tea ceremony.

Zephyr.def: The Greek god of the gentle west wind, often shown as a winged youth puﬀing air.

Zeus.def: King of the Greek gods, god of the sky and thunder. The Romans called him Jupiter. He carries a thunderbolt and often appears with an eagle.
Zeus.seen: No. 38 Great Altar of Zeus and Athena at Pergamon; No. 86 Henri IV Receives the Portrait (as Jupiter).

Zoroastrianism.def: The ancient Persian religion founded by the prophet Zoroaster, built around a struggle between good (Ahura Mazda) and evil, with fire as a sacred symbol.
Zoroastrianism.see: Ahura Mazda, Achaemenid. 8 Cultures, people and places Names of peoples, rulers, places and culture-specific ideas that the 250 works depend on.

Aboriginal Australians.def: The Indigenous peoples of Australia, with art and ceremony going back tens of thousands of years, tied to ancestral country and the Dreaming.

ʻahu ʻula.def: A Hawaiian feather cape or cloak worn by high chiefs, made of thousands of tiny red and yellow bird feathers tied to a net. It carried mana and served as spiritual protection.
ʻahu ʻula.seen: No. 215 ʻAhu ʻula (feather cape); No. 215 ‘Ahu ‘ula (feather cape).

al-Andalus.def: The Arabic name for the parts of Spain and Portugal under Muslim rule (711 to 1492), a meeting place of Muslim, Christian and Jewish cultures.
al-Andalus.seen: No. 56 Great Mosque of Córdoba; No. 57 Pyxis of al-Mughira; No. 65 Alhambra.

aliʻi.def: The chiefly ruling class of traditional Hawaiian society. Aliʻi held both political and sacred power, and only they could wear the redand-yellow feather capes and cloaks called ʻahu ʻula.
aliʻi.see: ʻahu ʻula, mana, feather cape, Hawaiʻi.

amanteca.def: Aztec professional featherworkers who made headdresses, shields and garments from tropical feathers.

Amarna.def: The capital built by the pharaoh Akhenaten for the sun god Aten, and the name for the unusual, relaxed art style of his reign.
Amarna.seen: No. 22 Akhenaton, Nefertiti, and three daughters.

Ancestral Puebloan.def: The ancient peoples of the Four Corners region of the U.S. Southwest (c. 100 to 1600 C.E.), builders of cliff dwellings, ancestors of today’s Pueblo peoples. Older books call them Anasazi.

ancien régime.def: ‘Old order’: French society under kings and aristocrats before the Revolution of 1789.
ancien régime.seen: No. 101 The Swing (Fragonard); No. 244 The Swing (after Fragonard).

Andes.def: The mountain range along western South America, home of the Chavín, Inka and other civilizations.
Andes.seen: No. 153 Chavín de Huántar; No. 159 City of Cusco; No. 161 Machu Picchu.

Angkor.def: The capital of the Khmer Empire in Cambodia, with Angkor Wat (Hindu) and Angkor Thom (Buddhist).
Angkor.seen: No. 199 Angkor Wat and Angkor Thom.

Anmatyerre.def: An Aboriginal people of central Australia; Emily Kame Kngwarreye was an Anmatyerre elder.

Asante.def: A powerful kingdom and people of Ghana, rich from gold. Also spelled Ashanti. Their king is the Asantehene, and the Golden Stool is the soul of the nation.

Asantehene.def: The title of the Asante king.

Ashoka.def: A Mauryan emperor (reigned c. 268 to 232 B.C.E.) who turned to Buddhism after a bloody war and spread it by building stupas and pillars.

Asmat.def: A people of southwest New Guinea who carve tall bisj poles to honor the dead and call for revenge.

Assyria.def: A warlike empire of northern Mesopotamia (peak c. 900 to 612 B.C.E.) whose palaces had giant guardian figures and relief carvings.

atoll.def: A ring-shaped coral island, or a ring of small islets, surrounding a lagoon. Atolls are common in Micronesia and Polynesia.
atoll.think: A coral doughnut in the ocean.

aurochs.def: A huge wild ox, the ancestor of modern cattle, that lived across Europe until the last one died in 1627. The giant bulls painted at Lascaux are aurochs.
aurochs.seen: No. 2 Great Hall of the Bulls.

Austronesian.def: A huge language family, and the seafaring peoples who spoke it, who spread from Taiwan through Southeast Asia and across the Pacific to Madagascar and Rapa Nui. The Lapita people were early Austronesian voyagers.

Babylon.def: An ancient city of Mesopotamia, capital of King Hammurabi (c. 1792 to 1750 B.C.E.).

Bamileke.def: A people of the grasslands of western Cameroon, known for beaded masks and royal arts.

Baule.def: A people of Côte d’Ivoire known for portrait masks and spirit spouse figures.

beadwork.def: Decoration made by sewing glass or shell beads onto cloth or leather. Glass trade beads from Europe became a major art form for Native North American and African artists.
beadwork.seen: No. 163 Bandolier bag; No. 178 Aka elephant mask; No. 177 Lukasa; No. 177 Lukasa (memory board).

Benin Bronzes.def: The thousands of brass plaques, heads and other objects looted from the royal palace of Benin by British soldiers in 1897 and scattered to museums worldwide. Some are now being returned.
Benin Bronzes.think: Mostly brass, not bronze, despite the name.
Benin Bronzes.seen: No. 169 Wall plaque, from Oba’s palace.

Benin (kingdom).def: A West African kingdom in today’s southern Nigeria (not the modern country called Benin), ruled by the Oba. Its brass casters made plaques and heads for the royal palace. British troops looted it in 1897.
Benin (kingdom).seen: No. 169 Wall plaque, from Oba’s palace.

bilongo.def: The medicines (earth, plants, bones and other powerful materials) packed into a Kongo nkisi to give it power, often sealed behind a mirror.

bisj pole.def: A tall Asmat memorial pole carved from a mangrove tree, with stacked ancestor figures, made for a feast honoring the recently dead.

Borobudur.def: The giant Buddhist monument in Java, Indonesia, built as a stepped mountain and mandala that pilgrims climb.

bundu.def: Another name for the Sande society and its sowei helmet mask.

bwami.def: A Lega society with many ranks that men and women climb through by learning moral teachings, taught with small ivory and wood figures and masks.

byeri.def: A Fang ancestor cult and the carved guardian figure placed on top of a bark box holding ancestors’ bones. Its calm, balanced forms deeply influenced European modern artists.

Byzantine Empire.def: The eastern half of the Roman Empire, which lasted until 1453, Christian and Greek-speaking, with its capital at Constantinople. Its art is famous for gold mosaics and icons.
Byzantine Empire.seen: No. 51 San Vitale; No. 52 Hagia Sophia; No. 54 Theotokos icon.

caliph.def: ‘Successor’: the political and religious leader of the Muslim community after Muhammad. The realm is a caliphate.
caliph.seen: No. 56 Great Mosque of Córdoba; No. 57 Pyxis of al-Mughira; No. 185 Dome of the Rock.

camelid.def: The animal family of camels and their South American relatives: llamas, alpacas, vicuñas and guanacos. The Tequixquiac sacrum comes from an extinct camelid.
camelid.seen: No. 3 Camelid sacrum in the shape of a canine.

casta.def: The Spanish colonial system of ranking people by their mix of Spanish, Indigenous and African ancestry, and the paintings that illustrated it as sets of family portraits.
casta.think: A colonial sorting chart turned into paintings.
casta.seen: No. 97 Spaniard and Indian Produce a Mestizo.

chicha.def: Corn beer brewed across the Andes, central to Inka feasts, offerings and politics. Rulers built loyalty by hosting huge feasts where chicha flowed.

Chilkat.def: A Tlingit weaving style for ceremonial robes of mountain-goat wool and cedar bark, with formline crest designs and long fringes.

chiton.def: A light, long tunic of linen or wool worn by ancient Greek women and men, falling in many fine folds. Sculptors loved carving its rippling cloth.

Chokwe.def: A people of Angola, the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Zambia, known for the pwo mask.

clan.def: A large family group that traces descent from a shared ancestor, often owning particular stories, crests, designs and lands.
clan.seen: No. 164 Transformation mask; No. 222 Malagan display; No. 218 Buk (mask).

Constantinople.def: The capital of the Byzantine Empire, founded on the old city of Byzantium in 330 C.E., later the Ottoman capital, now Istanbul.

contour rivalry.def: A Chavín carving trick in which lines can be read as two or more images at once, depending on how you look.

Country.def: For Aboriginal Australians, Country means the ancestral land a person belongs to and is responsible for, including its plants, animals, water, spirits and Dreaming stories. Painting it is a duty, not just a landscape.

creole.def: In colonial Spanish America, a person of Spanish descent born in the Americas (criollo). Creoles developed a proud local identity separate from Spain.
creole.seen: No. 95 Virgin of Guadalupe; No. 99 Portrait of Sor Juana.

criollo.def: A person of Spanish descent born in the Americas during the colonial period. Criollos ranked below Spanish-born people but above mixed-race people, and many adopted the Virgin of Guadalupe as a symbol of their own identity.
criollo.seen: No. 95 The Virgin of Guadalupe; No. 97 Spaniard and Indian Produce a Mestizo; No. 99 Portrait of Sor Juana.

cuneiform.def: The writing of ancient Mesopotamia, made of wedge-shaped marks pressed into clay with a reed or carved into stone. It was used for about 3,000 years.
cuneiform.seen: No. 19 Code of Hammurabi; No. 25 Lamassu.

Cusco.def: The Inka capital in the Peruvian highlands, said to be laid out in the shape of a puma. Also spelled Cuzco.

Cuzco School.def: Painters in colonial Cusco and the Andes who made Catholic images with flat, goldpatterned surfaces, often mixing in local ideas.
Cuzco School.seen: No. 90 Angel with Arquebus (La Paz School, a related tradition).

daimyo.def: A Japanese feudal lord who ruled a domain and commanded samurai under the shogun.

Djenné.def: A trading city in Mali, home of the Great Mosque built of mud brick.

Dogon.def: A people of Mali known for cliffside villages, granary doors, ancestor figures and masquerades.

Dutch Republic.def: The Protestant northern Netherlands, independent from Spain in the 1600s and rich from trade, with a booming art market of portraits, landscapes and still lifes.
Dutch Republic.seen: No. 87 SelfPortrait with Saskia; No. 92 Woman Holding a Balance; No. 96 Fruit and Insects.

Eastern Shoshone.def: A Native people of Wyoming, on the Wind River Reservation; Cotsiogo was an Eastern Shoshone painter.

Edo.def: The people of the Kingdom of Benin in southern Nigeria.
Edo.think: Not the same as the Edo period of Japan.
Edo.seen: No. 169 Wall plaque, from Oba’s palace.

enstoolment.def: The ceremony that installs a new Asante king or chief. The new Asantehene is lowered and raised over the Golden Stool without ever sitting on it. It is the Asante version of a coronation.

Etruscans.def: A people of central Italy (c. 800 to 100 B.C.E.) before the Roman takeover, known for lively tombs, terra cotta sculpture and temples.
Etruscans.seen: No. 29 Sarcophagus of the Spouses; No. 31 Temple of Minerva; No. 32 Tomb of the Triclinium.

Fang.def: A people of Gabon, Cameroon and Equatorial Guinea known for byeri reliquary guardian figures.

feather cape.def: A cape covered in bird feathers, a sign of rank and sacred power in Hawaiʻi and elsewhere in Polynesia.
feather cape.seen: No. 215 ʻAhu ʻula (feather cape); No. 158 Ruler’s feather headdress (a comparison).

Fiji.def: A Pacific island nation, a British colony from 1874 to 1970, where ceremonial gifts of mats and tapa build relationships.
Fiji.seen: No. 223 Presentation of Fijian mats and tapa cloths.

Flanders.def: The region of today’s Belgium where early Netherlandish painters like Jan van Eyck developed oil painting.
Flanders.seen: No. 66 Merode Altarpiece; No. 68 The Arnolfini Portrait.

Florence.def: A city in Tuscany, Italy, the birthplace of the Renaissance.
Florence.seen: No. 67 Pazzi Chapel; No. 69 David (Donatello); No. 70 Palazzo Rucellai.

formline.def: The Northwest Coast design system of swelling and tapering outlines, built from ovoids and U-shapes, that fills every surface.

French Revolution.def: The uprising (1789 to 1799) that overthrew France’s monarchy and aristocracy, inspired by Enlightenment ideas of liberty and equality.
French Revolution.seen: No. 103 The Oath of the Horatii (before it); No. 105 Self-Portrait (painted in exile); No. 244 The Swing (after Fragonard).

Gandhara.def: An ancient region of today’s Pakistan and Afghanistan where Buddhist art mixed with Greek and Roman styles, as in the wavy drapery of Buddha statues.

gbagba.def: Baule entertainment masquerade dances, at whose climax the mblo portrait mask appears.

glyph.def: A carved or painted sign standing for a word, sound or idea, especially in Maya and Aztec writing. The Yaxchilán lintels carry Maya glyphs naming the rulers and dates.

gogok.def: Comma-shaped jade or glass ornaments hung on Silla crowns, possibly standing for life, seeds or fertility.

Grand Tour.def: A long trip through Europe, especially Italy, made by wealthy young British and northern Europeans in the 1600s to 1800s to study ancient ruins and Renaissance art.
Grand Tour.think: A finishingschool road trip that spread Neoclassical taste.

Great Migration.def: The movement of about six million Black Americans from the rural South to Northern cities (c. 1910 to 1970) to escape segregation and find work.
Great Migration.seen: No. 141 The Migration of the Negro, Panel no. 49.

Great Zimbabwe.def: The stone capital of a rich Shona trading kingdom in southern Africa (c. 1000 to 1450), with huge mortarless granite walls. Its builders traded gold as far as China. Colonial writers falsely claimed Africans could not have built it.
Great Zimbabwe.seen: No. 167 Conical tower and circular wall of Great Zimbabwe.

Han.def: A long Chinese dynasty (206 B.C.E. to 220 C.E.) so important that Chinese people still call themselves ‘Han’.
Han.seen: No. 194 Funeral banner of Lady Dai.

Hawaiʻi.def: A Polynesian island chain, a kingdom until its overthrow by Americans in 1893 and later a U.S. state.

hei-tiki.def: A Māori neck pendant of greenstone (jade) shaped like a human figure, passed down as a family treasure.

hieroglyph.def: A picture-sign in the ancient Egyptian writing system. Some signs stand for sounds, others for whole words or ideas. The Narmer Palette writes the king’s name with a catfish and a chisel.
hieroglyph.seen: No. 13 Palette of King Narmer; No. 24 Last judgment of Hu-Nefer.
hieroglyph.see: cartouche, serekh, Book of the Dead.

Hopi.def: A Pueblo people of northeastern Arizona, known for katsina ceremonies and carved katsina dolls.

huipil.def: A loose, rectangular tunic woven and worn by Indigenous women in Mexico and Central America, still worn today.
huipil.seen: No. 97 Spaniard and Indian Produce a Mestizo.

ibol.def: A personal emblem carved on the front of a Kuba ndop that tells you which king it is.
ibol.think: Like a signature logo for each king.

Igbo.def: A large people of southeastern Nigeria.

Insular art.def: Art of Britain and Ireland c. 600 to 900 C.E. (‘insular’ means ‘of the islands’), mixing Celtic and Germanic interlace with Christian books. Also called Hiberno-Saxon.

islet.def: A very small island. Nan Madol was built on nearly 100 artificial islets of stacked stone and coral fill off the coast of Pohnpei.

Jahangir.def: The fourth Mughal emperor (reigned 1605 to 1627), a passionate art patron.
Jahangir.seen: No. 208 Jahangir Preferring a Sufi Shaikh to Kings.

Jingdezhen.def: China’s porcelain capital for over a thousand years, where imperial and export porcelain was made.
Jingdezhen.seen: No. 204 The David Vases; No. 250 Sunflower Seeds.

July Revolution.def: The 1830 uprising in Paris that replaced King Charles X with Louis-Philippe.

Justinian.def: Byzantine emperor (reigned 527 to 565 C.E.) who rebuilt Hagia Sophia and reconquered Italy. He appears in mosaic with his wife, Theodora.
Justinian.seen: No. 51 San Vitale; No. 52 Hagia Sophia.

kahu kiwi.def: A Māori cloak covered with kiwi feathers, worn by people of high rank.

Khajuraho.def: A site in central India with Hindu and Jain temples famed for their dense, sometimes erotic sculpture.

khipu.def: An Inka record-keeping device of knotted, colored cords, used for counting and possibly for stories. Also spelled quipu.

Kongo.def: A people and former kingdom of west-central Africa, in today’s Democratic Republic of the Congo, Republic of Congo and Angola. Famous for nkisi power figures.

Kuba.def: A kingdom in the Democratic Republic of the Congo famous for royal arts, textiles and the ndop royal figures.
Kuba.seen: No. 171 Ndop of King Mishe miShyaang maMbul.

Kuosi.def: A powerful Bamileke society of royals and wealthy titleholders who wear beaded elephant masks.

Kwakwaka’wakw.def: A Northwest Coast people of British Columbia, Canada, known for dramatic transformation masks used in potlatch dances.

Lakota.def: A Plains nation of the Dakotas (part of the Sioux), known for winter counts and ledger art.

ledger drawing.def: Drawings made by Plains artists in the late 1800s on pages of account books (ledgers) from traders and the army, often while confined on reservations or in prison, recording battles and daily life.

Lega.def: A people of the eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo whose life is organized by the bwami society.

Lenape.def: An Eastern Woodlands people, also called the Delaware, originally from the area of New Jersey, Delaware and New York.

literati.def: Educated scholargentlemen of China (and Korea and Japan) who painted, wrote poetry and practiced calligraphy as amateurs for self-expression, valuing personal style over polish.
literati.think: Painting as a gentleman’s hobby, not a job.
literati.seen: No. 227 Summer Trees (draws on literati ink tradition); No. 201 Travelers among Mountains and Streams.

Louis XIV.def: The ‘Sun King’ of France (reigned 1643 to 1715), who built Versailles as a stage for absolute royal power.

Luba.def: A people and former kingdom of the southeastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, known for royal art and the lukasa memory board.

malagan.def: Funeral ceremonies of New Ireland held months or years after a death, and the elaborate carvings and masks made for them. The carvings are often displayed once and then destroyed or sold.

Mali Empire.def: A rich West African empire (c. 1230 to 1600) famous for gold, trade across the Sahara, and Islamic learning in cities like Timbuktu and Djenné.

Manila galleon.def: Spanish trading ships that sailed between Manila in the Philippines and Acapulco in Mexico (1565 to 1815), carrying Asian silk, porcelain and screens to the Americas and silver to Asia.
Manila galleon.think: The first regular trade route linking Asia and the Americas.
Manila galleon.seen: No. 94 Screen with the Siege of Belgrade.

Mao Zedong.def: The leader of the Chinese Communist Party and founder of the People’s Republic of China (1949), shown everywhere as a sun-like hero.
Mao Zedong.seen: No. 212 Chairman Mao en Route to Anyuan; No. 250 Sunflower Seeds.

Māori.def: The Indigenous Polynesian people of Aotearoa (New Zealand), famous for carving, tā moko, cloaks and meeting houses.

marae.def: A Māori ceremonial courtyard and meeting place in front of a meeting house; in other parts of Polynesia, a stone temple platform.

Marshall Islands stick chart.def: A navigation chart of lashed palm ribs and shells showing ocean swell patterns around islands, studied on land by trained navigators and memorized before voyages.
Marshall Islands stick chart.think: A map of waves, not of coastlines.

masi.seen: No. 223 Fijian mats and tapa cloths.

Mbudye.def: A Luba society of ‘men of memory’ who kept and performed royal history and advised kings.

Medici.def: A rich banking family that ruled Florence and spent huge sums on art in the 1400s to 1500s. Two Medici became queens of France and several became popes.
Medici.think: The ultimate art patrons of the Renaissance.
Medici.seen: No. 72 Birth of Venus; No. 69 David (Donatello); No. 86 Marie de’ Medici Cycle.

Melanesia.def: The region of the southwest Pacific including Papua New Guinea, the Solomon Islands, Vanuatu, the Torres Strait area and Fiji.
Melanesia.seen: No. 222 Malagan display and mask; No. 218 Buk (mask); No. 9 The Ambum Stone.

Mende.def: A people of Sierra Leone and Liberia, known for the Sande society’s women’s masks.

Mesoamerica.def: The cultural region of southern Mexico and Central America where the Olmec, Teotihuacan, Maya and Aztec civilizations flourished, sharing maize farming, ball games, pyramids, calendars and blood sacrifice.
Mesoamerica.seen: No. 155 Yaxchilán; No. 157 Templo Mayor; No. 10 Tlatilco figurine.

Mesopotamia.def: ‘Land between the rivers’: the region between the Tigris and Euphrates in modern Iraq, home of Sumer, Babylon and Assyria.
Mesopotamia.seen: No. 12 White Temple; No. 19 Code of Hammurabi; No. 25 Lamassu.

mestizo.def: A person of mixed Spanish and Indigenous American ancestry.
mestizo.seen: No. 97 Spaniard and Indian Produce a Mestizo.

Mexica.def: The people usually called the Aztecs, who ruled an empire from their island capital, Tenochtitlan, until the Spanish conquest in 1521.
Mexica.seen: No. 157 Templo Mayor; No. 158 Ruler’s feather headdress; No. 81 Codex Mendoza.

Mexican muralism.def: A movement after the Mexican Revolution (1910 to 1920) in which artists like Diego Rivera painted public murals about Mexican history and Indigenous heritage for ordinary people.
Mexican muralism.seen: No. 143 Dream of a Sunday Afternoon in the Alameda Park; No. 143 Dream of a Sunday Afternoon.

Micronesia.def: ‘Small islands’: the region of tiny islands in the western Pacific, including the Marshall Islands, Pohnpei and Nukuoro.
Micronesia.seen: No. 213 Nan Madol; No. 217 Female deity, Nukuoro; No. 221 Navigation chart.

Ming.def: A Chinese dynasty (1368 to 1644) that built the Forbidden City and much of the Great Wall.

Mississippian.def: Native cultures of the Mississippi valley and Southeast (c. 800 to 1600 C.E.) that built large earthen mounds and towns such as Cahokia. The College Board labels the Great Serpent Mound Mississippian, though some scholars credit earlier peoples (Adena or Fort Ancient).

Mongol Empire.def: The largest connected land empire in history (1206 to 1368), founded by Genghis Khan, which linked China, Iran and Russia and boosted trade and artistic exchange.
Mongol Empire.seen: No. 189 Bahram Gur Fights the Karg; No. 204 The David Vases.

Motecuhzoma II.def: The Aztec ruler (often spelled Moctezuma or Montezuma) when the Spanish arrived in 1519.

mukanda.def: The Chokwe boys’ initiation into adulthood, at whose end masks such as pwo perform.

Nabataeans.def: An Arab trading people who controlled incense routes and carved their capital, Petra, from rock (c. 300 B.C.E. to 106 C.E.).

Nahua.def: The Nahuatl-speaking peoples of central Mexico, including the Mexica (Aztecs).

ndop.def: A carved wooden ‘portrait’ figure of a Kuba king, shown idealized and seated. It is identified by its ibol emblem, not by a facial likeness, and was believed to hold the king’s spirit.
ndop.seen: No. 171 Ndop of King Mishe miShyaang maMbul.

New Ireland.def: An island province of Papua New Guinea where malagan ceremonies are held.

New Spain.def: The Spanish colony that covered Mexico, Central America and more (1521 to 1821), ruled by a viceroy.
New Spain.seen: No. 81 Codex Mendoza; No. 95 Virgin of Guadalupe; No. 97 Spaniard and Indian Produce a Mestizo; No. 99 Portrait of Sor Juana.

nganga.def: A Kongo ritual specialist who activates nkisi figures and works as healer and diviner.

ngatu.def: Tongan tapa, made in large sheets by groups of women and given at weddings, funerals and royal occasions.

Niue.def: A small Polynesian island nation known for hiapo barkcloth.

nkisi n’kondi.def: A Kongo power figure that ‘hunts’ wrongdoers. A ritual specialist fills it with medicines, and people drive nails or blades into it to seal oaths, settle disputes or call for punishment. The plural of nkisi is minkisi.
nkisi n’kondi.think: Every nail is a record of a promise or a case, like a legal archive in wood.

Normans.def: Vikings who settled in Normandy, France, and conquered England in 1066 under William the Conqueror.

Nukuoro.def: A small Micronesian atoll whose people are culturally Polynesian, known for smooth, abstract deity figures.

oba.def: The title of the king of Benin, and also of Yoruba kings. The Oba of Benin is a sacred ruler shown frontal and larger than others, in coral-bead regalia.
oba.seen: No. 169 Wall plaque, from Oba’s palace.

Oceania.def: The Pacific Islands region, usually divided into Polynesia, Micronesia and Melanesia, sometimes with Australia.
Oceania.seen: No. 213 Nan Madol; No. 214 Moai; No. 222 Malagan.

Olowe of Ise.def: A famous Yoruba sculptor (c. 1875 to 1938), one of the few African artists of his time known by name, admired for his tall figures and deep undercutting.

Pachacuti.def: The Inka ruler (reigned c. 1438 to 1471) who turned a small kingdom into an empire and rebuilt Cusco; Machu Picchu was probably his estate.
Pachacuti.seen: No. 159 City of Cusco; No. 161 City of Machu Picchu.

pastoralism.def: A way of life based on herding animals, such as cattle, sheep or goats, often moving with the seasons. Much later Saharan rock art shows herders and their cattle.

patrician.def: A member of the old, inherited aristocracy of ancient Rome. Patricians prized ancestry and dignity.
patrician.seen: No. 42 Head of a Roman patrician.

peplos.def: A heavy woolen garment worn by ancient Greek women: a rectangle of cloth folded over at the top, belted and pinned at the shoulders, falling in thick, straight folds. Many scholars now think the Peplos Kore actually wears a different decorated garment.

Pergamon.def: A Hellenistic Greek kingdom in today’s Turkey, famous for its great altar.
Pergamon.seen: No. 38 Great Altar of Zeus and Athena.

Persia.def: The historic name for Iran and its empires, from the Achaemenids to the Safavids.
Persia.seen: No. 30 Persepolis; No. 186 Great Mosque, Isfahan; No. 190 The Court of Gayumars.

pictograph.def: A picture-sign that stands for a word or idea by showing it, like a little drawing of a hill meaning ‘hill’. Aztec manuscripts used pictographs for place names and events.
pictograph.think: Like the icons on a road sign or an emoji.
pictograph.seen: No. 81 Codex Mendoza; No. 165 Painted elk hide.

pisupo.def: The Samoan word for canned food, from ‘pea soup’, one of the first canned foods brought by Europeans. It now stands for an unhealthy imported diet.

Plains peoples.def: Native nations of the North American Great Plains, such as the Lakota, Shoshone and Crow, whose life centered on the buffalo. Their painted hides, ledger drawings and beadwork recorded history and visions.
Plains peoples.see: Sun Dance, winter count, ledger drawing.

Pohnpei.def: An island in Micronesia, site of Nan Madol.

Polynesia.def: ‘Many islands’: the huge triangle of Pacific islands from Hawaiʻi to New Zealand to Rapa Nui, settled by expert voyagers.
Polynesia.seen: No. 214 Moai; No. 215 ʻAhu ʻula; No. 216 Staff god; No. 220 Tamati Waka Nene.

Pompeii.def: A Roman town buried and preserved by the eruption of Mount Vesuvius in 79 C.E.
Pompeii.seen: No. 39 House of the Vettii; No. 40 Alexander Mosaic.

pope.def: The bishop of Rome and head of the Catholic Church, a giant art patron.
pope.seen: No. 75 Sistine Chapel; No. 76 School of Athens.

potlatch.def: A Northwest Coast ceremonial feast in which a host gives away goods and stages dances to confirm status, names and rights. Canada banned it from 1884 to 1951.

Pueblo peoples.def: Native peoples of New Mexico and Arizona, such as the Hopi and Tewa, who live in adobe or stone villages called pueblos.
Pueblo peoples.seen: No. 166 Black-on-black ceramic vessel; No. 154 Mesa Verde (ancestors).
Pueblo peoples.see: Ancestral Puebloan, Hopi, San Ildefonso Pueblo.

pukao.def: A red stone topknot or hat set on the head of some moai.

Qin.def: The short-lived dynasty (221 to 206 B.C.E.) that first unified China under Qin Shi Huang.

Qin Shi Huang.def: The first emperor of a unified China, who standardized writing, money and measures, and was buried with the terra cotta army.

Qorikancha.def: ‘Golden enclosure’: the main Inka temple in Cusco, dedicated to the sun, once covered in gold. A Spanish church was built on top of it.
Qorikancha.seen: No. 159 City of Cusco; No. 160 Maize cobs.

rangatira.def: A Māori chief or person of high rank. Tamati Waka Nene was a rangatira.

Rapa Nui.def: The Polynesian name for Easter Island and its people, famous for moai statues.

Rarotonga.def: The main island of the Cook Islands in central Polynesia, known for wrapped staff gods.

Ravenna.def: A city in northern Italy that was a western Byzantine capital, full of early Christian mosaics.

reservation.def: Land set aside by the U.S. government for a Native American nation, usually after forcing it off its homeland. Cotsiogo painted his elk hides on the Wind River Reservation in Wyoming.
reservation.see: Eastern Shoshone, Plains peoples, hide painting.

rock shelter.def: A shallow cave or overhanging rock that gives natural cover but stays open to daylight, unlike a deep cave. Much African rock art is found in them.
rock shelter.seen: No. 1 Apollo 11 Stones; No. 4 Running horned woman.

Rococo patrons.def: The French aristocrats of the 1700s who commissioned playful, flirtatious, pastel art for private homes.

Samoa.def: A Polynesian island nation. Many Samoans now live in New Zealand, where artists like Michel Tuffery work.

samurai.def: Japan’s hereditary warrior class, who served lords (daimyo) and followed a code of loyalty.
samurai.seen: No. 203 Night Attack on the Sanjô Palace.

San.def: Indigenous hunter-gatherer peoples of southern Africa, whose long rock art tradition is often linked to shamanic trance.
San.seen: No. 1 Apollo 11 Stones (region and later tradition).

San Ildefonso Pueblo.def: A Tewa pueblo in New Mexico, home of the potters Maria and Julian Martínez.

Sande.def: A women’s society among the Mende and neighbors that prepares girls for adulthood. It is one of the very few African traditions in which women wear masks.

Sapa Inka.def: ‘Unique Inka’: the title of the Inka emperor, believed to descend from the sun.

Saudeleur.def: The dynasty that ruled Pohnpei from Nan Madol, keeping local chiefs close to control them.

scarification.def: Making permanent patterns of small scars on the skin, practiced in many African cultures as a mark of beauty, identity, adulthood or status. Masks and figures often show it.
scarification.seen: No. 173 Female (Pwo) mask; No. 174 Portrait mask (Mblo).

scholar-oﬀicial.def: A government oﬀicial in China or Korea chosen through exams on the Confucian classics, often also a poet, calligrapher or painter.

secret society.def: A membership group, common in West and Central Africa, whose members learn restricted knowledge through initiation. Such societies often own masks, keep history, judge disputes and train young people. Scholars now often say ‘association’ or ‘initiation society’, since membership itself is usually public.
secret society.think: Like a powerful club with private rituals, not a hidden conspiracy.
secret society.seen: No. 175 Bundu mask (Sande); No. 177 Lukasa (Mbudye); No. 178 Aka elephant mask (Kuosi).

Sephardi.def: Jews of Spain and Portugal and their descendants, who were expelled from Spain in 1492.

serekh.def: An early Egyptian royal emblem: the king’s name written inside a rectangle shaped like a palace front. On the Narmer Palette it sits at the top between two cow heads. It came before the cartouche.

Shah Jahan.def: The fifth Mughal emperor (reigned 1628 to 1658), who built the Taj Mahal as a tomb for his wife, Mumtaz Mahal.

Shah Tahmasp.def: The second Safavid ruler of Iran (reigned 1524 to 1576), patron of a famous illustrated Shahnama.

shogun.def: Japan’s top military ruler, who held real power while the emperor was a figurehead, from 1192 to 1868.

Shona.def: The people of Zimbabwe whose ancestors built Great Zimbabwe.

sika dwa kofi.def: ‘Golden stool born on Friday’: the sacred Golden Stool of the Asante, believed to have come down from the sky. No one sits on it, and it never touches the ground.

Silk Road.def: The network of trade routes linking China with Central Asia, India, the Middle East and Europe, carrying silk, goods, religions (especially Buddhism) and art styles.
Silk Road.seen: No. 182 Bamiyan Buddhas; No. 195 Longmen caves.

Sinan.def: The chief Ottoman architect (c. 1490 to 1588), designer of hundreds of buildings, who sought to outdo Hagia Sophia’s dome.

Song.def: A Chinese dynasty (960 to 1279) famous for monumental landscape painting, NeoConfucianism and fine ceramics.
Song.seen: No. 201 Travelers among Mountains and Streams.

Spartacists.def: German revolutionary socialists, led by Karl Liebknecht and Rosa Luxemburg, crushed in 1919.
Spartacists.seen: No. 134 Memorial Sheet for Karl Liebknecht.

Sudano-Sahelian.def: The mud-brick building style of the Sahel region of West Africa, with thick walls, buttresses and wooden beams (toron) sticking out.

Sumer.def: The first cities of southern Mesopotamia (c. 4500 to 1900 B.C.E.), such as Uruk and Ur, inventors of writing (cuneiform).
Sumer.seen: No. 12 White Temple, Uruk; No. 14 Votive figures, Eshnunna; No. 16 Standard of Ur.

sunsum.def: The Asante word for soul or spirit. The Golden Stool holds the sunsum of the entire Asante nation.

symposium.def: An ancient Greek drinking party for men, with wine mixed in a krater, conversation, music and games. Much painted Greek pottery was made for it.
symposium.think: Today the word means an academic conference, a much soberer event.

t’oqapu.def: Small squares of geometric pattern woven into Inka textiles, each probably standing for a place, group or rank. Also spelled tocapu.

tā moko.def: Traditional Māori tattooing, especially of the face, carved into the skin with chisels. Each design records a person’s ancestry, rank and identity.
tā moko.think: Like a personal ID card and family tree written on the face.

Tang.def: A Chinese dynasty (618 to 907 C.E.), a golden age of Buddhism, poetry and Silk Road trade.

taonga.def: A Māori word for a treasure: any prized object, place, idea or tradition passed down through generations.
taonga.seen: No. 220 Tamati Waka Nene (cloak, hei-tiki, staff).

tapa.def: Barkcloth made by beating the inner bark of paper mulberry trees into sheets, then painting, stamping or dyeing it. It is made mostly by women and used for clothing, gifts and ceremonies. Called ngatu in Tonga, masi in Fiji, hiapo in Niue, siapo in Samoa.
tapa.seen: No. 219 Hiapo (tapa); No. 223 Fijian mats and tapa cloths; No. 216 Staff god (wrapped in tapa); No. 223 Presentation of Fijian mats and tapa; No. 216 Staff god.

tatanua.def: A type of malagan mask with a crested fiber ‘hairstyle’ representing the spirit of a dead person.

Tate Modern.def: The modern art museum in London, in a former power station whose Turbine Hall hosts giant commissions.

Tawantinsuyu.def: ‘The four parts together’: the Inka name for their empire.

Tehuana.def: A woman of the Isthmus of Tehuantepec in Oaxaca, Mexico, whose distinctive dress became a symbol of strong, Indigenous Mexican womanhood.

Tenochtitlan.def: The Aztec capital, built on an island in Lake Texcoco, now buried under Mexico City.
Tenochtitlan.seen: No. 157 Templo Mayor; No. 81 Codex Mendoza.

Teotihuacan.def: A vast ancient city near Mexico City (c. 100 B.C.E. to 550 C.E.) with the Pyramids of the Sun and Moon. The later Aztecs named it ‘place of the gods’.

the Academy.def: An oﬀicial art school and society, like France’s Royal Academy of Painting and Sculpture (1648), which taught rules, ranked subjects and controlled the Salon. ‘Academic art’ means art following its rules.
the Academy.seen: No. 105 Self-Portrait (Vigée Le Brun, an Academy member); No. 103 The Oath of the Horatii.

the Salon.def: The oﬀicial art exhibition of the French Academy in Paris. Getting accepted made careers; rejections led to rebel shows and modern art.
the Salon.think: Like a national talent show that decided who succeeded.
the Salon.seen: No. 103 The Oath of the Horatii; No. 113 The Stone Breakers; No. 115 Olympia.

Theodora.def: Byzantine empress and wife of Justinian, a former actress who became a powerful co-ruler.

Tibet.def: A high plateau region north of the Himalayas, center of Vajrayana Buddhism.

Tlingit.def: A Northwest Coast people of southeastern Alaska and Canada, known for Chilkat weaving, crest art and carved clan objects.

Torres Strait.def: The sea and islands between Australia and Papua New Guinea, whose peoples made masks from turtle shell.

Treaty of Waitangi.def: The 1840 agreement between the British Crown and many Māori chiefs that made New Zealand a British colony. The Māori and English versions differ, which still causes disputes.

Trobriand Islands.def: Islands off Papua New Guinea famous for the kula ring, a ceremonial exchange of shell valuables, and for carved, painted yam houses and canoe prows.

Upper and Lower Egypt.def: The two original parts of Egypt: Upper Egypt in the south (upriver) and Lower Egypt in the north (the Nile delta). The pharaoh ruled both and wore crowns for each.
Upper and Lower Egypt.think: ‘Upper’ is south because the Nile flows north.

Vatican.def: The pope’s headquarters and the smallest country in the world, inside Rome, with St. Peter’s Basilica and the Sistine Chapel.
Vatican.seen: No. 75 Sistine Chapel; No. 76 School of Athens.

Venice Biennale.def: A huge international art exhibition held every two years in Venice since 1895.

viceroyalty.def: A colony governed by a viceroy, who ruled on behalf of the Spanish king. New Spain and Peru were the two great viceroyalties.
viceroyalty.seen: No. 81 Codex Mendoza; No. 90 Angel with Arquebus.

wayfinding.def: Traditional Pacific navigation without instruments, reading stars, swells, winds and birds.

whare.def: A Māori house. A carved meeting house (whare whakairo) is seen as the body of an ancestor.

winter count.def: A Plains pictorial calendar, usually painted on a hide, with one picture for each year (‘winter’) recalling its main event.
winter count.think: A history book with one emoji per year.

Wu Zetian.def: The only woman to rule China as emperor in her own name (reigned 690 to 705 C.E.), a major Buddhist patron.

Yoruba.def: A large West African people, mostly in southwest Nigeria and Benin, with citykingdoms, orisha religion and famous carvers and bronze casters.
Yoruba.seen: No. 180 Veranda post (Opo Ogoga), Olowe of Ise.

Yuan.def: The Mongol dynasty that ruled China (1271 to 1368), founded by Kublai Khan.
Yuan.see: Mongol Empire. 9 Context, ideas and the exam Words for function, context and big ideas (patronage, propaganda, appropriation, repatriation), plus the vocabulary of the exam’s essay tasks.

abolition.def: The movement to end slavery and the slave trade. Britain banned the slave trade in 1807 and slavery in most of its colonies in 1833; the United States ended slavery in 1865.
abolition.think: Turner showed Slave Ship in 1840, the year a world antislavery convention met in London, so the painting joined a live debate.

absolutism.def: A system in which a monarch holds total power, unchecked by any parliament.

analyze.def: An AP task word: break a work or idea into its parts and explain how they relate and create meaning.

anonymous.def: Made by a maker whose name is not recorded. Most art in history is anonymous, which does not mean it was made without skill or individual style.
anonymous.seen: No. 33 Niobides Krater (Niobid Painter, a nickname); No. 169 Wall plaque, Benin.

antebellum.def: Latin for ‘before the war’. In U.S. history it means the South in the decades before the Civil War (1861 to 1865), the world of plantations and slavery.
antebellum.think: Think ‘plantation South’. Kara Walker’s silhouettes turn its romantic image into a nightmare.

apotropaic.def: Meant to ward off evil or bad luck.
apotropaic.seen: No. 25 Lamassu; No. 197 Todaiji (Nio); No. 172 Power figure.

apprentice.def: A young trainee who learned an art by working for years under a master in a workshop.

appropriation.def: Taking existing images, objects or styles and reusing them in a new work, often to change or question their meaning.
appropriation.seen: No. 147 Marilyn Diptych; No. 231 Untitled (No. 228); No. 244 The Swing (after Fragonard); No. 233 Trade.

art historical interpretation.def: A published argument by a scholar about a work’s meaning or importance. The AP exam may ask you to use or respond to one.

art market.def: The system of buying and selling art through dealers, galleries, auctions and collectors.
art market.seen: No. 148 Narcissus Garden; No. 96 Fruit and Insects.

artist.def: The maker of a work. In many cultures makers were seen as skilled craftspeople, often anonymous, rather than celebrated geniuses; the idea of the famous individual artist became strong in Renaissance Europe.
artist.seen: No. 74 Adam and Eve (Dürer signs his name); No. 188 Basin (signed six times); No. 180 Olowe of Ise.

atelier.def: French for an artist’s studio or workshop, especially a royal workshop of painters and calligraphers in Persian and Mughal courts.
atelier.seen: No. 190 The Court of Gayumars (Safavid royal atelier).

attribution.def: Deciding who made a work, or when and where, based on style, materials, documents and comparison. On the AP exam, the attribution question shows you an unknown work and asks you to name the likely artist or culture and justify it.
attribution.seen: No. 36 Grave stele of Hegeso (attributed to Kallimachos); No. 97 Spaniard and Indian Produce a Mestizo (attributed).

attribution question.def: The AP short-essay question that shows a work you have not studied and asks you to identify its likely artist, culture or period, using specific visual similarities to a work you know.
attribution question.think: Detective question: name a suspect, then show the clues.

audience.def: The people a work was made to be seen or used by: worshippers, a ruler’s subjects, visiting ambassadors, a small elite, a museum crowd. Ask who saw it, where, and how.
audience.seen: No. 25 Lamassu (foreign envoys); No. 79 Allegory of Law and Grace (ordinary Lutherans); No. 221 Navigation chart (trained navigators only).

bel composto.def: Italian for ‘beautiful whole’. Bernini’s idea of combining architecture, sculpture, painting and real light into one unified, theatrical experience.
bel composto.think: Like a stage show where the set, actors and lighting all work as one.

cache.def: A group of objects hidden or buried together on purpose. Archaeologists find caches of sacred objects that were buried rather than thrown away.

canon.def: Two meanings: (1) a set of rules for ideal proportions, like Polykleitos’ Canon; (2) the list of works considered the ‘greatest’ and most taught. The second canon has long favored European men, and the 250-work AP list is itself a canon.

ceremonial.def: Made for or used in formal public occasions, such as coronations, festivals, funerals or gift exchanges, rather than daily use.
ceremonial.seen: No. 13 Palette of King Narmer; No. 158 Ruler’s feather headdress; No. 223 Presentation of Fijian mats and tapa cloths.

citation.def: A deliberate reference in a work to an earlier work, like a footnote in pictures.
citation.seen: No. 115 Olympia (cites Venus of Urbino); No. 244 The Swing (after Fragonard).

civic virtue.def: Being a good citizen: putting the good of the community or republic before your own interests. Neoclassical art, inspired by ancient Rome, held it up as the highest ideal.
civic virtue.seen: No. 103 The Oath of the Horatii; No. 104 George Washington.

claim.def: A statement you argue is true and back up with evidence.

colonialism.def: One country taking control of another people’s land, government and resources, often settling it and imposing its religion and culture. European colonialism shaped how much of the world’s art was made, taken and seen.
colonialism.seen: No. 97 Spaniard and Indian Produce a Mestizo; No. 169 Wall plaque, Benin (looted); No. 220 Tamati Waka Nene; No. 244 The Swing (after Fragonard).

commemorative.def: Made to honor and preserve the memory of a person or event.
commemorative.seen: No. 13 Palette of King Narmer; No. 171 Ndop; No. 225 Vietnam Veterans Memorial.

commission.def: A formal order and payment for an artist to make a specific work, often with a contract setting the subject, materials and deadline. Also used as a verb (‘the queen commissioned it’).
commission.think: Made to order, not made on spec.
commission.seen: No. 101 The Swing (commissioned to a courtier’s specifications); No. 86 Marie de’ Medici Cycle; No. 107 La Grande Odalisque.

commodification.def: Turning something (art, culture, identity, people) into a product to be bought and sold.
commodification.seen: No. 147 Marilyn Diptych; No. 148 Narcissus Garden; No. 230 Pink Panther.

comparison.def: Discussing two or more works together, showing both similarities and differences and explaining why. The AP long-essay comparison question pairs a given work with one you choose.
comparison.think: Always give both ‘alike’ and ‘different’, with reasons.
comparison.see: thesis, line of reasoning, continuity and change.

complexity.def: A more sophisticated argument, such as explaining both sides, several causes, or how a work both continues and breaks a tradition. The strongest AP long essays show it.
complexity.think: Going beyond ‘this is true’ to ‘this is true, and here is the nuance’.

connoisseurship.def: Identifying who made a work through expert, close study of its style and technique.

conservation.def: The science of protecting works from decay, damage and environment, preferably changing as little as possible.
conservation.seen: No. 73 Last Supper (flaking paint); No. 151 Spiral Jetty (submerged and changing).

consumerism.def: A culture focused on buying goods, and the idea that buying makes us happy or defines who we are.
consumerism.seen: No. 147 Marilyn Diptych; No. 237 Pisupo Lua Afe; No. 230 Pink Panther.

content.def: The subject matter of a work: what or who is shown, the story, the symbols and the message.

content area.def: One of the ten geographic and timebased units of the AP Art History course, such as ‘Global Prehistory’ or ‘Africa’.

context.def: The circumstances around a work: when, where, by and for whom it was made, its original setting and use, and later history. Context explains why a work looks the way it does.
context.seen: No. 173 Pwo mask (danced, not hung on a wall); No. 165 Painted elk hide.

contextual analysis.def: Explaining how a work’s context (time, place, patron, function, audience, beliefs) shaped it and its meaning. One of the AP short-essay question types.

continuity and change.def: How traditions carry on (continuity) and how they shift (change) over time. The AP continuity and change question asks how a work relates to earlier or later art traditions.
continuity and change.seen: No. 220 Tamati Waka Nene; No. 245 Old Man’s Cloth; No. 244 The Swing (after Fragonard).

contract.def: A written agreement between patron and artist listing what is to be made, materials (such as how much gold or blue), price and deadline.

court art.def: Art made for a royal or princely court, usually by artists the ruler employed, to show the ruler’s wealth, taste and power. Safavid manuscripts and the Ardabil Carpet came from court workshops.
court art.seen: No. 190 The Court of Gayumars; No. 191 Ardabil Carpet.

craft.def: Skilled handmade work, especially textiles, ceramics, metalwork and furniture, long ranked below painting and sculpture in Europe. That ranking is now widely questioned.
craft.seen: No. 232 Dancing at the Louvre (quilt); No. 166 Black-on-black vessel; No. 219 Hiapo.
craft.see: high and low art, decorative arts, feminist art.

critique.def: A work or argument that questions or criticizes something, such as power, the art world, gender roles or colonialism.
critique.seen: No. 148 Narcissus Garden (critique of the art market); No. 243 Darkytown Rebellion; No. 233 Trade.

cult of personality.def: Using propaganda, images and mass media to turn a political leader into an idolized, almost godlike hero. In Mao’s China his image was everywhere.
cult of personality.seen: No. 212 Chairman Mao en Route to Anyuan.

cultural exchange.def: The flow of ideas, materials, styles and beliefs between cultures through trade, travel, conquest or migration. On the exam it is one of the most useful themes for comparisons.
cultural exchange.seen: No. 182 Bamiyan Buddhas (Greek and Indian); No. 204 The David Vases (Persian cobalt, Chinese porcelain); No. 94 Biombo; No. 208 Jahangir (European prints).

cultural patrimony.def: Objects and traditions that belong to a whole people or nation as their shared heritage, not to any one owner.
cultural patrimony.seen: No. 170 Golden Stool; No. 220 Tamati Waka Nene (taonga).

decorative arts.def: Useful objects made beautifully: furniture, ceramics, textiles, metalwork, glass.
decorative arts.seen: No. 188 Basin (Baptistère de St. Louis); No. 191 Ardabil Carpet; No. 204 The David Vases.

degenerate art.def: The Nazi label (in German, Entartete Kunst) for modern art they banned, including Expressionism and abstraction. In 1937 they seized thousands of works from German museums and mocked many of them in a touring exhibition.

describe.def: An AP task word: give the relevant features of something in detail, more than just naming it.

devotional.def: Made to help someone pray or feel closer to God, often for private use.
devotional.seen: No. 62 Röttgen Pietà; No. 66 Merode Altarpiece; No. 54 Theotokos icon.

diaspora.def: A people scattered from their homeland and living in other countries, often keeping ties to their culture. Diaspora artists often explore belonging between two worlds.
diaspora.seen: No. 232 Dancing at the Louvre; No. 236 En la Barberia no se Llora; No. 237 Pisupo Lua Afe; No. 235 Rebellious Silence.

didactic.def: Made to teach a lesson, usually moral or religious.
didactic.seen: No. 79 Allegory of Law and Grace; No. 98 The Tête à Tête (Marriage à la Mode); No. 198 Borobudur (reliefs teach pilgrims).

digital art.def: Art made or shown with computers and digital technology.
digital art.seen: No. 241 Pure Land (digital compositing); No. 240 Guggenheim Museum Bilbao (computer-aided design).

diplomacy.def: Relations between states. Art served it through gifts, portraits and ceremonies.
diplomacy.seen: No. 223 Presentation of Fijian mats and tapa to Queen Elizabeth II ; No. 208 Jahangir Preferring a Sufi Shaikh to Kings.

donor.def: A person who pays for a religious work as a gift to a church or shrine, often shown kneeling inside the work. A ‘donor portrait’ records them.
donor.seen: No. 66 Merode Altarpiece (donors in left wing); No. 63 Arena Chapel; No. 204 The David Vases (inscribed donor).

entropy.def: A scientific idea: everything gradually breaks down into disorder. Robert Smithson welcomed it, letting Spiral Jetty sink, crust with salt and erode.
entropy.think: Like a sandcastle slowly flattened by the tide.

epic.def: A long poem or story about heroes, battles and the founding of a people. Ferdowsi’s Shahnama (Book of Kings) is the national epic of Iran, and many Persian paintings illustrate it.
epic.think: The Persian equivalent of the Iliad or The Lord of the Rings.
epic.seen: No. 189 Bahram Gur Fights the Karg; No. 190 The Court of Gayumars.

Eurocentrism.def: Judging the world’s art by European standards, or treating European art as the norm and everything else as ‘other’.

evidence.def: Specific facts that support a claim: visual details you can point to and contextual facts (dates, patrons, functions, beliefs). On the AP exam vague evidence earns little; precise evidence earns points.
evidence.think: Point to it on the work, or name the fact.

exoticism.def: Treating other cultures as strange, thrilling and foreign, usually seen from outside without real understanding.
exoticism.seen: No. 107 La Grande Odalisque; No. 123 Where Do We Come From?.

explain.def: An AP task word: give reasons and show how or why, linking cause and effect. Most points on the exam need explaining, not just describing.

feminism.def: The belief in, and movement for, equal rights and opportunities for women. Feminist art since the 1970s questions how women have been shown in art and who gets to be an artist.

fetish.def: An old European word for African sacred objects, now avoided because it carries insulting colonial ideas of ‘superstition’. Scholars say ‘power figure’ instead.

four humors.def: An old medical theory that health and personality depend on balancing four body fluids: blood, yellow bile, black bile and phlegm. Too much of one made a person sanguine (cheerful), choleric (angry), melancholic (sad) or phlegmatic (sluggish).
four humors.think: In Dürer’s Adam and Eve, a cat, rabbit, elk and ox stand for the four humors, still in balance before the Fall.

free-response question.def: An AP essay question (FRQ). The AP Art History exam has two long essays and four short essays: visual analysis, contextual analysis, attribution, and continuity and change.

function.def: What a work was made to do: worship, burial, protection, teaching, persuasion, decoration, record-keeping, display of status, and so on. Function is one of the main things the AP exam asks about.
function.seen: No. 172 Power figure (seals oaths); No. 177 Lukasa (memory aid); No. 221 Navigation chart (teaching navigation).

funerary.def: Having to do with death, burial and memory of the dead: tombs, coﬀins, grave goods, memorials.
funerary.seen: No. 23 Tutankhamun’s coﬀin; No. 29 Sarcophagus of the Spouses; No. 193 Terra cotta warriors; No. 222 Malagan.

gender.def: The roles, behaviors and identities a society expects of women and men. Asking ‘how does this work show gender?’ is a powerful analysis tool.
gender.seen: No. 103 The Oath of the Horatii; No. 180 Opo Ogoga; No. 236 En la Barberia no se Llora; No. 175 Bundu mask.

genealogy.def: A family’s line of descent, traced back through generations of ancestors. Art often displayed genealogies to prove a ruler’s or chief’s right to power.
genealogy.seen: No. 177 Lukasa (memory board); No. 216 Staff god.

Gesamtkunstwerk.def: German for ‘total work of art’. A project that unites many arts, such as architecture, painting, decoration, music and design, into one whole. Klimt and the Vienna Secession embraced the idea.
Gesamtkunstwerk.see: Vienna Secession, bel composto, Art Nouveau.

gift exchange.def: The giving and receiving of valuable objects to create bonds, show rank and build obligations between people or groups.
gift exchange.seen: No. 223 Presentation of Fijian mats and tapa; No. 164 Transformation mask (potlatch); No. 184 Jowo Rinpoche (dowry).

global contemporary.def: Art made around the world from about 1980 to now, often dealing with globalization, identity, politics and new media, and shown at international biennials.
global contemporary.seen: No. 245 Old Man’s Cloth; No. 250 Sunflower Seeds; No. 248 Shibboleth; No. 246 Stadia II.

global trade.def: Worldwide trade networks, especially after 1500, that moved silver, silk, porcelain, enslaved people and art between continents.
global trade.seen: No. 94 Screen with the Siege of Belgrade; No. 244 The Swing (after Fragonard); No. 245 Old Man’s Cloth.

globalization.def: The growing connection of the world’s economies, cultures and people through trade, travel, media and the internet.
globalization.seen: No. 238 Electronic Superhighway; No. 246 Stadia II ; No. 250 Sunflower Seeds.

gravitas.def: Latin for ‘weight’ or ‘seriousness’. The Roman virtue of dignity, self-control and moral seriousness, shown in stern, wrinkled, veristic portraits.
gravitas.seen: No. 42 Head of a Roman patrician.

guerrilla.def: Spanish for ‘little war’. Fighting by small, irregular bands who ambush a larger army. The word comes from Spain’s resistance to Napoleon’s troops (1808 to 1814), the war Goya recorded in The Disasters of War.

guild.def: An association of craftsmen in a trade (such as painters or goldsmiths) that set standards, trained apprentices and controlled who could sell work in a city.
guild.think: A medieval trade union and licensing board in one.

happening.def: An unscripted, often audience-involving art event of the late 1950s and 1960s, a forerunner of performance art.

heliocentric.def: Sun-centered: the idea, argued by Copernicus and confirmed by Galileo and Kepler, that the Earth and planets orbit the sun.
heliocentric.seen: No. 100 A Philosopher Giving a Lecture on the Orrery.

hierarchy.def: A ranking of people from most to least important. Art often shows it through size, position and dress.
hierarchy.seen: No. 13 Palette of King Narmer; No. 169 Wall plaque, Benin; No. 51 San Vitale.

hierarchy of genres.def: The Academy’s ranking of painting subjects: history painting (big stories from the Bible, myth or history) at the top, then portraits, everyday scenes, landscape, and still life at the bottom.
hierarchy of genres.think: Realists broke the rule by painting ordinary people at history-painting size.
hierarchy of genres.seen: No. 103 The Oath of the Horatii (history painting); No. 113 The Stone Breakers; No. 96 Fruit and Insects (still life).

high and low art.def: The traditional split between ‘fine’ art for elites and museums (high) and popular culture, crafts or commercial images (low). Pop and later art erased the boundary.
high and low art.seen: No. 147 Marilyn Diptych; No. 230 Pink Panther; No. 226 Horn Players.

homage.def: A work made to honor an earlier artist or work.

humanism.def: A Renaissance movement that revived the study of ancient Greek and Roman writings and celebrated human ability, reason and the individual, alongside Christian faith.
humanism.seen: No. 69 David (Donatello); No. 76 School of Athens.

hybridity.def: The mixing of different cultures, styles or identities in one work or person, creating something new rather than simply one or the other.
hybridity.seen: No. 81 Codex Mendoza; No. 163 Bandolier bag; No. 244 The Swing (after Fragonard); No. 247 Preying Mantra.

iconology.def: A deeper study than iconography: explaining what a work’s symbols and subjects reveal about the beliefs and attitudes of its time and culture.
iconology.think: Iconography asks ‘what is the lily?’; iconology asks ‘why did this society care about it?’

idealization.def: Showing a person or thing as more perfect than in real life, according to a culture’s ideal of beauty, virtue or power. Many ‘portraits’ outside Europe, and royal images everywhere, are idealized rather than true likenesses.
