idealization.seen: No. 171 Ndop (ageless king); No. 175 Bundu mask (ideal female beauty); No. 18 King Menkaura and queen.

identify.def: An AP task word: name or state something specific (an artist, a culture, a function), with no explanation needed.

identity.def: Who a person or group is, or believes they are, including race, ethnicity, nationality, religion, gender and class. Much modern and contemporary art explores identity.
identity.seen: No. 140 The Two Fridas; No. 231 Untitled (No. 228); No. 232 Dancing at the Louvre; No. 233 Trade.

image set.def: The 250 required works of the AP Art History course. Exam questions may also allow works ‘beyond the image set’ that you know well.

imperialism.def: Building an empire by extending power over other lands, through conquest, colonies or economic control.
imperialism.seen: No. 43 Augustus of Prima Porta; No. 170 Golden Stool (War of the Golden Stool); No. 223 Fijian mats presentation.

indigenous.def: Native to a place; Indigenous peoples are the original inhabitants of lands later colonized by others.
indigenous.seen: No. 166 Black-onblack vessel; No. 234 Earth’s Creation; No. 233 Trade.

Industrial Revolution.def: The change from hand production to machines and factories, starting in Britain around 1760, which brought railways, cities, new materials and photography.
Industrial Revolution.seen: No. 116 The SaintLazare Station; No. 124 Carson, Pirie, Scott Building; No. 111 Slave Ship.

installation.def: A work that fills or transforms a whole space, which the viewer often walks into or around, rather than a single object on a wall or pedestal.
installation.seen: No. 236 En la Barberia no se Llora; No. 243 Darkytown Rebellion; No. 250 Sunflower Seeds; No. 248 Shibboleth; No. 229 A Book from the Sky; No. 236 No Crying Allowed in the Barbershop; No. 148 Narcissus Garden.

institutional critique.def: Art that questions the institutions of art itself (museums, galleries, the market) and who they include or exclude.

interpretation.def: An explanation of what a work means. Interpretations can differ, so on the exam you support yours with evidence.
interpretation.seen: No. 92 Woman Holding a Balance; No. 85 Calling of Saint Matthew (which figure is Matthew?).

justify.def: An AP task word: support a claim with evidence and reasoning, as in the attribution question.

kitsch.def: Cheap, sentimental, mass-market art or decoration seen as being in bad taste. Some artists use it on purpose.

legitimacy.def: The right to rule, or a claim to it. Rulers commissioned art linking themselves to gods, ancestors or great past empires to look legitimate.
legitimacy.seen: No. 43 Augustus of Prima Porta; No. 57 Pyxis of al-Mughira; No. 189 Bahram Gur Fights the Karg (Mongols claiming Persian kingship).

lex talionis.def: Latin for ‘law of retaliation’: punishment that matches the crime, ‘an eye for an eye’. Hammurabi’s laws apply it, though penalties also depended on the social rank of victim and offender.

limpieza de sangre.def: Spanish for ‘purity of blood’. A colonial idea that ranked people by ancestry, favoring ‘pure’ Spanish Christian descent. It underlay the casta system of New Spain.
limpieza de sangre.seen: No. 97 Spaniard and Indian Produce a Mestizo.

line of reasoning.def: The logical chain that connects your evidence to your thesis, explaining how and why each piece supports it. AP essay scoring rewards a clear one.
line of reasoning.think: The ‘because’ that ties evidence to argument.

looting.def: Stealing objects, especially in war or from archaeological sites without permission.

luxury object.def: A small, precious, finely made item for an elite owner, often of ivory, gold, silk or rare pigments.
luxury object.seen: No. 57 Pyxis of al-Mughira; No. 50 Vienna Genesis; No. 191 Ardabil Carpet.

machismo.def: An exaggerated sense of masculine pride and toughness, including the idea that real men never show emotion. Pepón Osorio’s barbershop installation, titled No Crying Allowed in the Barbershop, questions it.
machismo.seen: No. 236 No Crying Allowed in the Barbershop.

male gaze.def: A term from film critic Laura Mulvey (1975): images that present women as objects for a presumed male viewer.
male gaze.seen: No. 80 Venus of Urbino; No. 107 La Grande Odalisque.

mass media.def: Newspapers, magazines, radio, film, TV and the internet: forms that reach huge audiences at once.
mass media.seen: No. 147 Marilyn Diptych; No. 238 Electronic Superhighway; No. 247 Preying Mantra.

mass production.def: Making large numbers of identical items, by molds, machines or assembly lines.
mass production.seen: No. 193 Terra cotta warriors (molds); No. 147 Marilyn Diptych (silkscreen); No. 250 Sunflower Seeds (looks mass-produced but is handmade).

memorial.def: A structure or object made to remember the dead or a tragic event.
memorial.seen: No. 225 Vietnam Veterans Memorial; No. 134 Memorial Sheet for Karl Liebknecht; No. 209 Taj Mahal (a tomb).

Mexicanidad.def: Spanish for ‘Mexicanness’. A movement after the Mexican Revolution to celebrate Mexico’s Indigenous and folk heritage as the heart of national identity. Frida Kahlo embraced it in her Tehuana dress and imagery.

mnemonic device.def: Anything that helps you remember, like a rhyme, a pattern or an object. The Luba lukasa and the Marshall Islands stick chart were memory aids for trained experts.
mnemonic device.think: Like ‘Please Excuse My Dear Aunt Sally’ for the order of operations.
mnemonic device.seen: No. 177 Lukasa (memory board); No. 221 Navigation chart.

modernity.def: The condition of modern life after the Industrial Revolution: cities, railways, factories, crowds, speed and new technology. Artists like Monet made it their subject.

monument.def: A large public work meant to last and to make a statement to everyone who passes, usually about power, memory or identity.
monument.seen: No. 17 Great Pyramids; No. 225 Vietnam Veterans Memorial; No. 150 Lipstick (Ascending) on Caterpillar Tracks.

multimedia.def: A work that combines different media such as video, sound, light and objects.
multimedia.seen: No. 238 Electronic Superhighway; No. 239 The Crossing.

museum.def: An institution that collects, preserves and displays objects. Museums shape how we see works, often removing them from their original setting.
museum.seen: No. 240 Guggenheim Museum Bilbao; No. 249 MAXXI.

national identity.def: A shared sense of what makes a people a nation: history, land, language and heroes. Art from the 1800s on often tries to shape it, as in Velasco’s grand views of the Valley of Mexico.

nationalism.def: Strong loyalty to one’s nation, sometimes claiming superiority over others. Art has often built national identity.
nationalism.seen: No. 143 Dream of a Sunday Afternoon; No. 112 Palace of Westminster; No. 246 Stadia II.

Neoplatonism.def: A philosophy based on Plato, revived in Renaissance Florence, that saw physical beauty as a reflection of divine, spiritual beauty. It let a nude pagan goddess like Botticelli’s Venus carry Christian-friendly meanings.

Old Masters.def: The great European painters from about 1300 to 1800, such as Leonardo, Rembrandt and Velázquez, and their works.
Old Masters.seen: No. 91 Las Meninas; No. 87 Self-Portrait with Saskia; No. 231 Untitled (No. 228) (parodies them).

oral history.def: History passed down by speaking and memory rather than by writing: genealogies, migrations and legends. Many African and Pacific cultures preserved it through trained specialists.

parody.def: An imitation that mocks or comments on its source.
parody.seen: No. 114 Nadar Raising Photography to the Height of Art; No. 231 Untitled (No. 228).

participatory art.def: Art that requires the audience to take part to be complete.
participatory art.seen: No. 148 Narcissus Garden; No. 238 Electronic Superhighway (live camera of viewers); No. 243 Darkytown Rebellion (viewers’ shadows).

patron.def: The person or group who pays for and often directs the making of a work of art, such as a ruler, church, guild or rich family. Patrons usually decided the subject, size and materials.
patron.think: The client. Ask ‘who paid for this, and what did they want from it?’
patron.seen: No. 63 Arena Chapel (Enrico Scrovegni); No. 72 Birth of Venus (Medici circle); No. 195 Longmen caves (Empress Wu); No. 209 Taj Mahal (Shah Jahan).

patronage.def: The support that patrons give artists by buying or ordering their work. Systems of patronage (church, court, city, private buyers) shape what art gets made.
patronage.seen: No. 75 Sistine Chapel (papal patronage); No. 86 Marie de’ Medici Cycle; No. 195 Longmen caves.

portable.def: Small and light enough to carry. Portable art can travel through trade, gifts, pilgrimage or migration, spreading styles.
portable.seen: No. 1 Apollo 11 Stones; No. 53 Merovingian fibulae; No. 66 Merode Altarpiece.

postcolonial.def: Describes the period after colonies won independence, and art or ideas that examine the lasting effects of colonialism on identity, power and culture.
postcolonial.seen: No. 245 Old Man’s Cloth; No. 244 The Swing (after Fragonard); No. 233 Trade.

prestige object.def: An object whose main job is to signal that its owner is important, often made of rare materials or by rare skill.
prestige object.seen: No. 7 Jade cong; No. 53 Merovingian fibulae; No. 162 All-T’oqapu tunic.

propaganda.def: Art or media made to spread a political or religious message and shape what people believe, often by glorifying a leader or cause.
propaganda.seen: No. 43 Augustus of Prima Porta; No. 59 Bayeux Tapestry; No. 86 Marie de’ Medici Cycle; No. 212 Chairman Mao en Route to Anyuan.

provenance.def: The history of who has owned a work and where it has been since it was made. Gaps or ‘collected in 1897’ can signal looting.
provenance.think: A work’s ownership history, like a car’s Carfax report.
provenance.seen: No. 169 Wall plaque, Benin (looted 1897); No. 188 Basin (Baptistère de St. Louis).

quotation.def: Borrowing a recognizable pose, figure or composition from an earlier work.
quotation.seen: No. 115 Olympia; No. 43 Augustus of Prima Porta (Doryphoros pose); No. 230 Pink Panther (Baroque nude pose).

radiocarbon dating.def: A scientific method that dates once-living material, like charcoal, wood or bone, by measuring how much of a radioactive form of carbon has decayed. It works back to about 50,000 years.
radiocarbon dating.seen: No. 1 Apollo 11 Stones; No. 156 Great Serpent Mound.

readymade.def: An ordinary manufactured object chosen and presented as art by an artist, as Marcel Duchamp did. The idea, not the handwork, makes it art.

reception.def: How people responded to a work at the time and later: praise, scandal, rejection, copying, censorship.
reception.seen: No. 115 Olympia (scandal); No. 107 La Grande Odalisque (attacked); No. 144 Fountain (rejected).

reciprocity.def: Giving and returning gifts or help, which builds relationships and obligations. It is central to Pacific gift exchange and to how the Inka state ran.
reciprocity.think: You help me, I help you, and we’re tied together.
reciprocity.seen: No. 223 Presentation of Fijian mats and tapa.

refraction.def: The bending of waves as they pass around or over something. In Marshall Islands stick charts, curved sticks show ocean swells bending around islands.

regalia.def: The special clothing and objects that show royal or high rank, such as crowns, scepters, capes, stools and jewelry.
regalia.seen: No. 158 Ruler’s feather headdress; No. 215 ʻAhu ʻula; No. 170 Golden Stool; No. 169 Wall plaque (coral-bead regalia).

regent.def: Someone who rules on behalf of a monarch who is too young, absent or unable to rule. Blanche of Castile was regent of France for her young son, Louis IX.

repatriation.def: Returning objects to the country or community they came from, especially objects taken by looting or under colonial rule.
repatriation.seen: No. 169 Wall plaque, Benin; No. 164 Transformation mask (potlatch objects returned).

reproducibility.def: The ability to make many copies of an image, as with prints and photographs. It spreads images widely and raises questions about originality.
reproducibility.seen: No. 79 Allegory of Law and Grace; No. 211 Under the Wave off Kanagawa; No. 212 Chairman Mao en Route to Anyuan.

restitution.def: Returning property, such as looted art, to its rightful owners. Debates over the Benin Bronzes taken by British troops in 1897 are a key example.
restitution.seen: No. 169 Wall plaque from Oba’s palace.

restoration.def: Repairing a damaged work and sometimes replacing missing parts or cleaning it to look closer to its original state. Restorations can be controversial if they change the work too much.
restoration.seen: No. 75 Sistine Chapel (cleaned 1980s to 1990s); No. 73 Last Supper.

ritual.def: A set of actions performed in a fixed, meaningful way, usually religious. Many objects only make full sense inside the ritual they were made for.
ritual.seen: No. 155 Yaxchilán (bloodletting); No. 172 Power figure; No. 202 Shiva as Lord of Dance (processions).

Royal Academy.def: The oﬀicial art academy of a kingdom: in France, the Royal Academy of Painting and Sculpture (1648); in Britain, the Royal Academy of Arts (1768). They trained artists, held exhibitions and ranked the genres. Vigée Le Brun was one of very few women admitted in France.
Royal Academy.see: the Academy, the Salon, hierarchy of genres.

satire.def: Using humor, exaggeration or irony to criticize people, habits or institutions.
satire.seen: No. 98 The Tête à Tête (Hogarth); No. 114 Nadar Raising Photography; No. 237 Pisupo Lua Afe.

secular.def: Not religious; worldly. Secular art includes portraits, scenes of daily life, entertainment masks and luxury objects for the court. Islamic art avoids figures mainly in religious settings, so secular Islamic objects are often full of people and animals.
secular.seen: No. 57 Pyxis of al-Mughira; No. 174 Portrait mask (Mblo); No. 188 Basin (Baptistère de St. Louis).
secular.see: genre scene, court art, luxury object.

shibboleth.def: A word, custom or test used to tell insiders from outsiders. In the Bible (Judges 12), fleeing men were killed if they could not pronounce it. Doris Salcedo used it as the title of her crack in the Tate Modern floor, about exclusion and racism.

signature.def: The artist’s name written on a work. Signing was rare in many periods, so a signature can be a bold claim to fame or authorship.
signature.seen: No. 74 Adam and Eve (Dürer’s tablet); No. 188 Basin (Baptistère de St. Louis); No. 166 Black-on-black vessel (signed); No. 144 Fountain (‘R. Mutt’).

social practice.def: Art in which the main ‘work’ is engaging people and communities in collaboration or social change, rather than making objects.

sovereignty.def: Supreme, independent power to govern. The Golden Stool embodies the sovereignty and soul of the whole Asante nation.

status.def: A person’s rank or prestige in society. Many works are made to display or claim status, through costly materials, size, rare skills or exclusive use.
status.seen: No. 39 House of the Vettii; No. 178 Aka elephant mask; No. 15 Seated scribe.

stratigraphy.def: Dating finds by the layers of earth (strata) in which they lie: in undisturbed ground, lower layers are older.
stratigraphy.think: Like a stack of mail: what’s at the bottom arrived first.

style.def: The recognizable way something is made, which can belong to an artist, a workshop, a culture or a period. Learning styles lets you attribute unknown works.
style.think: Like recognizing a singer by their voice.

swell.def: A long, rolling ocean wave that travels far from the wind that created it. Marshall Islands navigators read swells, and how islands bend them, to find land.

syncretism.def: The blending of different religions or beliefs into a new combined form.
syncretism.think: Mixing two belief systems into one.
syncretism.seen: No. 90 Angel with Arquebus; No. 95 Virgin of Guadalupe; No. 142 The Jungle (Santería); No. 48 Catacomb of Priscilla (pagan forms, Christian meaning).

synesthesia.def: A mixing of the senses, such as seeing colors when hearing music. Kandinsky compared colors to musical tones and wanted his paintings to work on viewers like music.

the gaze.def: The way a work positions the viewer to look, and the power in that looking. The ‘male gaze’ means images made for men’s pleasure in looking at women.
the gaze.seen: No. 80 Venus of Urbino; No. 115 Olympia (stares back); No. 101 The Swing; No. 231 Untitled (No. 228).

thesis.def: A clear, defensible claim that answers the question and that the rest of the essay proves. On the AP rubric it must do more than restate the question.
thesis.think: The one sentence a reader should remember.

tourist art.def: Objects made by local artists to sell to outsiders. It can still be serious art and can preserve or adapt traditions.
tourist art.seen: No. 165 Painted elk hide; No. 166 Black-on-black vessel.

trade.def: The exchange of goods over distance. Trade brought new materials (brass, beads, cobalt, silk) and new ideas to artists.
trade.seen: No. 169 Wall plaque (brass from Europe); No. 204 The David Vases (Persian cobalt); No. 163 Bandolier bag (glass beads); No. 181 Petra.
trade.see: cultural exchange, Silk Road, global trade.

tradition.def: Ways of making, believing or doing passed down through generations. Many works keep a tradition alive or change it.
tradition.seen: No. 166 Black-onblack vessel (revived); No. 227 Summer Trees; No. 234 Earth’s Creation.

tribute.def: Payments of goods (feathers, cloth, gold, food) that conquered or lesser groups had to send to a ruler.
tribute.seen: No. 158 Ruler’s feather headdress; No. 81 Codex Mendoza; No. 215 ʻAhu ʻula.

uncanny.def: Familiar but strangely disturbing. Freud described it as the eerie feeling when something homely turns strange, and the Surrealists sought it out, as in Oppenheim’s fur-covered teacup.

usury.def: Lending money at interest, which the medieval Church condemned as a sin. Enrico Scrovegni may have built the Arena Chapel partly to make up for his family’s usury.

visual analysis.def: Describing a work’s form (materials, technique, composition, color, line, scale) and explaining how those choices create meaning. One of the AP short-essay question types.
visual analysis.think: Say what you see, then say why it matters.

votive.def: Offered to a god as a gift or to fulfill a promise (a vow). Votive figures could ‘pray’ on the giver’s behalf.
votive.seen: No. 14 Statues of votive figures, Eshnunna.

wabi-sabi.def: A Japanese idea of beauty that values simple, imperfect, weathered and impermanent things, linked to Zen Buddhism and the tea ceremony.
wabi-sabi.think: A cracked old tea bowl can be more beautiful than a perfect new one.

women artists.def: Women who made art, often against barriers like exclusion from academies, nude-model classes and guilds. Many were left out of histories until recently.
women artists.seen: No. 96 Fruit and Insects (Rachel Ruysch); No. 105 Self-Portrait (Vigée Le Brun); No. 166 Black-on-black vessel (Maria Martínez); No. 175 Bundu mask (Sande women).

workshop.def: An artist’s studio where a master, assistants and apprentices worked together. Many works ‘by’ a famous artist were partly or mostly made by the workshop.
workshop.think: Like a small company with the master as brand name.
workshop.seen: No. 66 Merode Altarpiece (workshop of Robert Campin); No. 197 Todai-ji (Nio by Unkei and Kaikei’s workshop).

order: Churning of the Ocean of Milk

questions.prompt: A slanted line or direction. thiss feel active and unstable compared with calm horizontals and verticals.
Art that tells a story or shows an event from a story.
How a surface feels, or looks like it would feel: rough, smooth, soft, bumpy, glossy. Actual this can be touched; implied this is only painted.
A color made lighter by adding white.
An accepted, repeated way of showing something in a particular culture, even if it is not realistic. Viewers in that culture understand it automatically.
The line where the land or sea seems to meet the sky. In linear perspective, the vanishing point usually sits on it, at the viewer’s eye level.
One horizontal band in a work that is divided into stacked rows, like shelves. Each this often shows a different scene or level of importance.
Placing one image on top of another so they overlap, as when prehistoric painters added new animals over older ones on the same wall.
How strong, pure or intense a color is. A highly saturated red is vivid; a low-this red is dull and grayish. Also called intensity or chroma.
Tricks that make a flat surface seem to have real depth, space or objects, so the wall or ceiling seems to open up.

Art that simplifies, exaggerates or rearranges what things really look like, so you may only partly recognize the subject (or not at all). The word describes how far an image has moved away from a photo-like copy.

Showing different parts of one body from their most recognizable angles at the same time: head in profile, eye from the front, shoulders from the front, legs in profile. Common in Egyptian and Near Eastern art. Also called twisted perspective.
Cutting off part of a scene at the edge of the frame, so figures or objects are only partly shown. It makes an image feel like a quick snapshot.
A round or oval framed area holding a design or figure, often used as the central motif of carpets, ivories and ceilings.
A strong difference between two things placed together: light and dark, rough and smooth, big and small, bright and dull. this grabs attention.
Orange, green and purple: the colors you get by mixing two primary colors.
Colors that sit next to each other on the color wheel, such as yellow, yellow-orange and orange. Used together they feel calm and unified rather than clashing.
Using differences in shape, color, size or texture to keep a work interesting. Usually balanced against unity.

A way of showing depth used in Chinese and Japanese painting: the sides of buildings are drawn as parallel diagonal lines that never meet, so the scene can unroll sideways without one fixed viewpoint.
How smooth or rough the final surface is. A high this hides brushstrokes completely; a loose this leaves them visible.
The position from which the viewer seems to see the scene: low, high, straight on, from the side. Also called vantage point.
Made of regular, measurable shapes such as squares, circles, triangles and straight lines. The opposite of organic.
Stretching, twisting or exaggerating forms on purpose, usually to show emotion or a new idea rather than accuracy.
Drawing something that points toward or away from you so it looks squashed and shorter, which makes it seem to stick out in space.
A flat, enclosed area with only height and width, such as a circle or a blob.
A shape that has (or looks like it has) three dimensions: height, width and depth. In art talk ‘this’ can also mean all the visual parts of a work together, as opposed to its subject.
Showing people’s inner emotions and states of mind truthfully, not just their outward appearance. Each of Rodin’s Burghers of Calais shows his own kind of despair.
Facing straight out at the viewer, square to the front. this figures often look formal, stiff and powerful.
A wide view showing a large stretch of land or city, as if you can turn your head and take it all in.
A decoration of bands, ribbons or animal bodies that weave over and under each other in complicated knots.
Reds, oranges and yellows. They feel warm, energetic or emotional and tend to seem to come toward you.

An imaginary straight line running through the center of a body, object or building, around which its parts are arranged. A standing figure usually has a vertical this; in contrapposto that this bends.
Egg-shaped. In Northwest Coast art, the this is a rounded, slightly squarish oval used as a basic building block of formline designs.
The part of a picture that seems closest to you, at the bottom or front of the scene.
How the visual ‘weight’ of shapes, colors and objects is spread around a work so it feels stable instead of tipping to one side. It can be symmetrical, asymmetrical or radial.
The real, everyday color of an object in normal light, such as a lemon’s yellow or grass’s green.
A mark that is longer than it is wide. thiss can be straight, curved, thick, thin, calm or agitated, and they outthis shapes, show movement or carry feeling.
Made to show strong feeling. An this work uses color, line or distortion to make you feel something rather than to record what things look like.
The way an artist makes one part stand out more than the rest, using light, color, size, placement or lines that point to it.
Filling every inch of a surface with figures or decoration so no empty space is left. Latin for ‘fear of empty space’.
A circle that arranges colors in rainbow order so you can see which colors are related. Opposite colors are complementary; neighbors are analogous.
Showing things the way they actually look in the real world, with accurate details, proportions, light and texture.
In linear perspective, the diagonal lines (real or implied) that run back into the picture and meet at the vanishing point, such as the edges of a ceiling or floor tiles.
Placing one thing partly in front of another. The one that blocks the other looks closer. It is the simplest way to show depth.
How strongly a part of a work pulls your attention. Big, dark, bright or busy areas feel heavier than small, pale or plain ones.
How the main shapes (the figure) stand out from what is behind them (the ground). Some works play with this so you are not sure which is which.

Avoiding pictures of people, animals or gods, especially in a religious setting. Instead the art uses writing, patterns and plants. Common in Islamic religious spaces and in very early Buddhist art, where the Buddha was shown only by symbols such as a footprint or an empty throne.
The size of one part compared with another part or with the whole, such as head to body.
Breaking forms into pieces, planes or shards, often reassembled in a new way. Central to Cubism.
Describing and explaining a work by looking only at its visual parts: line, color, shape, space, texture, composition and so on, before talking about meaning.
The plain name of a color: red, blue, green and so on.
Making the most important person the biggest, no matter where they stand in the scene. Size shows rank, not distance.
Art that shows recognizable things from the real world, whether realistic or stylized.
The pose or hand movement of a figure that communicates something, like pointing, blessing or reaching.
The zone of a picture between the foreground and the background.
A style that relies on clear outlines and sharp edges between forms, so shapes look crisp and polished. Often contrasted with a painterly style.
A line you do not actually see but your eye follows anyway, such as the direction of a pointing finger, a gaze, or a row of objects.
A set of rules for the ideal size of each body part compared with the others, used so every figure looks ‘correct’. The Greek sculptor Polykleitos wrote one; Egyptian artists used a grid system.
A style where you can see loose brushstrokes and soft edges, with color and texture more important than crisp outlines.
Texture that is painted or drawn to look rough, soft or shiny, even though the actual surface is smooth.
Made in one color, or in shades of a single color (including just black ink and grays). Also called monochromatic.
Surrounding the viewer with sound, image or space, so you feel you are inside the work rather than looking at it.
Shown in a simplified, exaggerated or decorative way that follows a set style rather than copying nature exactly.
Lining up all the heads in a crowd at the same height, whether the figures are standing, riding or walking. It keeps a long frieze tidy.
Strong, focused light that throws some areas into bright highlight and leaves others in deep shadow, raising the emotional temperature of a scene.
Burnt wood (or bone) used as a black drawing material. One of the oldest art materials.
Opaque watercolor: water-based paint with extra white or chalk added so it covers what is underneath, drying flat and matte.
A type of painting from colonial Mexico (1700s) showing families of mixed racial background in sets, each labeled with a category name. They recorded a colonial system of racial ranking.
Paint made with pigment mixed in a drying oil, usually linseed oil. It dries slowly, so artists can blend smoothly and build up thin glazes; it became the main European painting medium by the 1500s.
A painting made on a portable support, like canvas or panel, that can be moved and hung anywhere, as opposed to a mural fixed to a wall.
A work made by gluing paper, photos, fabric or other materials onto a flat surface. From the French ‘coller’, to glue.
A dark box or room with a tiny hole or lens that projects an upsidedown image of the outside scene onto a wall or screen. Artists could trace it, and it led to the camera.
A picture whose main subject is natural scenery: land, sky, trees and water. It was a major subject in China by the 900s and became one in Europe from the 1500s.
Painting with pigment mixed into hot melted wax. The colors stay bright and glossy for centuries. Used for Roman-Egyptian mummy portraits and early icons.
A thin, watery layer of ink or paint brushed over an area to give a soft, even tone.
A printed image, such as an engraving, that an artist copied or adapted. Colonial painters in the Americas often worked from European prints, so poses and compositions traveled across the ocean.
A handwritten book decorated with painted pictures, colored letters and often gold or silver. Before printing, every book was made by hand.
Painting done entirely in shades of gray, often to imitate stone sculpture.
The surface a painting or drawing is made on, such as wood panel, canvas, paper, silk, vellum, plaster or hide.

Italian for ‘changing’. Painting the shadows of a fabric in a different, often lighter or brighter color instead of a darker shade of the same one, so the cloth seems to shimmer. Mannerists like Pontormo loved it.
A vertical scroll painting mounted on silk or paper with a rod at the bottom, made to hang on a wall and be rolled up for storage.

In Chinese painting, a type of brushstroke (cun) used to show the texture of rocks and mountains, such as ‘raindrop’ or ‘axe-cut’ strokes. Fan Kuan’s mountains are built from thousands of raindrop strokes.
Making marks on a surface with a tool like pencil, charcoal, chalk or ink, usually emphasizing line. thiss can be finished works or sketches for later projects.
Gold hammered into sheets thinner than tissue paper and applied to a surface to make it shine.
A background covered with gold leaf instead of a landscape or room, making holy figures seem to exist in heaven rather than on earth.
The museum-label name for acrylic and similar plastic-based paints. They dry fast and come in bright colors.
An early photographic print (about 1850 to 1890) made on paper coated with egg white, which held the light-sensitive chemicals and gave a fine, glossy image.
A Persian, Mughal or Ottoman album that collected paintings and samples of calligraphy, often set in decorated borders, for a royal or elite collector.
Pouring very thin paint onto raw, unprimed canvas so it soaks into the cloth, leaving soft, see-through pools of color. Pioneered by Helen Frankenthaler.
A thin, tough, smooth plastic film. Some contemporary artists paint and collage on it instead of paper or canvas.
Chinese for ‘mountain-water’: the Chinese tradition of landscape painting with mountains, rivers and mist, expressing harmony between people and nature.
A Japanese folding screen made of hinged panels, often painted on gold-leafed paper, used to divide rooms and decorate homes.
A print made by carving a picture into a block of wood, inking the raised surface and pressing paper onto it. Japanese color thiss used a separate block for each color.
A white mix of chalk or plaster and glue brushed onto wood panels or canvas to make a smooth, bright surface for painting.
A printmaking technique, related to etching, that uses acid eating through a powdered resin layer to make soft areas of tone that look like watercolor washes, instead of only lines.
Italian for ‘nude’. One of the twenty muscular nude young men Michelangelo painted on the Sistine Chapel ceiling, seated at the corners of the smaller Genesis scenes. Plural: ignudi.
Shading made by drawing sets of fine parallel lines that cross each other. The closer the lines, the darker the area.
A long roll of papyrus, paper or silk with writing or images, unrolled to read and rolled up to store.
An early, angular style of Arabic script with straight lines and sharp corners, used in the first centuries of Islam for copying the Qur’an and in architecture.
A painting of non-moving objects, such as fruit, flowers, cups or skulls, arranged by the artist.
A flat board, usually wood, used as a surface to paint on. Before canvas took over, most European paintings were on thiss.
Painting with separate, unblended dabs of color placed side by side so they mix in the viewer’s eye instead of on the palette. A key Impressionist technique.
Individual letters or characters made as separate pieces that can be arranged into text, printed, and then reused.
Light thrown onto a wall or screen from a projector, used by some contemporary artists as part of an installation, so viewers’ shadows can join the scene.
Painting on animal skin. Plains and Plateau peoples of North America painted hides to record histories, events and visions.
The drawing an artist makes on a surface before painting over it. Scientists can often see it with infrared light.
Shading made with many fine parallel lines close together.
A painting of ordinary people doing everyday things, like working, cooking or chatting.
Painting a design directly by hand, without stencils, stamps or rubbing boards. Niuean hiapo stands out because its fine, dense patterns were painted freehand.
Words written, painted or carved on a work, such as a title, poem, name or dedication.
Oil paint formed into a solid stick, like a giant crayon, so artists can draw directly with paint. Basquiat used it in Horn Players.
A small scene or picture set within a larger composition or border. Four corner thiss in the Virgin of Guadalupe painting tell the story of her appearances.

The family of printmaking methods where lines are cut or etched into a metal plate. Ink sits in the grooves, and strong pressure pulls it onto paper. Engraving, etching, drypoint and aquatint are all this.
Canvas not coated with gesso or primer, so thinned paint soaks straight into the fabric. Helen Frankenthaler poured paint onto it in her soak-stain technique.
A woman in an Ottoman harem; in European painting, a reclining nude in an imagined ‘Oriental’ setting, a favorite subject of Orientalism.
A note written in the margin or between the lines of a text to explain or translate it. Spanish thises label the Aztec pictures in the Codex Mendoza.
Animal skin (usually sheep or goat) soaked, scraped, stretched and dried to make a smooth, tough writing surface. Fine calfskin this is called vellum.
Shapes cut out of paper and arranged or pasted as a work of art. Kara Walker uses large black cut-paper silhouettes on white walls.
An intaglio print made by cutting lines into a metal plate with a burin, filling the grooves with ink, wiping the surface clean and pressing paper onto it. It gives sharp, precise lines.
A work made of two panels, often hinged together.
A large painting done directly on a wall or ceiling.
Short for thismono: a Japanese illustrated handscroll that combines pictures and text to tell a story, unrolled section by section from right to left.
A Spanish word for a folding screen, borrowed from the Japanese ‘byōbu’. thiss were made in colonial Mexico after Japanese screens arrived by trade.
A book or document written by hand. Before printing, every book was a this, and luxury ones were richly painted.
Fine, smooth parchment made from calfskin, used for the best medieval manuscripts. Some luxury manuscripts were dyed purple, the royal color.
Painting on plaster on a wall or ceiling. In true (buon) this the plaster is still wet; in this secco it is dry.
A painting whose main subject is the sea.
Photography that records images as computer data instead of on film, which makes pictures easy to edit and combine. Mariko Mori used digital tools to build Pure Land.
In color woodblock printing, the block carved with the main black outlines. The separate color blocks are cut to line up with it.
An intaglio printmaking method where the artist scratches lines straight into a metal plate with a sharp needle. The scratch throws up a rough edge (burr) that prints soft, velvety lines.
A side panel of an altarpiece, often hinged so it can close over the center panel. thiss were often painted on both sides, with different scenes shothis when open or closed.
A print made by drawing with a greasy crayon on a flat stone or metal plate. The surface is wet, so greasy ink sticks only to the drawing (oil and water don’t mix). Invented about 1796.
Color made by grinding up colored rocks and earth, such as red and yellow ochre or black manganese. The oldest paints.
A technique, used by Cézanne and the Cubists, of leaving edges open so one plane flows into the next, blurring the boundaries between objects and space.

Italian for both ‘drawing’ and ‘design’. The Florentine and Roman belief that great art begins with drawing and careful intellectual planning, praised in artists like Michelangelo. It was debated against Venetian colorito.
A single sheet or page of a manuscript or book. thiss are numbered with r (recto, the front) and v (verso, the back).
A style of contemporary Aboriginal Australian painting built up from many dabs or dots of color, connected to body painting and ceremonial designs about ancestral land.
A Japanese technique of dropping ink or paint onto an area that is still wet, so the colors pool and blur into soft, mottled patches.

A single painting or sheet of calligraphy made to be mounted in an album, rather than to illustrate the text of a book. Persian, Mughal and Ottoman collectors gathered such pages into albums called muraqqa.
The soft gray carbon inside an ordinary pencil, used for drawing.
A flat panel, often of metal or stone, decorated with relief and attached to a wall.
Carved directly out of a natural cliff or rock face, rather than built from separate blocks.
An ordinary object, natural or manufactured, that an artist uses in a work of art, either as is or changed. Often called by the French ‘objet trouvé’.
Art made by tying, gluing or sewing feathers onto a backing to create garments, headdresses or images. Rare, bright feathers were a sign of high rank in Polynesia and Mesoamerica.
A carved wooden shrine figure of the Igbo people of Nigeria, with ram’s horns, honoring a man’s right hand, his personal drive and success. A man kept one and made offerings to it.
An elaborate hairstyle. African masks often carve detailed thiss to show beauty, status or the fashions of a time and place.
A likeness of a specific person, showing their appearance, status or character. It can be painted, carved, cast or photographed, and it can be naturalistic or symbolic.
A soft, porous rock formed from compacted volcanic ash. Rapa Nui’s moai were carved from it. The volcanic stone of the Roman catacombs, often called tufa, is geologically this too.

The crossing balance in a contrapposto figure: the tense, working parts sit diagonally across from each other, and so do the relaxed parts. In the Doryphoros the straight weight-bearing right leg pairs with the bent, spear-holding left arm.
The threads woven crosswise over and under the warp threads on a loom. In tapestry, colored thiss make the picture.
A hard, dark gray sandstone. Egyptian sculptors used it for royal statues and objects because it could be polished to a smooth finish.
A female mask of the Chokwe people (Angola and Congo) honoring the ideal woman and the founding ancestress. Ironically, it is danced by men, dressed as women.
Built from standard, interchangeable parts. The Terracotta Warriors were assembled from mold-made legs, torsos, arms and heads, then finished by hand so each looks individual.
The large triangular bone at the base of the spine; the name is Latin for ‘sacred bone’. The Tequixquiac this, from an extinct camelid, was carved so it looks like the head of a dog or coyote.
A huge Assyrian guardian figure with a bull or lion body, eagle wings and a bearded human head, placed at palace gateways. Some have five legs so they look correct from the front and the side.
Pressing or punching small patterns into a surface, such as gold leaf, leather or metal, with small tools. The gold backgrounds of the Golden Haggadah are tooled.
A hard, gray volcanic stone. Borobudur in Java was built from enormous numbers of this blocks, and its long relief panels are carved into them.
A paste of lime or gypsum, sand and water that hardens as it dries. Used to coat walls (for fresco), to model details and to make casts.
Making a sculpture by removing material, carving or cutting it away from a block. The opposite of additive.
On a loom, the threads stretched lengthwise and held tight. The weft threads are woven over and under them.

Sculpture made from soft materials like vinyl, cloth or foam, often making hard everyday things floppy. Claes Oldenburg is its best-known maker; Lipstick (Ascending) first had a soft vinyl tip that was pumped up with air.
A cast taken directly from a living person’s face, usually in plaster, so a sculptor can get a precise likeness. Houdon made a this of George Washington at Mount Vernon in 1785.
Sculpture that is fully three-dimensional and meant to be seen from all sides, not attached to a background like relief.
A sculpture of a person’s head, neck and usually shoulders and upper chest.

A helmet mask of the Sande society of the Mende (Sierra Leone), worn by women leaders when initiating girls into adulthood, one of the few African masks danced by women. Its neck rolls signal health and beauty. Also called a Bundu mask.
Carving or metalwork pierced with holes so you can see through it, making a lacy pattern.
The small cubes of stone, glass or tile used to make a mosaic. Singular: tessera. Glass this backed with gold leaf make glittering gold backgrounds.
A mask of the Kwakwaka’wakw and other Northwest Coast peoples that opens with strings during a dance to reveal a second face inside, showing a being changing from animal to human or ancestor.
Art made for one particular place, so that its meaning depends on that location. Moving it would change or destroy the work.
Shaping wood with knives, adzes and chisels. Many of the 250 works from Africa and the Pacific are carved wood, often from a single piece.
A tree whose inner bark is beaten into barkcloth (tapa) across Polynesia, and made into paper in East Asia.
Decorating cloth by stitching designs onto it with colored thread.
A hand-held wooden ‘memory board’ of the Luba people (Congo), covered in beads, shells and metal pins. Trained experts touched it while reciting history, king lists and sacred knowledge.
The hard, creamy-white material of elephant tusks (and some other animal teeth), prized for fine carving. Today the this trade is mostly banned to protect elephants.
A hard sandstone found in southern England. Stonehenge’s huge outer circle and trilithons are thiss; the smaller ‘bluestones’ came from Wales.
Reddish-brown baked clay used for sculpture, pottery and roof tiles. Italian for ‘baked earth’.

A flat jade disk with a round hole in the center, made in China from Neolithic times on and often buried with the elite. Later Chinese texts link the this with heaven; on Lady Dai’s funeral banner two dragons loop through one.
A light, strong, silvery metal that does not rust. Gehry covered the Guggenheim Bilbao in thin this panels that shimmer like fish scales.
An embroidery method in which threads are laid across the surface of the cloth and tied down with small stitches. The Bayeux Tapestry fills its figures with laid-and-couched work.
The pose of a Roman general or emperor with one arm raised, addressing his troops. The word is Latin for ‘speech’ or ‘address’.
A brilliant deep blue pigment made from ground lapis lazuli from Afghanistan. Before a synthetic version was invented in the 1820s it could cost more than gold; Vermeer used it lavishly.
A carved wooden post that holds up the roof of a veranda (covered porch) of a palace. The Yoruba sculptor Olowe of Ise carved posts with figures that seem to carry the roof.
A small statue, usually of a person or animal, often small enough to hold in your hand.
A technique where thin metal strips are attached to a surface to make little walled cells (cloisons), which are then filled with colored enamel or cut stones like garnets.
Wax masks of a noble Roman family’s ancestors, kept in the atrium of the house and worn by actors in family funeral processions. They may help explain the stern realism of Roman portrait busts.
A small round box with a lid, used for jewelry, cosmetics or perfume. Plural: pyxides.
Sculpture that projects from a flat background instead of standing free. It can be low (bas-this), high, or sunken.
A way to cast metal. The artist makes a model in wax, covers it in clay, and heats it so the wax melts out (‘is lost’). Molten metal is poured into the empty space, and the clay is broken away.
The shiny, rainbow-colored inner layer of some seashells, cut and inlaid into wood, lacquer or paintings.
Glowing, gas-filled glass tubes bent into lines or letters, as in signs. Paik outlined the U.S. states in this in Electronic Superhighway.
A staged scene in which figures are arranged and frozen as if in a painting. Yinka Shonibare’s The Swing (after Fragonard) turns a painting into a three-dimensional this you can walk around.
A soft, pale, slightly see-through stone that is easy to carve and polish.
A three-dimensional work made by putting together found or readymade objects and materials. The 3D cousin of collage.
Showing a person on horseback. this statues of rulers were a classic way to show power and command.
Any object made of clay and hardened by heat (firing). Includes earthenware, terracotta, stoneware and porcelain.
Seathis and turtle this used as a material for inlay, ornament, beads and, in the Pacific, even whole masks.
A mask made of cloth, beads or fiber that is pulled over the whole head like a hood. The Bamileke Aka elephant mask is a beaded this.
A metal made by melting two or more metals together, such as bronze (copper plus tin) or brass (copper plus zinc). Inka metalworkers used gold and silver thiss.
A carved wooden figure from Rarotonga (Cook Islands) with a god’s head at the top, wrapped in a huge roll of tapa cloth. Christian missionaries removed and destroyed many wrappings.
The modernist belief that a material should look like itself: stone should feel like stone, and wood should show its grain. Brancusi’s direct carving follows it.
A tropical plant whose long leaves are dried, split and woven into mats, baskets and sails across the Pacific. Fine this mats are valuable gifts.
Covering a surface with a thin layer of gold, as gold leaf or gold paint. Something gilded is called ‘gilt’.
A fine white clay, the key ingredient of porcelain. Its name comes from Gaoling, a hill near the porcelain city of Jingdezhen in China.
Animal this used as a material for carving or shaping. One of the earliest art materials.
Fine, hard, white ceramic made from a special clay (kaolin) fired at very high heat. It can be so thin light glows through it. First perfected in China.
Carving straight into stone or wood without first making a clay model to copy, letting the material guide the shape. Championed by early modern sculptors like Brancusi.
Inlay of cut and polished colored stones fitted together into marble to make flowers, vines and patterns. Italian for ‘hard stone’.
A broken piece of pottery, also called a potthis. Archaeologists use thiss to date sites and identify cultures, because fired clay survives well.
Relief where the figures are cut into the surface, so their highest points are level with (or below) the flat surface around them. Common in Egypt; it holds up well in bright sun.
Robert Rauschenberg’s name for his works that this painting with real objects attached to the surface, part painting and part sculpture. Jaune Quick-to-See Smith’s Trade follows the idea.
A stone head with a long peg (tenon) on the back so it can be set into a wall. At Chavín de Huántar they show a human face changing step by step into a snarling jaguar.

A Greek vase-painting technique where the background is painted black and the figures are left the red-orange color of the clay, with details drawn in with a brush. It allowed more lifelike detail than black-figure.
A hollow form into which liquid material like clay, plaster or metal is pressed or poured to make a shape. thiss let makers produce many matching parts.
A likeness of a person, especially a sculpture on a tomb or a figure used in a ritual. Among the cast-gold pieces hanging from the Golden Stool are eﬀigies of enemy rulers the Asante defeated.
A type of steel that forms a stable, rusty-orange outer layer, which protects the metal from further rust. Popular for outdoor sculpture since the 1960s.
A mask that covers the whole head like a helmet, rather than just the face. The Sande society’s sowei (Bundu) mask is a famous example.
A gold-colored metal made by mixing copper and zinc. It can be hammered or cast, and it shines like gold when polished.

A carving style in which thin cloth seems wet and clings to the body, revealing it while forming rippling folds. It began on the Parthenon sculptures and continued in Hellenistic works like the Winged Victory.
Video sent live from a camera straight to monitors in the same place, without broadcasting it. Nam June Paik used it so viewers suddenly see themselves on screen inside the work.
Shaping a sculpture by cutting, chiseling or scraping material away from a block of stone, wood, ivory or jade.
Sculpture made to be part of a building, such as figures on a roof, carved bands along a wall, or a carved panel over a doorway.
Latin for ‘worm-like work’. The finest Roman mosaic technique, using tiny tesserae laid in curving rows that follow the outlines of forms, allowing painterly shading.
A picture or pattern made by setting many small pieces of colored stone, glass or tile (tesserae) into plaster or cement.

Native American decoration made from dyed porcupine quills, flattened and sewn or wrapped onto hide or birchbark. Glass beadwork, like that on the Lenape bandolier bag (No. 163), largely replaced it once trade beads were plentiful.
A resist-dye technique: cloth is tied, folded or bound so parts of it don’t take the dye, creating patterns. Faith Ringgold framed Dancing at the Louvre with thisd fabric.
Rubbing a surface hard with a smooth stone or tool to make it shiny. Potters burnish clay before firing to make it gleam; printmakers burnish metal plates to smooth out areas and lighten them.
Art installed in public spaces, like parks, plazas or streets, where anyone can see it, often paid for by governments or communities.

A Japanese technique (yosegi-zukuri) for making large wooden statues from many separately carved blocks fitted together, which makes them lighter and less likely to crack. Unkei and Kaikei’s Nio guardians at Todai-ji were made this way.
Delicate ornament made from very fine twisted wires of gold or silver soldered into lacy patterns.
Making a sculpture by pouring a liquid material, such as molten metal or plaster, into a mold and letting it harden. Many copies can come from one mold.
Shaping a soft material like clay or wax with hands and tools to make a sculpture. It is additive, building form up.
Threads or strands from plants (cotton, bark, pandanus, coconut husk) or animals (wool, camelid hair, silk) used for weaving, netting, tying and binding.
Painting a sculpture or building in many colors. Greek and Roman marble statues were originally painted; the color has mostly worn off. Adjective: polychrome.
Portable prehistoric art, such as carved figurines or decorated stones that could be carried, as opposed to paintings fixed to cave walls. Also called portable art.
An upright post, usually round, that holds up a roof or beam. A classical this has three parts: a base at the bottom, a long shaft, and a decorated capital on top.

Decoration attached to the surface of a building rather than growing out of its structure. In Postmodern architecture, like Venturi’s House in New Castle County, flat cut-out columns and arches are openly stuck on as signs.
A Persian-style garden divided into four parts by water channels or paths, often seen as an image of paradise, which the Qur’an describes as having four rivers.
A dome built over an oval rather than a circle, favored in the Baroque for its sense of movement and tension. Borromini’s San Carlo has one.
A tomb-like monument that does not hold the body. In the Taj Mahal, the thiss of Mumtaz Mahal and Shah Jahan sit in the main hall, while their real graves lie in a crypt below.
A small dome, often on top of a roof or a larger dome, sometimes used as a lookout or to let in light.
A flat, level step cut into a slope or built up as a platform. Inka farmers carved mountains into thiss; Hatshepsut’s temple and Borobudur rise in thiss.
A prehistoric circular area surrounded by a ditch and a bank of earth, sometimes with stones or timber posts set inside. Stonethis is the famous example.

A walkway that goes around something, such as the apse of a church or the central space of a round shrine. It let pilgrims circle relics without disturbing services. The Dome of the Rock has two ambulatories around its sacred rock.
Walls made of stone blocks cut and smoothed so precisely that they fit tightly without mortar. Inka ashlar is so exact that a knife blade cannot slip between the stones.

In Chinese and Japanese wooden buildings, interlocking wooden blocks and arms (called dougong in Chinese) that sit on top of the columns and carry the heavy, overhanging tile roof. The more elaborate the brackets, the higher the building’s rank.
The top step of a Greek temple’s platform, the floor that the columns stand on.
A fortified stronghold, often on high ground, protecting a city’s palace and temples. Sargon II’s palace at Dur Sharrukin stood within a walled this guarded by lamassu.
One of the square panels in a Doric frieze, set between triglyphs. thiss were often carved with relief sculpture, such as battles on the Parthenon.
The top, projecting layer of an entablature, or any strong ledge that sticks out along the top of a wall. It throws rainwater away from the wall and gives a building a firm ‘lid’.
A long, shelf-like slot cut into a catacomb wall to hold a body, sealed with a slab or tiles. Plural: loculi.
The dining hall of a monastery or convent. Leonardo painted the Last Supper on the this wall of Santa Maria delle Grazie, so the friars ate with Christ and the apostles.
A monumental entrance gateway tower in the outer walls of a Hindu temple complex, especially in south India and Cambodia.
A hall or porch in a Hindu temple where worshippers gather before approaching the shrine. Larger temples have a series of them leading to the garbhagriha.
An arrangement of five things: four at the corners of a square and one in the middle, like the five dots on dice. Angkor Wat’s five towers form one, standing for the five peaks of Mount Meru.
A storehouse for grain. The Conical Tower at Great Zimbabwe may imitate a Shona this, possibly as a symbol of the ruler’s generosity and wealth.

In the style of Andrea Palladio, a 16th-century Italian architect who designed symmetrical villas with temple-like porticoes and pediments. His style spread to England and America, including Jefferson’s Monticello.
Ceramic tiles covered in a shiny, colored glassy coat, used to cover walls and domes in bright patterns. Persian and Ottoman builders were masters of it.
A skeleton of steel beams and columns that carries a building’s whole weight, so walls do not have to. It made skyscrapers possible in the late 1800s.
A half-moon-shaped wall area under an arch or vault, often filled with a painting or relief. The School of Athens fills one.
A medieval church built to handle crowds of travelers visiting holy relics. It has wide aisles, an ambulatory, and radiating chapels so people can flow past the relics without disturbing Mass.
One of the curved bands that frame the tympanum of a church doorway, often carved with small figures.
A round building or round room, usually covered by a dome.

In East Asian architecture, a large rectangular wooden building on a stone platform, used for worship or government. The Great Buddha this at Todai-ji and the this of Supreme Harmony in the Forbidden City are famous examples.

A Japanese Zen garden (in Japanese, karesansui, said kah-raysahn-SOO-ee) made of raked gravel and carefully placed rocks, with little or no water or plants. The gravel suggests water and the rocks suggest islands or mountains. It is for looking at and meditating on, not walking through.
Stonework of many-sided blocks cut to fit together like a jigsaw puzzle, without mortar. The Inka walls of Cusco and Saqsaywaman are famous examples.
Buildings made mainly of earth, including mud brick, rammed earth and mud plaster. It stays cool in hot climates but must be repaired regularly.
A wide window with a large fixed glass pane in the middle and a narrow window on each side that can open. A steel frame made it possible.
A vault supported by a framework of thin stone arches (ribs) that cross diagonally. The ribs carry the weight to specific points, so the panels between them can be thinner and lighter.

Tiny, deliberate bends in a building that correct tricks of the eye. On the Parthenon the floor bulges up, the columns lean slightly inward, and the shafts swell, so the whole temple looks perfectly straight and alive.
A tall, often lacy stone crest built on the roof of a Maya temple to make it look taller and to display painted or sculpted images.
A ribbed, disk-shaped stone that caps the shikhara of a north Indian temple, shaped like a segmented fruit.

A sealed room in an Egyptian tomb holding a statue of the dead person for their ka (life force), sometimes with a small slit so the statue could ‘see’ offerings. The Seated Scribe probably stood in a tomb chapel or this.
A garden laid out in strict geometric patterns, with straight paths, clipped hedges, pools and fountains arranged on an axis. Versailles’ gardens show the king controlling even nature.
Latin for ‘net work’. Ancient Roman wall facing made of small square stones set diagonally in a diamond net pattern. Alberti imitated it at the base of the Palazzo Rucellai.
A curved structure that spans an opening. Wedge-shaped stones (voussoirs) press against each other and pass the weight down to the sides. thises can span wider gaps than a single beam.
The direction of Mecca, which Muslims face when they pray. The this wall of a mosque faces Mecca and holds the mihrab.
A pier with several thinner shafts attached to it. Each shaft lines up with an arch or rib above, so the wall’s structure reads as a set of lines rising to the vault.
An Ottoman complex built around a mosque, which could also include schools, a hospital, a soup kitchen, baths and the founder’s tomb.
A block with three vertical grooves that alternates with metopes in a Doric frieze. It probably recalls the ends of wooden beams in earlier wooden temples.
Bundles of palm wood that stick out from the walls of West African mud buildings. They act as built-in scaffolding for the yearly re-plastering and also decorate the walls.
The earliest type of mosque: a large prayer hall filled with rows of columns, usually beside an open courtyard. It can be enlarged simply by adding more rows of columns.
Pieces of colored glass held together by strips of lead to form pictures in a window. In Gothic churches the colored light was meant to feel like heavenly light.
Louis Sullivan’s famous idea that a building’s shape should come from what it is used for. It became a motto of modern architecture.
A large open public square in a town or ceremonial center, used for gatherings, markets or ritual.
Greek for ‘city of the dead’. A large ancient cemetery, often with tombs laid out like streets and houses.
The wedge-shaped stone at the very top center of an arch. It is the last stone put in, and it locks the others in place.
A long side passage that runs parallel to the nave of a church, separated from it by a row of columns or piers.
A rounded roof shaped like half a sphere (or taller, like an onion). A this is basically an arch spun in a circle.
Mies van der Rohe’s motto: simple, stripped-down design with no extra ornament is more powerful. Robert Venturi later joked back, ‘less is a bore.’
A tall platform that an Etruscan or Roman temple stands on, with stairs only at the front. It makes the temple face one way, unlike a Greek temple you can approach from all sides.
An arch that curves in past its widest point before meeting its supports, like a horseshoe. A hallmark of Islamic Spain.

Iron melted and poured into molds. Strong and cheap in the 1800s, it was used for building frames and for intricate ornament, like the swirling decoration over the entrance of Sullivan’s Carson, Pirie, Scott store.
A large hall whose roof is held up by many rows of columns. The word means ‘under columns.’ Ancient Egyptians, Persians and early Islamic mosque builders all used it.
One repeated section of a building, marked off by columns, piers, or vault ribs. A Gothic nave is a row of identical thiss.
Brilliant ceramic tiles made in the Ottoman town of Iznik (Turkey), famous for vivid blue, turquoise and tomato-red flowers on white. Used inside Sinan’s mosques.
A temple designed as a model of a sacred mountain, usually Mount Meru, the center of the universe in Hindu and Buddhist belief, with towers or terraces rising to a high center.
Design in which computer formulas generate and adjust a building’s shapes. It is associated with the flowing, curving forms of Zaha Hadid.
A zigzag or V-shaped pattern. At Great Zimbabwe, a chevron band runs along the top of the Great Enclosure wall.
A very tall building made possible by steel frames and elevators. It started in Chicago and New York in the late 1800s.
A precise line drawing, such as a plan, elevation or section, used to design or record a building. Julie Mehretu layers drawings of stadiums and buildings into her paintings.
A carved stone outcrop at Inka sites, thought to be linked to the sun and the calendar. The name is often translated as ‘hitching post of the sun.’
The main church of a bishop’s district, holding the bishop’s throne (the ‘cathedra’). Medieval thiss were the biggest, most expensive buildings in their towns.
The triangular upper part of a wall at the end of a pitched roof. In classical buildings, a decorated this is a pediment. Venturi’s House in New Castle County hides behind a big farmhouse this.
A slight swelling in the middle of a column shaft. It makes columns look straight and strong rather than pinched, because perfectly straight columns can look thin in the middle from a distance.
The dining room of a Roman house, named for its three couches, arranged in a U, where diners reclined. The Etruscan Tomb of the this is named for its painted banquet scenes.
A ceiling made by extending a round arch in a straight line, like a tunnel. Also called a tunnel vault. It is heavy and pushes outward along its whole length, so the walls below must be thick.

The top of an Egyptian column carved to look like a bundle of papyrus plants, either open like a flower or closed like a bud. It turns a stone hall into a symbolic marsh, where Egyptians believed creation began.
The fermented mud mixture used to build and plaster mosques and houses in Mali. At Djenné it is re-applied every year.
A tall, rounded, finger-like tower of a Thai or Khmer-style temple, descended from Khmer prasats like those at Angkor Wat.
A Chinese system for siting and arranging buildings in harmony with the land, water and cosmic forces. The Forbidden City faces south, with protective hills to the north.
Everything that sits on top of the columns in a classical building and below the roof: the architrave, the frieze, and the cornice, stacked in that order.
Sun-dried brick made from clay, sand and straw, or the mud mortar and plaster made from the same mix. Used from Africa to the American Southwest.
An outer covering or skin attached to a building’s frame, such as terra cotta, glass, stone or titanium.
A tomb with one or more rooms built or cut underground, often decorated like a house for the dead. Etruscan families were buried in painted thiss.
A massive, tower-flanked front block at the west end of Carolingian and Ottonian churches, holding an entrance, chapels and an upper gallery.
A long row of columns spaced at regular intervals, usually holding up a roof or entablature.
A round opening at the top of a dome that lets in light (and rain). The Pantheon’s this is about 30 feet wide and is the only light source inside.
A door, window or niche that is narrower at the top than at the bottom. The Inka used it because it is very stable in earthquakes.
Columns that look like early versions of the Greek Doric column: plain, fluted and many-sided. Hatshepsut’s mortuary temple has them, about a thousand years before the first Greek Doric temples.
An underground space. At the Colosseum, the this under the arena floor held tunnels, cages and lifts for animals and fighters.
A huge stepped platform of mud brick built in ancient Mesopotamia (modern Iraq), with a temple on top. Raising the temple high lifted it closer to the gods and made it visible across the flat plain.
Stone walls built without any mortar. The stones hold together through careful fitting and their own weight.
A building structure made of a wooden skeleton of posts and beams, with the walls only filling the gaps. Traditional Chinese and Japanese temples and palaces use it.
An enclosed garden courtyard surrounded by a covered walkway, part of a monastery or convent. The Spanish built a convent with a this on top of the Inka sun temple in Cusco.
A dome built on a framework of crossing arches or ribs, which often form a star pattern. The dome in front of Córdoba’s mihrab is a famous early example.
A temple at the edge of the Nile floodplain where a pharaoh’s funeral began, linked by a causeway to the mortuary temple beside his pyramid.
Pieces taken from older buildings and reused in new ones, such as columns, capitals or carvings. It saves work and can also show victory over, or connection to, the past.
Bricks made of mud (often mixed with straw) and dried in the sun instead of fired in a kiln. Cheap and easy where stone and wood are scarce, but it wears away and needs constant repair.
Le Corbusier’s phrase for a modern house: an eﬀicient, functional object designed like a machine around how people actually live.
The path for circumambulation, the ritual of walking clockwise around a holy object like a stupa or a temple’s sanctum. At Borobudur, pilgrims circle and climb through the terraces toward the top.
An arch whose inner edge is cut into a series of curves or ‘lobes’ like a scalloped edge. Used near the mihrab at Córdoba, sometimes in interlacing layers.
A large vaulted hall that is walled on three sides and completely open on the fourth, usually facing a courtyard. A standard feature of Persian and later Islamic architecture.
Originally a long Roman public hall used for law courts and business, with a central nave, side aisles and an apse at the end. Early Christians copied this plan for their churches.
An outside wall that can be designed freely, with windows placed anywhere, because it carries no weight. One of Le Corbusier’s Five Points.
A modern architecture style of the 1920s to 1960s, spread worldwide: boxy shapes, flat roofs, white walls or glass skins, steel and concrete frames, and no ornament.
A very large stone used to build a monument, usually without mortar. ‘thisic’ describes structures made of such stones, mostly from prehistoric times.
A row of columns surrounding a building or a courtyard. A Greek temple like the Parthenon is wrapped in a this; a Roman house has a this garden, a courtyard ringed by columns.
A private townhouse of a wealthy Roman family. It turned inward around an atrium and a peristyle garden, with few windows on the street.

A paste, such as mud, lime or cement, spread between stones or bricks to bind them. Mesa Verde’s sandstone blocks sit in mud this; Inka builders famously used none, fitting stones so tightly they did not need it.
The small, dark, innermost shrine of a Hindu temple, where the main image of the god is kept. Only priests may enter.
A Maya staircase whose steps are carved with writing (glyphs) and images that record a ruler’s history and deeds.
A formal garden of flat, level beds laid out in symmetrical patterns, often edged with low clipped hedges and gravel paths, as at Versailles.
A Buddhist monument shaped like a solid dome or mound that holds relics of the Buddha or a holy teacher. You cannot go inside; instead, worshippers walk around it clockwise.
A building laid out around a central point, so all sides are equal or nearly so, such as a circle, square, octagon or Greek cross. It usually has a dome over the middle.
A church or shrine built over the grave of a martyr or at a site linked to Christ’s life, often with a central plan. San Vitale honors the martyr Saint Vitalis.
A building laid out as an eight-sided shape. San Vitale and the Dome of the Rock both use octagons, a shape halfway between a square (earth) and a circle (heaven).
The tall, curving tower that rises over the garbhagriha of a north Indian Hindu temple. Clusters of smaller towers climb toward it like a mountain range, evoking Mount Meru, home of the gods.

A great audience hall of the ancient Persian kings, a hypostyle hall where the king received visitors and gifts. The one at Persepolis stood on a raised platform reached by staircases carved with processions of tribute bearers.
A large mosque where a whole community gathers for the Friday noon prayer and sermon. Also called a Friday mosque or, in Persian, masjid-e jameh.
A building front that curves in and out in waves instead of being flat. Borromini’s San Carlo is the classic Baroque example.
A tall rectangular frame around an iwan’s arched opening, which makes the entrance look bigger and grander. Persian and Mughal buildings use it; the Taj Mahal has one on each side.
A tall, thin, four-sided stone pillar that narrows as it rises and ends in a small pyramid point. Egyptian pharaohs set them up in pairs at temple entrances to honor the sun god.
A row of arches held up by columns or piers.
A tall, pointed, cone- or pyramid-shaped structure on top of a tower, especially on a church.
A meeting room attached to a monastery or cathedral, where monks or clergy gathered to discuss business and hear readings.
A sacred area set apart for a god, often walled, that contains temples, altars and offerings.
A building material made by mixing lime, sand, water and rubble that hardens like stone. Romans used it to pour huge curved shapes like domes and vaults, which changed architecture forever.
A gallery or porch that is open on one or more sides, usually with columns or arches, and part of a larger building. It is an indoor-outdoor space for shade and air.
A screened-off area in a mosque near the mihrab, reserved for the ruler to pray in safety and in style.
The solid, hemispherical dome of a stupa, which covers the relics and stands for the dome of heaven or the world mountain.
A building that forms the guarded entrance to a temple or palace compound. Todai-ji’s Great South Gate holds two giant guardian figures.
A sunken square or other shaped panel set into a ceiling or dome. thiss make a dome lighter and decorate it with a grid pattern.

Beautiful writing used as decoration on a building, often Qur’an verses or poetry, carved in stone or stucco or laid in tile and mosaic. On the Taj Mahal the letters get larger near the top so they look the same size from the ground.
An extra block placed between a column’s capital and the arch above it, helping to carry the weight. Used in Byzantine churches like San Vitale.
A thick, solid upright support, usually square or rectangular, bigger and stronger than a column.

A tall, many-storied tower with roofs at each level, found in Buddhist temples in China, Korea and Japan. It grew out of the Indian stupa and often holds relics. Todai-ji once had two huge thiss, now lost.
A school for Islamic religious learning, often attached to a mosque.
A roof that slopes down on all four sides. In China, a double-eaved this (two layers) was reserved for the most important imperial halls.
A round, partly underground room used by Puebloan peoples for ceremonies and meetings. A small hole in the floor (the sipapu) stands for the place where people emerged into this world.
A shallow basin in the floor of a Roman atrium that caught rainwater falling through the opening in the roof above.

An art tradition of the nomads of the Eurasian steppes and of early medieval northern Europe in which animals, such as birds of prey, beasts and fish, are twisted, stretched and woven into patterns on small, portable metal objects.
A Russian movement of about 1915 to the 1930s that wanted art to serve the new Soviet society, using geometric forms, industrial materials, graphic design and photomontage.
An Italian movement founded in 1909 that celebrated speed, machines, cities, technology and even war, showing motion with repeated forms and fractured lines.
Italian art of about 1280 to 1400 that started to move toward the Renaissance, especially in Giotto’s frescoes, which give figures real weight, space around them and human emotion.
Piet Mondrian’s name for his pure abstract style: only straight horizontal and vertical lines, the three primary colors, and black, white and gray. He hoped it would express universal harmony.
A Hindu dynasty of central India, 9th to 13th centuries C.E., which built the temples of Khajuraho with their towering shikharas and dense, sensual sculpture.
Japan’s period from 710 to 794 C.E., when the capital was at Nara and emperors sponsored Buddhism as a state religion, building Todai-ji.
The Abstract Expressionist artists active in New York City in the 1940s and 1950s, such as Pollock, de Kooning and Rothko, who made New York the center of the art world.

Art made in Spain’s American colonies (the viceroyalties of New Spain and Peru) from the 1500s to the early 1800s. It blends European styles with Indigenous materials, ideas and artists, from feather and shell inlay to casta paintings.

Art made by the rules of oﬀicial art schools (academies), like the French Academy, from the 1600s to the 1800s: polished finish, perfect drawing and serious historical or mythological subjects. Shown at the yearly Salon in Paris.
The last Muslim dynasty in Spain, ruling Granada from 1232 until 1492, when it fell to Ferdinand and Isabella. It built the Alhambra palace.
A type of Abstract Expressionism using large areas of flat or stained color to create calm, immersive, spiritual effects. Frankenthaler poured thinned paint into raw canvas.
Korea’s longest dynasty, 1392 to 1910, guided by Confucian ideals. Oﬀicial portraits of scholars and oﬀicials show them formally and soberly in court dress.
A flowering of African American art, music and literature centered in Harlem, New York, in the 1920s and 1930s, celebrating Black identity, history and culture. Jacob Lawrence grew up in its world.

Japanese for ‘Japanese-style painting’. A style that grew up in the Heian period, with bright colors, high angled views, roofs left off to show interiors, and Japanese stories and places, in contrast to Chinese-style painting.

The broad movement, from roughly the 1860s to the 1970s, of artists rejecting tradition to invent new forms suited to modern life. It includes Impressionism through Abstract Expressionism and the International Style.

Roman art under the emperors, starting with Augustus in 27 B.C.E. It mixes idealized Greek-style portraits of rulers with huge engineering projects in concrete, like the Colosseum and Pantheon, all promoting the emperor’s power.
The approach Gauguin and his circle developed in the late 1880s: flat areas of bold color, strong outlines and simplified forms that combine what the artist saw with memory, feeling and symbols.
A Neolithic culture in the Yangtze River delta of China, about 3300 to 2200 B.C.E., known for finely carved jade objects such as the cong, a square tube with a round hole.

A revolutionary movement started in Paris around 1907 by Picasso and Braque. It breaks objects into flat, geometric pieces and shows them from several angles at once, abandoning single-point perspective.
Art under Charlemagne and his heirs, about 768 to 900 C.E., in France and Germany. It deliberately revived Roman and Early Christian models in manuscripts, metalwork and churches with westworks.

Japan’s period from 794 to 1185 C.E., when the court in Heian (Kyoto) produced refined literature and painting. It ended in civil wars between the Taira and Minamoto clans, the war shown in the later Night Attack scroll.
Work leading up to Cubism, especially Picasso’s Les Demoiselles d’Avignon (1907), which broke figures into flat, angular planes before Cubism was fully developed.
The Muslim dynasty that ruled most of South Asia from 1526 to 1857, mixing Persian, Indian and Islamic traditions. Known for the Taj Mahal and refined, detailed miniature paintings.

Christian art from about 200 to 500 C.E. At first hidden in catacomb paintings with simple symbols, it became public after Christianity was legalized in 313, when churches were built on the basilica plan.
Art, especially in Germany around 1905 to 1925, that distorts form and color to express strong inner emotions such as anxiety, anger or spiritual feeling, rather than show the world accurately.

Japanese woodblock prints and paintings of the Edo period showing the ‘floating world’ of entertainment, actors, beauties and later landscapes. Cheap and popular, they deeply influenced European artists.
Art made with and for a particular community, often through conversations, workshops and shared stories, and shown in that neighborhood rather than only in museums.
The second phase of Cubism (from about 1912). Instead of breaking objects down, artists built pictures up from flat, simpler shapes, brighter colors, and real materials glued on (collage).
‘The Blue Rider,’ a German Expressionist group founded in Munich in 1911 by Kandinsky and Franz Marc, which moved toward spiritual abstraction using color like music.

Art of Sumer, the world’s first civilization of cities, in southern Mesopotamia (modern Iraq), about 3500 to 2000 B.C.E. It includes ziggurats, wide-eyed praying statues and inlaid objects, and it invented writing (cuneiform).

A German art and design school (1919 to 1933) that joined art, craft and industry. It taught clean, functional, geometric design and shaped modern architecture and furniture. Mies van der Rohe was its last director.
