A movement launched in 1924 that explored dreams, the unconscious mind and strange combinations of images, inspired by Freud’s ideas.
Roman art from 509 to 27 B.C.E., when Rome was a republic governed by elected oﬀicials. Portraits of older men are ‘veristic’: brutally realistic, showing wrinkles to signal wisdom and service.

The seafaring culture, about 1500 to 500 B.C.E., that first settled the islands of the western Pacific. It is known for pottery decorated with stamped and incised patterns, many later found in Polynesian tattoo and tapa designs.
Art of the Franks under the this kings (about 481 to 751 C.E.) in what is now France and Germany, known for jeweled metalwork such as brooches (fibulae) with garnets and animal shapes.
The peak of the Italian Renaissance, about 1495 to 1520 (longer in Venice). Leonardo, Michelangelo, Raphael and Titian created balanced, monumental, idealized works.
French for ‘courtly party’. A Rococo type of painting showing elegant aristocrats flirting and amusing themselves in dreamy parks and gardens.
A light, playful style of about 1720 to 1780, mostly in France. Pastel colors, curving lines, frothy decoration and flirty scenes of aristocrats at leisure.

Art of about 1886 to 1905 by painters who began with Impressionism but went further in their own directions: Van Gogh (emotional color), Gauguin (flat symbolic color), Cézanne (solid geometric structure), Seurat (dots of color).

The New Stone Age, beginning around 10,000 to 8000 B.C.E. in the Near East and later elsewhere, when people started farming, raising animals and living in villages. It brought pottery, polished stone tools and huge stone monuments.
Greek art of about 480 to 323 B.C.E., centered on Athens. It aims for ideal balance and calm: perfect human bodies in natural poses (contrapposto), harmonious proportions and the Parthenon.
A movement from the 1970s on that rejects Modernism’s belief in purity and progress. It mixes styles, quotes the past, uses irony and questions ideas of originality and identity.
Egypt before and around the time its first kings united Upper and Lower Egypt, about 3000 B.C.E. The Narmer Palette already shows the conventions Egyptian art kept for 3,000 years.
Art and attitudes that attack the very idea of art: its skill, beauty, museums and market. Dada artists, above all Marcel Duchamp with his readymades, made this to question what counts as art at all.

A Mesoamerican civilization of southern Mexico and Central America, at its height about 250 to 900 C.E. this city-states built pyramid temples with roof combs and carved stone reliefs with hieroglyphic writing recording rulers’ histories.

The period from about 200 to 600 C.E., when the Roman world was turning Christian. Art becomes less naturalistic and more symbolic, with crowded or flattened figures, and Christian art begins in catacombs and basilicas.

The many painters across Europe in the early 1600s who copied Caravaggio’s style: harsh light against deep darkness, ordinary-looking people and closeup, real-life drama. Caravaggio’s Calling of Saint Matthew (No. 85) shows the model they followed.

Italian art of about 1520 to 1600, after the High Renaissance. Figures are stretched and twisted, colors are strange, space is crowded or unclear, and the mood is tense: elegance and artificiality over balance.

European art of about 500 to 1000 C.E., after the fall of Rome, made by peoples such as the Franks, Anglo-Saxons and Irish. Much of it is portable metalwork and illuminated manuscripts with dense interlaced patterns.
The Native American culture region along the Pacific coast of Canada and Alaska, home to peoples like the Kwakwaka’wakw, known for carved masks, totem poles and potlatch ceremonies.
Large artworks, from the 1960s on, that fill or transform a whole room or site, so viewers walk into and experience them.
The first main phase of Cubism (about 1909 to 1912). Objects are broken into many small, overlapping facets in a narrow range of browns and grays, so the subject is hard to read.
Japan’s period from 1185 to 1333, when samurai warlords (shoguns) took power. Art became more realistic and energetic, from narrative war scrolls to muscular guardian sculptures.
A short movement in France (about 1905 to 1908), led by Henri Matisse, using wild, bright, unnatural colors and loose brushwork to express feeling.
One of the Three Kingdoms of ancient Korea (57 B.C.E. to 935 C.E.), later ruling a unified Korea. Its royal tombs held spectacular gold crowns shaped like trees and antlers.
Renaissance painting in Venice, led by artists like Titian, which stressed rich color, soft light and the texture of oil paint more than precise drawing.
The dynasty that ruled Iran from 1501 to 1736 and made Shia Islam the state religion. Its court produced dazzling illustrated manuscripts, carpets and tiled buildings.
Art in which the work is a live action by the artist, sometimes with the audience, rather than an object. It became a major form from the 1960s on.
Art of the German emperors named Otto and their successors, about 919 to 1024 C.E. It produced massive churches, bronze doors and solemn manuscripts that bridge Carolingian and Romanesque art.

An art and culture movement that mixes African and African diaspora history and myth with science fiction, technology and imagined futures, to picture Black life beyond the limits of the past and present.

Japan’s period from 1615 to 1868, under the Tokugawa shoguns in Edo (Tokyo), when the country was largely closed to the outside world. A wealthy merchant class enjoyed Rinpa painting and ukiyo-e woodblock prints.
European art and architecture of about 1000 to 1150 C.E. Churches have thick walls, round arches, barrel vaults, small windows and sculpted portals, often built along pilgrimage roads.

The 1600s in the Dutch Republic, a rich Protestant trading nation. Artists sold to middle-class buyers on an open market, painting portraits, still lifes, landscapes and everyday scenes in exquisite detail.

Greek art after Alexander the Great, 323 to 31 B.C.E., spread across a huge territory from Egypt to Asia. It is dramatic and emotional, shows twisting motion, and includes real people: the old, the poor and the suffering.

Buddhist art of Gandhara (today’s Pakistan and Afghanistan), about the first to eighth centuries C.E., which blended Indian Buddhism with Greek and Roman sculpture, giving the Buddha wavy hair and toga-like robes.
Art of Babylon in Mesopotamia. The Old this period (about 1900 to 1600 B.C.E.) under King Hammurabi produced the famous carved law code; a later Neo-this empire flourished in the 600s B.C.E.
The early Tibetan kingdom (7th to 9th centuries C.E.) that brought Buddhism to Tibet. Its king Songtsen Gampo is linked to the arrival of the Jowo Rinpoche statue in Lhasa.

Art of the thiss, Arab traders who controlled desert caravan routes and built the city of Petra (Jordan), about 400 B.C.E. to 106 C.E. They carved huge tomb facades into cliffs, mixing Greek and Roman forms with local taste.
Belief in only one god, as in Judaism, Christianity and Islam, and briefly in Akhenaten’s Egypt.
The fig tree under which the Buddha meditated and reached enlightenment. In early Buddhist art a tree can stand in for the Buddha himself.
A Maya ritual in which rulers and nobles drew their own blood, for example through the tongue, as an offering to gods and to call up ancestors in visions.
Life after death. Belief in an this drove huge amounts of art: tombs, coﬀins, grave goods and guardian figures meant to help or protect the dead.
The scene of Jesus’ body being carried to and laid in his tomb after the Crucifixion.
An Egyptian symbol shaped like a cross with a loop on top, meaning ‘life’. Gods hold it to give life to the king.
A small shrine or carved image set up in a private home for family worship. The relief of Akhenaton, Nefertiti and their daughters was a this honoring the royal family and the sun god Aten.
Japan’s native religion, honoring kami: spirits found in nature, places and ancestors. It coexists with Buddhism in Japan.
A crown with stacked pairs of horns, worn only by gods in Mesopotamian art. It tells you the figure is divine, like Shamash on the Code of Hammurabi.
Greek goddess of love and beauty, called Venus by the Romans. She was born from sea foam, and Julius Caesar’s family (including Augustus) claimed to descend from her.
A sacred mountain spirit in Andean belief. Inka sites were laid out to frame views of these holy peaks.
Jesus’ final meal with his twelve apostles before his arrest. He announces that one of them (Judas) will betray him, and he shares bread and wine, which became the Christian rite of the Eucharist.
A Japanese school of Buddhism (Chan in Chinese) that stresses meditation, simplicity and sudden insight over texts and rituals. this shaped Japanese gardens, ink painting and the tea ceremony.
The Greek goddess who is the Earth itself, mother of the Giants.

The founding father of Judaism, Christianity and Islam. God tested him by asking him to sacrifice his son (Isaac in the Bible, Ishmael in Muslim tradition). Muslims believe he and Ishmael built the Kaaba.
The supreme god of Zoroastrianism, the religion of ancient Persia’s kings, sometimes symbolized by a winged disk.
An upright, rounded pillar that stands for Shiva’s creative energy. It is the main object of worship in most Shiva temples.
The ‘turning the wheel of the law’ gesture, with both hands at the chest forming circles with the fingers. It stands for the Buddha’s first sermon.
The vulture goddess of Upper Egypt and the cobra goddess of Lower Egypt, protectors of the king. Together they stand for the united land.
The Bible story of the Israelites escaping slavery in Egypt, with the ten plagues and the parting of the Red Sea. Also the name of the second book of the Bible.
A mythical bird. In China it is a sign of peace, virtue and the empress, often paired with the dragon; in the West it is reborn from its own ashes.
An Egyptian collection of spells and pictures, written on papyrus and buried with the dead to guide them safely through the underworld to the afterlife.

Greek for ‘ruler of all’. A Byzantine image of Christ as stern ruler of the universe, seen from the chest up, holding a book and blessing with his right hand. It usually fills the central dome of a Byzantine church.
The room in a monastery where monks copied and decorated books by hand.
The art of beautiful handwriting. In Islam it is the most honored art form because it records God’s words. Chinese and Japanese this is also a high art, done with brush and ink.
Focusing and quieting the mind, a central practice in Buddhism and especially in Zen, which seeks enlightenment through direct experience. Zen gardens like Ryoan-ji are aids to quiet contemplation.
In Hinduism, final release from the cycle of rebirth.
In Aboriginal Australian belief, the time and ongoing reality in which ancestral beings created the land, laws and living things. Aboriginal art often maps a person’s this and country.
The Egyptian judgment after death: the heart is weighed against the feather of Ma’at. A light heart (a good life) wins eternal life with Osiris; a heavy one is eaten by Ammit.
One of the twelve chosen followers of Jesus, such as Peter, John, Matthew and Judas. The word means ‘one who is sent out’.
The Greek god of the gentle west wind, often shown as a winged youth puﬀing air.
Aztec moon goddess who led an attack on her mother Coatlicue and was killed and cut apart by her brother Huitzilopochtli. A stone disk of her broken body lay at the foot of the Templo Mayor.
A priest or priestess through whom a god was believed to answer questions about the future, or the sacred place where this happened. Chavín de Huántar may have housed an this at the Lanzón.
The king of ancient Egypt, believed to be a living god, the earthly form of Horus. thiss are shown idealized, calm and young forever.
Greek and Roman god of the sun, light, music, poetry and prophecy, always shown young and handsome. Twin brother of Artemis.
A giant snake in Maya art from whose mouth an ancestor or god appears, called up through bloodletting rituals.

A religion founded in India around 500 B.C.E. by Siddhartha Gautama, the Buddha. It teaches that life is full of suffering caused by desire, and that one can escape the cycle of rebirth by reaching enlightenment. It spread across Asia along trade routes.
In art history, simply the worship and rituals given to a particular god, saint or image, as in ‘this statue’. It does not mean a strange sect.
Belief in many gods, as in ancient Egypt, Greece, Rome, the Aztec Empire and Hinduism.

A holy object: part of a saint’s body (bones, hair) or something they touched (clothing). People believed thiss could heal and protect, so churches that owned them drew crowds of pilgrims. Buddhists also honor thiss of the Buddha.
Honoring dead family members as spirits who still protect and guide the living. Many works are made to house, remember or honor ancestors.
Latin for ‘remember that you will die’. An object or image, like a skull or rotting fruit, that reminds viewers that life is short.
A modern name for the creature on the Narmer Palette that is part serpent (a long snaky neck) and part leopard (the body). Two with intertwined necks form the circle in the palette’s center.
choices: Churning of the Ocean of Milk

questions.prompt: Finding hidden knowledge or the future by ritual means, such as reading objects, casting lots or consulting spirits.
choices: Churning of the Ocean of Milk

questions.prompt: The meditation gesture: both hands rest in the lap, palms up, one on top of the other.
A large seabird that appears on Torres Strait masks and other Pacific art, linked to clans, ancestors and seafaring.
An Arabic title for a respected elder, religious scholar or Sufi master. Also spelled sheikh or shaikh.
Latin for ‘axis of the world’: an imagined central pole connecting earth with heaven and the underworld. A mountain, tree, pillar or temple can play this role.
choices: Churning of the Ocean of Milk

questions.prompt: The Christian ritual of sharing bread and wine in memory of the Last Supper. Catholics believe the bread and wine become Christ’s body and blood. Also called Holy Communion or the Mass.
The bump on top of the Buddha’s head, a sign of his expanded wisdom. It is one of the fixed marks (lakshanas) of a Buddha.
An Afro-Cuban religion blending Yoruba orisha worship with Catholic saints, created by enslaved Africans in Cuba.
An object or feature that identifies a figure, like Zeus’s thunderbolt, a saint’s tool of martyrdom, or Shiva’s drum and flame.
The closed meeting in which the Catholic cardinals elect a new pope. Today it is held in the Sistine Chapel.
The ritual prayer Muslims perform five times a day, facing Mecca. Mosques are designed around it.
Four jars that held a mummy’s removed organs (liver, lungs, stomach, intestines), each lid often shaped as the head of a protective god.
One of the main Hindu gods, the destroyer and re-creator of the universe. He is often shown with a third eye, matted hair, a snake and a trident, and is worshipped as the lingam.
Ibis-headed Egyptian god of writing and wisdom, who records the result of the weighing of the heart.

‘Serpent Skirt’: the Aztec earth goddess, mother of the war god Huitzilopochtli. In the myth, she gave birth to him on Serpent Mountain (Coatepec) as her daughter Coyolxauhqui attacked her. The Templo Mayor re-creates that mountain.
The person who calls Muslims to prayer five times a day, traditionally from a minaret.
‘Serpent Mountain’: the mythical mountain where Huitzilopochtli was born and defeated Coyolxauhqui. The Templo Mayor’s Huitzilopochtli side was built as this.

The Catholic Church’s response to the Reformation, set out at the Council of Trent (1545 to 1563). It wanted art that was clear, emotional and dramatic to pull believers back to Catholicism. This fueled Baroque art.

A full-length cloak, usually black, worn by many women in Iran that covers the head and body but leaves the face open. Shirin Neshat’s Women of Allah photographs use it to explore Iranian women’s identity.
A spirit being of the Hopi and other Pueblo peoples who brings rain and blessings. Masked dancers embody thiss, and carved this dolls teach children about them. Also spelled kachina.
In Hinduism and Buddhism, the endless cycle of birth, death and rebirth that a soul is trapped in until it is released.
A chubby, naked baby boy, often with wings, in European art. The plural is putti. They can be cupids or baby angels.
A work in which characters and events stand for bigger ideas, so the whole thing carries a second, hidden meaning.
Latin for ‘sorrowful mother’. The Virgin Mary grieving over Christ’s suffering and death, a favorite late medieval devotional subject.
The five basic duties of Islam: declaring faith in one God and Muhammad as his prophet, praying five times a day, giving to the poor, fasting in Ramadan, and making the hajj if possible.
Queen of the Greek gods, wife of Zeus, goddess of marriage. The Romans called her Juno; her symbol is the peacock.
A gift given to a god, spirit or ancestor, such as food, flowers, precious objects or a statue.
Greek god of wine, theater and wild celebration, called Bacchus by the Romans. His followers included frenzied women (maenads) and satyrs.
A god or goddess.

A Chinese philosophy based on the teachings of Confucius (551 to 479 B.C.E.), stressing proper behavior, respect for elders and ancestors, loyalty to rulers, and education. It shaped government and family life in China and Korea.
The Inka sun god, ancestor of the Inka ruler. His main temple was the Qorikancha in Cusco.
A figure that holds spiritual power gathered by a ritual specialist, used to protect, heal, seal oaths or punish wrongdoers. The Kongo nkisi n’kondi is the best-known example.
Offering something valuable, such as an animal, food, one’s own blood or even a human life, to a god. Mesoamerican religions held that the gods needed blood to keep the universe running.
A female nature spirit of fertility in Indian art, often shown as a curvy woman clinging to a tree. thiss decorate Buddhist and Hindu monuments.
The mythical battle between the Greek gods and the Giants. Greeks used it as a symbol of civilization (or their own side) defeating chaos and barbarians.
A bundle of rods tied around an axe, carried in front of ancient Roman oﬀicials as a sign of their power. Houdon’s George Washington rests his hand on a this of 13 rods, one for each original state.

Lower-case ‘church’ can mean a building for Christian worship; capital-C ‘the Church’ means the organization of Christianity itself, with its leaders (popes, bishops, priests). The Church was the biggest art patron in Europe for over a thousand years.
In Buddhism, the final state of peace in which desire and suffering are blown out and the cycle of rebirth ends. The Buddha’s death is called his parithis (‘complete this’).
A wheel (dharmachakra) standing for the Buddha’s teaching, which he ‘set in motion’ with his first sermon. Early Buddhist art used it instead of showing the Buddha.
A heavenly female dancer or nymph in Hindu and Buddhist belief. Hundreds of carved thiss decorate the walls of Angkor Wat.
Egyptian sun god, also spelled Re, who sails across the sky by day. He merged with other gods, as in Amun-Re.
Excessive pride that challenges the gods; in Greek myth it is always punished.
In the Shahnama, the first king of the world, who ruled from a mountaintop when people wore leopard skins and had not yet learned cooking or clothing.
A revived form of Confucianism from the Song dynasty onward that blended in ideas from Daoism and Buddhism about the order of the universe. It became the oﬀicial philosophy of Joseon Korea.
A holy place or container for a god, saint, relic or sacred image, from a tiny household altar to a whole building.

The destruction of religious images, or a belief that such images are wrong. The Byzantine Empire banned and destroyed icons in 726 to 843 C.E.; Protestants smashed church images in the 1500s; the Taliban blew up the Bamiyan Buddhas in 2001.
The Christian ritual of washing or dipping in water to welcome a person into the faith and wash away sin.
‘Feathered Serpent’: a major Mesoamerican god of wind, learning and priests, worshipped from Teotihuacan to the Aztecs.
Sanskrit for ‘god-king’. A royal cult in the Khmer Empire that linked the king with a Hindu god, usually Shiva or Vishnu, so that royal temples were also the god’s palaces.
In Hinduism and Buddhism, the idea that your actions decide what happens to you in future lives. Good deeds bring a better rebirth.
Egyptian goddess of love, music and motherhood, shown as a cow or a woman with cow ears or horns.
The Christian belief that one God exists as three persons: the Father, the Son (Jesus) and the Holy Spirit (often shown as a dove).
The longest or shortest day of the year. Many ancient monuments line up with the this sunrise or sunset.
The religion founded in Arabia in the 600s C.E. by the Prophet Muhammad, who Muslims believe received God’s final message, the Qur’an. A follower is a Muslim. this spread quickly from Spain to India.
A glass or metal hanging lamp used in mosques and shrines. It echoes a famous Qur’an verse comparing God’s light to a lamp.
The raising of a person to the status of a god, often shown as being carried up into heaven.
In Egyptian belief, a person’s personality or soul, shown as a bird with a human head. It could fly out of the tomb by day and return at night.
A people’s picture of how the universe is arranged: heaven, earth, underworld, and how they connect. Many buildings and objects are maps of a this.
Greek goddess of wisdom, war strategy and crafts, and protector of Athens. The Romans called her Minerva. She wears a helmet and carries a shield and spear.
A ring or disc of light around a holy person’s head, showing their holiness or (for rulers) their god-given power. Also called a nimbus. Christ’s this often has a cross in it.
In Buddhism, spiritual credit earned by good acts like paying for a temple or image. Rulers and donors sponsored Buddhist art partly to gain this.
A seven-branched lamp that stood in the ancient Temple in Jerusalem, a lasting symbol of Judaism. (A nine-branched version is used at Hanukkah.)
A community where monks (or nuns, in a convent) live apart from the world to pray and work under strict rules. Medieval monasteries copied and decorated most books in Europe.
An Aztec painter-scribe who wrote by painting pictures in codices.
Greek god of desire, called Cupid by the Romans: a winged boy with a bow whose arrows make people fall in love.
A ceremony that makes a building or object sacred, setting it apart for religious use. Todai-ji’s Great Buddha was consecrated in 752 with an ‘eye-opening’ ceremony.

The religion built around Jesus of Nazareth, whom Christians believe is the Son of God who died and rose again to save people from sin. It became the main religion of Europe, so most European art from about 300 to 1700 C.E. is Christian art.
Italian for ‘pity’. An image of the Virgin Mary alone holding the dead body of Jesus across her lap. It is a close-up, private version of the Lamentation.

An ancient religious group with secret rites revealed only to initiates, who were promised protection or a better afterlife. The Sanctuary of the Great Gods on Samothrace, where the Winged Victory stood, was the center of one.
A sacred text recording the teachings of the Buddha (or, in Hinduism, short teachings). Copying thiss was a way to earn merit.
A Buddhist paradise, especially Amida Buddha’s Western Paradise. this Buddhism, very popular in Japan, teaches that faith in Amida brings rebirth there.
The ‘earth-touching’ gesture: the right hand reaches down to touch the ground. It recalls the moment the Buddha called the earth to witness his enlightenment.
The Bible story in which Adam and Eve disobey God by eating the forbidden fruit and are thrown out of the Garden of Eden. Christians call this the origin of sin and death.
In Mahayana Buddhism, a being who has reached enlightenment but chooses to stay in the world to help others. thiss are often shown as richly dressed princes, unlike the plain-robed Buddha.

The cube-shaped shrine in Mecca, the holiest site in Islam. Muslims everywhere face it when they pray, and pilgrims walk around it seven times during the hajj. It is covered by a black cloth, the kiswa.
The Buddha of Infinite Light (Amitabha in Sanskrit), who rules a Western Paradise called the Pure Land. Believers who call his name hope to be reborn there.
A performance with masks, full costumes, music and dance, in which the masker becomes a spirit or character. The mask is only one part of the work.
A vision of the Virgin Mary that appeared to Juan Diego, an Indigenous man in Mexico, in 1531, leaving her image on his cloak. She became the patron of Mexico and a symbol of Mexican identity.
The world of the dead, usually imagined below the earth.
The gift-giving gesture: hand lowered, palm facing out, offering blessings or wishes granted.
A ritual meant to make crops, animals or fish multiply and the community prosper.
A symbolic hand gesture in Buddhist and Hindu art. Each has a fixed meaning, so you can tell what a figure is ‘saying’ by its hands.
The Hebrew prophet who led the Israelites out of Egypt and received the Ten Commandments (God’s law) on Mount Sinai.
A major summer ceremony of many Plains peoples involving fasting, dance and sacrifice for the renewal of the community. The U.S. government banned it in the late 1800s.
The twelve major gods of ancient Greece, believed to live on Mount Olympus. The Romans adopted them under Latin names (Zeus became Jupiter, Athena became Minerva, and so on).
A Muslim building for communal prayer. Key parts: a wall facing Mecca (qibla) with a niche (mihrab), a pulpit (minbar), often a courtyard, and towers (minarets). ‘Masjid’ is the Arabic word.
In Hinduism, seeing and being seen by a god through its sacred image. The exchange of looks is itself a blessing, which is why images have large, open eyes and are paraded in processions.

The holy book of Christianity. It has two parts: the Old Testament (the Hebrew scriptures, shared with Judaism) and the New Testament (about Jesus and his followers). Most Christian art illustrates a this story.
Italian for ‘my lady’. A name for the Virgin Mary, and for any painting or statue of her, usually holding the baby Jesus.
Across cultures the sun stands for life, kingship and the divine: the Aten, Inti, the Mughal emperor’s halo, Mao as the ‘sun’ of China.
The striped cloth headdress with side flaps worn by Egyptian kings.
The execution of Jesus by nailing him to a wooden cross, the central event of Christianity. Images range from calm and triumphant to bloody and painful.
The pursuit of direct, personal union with God through prayer, vision or trance, beyond ordinary thinking.
In Baule belief, a spirit husband or wife from the other world who can cause trouble in one’s life. A diviner may advise carving a figure of the this and caring for it.
In Benin and Yoruba belief, the god of the sea and wealth. The Oba is linked to him through coral beads and river-leaf patterns.
The meaning of the images and symbols in a work: who is shown, what the objects stand for, and what story is told. Also, the study of that meaning.
Among the Kongo peoples, any object filled with spiritual power and medicines by a ritual specialist (nganga). The this n’kondi is one powerful type. Plural: mithis.
choices: Churning of the Ocean of Milk

questions.prompt: The Jewish scriptures (the Tanakh), written mostly in Hebrew. Christians call it the Old Testament. Hebrew is read right to left, so Jewish manuscripts read right to left too.
choices: Churning of the Ocean of Milk

questions.prompt: A person sent to spread their religion to other peoples. Christian missionaries in the Americas, Africa and the Pacific changed local art, often destroying or hiding ‘pagan’ objects.
A garden divided into four parts by water channels, picturing the Qur’an’s description of paradise with its four rivers. The Persian name is charbagh (‘four gardens’).
Christianity’s belief that Jesus rose from the dead three days after he died. In art he often bursts from the tomb surrounded by light.
The mud-brick building style of the Sahel region of West Africa, with thick walls, buttresses and wooden beams (toron) sticking out.
A large West African people, mostly in southwest Nigeria and Benin, with city-kingdoms, orisha religion and famous carvers and bronze casters.
A people of Mali known for cliffside villages, granary doors, ancestor figures and masquerades.
The largest connected land empire in history (1206 to 1368), founded by Genghis Khan, which linked China, Iran and Russia and boosted trade and artistic exchange.
Vikings who settled in Normandy, France, and conquered England in 1066 under William the Conqueror.
Small squares of geometric pattern woven into Inka textiles, each probably standing for a place, group or rank. Also spelled tocapu.

A huge language family, and the seafaring peoples who spoke it, who spread from Taiwan through Southeast Asia and across the Pacific to Madagascar and Rapa Nui. The Lapita people were early this voyagers.
The Polynesian name for Easter Island and its people, famous for moai statues.
A Māori cloak covered with kiwi feathers, worn by people of high rank.
A Tewa pueblo in New Mexico, home of the potters Maria and Julian Martínez.
Byzantine empress and wife of Justinian, a former actress who became a powerful co-ruler.
The chief Ottoman architect (c. 1490 to 1588), designer of hundreds of buildings, who sought to outdo Hagia Sophia’s dome.
A shallow cave or overhanging rock that gives natural cover but stays open to daylight, unlike a deep cave. Much African rock art is found in them.
A rich banking family that ruled Florence and spent huge sums on art in the 1400s to 1500s. Two this became queens of France and several became popes.
A ring-shaped coral island, or a ring of small islets, surrounding a lagoon. thiss are common in Micronesia and Polynesia.
The chiefly ruling class of traditional Hawaiian society. this held both political and sacred power, and only they could wear the red-and-yellow feather capes and cloaks called ʻahu ʻula.
A colony governed by a viceroy, who ruled on behalf of the Spanish king. New Spain and Peru were the two great viceroyalties.
A warlike empire of northern Mesopotamia (peak c. 900 to 612 B.C.E.) whose palaces had giant guardian figures and relief carvings.
A Lega society with many ranks that men and women climb through by learning moral teachings, taught with small ivory and wood figures and masks.
The bishop of Rome and head of the Catholic Church, a giant art patron.
German revolutionary socialists, led by Karl Liebknecht and Rosa Luxemburg, crushed in 1919.
An Inka record-keeping device of knotted, colored cords, used for counting and possibly for stories. Also spelled quipu.
The Mongol dynasty that ruled China (1271 to 1368), founded by Kublai Khan.
A picture-sign in the ancient Egyptian writing system. Some signs stand for sounds, others for whole words or ideas. The Narmer Palette writes the king’s name with a catfish and a chisel.
A long trip through Europe, especially Italy, made by wealthy young British and northern Europeans in the 1600s to 1800s to study ancient ruins and Renaissance art.
A very small island. Nan Madol was built on nearly 100 artificial thiss of stacked stone and coral fill off the coast of Pohnpei.
The ‘Sun King’ of France (reigned 1643 to 1715), who built Versailles as a stage for absolute royal power.
A high plateau region north of the Himalayas, center of Vajrayana Buddhism.
A people of the eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo whose life is organized by the bwami society.
A tall Asmat memorial pole carved from a mangrove tree, with stacked ancestor figures, made for a feast honoring the recently dead.
A Northwest Coast people of British Columbia, Canada, known for dramatic transformation masks used in potlatch dances.
An island province of Papua New Guinea where malagan ceremonies are held.
A powerful Bamileke society of royals and wealthy titleholders who wear beaded elephant masks.
Jews of Spain and Portugal and their descendants, who were expelled from Spain in 1492.
An ancient region of today’s Pakistan and Afghanistan where Buddhist art mixed with Greek and Roman styles, as in the wavy drapery of Buddha statues.
Land set aside by the U.S. government for a Native American nation, usually after forcing it off its homeland. Cotsiogo painted his elk hides on the Wind River this in Wyoming.
A Polynesian island nation. Many thisns now live in New Zealand, where artists like Michel Tuffery work.
Japan’s hereditary warrior class, who served lords (daimyo) and followed a code of loyalty.
The Spanish colonial system of ranking people by their mix of Spanish, Indigenous and African ancestry, and the paintings that illustrated it as sets of family portraits.
A huge wild ox, the ancestor of modern cattle, that lived across Europe until the last one died in 1627. The giant bulls painted at Lascaux are this.
The title of the Asante king.
A woman of the Isthmus of Tehuantepec in Oaxaca, Mexico, whose distinctive dress became a symbol of strong, Indigenous Mexican womanhood.
In colonial Spanish America, a person of Spanish descent born in the Americas (criollo). thiss developed a proud local identity separate from Spain.
The modern art museum in London, in a former power station whose Turbine Hall hosts giant commissions.
A Pueblo people of northeastern Arizona, known for katsina ceremonies and carved katsina dolls.
A Roman town buried and preserved by the eruption of Mount Vesuvius in 79 C.E.
The capital of the Khmer Empire in Cambodia, with this Wat (Hindu) and this Thom (Buddhist).
The French aristocrats of the 1700s who commissioned playful, flirtatious, pastel art for private homes.
The main island of the Cook Islands in central Polynesia, known for wrapped staff gods.

For Aboriginal Australians, this means the ancestral land a person belongs to and is responsible for, including its plants, animals, water, spirits and Dreaming stories. Painting it is a duty, not just a landscape.
Traditional Māori tattooing, especially of the face, carved into the skin with chisels. Each design records a person’s ancestry, rank and identity.
The historic name for Iran and its empires, from the Achaemenids to the Safavids.

A Kongo power figure that ‘hunts’ wrongdoers. A ritual specialist fills it with medicines, and people drive nails or blades into it to seal oaths, settle disputes or call for punishment. The plural of nkisi is minkisi.
The sea and islands between Australia and Papua New Guinea, whose peoples made masks from turtle shell.

An oﬀicial art school and society, like France’s Royal Academy of Painting and Sculpture (1648), which taught rules, ranked subjects and controlled the Salon. ‘Academic art’ means art following its rules.
A Māori neck pendant of greenstone (jade) shaped like a human figure, passed down as a family treasure.
Native peoples of New Mexico and Arizona, such as the Hopi and Tewa, who live in adobe or stone villages called pueblos.
A Māori chief or person of high rank. Tamati Waka Nene was a this.
The pope’s headquarters and the smallest country in the world, inside Rome, with St. Peter’s Basilica and the Sistine Chapel.
A Chinese dynasty (960 to 1279) famous for monumental landscape painting, Neo-Confucianism and fine ceramics.
An ancient city of Mesopotamia, capital of King Hammurabi (c. 1792 to 1750 B.C.E.).
A personal emblem carved on the front of a Kuba ndop that tells you which king it is.
The writing of ancient Mesopotamia, made of wedge-shaped marks pressed into clay with a reed or carved into stone. It was used for about 3,000 years.
A people of Gabon, Cameroon and Equatorial Guinea known for byeri reliquary guardian figures.
The first cities of southern Mesopotamia (c. 4500 to 1900 B.C.E.), such as Uruk and Ur, inventors of writing (cuneiform).
A Pacific island nation, a British colony from 1874 to 1970, where ceremonial gifts of mats and tapa build relationships.
A people of central Italy (c. 800 to 100 B.C.E.) before the Roman takeover, known for lively tombs, terra cotta sculpture and temples.
A people and former kingdom of the southeastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, known for royal art and the lukasa memory board.
An island in Micronesia, site of Nan Madol.
The people usually called the Aztecs, who ruled an empire from their island capital, Tenochtitlan, until the Spanish conquest in 1521.
A government oﬀicial in China or Korea chosen through exams on the Confucian classics, often also a poet, calligrapher or painter.
China’s porcelain capital for over a thousand years, where imperial and export porcelain was made.

A West African kingdom in today’s southern Nigeria (not the modern country called Benin), ruled by the Oba. Its brass casters made plaques and heads for the royal palace. British troops looted it in 1897.
A Luba society of ‘men of memory’ who kept and performed royal history and advised kings.
A famous Yoruba sculptor (c. 1875 to 1938), one of the few African artists of his time known by name, admired for his tall figures and deep undercutting.
Byzantine emperor (reigned 527 to 565 C.E.) who rebuilt Hagia Sophia and reconquered Italy. He appears in mosaic with his wife, Theodora.
A type of malagan mask with a crested fiber ‘hairstyle’ representing the spirit of a dead person.
A Tlingit weaving style for ceremonial robes of mountain-goat wool and cedar bark, with formline crest designs and long fringes.
The movement of about six million Black Americans from the rural South to Northern cities (c. 1910 to 1970) to escape segregation and find work.
A Plains pictorial calendar, usually painted on a hide, with one picture for each year (‘winter’) recalling its main event.
A large people of southeastern Nigeria.

Barkcloth made by beating the inner bark of paper mulberry trees into sheets, then painting, stamping or dyeing it. It is made mostly by women and used for clothing, gifts and ceremonies. Called ngatu in Tonga, masi in Fiji, hiapo in Niue, siapo in Samoa.
A Māori house. A carved meeting house (this whakairo) is seen as the body of an ancestor.
The Arabic name for the parts of Spain and Portugal under Muslim rule (711 to 1492), a meeting place of Muslim, Christian and Jewish cultures.
A site in central India with Hindu and Jain temples famed for their dense, sometimes erotic sculpture.
A way of life based on herding animals, such as cattle, sheep or goats, often moving with the seasons. Much later Saharan rock art shows herders and their cattle.
A small Polynesian island nation known for hiapo barkcloth.
A powerful kingdom and people of Ghana, rich from gold. Also spelled Ashanti. Their king is the thishene, and the Golden Stool is the soul of the nation.
Traditional Pacific navigation without instruments, reading stars, swells, winds and birds.
A Japanese feudal lord who ruled a domain and commanded samurai under the shogun.
Painters in colonial Cusco and the Andes who made Catholic images with flat, gold-patterned surfaces, often mixing in local ideas.
The Inka capital in the Peruvian highlands, said to be laid out in the shape of a puma. Also spelled Cuzco.
Comma-shaped jade or glass ornaments hung on Silla crowns, possibly standing for life, seeds or fertility.
The region of the southwest Pacific including Papua New Guinea, the Solomon Islands, Vanuatu, the Torres Strait area and Fiji.
The first emperor of a unified China, who standardized writing, money and measures, and was buried with the terra cotta army.

Native cultures of the Mississippi valley and Southeast (c. 800 to 1600 C.E.) that built large earthen mounds and towns such as Cahokia. The College Board labels the Great Serpent Mound this, though some scholars credit earlier peoples (Adena or Fort Ancient).
A Northwest Coast ceremonial feast in which a host gives away goods and stages dances to confirm status, names and rights. Canada banned it from 1884 to 1951.
The bending of waves as they pass around or over something. In Marshall Islands stick charts, curved sticks show ocean swells bending around islands.
The great European painters from about 1300 to 1800, such as Leonardo, Rembrandt and Velázquez, and their works.
Made to teach a lesson, usually moral or religious.
Newspapers, magazines, radio, film, TV and the internet: forms that reach huge audiences at once.
Offered to a god as a gift or to fulfill a promise (a vow). this figures could ‘pray’ on the giver’s behalf.
An object whose main job is to signal that its owner is important, often made of rare materials or by rare skill.
The traditional split between ‘fine’ art for elites and museums (high) and popular culture, crafts or commercial images (low). Pop and later art erased the boundary.
Lending money at interest, which the medieval Church condemned as a sin. Enrico Scrovegni may have built the Arena Chapel partly to make up for his family’s this.
A deliberate reference in a work to an earlier work, like a footnote in pictures.
Familiar but strangely disturbing. Freud described it as the eerie feeling when something homely turns strange, and the Surrealists sought it out, as in Oppenheim’s fur-covered teacup.
The person or group who pays for and often directs the making of a work of art, such as a ruler, church, guild or rich family. thiss usually decided the subject, size and materials.
Relations between states. Art served it through gifts, portraits and ceremonies.
How traditions carry on (continuity) and how they shift (change) over time. The AP this question asks how a work relates to earlier or later art traditions.
An AP task word: give reasons and show how or why, linking cause and effect. Most points on the exam need thising, not just describing.
Made to honor and preserve the memory of a person or event.
Objects and traditions that belong to a whole people or nation as their shared heritage, not to any one owner.
Worldwide trade networks, especially after 1500, that moved silver, silk, porcelain, enslaved people and art between continents.
Cheap, sentimental, mass-market art or decoration seen as being in bad taste. Some artists use it on purpose.
Explaining how a work’s context (time, place, patron, function, audience, beliefs) shaped it and its meaning. One of the AP short-essay question types.
Using humor, exaggeration or irony to criticize people, habits or institutions.
Art or media made to spread a political or religious message and shape what people believe, often by glorifying a leader or cause.
Describes the period after colonies won independence, and art or ideas that examine the lasting effects of colonialism on identity, power and culture.
The science of protecting works from decay, damage and environment, preferably changing as little as possible.
A mixing of the senses, such as seeing colors when hearing music. Kandinsky compared colors to musical tones and wanted his paintings to work on viewers like music.

The Nazi label (in German, Entartete Kunst) for modern art they banned, including Expressionism and abstraction. In 1937 they seized thousands of works from German museums and mocked many of them in a touring exhibition.

A philosophy based on Plato, revived in Renaissance Florence, that saw physical beauty as a reflection of divine, spiritual beauty. It let a nude pagan goddess like Botticelli’s Venus carry Christian-friendly meanings.
The recognizable way something is made, which can belong to an artist, a workshop, a culture or a period. Learning thiss lets you attribute unknown works.
The roles, behaviors and identities a society expects of women and men. Asking ‘how does this work show this?’ is a powerful analysis tool.
Made by a maker whose name is not recorded. Most art in history is this, which does not mean it was made without skill or individual style.
Sun-centered: the idea, argued by Copernicus and confirmed by Galileo and Kepler, that the Earth and planets orbit the sun.

Not religious; worldly. this art includes portraits, scenes of daily life, entertainment masks and luxury objects for the court. Islamic art avoids figures mainly in religious settings, so this Islamic objects are often full of people and animals.

The maker of a work. In many cultures makers were seen as skilled craftspeople, often anonymous, rather than celebrated geniuses; the idea of the famous individual this became strong in Renaissance Europe.

Spanish for ‘Mexicanness’. A movement after the Mexican Revolution to celebrate Mexico’s Indigenous and folk heritage as the heart of national identity. Frida Kahlo embraced it in her Tehuana dress and imagery.
Latin for ‘weight’ or ‘seriousness’. The Roman virtue of dignity, self-control and moral seriousness, shown in stern, wrinkled, veristic portraits.
Supreme, independent power to govern. The Golden Stool embodies the this and soul of the whole Asante nation.
Using propaganda, images and mass media to turn a political leader into an idolized, almost godlike hero. In Mao’s China his image was everywhere.
A work made to honor an earlier artist or work.
A scientific idea: everything gradually breaks down into disorder. Robert Smithson welcomed it, letting Spiral Jetty sink, crust with salt and erode.
The special clothing and objects that show royal or high rank, such as crowns, scepters, capes, stools and jewelry.
Italian for ‘beautiful whole’. Bernini’s idea of combining architecture, sculpture, painting and real light into one unified, theatrical experience.
The artist’s name written on a work. Signing was rare in many periods, so a this can be a bold claim to fame or authorship.
Skilled handmade work, especially textiles, ceramics, metalwork and furniture, long ranked below painting and sculpture in Europe. That ranking is now widely questioned.
Borrowing a recognizable pose, figure or composition from an earlier work.
A more sophisticated argument, such as explaining both sides, several causes, or how a work both continues and breaks a tradition. The strongest AP long essays show it.
Turning something (art, culture, identity, people) into a product to be bought and sold.
Useful objects made beautifully: furniture, ceramics, textiles, metalwork, glass.
An association of craftsmen in a trade (such as painters or goldsmiths) that set standards, trained apprentices and controlled who could sell work in a city.
French for an artist’s studio or workshop, especially a royal workshop of painters and calligraphers in Persian and Mughal courts.
A shared sense of what makes a people a nation: history, land, language and heroes. Art from the 1800s on often tries to shape it, as in Velasco’s grand views of the Valley of Mexico.

An exaggerated sense of masculine pride and toughness, including the idea that real men never show emotion. Pepón Osorio’s barbershop installation, titled No Crying Allowed in the Barbershop, questions it.
A family’s line of descent, traced back through generations of ancestors. Art often displayed genealogies to prove a ruler’s or chief’s right to power.
Spanish for ‘purity of blood’. A colonial idea that ranked people by ancestry, favoring ‘pure’ Spanish Christian descent. It underlay the casta system of New Spain.
Discussing two or more works together, showing both similarities and differences and explaining why. The AP long-essay this question pairs a given work with one you choose.

The oﬀicial art academy of a kingdom: in France, the this of Painting and Sculpture (1648); in Britain, the this of Arts (1768). They trained artists, held exhibitions and ranked the genres. Vigée Le Brun was one of very few women admitted in France.

Deciding who made a work, or when and where, based on style, materials, documents and comparison. On the AP exam, the this question shows you an unknown work and asks you to name the likely artist or culture and justify it.
The mixing of different cultures, styles or identities in one work or person, creating something new rather than simply one or the other.
Art made for a royal or princely court, usually by artists the ruler employed, to show the ruler’s wealth, taste and power. Safavid manuscripts and the Ardabil Carpet came from court workshops.
The change from hand production to machines and factories, starting in Britain around 1760, which brought railways, cities, new materials and photography.
The exchange of goods over distance. this brought new materials (brass, beads, cobalt, silk) and new ideas to artists.
A long, rolling ocean wave that travels far from the wind that created it. Marshall Islands navigators read thiss, and how islands bend them, to find land.
A term from film critic Laura Mulvey (1975): images that present women as objects for a presumed male viewer.

An old medical theory that health and personality depend on balancing four body fluids: blood, yellow bile, black bile and phlegm. Too much of one made a person sanguine (cheerful), choleric (angry), melancholic (sad) or phlegmatic (sluggish).
A written agreement between patron and artist listing what is to be made, materials (such as how much gold or blue), price and deadline.
Latin for ‘law of retaliation’: punishment that matches the crime, ‘an eye for an eye’. Hammurabi’s laws apply it, though penalties also depended on the social rank of victim and offender.
The condition of modern life after the Industrial Revolution: cities, railways, factories, crowds, speed and new technology. Artists like Monet made it their subject.
The system of buying and selling art through dealers, galleries, auctions and collectors.
The flow of ideas, materials, styles and beliefs between cultures through trade, travel, conquest or migration. On the exam it is one of the most useful themes for comparisons.
Art made around the world from about 1980 to now, often dealing with globalization, identity, politics and new media, and shown at international biennials.
A Japanese idea of beauty that values simple, imperfect, weathered and impermanent things, linked to Zen Buddhism and the tea ceremony.
A clear, defensible claim that answers the question and that the rest of the essay proves. On the AP rubric it must do more than restate the question.
A statement you argue is true and back up with evidence.

Showing a person or thing as more perfect than in real life, according to a culture’s ideal of beauty, virtue or power. Many ‘portraits’ outside Europe, and royal images everywhere, are idealized rather than true likenesses.
Describing a work’s form (materials, technique, composition, color, line, scale) and explaining how those choices create meaning. One of the AP short-essay question types.
Stealing objects, especially in war or from archaeological sites without permission.

rows.1: diagonal: A slanted line or direction. Diagonals feel active and unstable compared with calm horizontals and verticals. Looking and describing
rows.2: narrative: Art that tells a story or shows an event from a story. Looking and describing
rows.3: texture: How a surface feels, or looks like it would feel: rough, smooth, soft, bumpy, glossy. Actual texture can be touched; implied texture is only painted. Looking and describing
rows.4: tint: A color made lighter by adding white. Looking and describing
rows.5: convention: An accepted, repeated way of showing something in a particular culture, even if it is not realistic. Viewers in that culture understand it automatically. Looking and describing
rows.6: horizon line: The line where the land or sea seems to meet the sky. In linear perspective, the vanishing point usually sits on it, at the viewer’s eye level. Looking and describing
rows.7: register: One horizontal band in a work that is divided into stacked rows, like shelves. Each register often shows a different scene or level of importance. Looking and describing
rows.8: superimposition: Placing one image on top of another so they overlap, as when prehistoric painters added new animals over older ones on the same wall. Looking and describing
rows.9: saturation: How strong, pure or intense a color is. A highly saturated red is vivid; a low-saturation red is dull and grayish. Also called intensity or chroma. Looking and describing
rows.10: illusionism: Tricks that make a flat surface seem to have real depth, space or objects, so the wall or ceiling seems to open up. Looking and describing
rows.11: abstract: Art that simplifies, exaggerates or rearranges what things really look like, so you may only partly recognize the subject (or not at all). The word describes how far an image has moved away from a photo-like copy. Looking and describing
rows.12: composite view: Showing different parts of one body from their most recognizable angles at the same time: head in profile, eye from the front, shoulders from the front, legs in profile. Common in Egyptian and Near Eastern art. Also called twisted perspective. Looking and describing
rows.13: cropping: Cutting off part of a scene at the edge of the frame, so figures or objects are only partly shown. It makes an image feel like a quick snapshot. Looking and describing 228 # Ans. Why Rule (category)
rows.14: medallion: A round or oval framed area holding a design or figure, often used as the central motif of carpets, ivories and ceilings. Looking and describing
rows.15: contrast: A strong difference between two things placed together: light and dark, rough and smooth, big and small, bright and dull. Contrast grabs attention. Looking and describing
rows.16: secondary colors: Orange, green and purple: the colors you get by mixing two primary colors. Looking and describing
rows.17: analogous colors: Colors that sit next to each other on the color wheel, such as yellow, yellow-orange and orange. Used together they feel calm and unified rather than clashing. Looking and describing
rows.18: variety: Using differences in shape, color, size or texture to keep a work interesting. Usually balanced against unity. Looking and describing
rows.19: oblique perspective: A way of showing depth used in Chinese and Japanese painting: the sides of buildings are drawn as parallel diagonal lines that never meet, so the scene can unroll sideways without one fixed viewpoint. Looking and describing
rows.20: finish: How smooth or rough the final surface is. A high finish hides brushstrokes completely; a loose finish leaves them visible. Looking and describing
rows.21: viewpoint: The position from which the viewer seems to see the scene: low, high, straight on, from the side. Also called vantage point. Looking and describing
rows.22: geometric: Made of regular, measurable shapes such as squares, circles, triangles and straight lines. The opposite of organic. Looking and describing
rows.23: distortion: Stretching, twisting or exaggerating forms on purpose, usually to show emotion or a new idea rather than accuracy. Looking and describing
rows.24: foreshortening: Drawing something that points toward or away from you so it looks squashed and shorter, which makes it seem to stick out in space. Looking and describing
rows.25: shape: A flat, enclosed area with only height and width, such as a circle or a blob. Looking and describing
rows.26: form: A shape that has (or looks like it has) three dimensions: height, width and depth. In art talk ‘form’ can also mean all the visual parts of a work together, as opposed to its subject. Looking and describing
rows.27: psychological realism: Showing people’s inner emotions and states of mind truthfully, not just their outward appearance. Each of Rodin’s Burghers of Calais shows his own kind of despair. Looking and describing
rows.28: frontal: Facing straight out at the viewer, square to the front. Frontal figures often look formal, stiff and powerful. Looking and describing
rows.29: panoramic: A wide view showing a large stretch of land or city, as if you can turn your head and take it all in. Looking and describing
rows.30: interlace: A decoration of bands, ribbons or animal bodies that weave over and under each other in complicated knots. Looking and describing
rows.31: warm colors: Reds, oranges and yellows. They feel warm, energetic or emotional and tend to seem to come toward you. Looking and describing 229 # Ans. Why Rule (category)
rows.32: axis: An imaginary straight line running through the center of a body, object or building, around which its parts are arranged. A standing figure usually has a vertical axis; in contrapposto that axis bends. Looking and describing
rows.33: ovoid: Egg-shaped. In Northwest Coast art, the ovoid is a rounded, slightly squarish oval used as a basic building block of formline designs. Looking and describing
rows.34: foreground: The part of a picture that seems closest to you, at the bottom or front of the scene. Looking and describing
rows.35: balance: How the visual ‘weight’ of shapes, colors and objects is spread around a work so it feels stable instead of tipping to one side. It can be symmetrical, asymmetrical or radial. Looking and describing
rows.36: local color: The real, everyday color of an object in normal light, such as a lemon’s yellow or grass’s green. Looking and describing
rows.37: line: A mark that is longer than it is wide. Lines can be straight, curved, thick, thin, calm or agitated, and they outline shapes, show movement or carry feeling. Looking and describing
rows.38: expressive: Made to show strong feeling. An expressive work uses color, line or distortion to make you feel something rather than to record what things look like. Looking and describing
rows.39: emphasis: The way an artist makes one part stand out more than the rest, using light, color, size, placement or lines that point to it. Looking and describing
rows.40: horror vacui: Filling every inch of a surface with figures or decoration so no empty space is left. Latin for ‘fear of empty space’. Looking and describing
rows.41: color wheel: A circle that arranges colors in rainbow order so you can see which colors are related. Opposite colors are complementary; neighbors are analogous. Looking and describing
rows.42: naturalism: Showing things the way they actually look in the real world, with accurate details, proportions, light and texture. Looking and describing
rows.43: orthogonal: In linear perspective, the diagonal lines (real or implied) that run back into the picture and meet at the vanishing point, such as the edges of a ceiling or floor tiles. Looking and describing
rows.44: overlapping: Placing one thing partly in front of another. The one that blocks the other looks closer. It is the simplest way to show depth. Looking and describing
rows.45: visual weight: How strongly a part of a work pulls your attention. Big, dark, bright or busy areas feel heavier than small, pale or plain ones. Looking and describing
rows.46: figure-ground relationship: How the main shapes (the figure) stand out from what is behind them (the ground). Some works play with this so you are not sure which is which. Looking and describing
rows.47: aniconic: Avoiding pictures of people, animals or gods, especially in a religious setting. Instead the art uses writing, patterns and plants. Common in Islamic religious spaces and in very early Buddhist art, where the Buddha was shown only by symbols such as a footprint or an empty throne. Looking and describing
rows.48: proportion: The size of one part compared with another part or with the whole, such as head to body. Looking and describing 230 # Ans. Why Rule (category)
rows.49: fragmentation: Breaking forms into pieces, planes or shards, often reassembled in a new way. Central to Cubism. Looking and describing
rows.50: formal analysis: Describing and explaining a work by looking only at its visual parts: line, color, shape, space, texture, composition and so on, before talking about meaning. Looking and describing
rows.51: hue: The plain name of a color: red, blue, green and so on. Looking and describing
rows.52: hierarchical scale: Making the most important person the biggest, no matter where they stand in the scene. Size shows rank, not distance. Looking and describing
rows.53: representational: Art that shows recognizable things from the real world, whether realistic or stylized. Looking and describing
rows.54: gesture: The pose or hand movement of a figure that communicates something, like pointing, blessing or reaching. Looking and describing
rows.55: middle ground: The zone of a picture between the foreground and the background. Looking and describing
rows.56: linear style: A style that relies on clear outlines and sharp edges between forms, so shapes look crisp and polished. Often contrasted with a painterly style. Looking and describing
rows.57: implied line: A line you do not actually see but your eye follows anyway, such as the direction of a pointing finger, a gaze, or a row of objects. Looking and describing
rows.58: canon of proportions: A set of rules for the ideal size of each body part compared with the others, used so every figure looks ‘correct’. The Greek sculptor Polykleitos wrote one; Egyptian artists used a grid system. Looking and describing
rows.59: painterly: A style where you can see loose brushstrokes and soft edges, with color and texture more important than crisp outlines. Looking and describing
rows.60: implied texture: Texture that is painted or drawn to look rough, soft or shiny, even though the actual surface is smooth. Looking and describing
rows.61: monochrome: Made in one color, or in shades of a single color (including just black ink and grays). Also called monochromatic. Looking and describing
rows.62: immersive: Surrounding the viewer with sound, image or space, so you feel you are inside the work rather than looking at it. Looking and describing
rows.63: stylized: Shown in a simplified, exaggerated or decorative way that follows a set style rather than copying nature exactly. Looking and describing
rows.64: isocephaly: Lining up all the heads in a crowd at the same height, whether the figures are standing, riding or walking. It keeps a long frieze tidy. Looking and describing
rows.65: dramatic lighting: Strong, focused light that throws some areas into bright highlight and leaves others in deep shadow, raising the emotional temperature of a scene. Looking and describing
rows.66: charcoal: Burnt wood (or bone) used as a black drawing material. One of the oldest art materials. Painting, drawing and printmaking
rows.67: gouache: Opaque watercolor: water-based paint with extra white or chalk added so it covers what is underneath, drying flat and matte. Painting, drawing and printmaking 231 # Ans. Why Rule (category)
rows.68: casta painting: A type of painting from colonial Mexico (1700s) showing families of mixed racial background in sets, each labeled with a category name. They recorded a colonial system of racial ranking. Painting, drawing and printmaking
rows.69: oil paint: Paint made with pigment mixed in a drying oil, usually linseed oil. It dries slowly, so artists can blend smoothly and build up thin glazes; it became the main European painting medium by the 1500s. Painting, drawing and printmaking
rows.70: easel painting: A painting made on a portable support, like canvas or panel, that can be moved and hung anywhere, as opposed to a mural fixed to a wall. Painting, drawing and printmaking
rows.71: collage: A work made by gluing paper, photos, fabric or other materials onto a flat surface. From the French ‘coller’, to glue. Painting, drawing and printmaking
rows.72: camera obscura: A dark box or room with a tiny hole or lens that projects an upside-down image of the outside scene onto a wall or screen. Artists could trace it, and it led to the camera. Painting, drawing and printmaking
rows.73: landscape: A picture whose main subject is natural scenery: land, sky, trees and water. It was a major subject in China by the 900s and became one in Europe from the 1500s. Painting, drawing and printmaking
rows.74: encaustic: Painting with pigment mixed into hot melted wax. The colors stay bright and glossy for centuries. Used for Roman-Egyptian mummy portraits and early icons. Painting, drawing and printmaking
rows.75: wash: A thin, watery layer of ink or paint brushed over an area to give a soft, even tone. Painting, drawing and printmaking
rows.76: print source: A printed image, such as an engraving, that an artist copied or adapted. Colonial painters in the Americas often worked from European prints, so poses and compositions traveled across the ocean. Painting, drawing and printmaking
rows.77: illuminated manuscript: A handwritten book decorated with painted pictures, colored letters and often gold or silver. Before printing, every book was made by hand. Painting, drawing and printmaking
rows.78: grisaille: Painting done entirely in shades of gray, often to imitate stone sculpture. Painting, drawing and printmaking
rows.79: support: The surface a painting or drawing is made on, such as wood panel, canvas, paper, silk, vellum, plaster or hide. Painting, drawing and printmaking
rows.80: cangiante: Italian for ‘changing’. Painting the shadows of a fabric in a different, often lighter or brighter color instead of a darker shade of the same one, so the cloth seems to shimmer. Mannerists like Pontormo loved it. Painting, drawing and printmaking
rows.81: hanging scroll: A vertical scroll painting mounted on silk or paper with a rod at the bottom, made to hang on a wall and be rolled up for storage. Painting, drawing and printmaking
rows.82: texture stroke: In Chinese painting, a type of brushstroke (cun) used to show the texture of rocks and mountains, such as ‘raindrop’ or ‘axe-cut’ strokes. Fan Kuan’s mountains are built from thousands of raindrop strokes. Painting, drawing and printmaking
rows.83: drawing: Making marks on a surface with a tool like pencil, charcoal, chalk or ink, usually emphasizing line. Drawings can be finished works or sketches for later projects. Painting, drawing and printmaking
rows.84: gold leaf: Gold hammered into sheets thinner than tissue paper and applied to a surface to make it shine. Painting, drawing and printmaking 232 # Ans. Why Rule (category)
rows.85: gold ground: A background covered with gold leaf instead of a landscape or room, making holy figures seem to exist in heaven rather than on earth. Painting, drawing and printmaking
rows.86: synthetic polymer paint: The museum-label name for acrylic and similar plastic-based paints. They dry fast and come in bright colors. Painting, drawing and printmaking
rows.87: albumen print: An early photographic print (about 1850 to 1890) made on paper coated with egg white, which held the light-sensitive chemicals and gave a fine, glossy image. Painting, drawing and printmaking
rows.88: muraqqa: A Persian, Mughal or Ottoman album that collected paintings and samples of calligraphy, often set in decorated borders, for a royal or elite collector. Painting, drawing and printmaking
rows.89: soak-stain: Pouring very thin paint onto raw, unprimed canvas so it soaks into the cloth, leaving soft, see-through pools of color. Pioneered by Helen Frankenthaler. Painting, drawing and printmaking
rows.90: Mylar: A thin, tough, smooth plastic film. Some contemporary artists paint and collage on it instead of paper or canvas. Painting, drawing and printmaking
rows.91: shanshui: Chinese for ‘mountain-water’: the Chinese tradition of landscape painting with mountains, rivers and mist, expressing harmony between people and nature. Painting, drawing and printmaking
rows.92: byōbu: A Japanese folding screen made of hinged panels, often painted on gold-leafed paper, used to divide rooms and decorate homes. Painting, drawing and printmaking
rows.93: woodblock print: A print made by carving a picture into a block of wood, inking the raised surface and pressing paper onto it. Japanese color woodblock prints used a separate block for each color. Painting, drawing and printmaking
rows.94: gesso: A white mix of chalk or plaster and glue brushed onto wood panels or canvas to make a smooth, bright surface for painting. Painting, drawing and printmaking
rows.95: aquatint: A printmaking technique, related to etching, that uses acid eating through a powdered resin layer to make soft areas of tone that look like watercolor washes, instead of only lines. Painting, drawing and printmaking
rows.96: ignudo: Italian for ‘nude’. One of the twenty muscular nude young men Michelangelo painted on the Sistine Chapel ceiling, seated at the corners of the smaller Genesis scenes. Plural: ignudi. Painting, drawing and printmaking
rows.97: cross-hatching: Shading made by drawing sets of fine parallel lines that cross each other. The closer the lines, the darker the area. Painting, drawing and printmaking
rows.98: scroll: A long roll of papyrus, paper or silk with writing or images, unrolled to read and rolled up to store. Painting, drawing and printmaking
rows.99: Kufic: An early, angular style of Arabic script with straight lines and sharp corners, used in the first centuries of Islam for copying the Qur’an and in architecture. Painting, drawing and printmaking
rows.100: still life: A painting of non-moving objects, such as fruit, flowers, cups or skulls, arranged by the artist. Painting, drawing and printmaking
rows.101: panel: A flat board, usually wood, used as a surface to paint on. Before canvas took over, most European paintings were on panels. Painting, drawing and printmaking 233 # Ans. Why Rule (category)
rows.102: broken color: Painting with separate, unblended dabs of color placed side by side so they mix in the viewer’s eye instead of on the palette. A key Impressionist technique. Painting, drawing and printmaking
rows.103: movable type: Individual letters or characters made as separate pieces that can be arranged into text, printed, and then reused. Painting, drawing and printmaking
rows.104: projection: Light thrown onto a wall or screen from a projector, used by some contemporary artists as part of an installation, so viewers’ shadows can join the scene. Painting, drawing and printmaking
rows.105: hide painting: Painting on animal skin. Plains and Plateau peoples of North America painted hides to record histories, events and visions. Painting, drawing and printmaking
rows.106: underdrawing: The drawing an artist makes on a surface before painting over it. Scientists can often see it with infrared light. Painting, drawing and printmaking
rows.107: hatching: Shading made with many fine parallel lines close together. Painting, drawing and printmaking
rows.108: genre scene: A painting of ordinary people doing everyday things, like working, cooking or chatting. Painting, drawing and printmaking
rows.109: freehand painting: Painting a design directly by hand, without stencils, stamps or rubbing boards. Niuean hiapo stands out because its fine, dense patterns were painted freehand. Painting, drawing and printmaking
rows.110: inscription: Words written, painted or carved on a work, such as a title, poem, name or dedication. Painting, drawing and printmaking
rows.111: oil paintstick: Oil paint formed into a solid stick, like a giant crayon, so artists can draw directly with paint. Basquiat used it in Horn Players. Painting, drawing and printmaking
rows.112: vignette: A small scene or picture set within a larger composition or border. Four corner vignettes in the Virgin of Guadalupe painting tell the story of her appearances. Painting, drawing and printmaking
rows.113: intaglio: The family of printmaking methods where lines are cut or etched into a metal plate. Ink sits in the grooves, and strong pressure pulls it onto paper. Engraving, etching, drypoint and aquatint are all intaglio. Painting, drawing and printmaking
rows.114: unprimed canvas: Canvas not coated with gesso or primer, so thinned paint soaks straight into the fabric. Helen Frankenthaler poured paint onto it in her soak-stain technique. Painting, drawing and printmaking
rows.115: odalisque: A woman in an Ottoman harem; in European painting, a reclining nude in an imagined ‘Oriental’ setting, a favorite subject of Orientalism. Painting, drawing and printmaking
rows.116: gloss: A note written in the margin or between the lines of a text to explain or translate it. Spanish glosses label the Aztec pictures in the Codex Mendoza. Painting, drawing and printmaking
rows.117: parchment: Animal skin (usually sheep or goat) soaked, scraped, stretched and dried to make a smooth, tough writing surface. Fine calfskin parchment is called vellum. Painting, drawing and printmaking
rows.118: cut paper: Shapes cut out of paper and arranged or pasted as a work of art. Kara Walker uses large black cut-paper silhouettes on white walls. Painting, drawing and printmaking 234 # Ans. Why Rule (category)
rows.119: engraving: An intaglio print made by cutting lines into a metal plate with a burin, filling the grooves with ink, wiping the surface clean and pressing paper onto it. It gives sharp, precise lines. Painting, drawing and printmaking
rows.120: diptych: A work made of two panels, often hinged together. Painting, drawing and printmaking
rows.121: mural: A large painting done directly on a wall or ceiling. Painting, drawing and printmaking
rows.122: emaki: Short for emakimono: a Japanese illustrated handscroll that combines pictures and text to tell a story, unrolled section by section from right to left. Painting, drawing and printmaking
rows.123: biombo: A Spanish word for a folding screen, borrowed from the Japanese ‘byōbu’. Biombos were made in colonial Mexico after Japanese screens arrived by trade. Painting, drawing and printmaking
rows.124: manuscript: A book or document written by hand. Before printing, every book was a manuscript, and luxury ones were richly painted. Painting, drawing and printmaking
rows.125: vellum: Fine, smooth parchment made from calfskin, used for the best medieval manuscripts. Some luxury manuscripts were dyed purple, the royal color. Painting, drawing and printmaking
rows.126: fresco: Painting on plaster on a wall or ceiling. In true (buon) fresco the plaster is still wet; in fresco secco it is dry. Painting, drawing and printmaking
rows.127: seascape: A painting whose main subject is the sea. Painting, drawing and printmaking
rows.128: digital photography: Photography that records images as computer data instead of on film, which makes pictures easy to edit and combine. Mariko Mori used digital tools to build Pure Land. Painting, drawing and printmaking
rows.129: key block: In color woodblock printing, the block carved with the main black outlines. The separate color blocks are cut to line up with it. Painting, drawing and printmaking
rows.130: drypoint: An intaglio printmaking method where the artist scratches lines straight into a metal plate with a sharp needle. The scratch throws up a rough edge (burr) that prints soft, velvety lines. Painting, drawing and printmaking
rows.131: wing: A side panel of an altarpiece, often hinged so it can close over the center panel. Wings were often painted on both sides, with different scenes showing when open or closed. Painting, drawing and printmaking
rows.132: lithograph: A print made by drawing with a greasy crayon on a flat stone or metal plate. The surface is wet, so greasy ink sticks only to the drawing (oil and water don’t mix). Invented about 1796. Painting, drawing and printmaking
rows.133: mineral pigment: Color made by grinding up colored rocks and earth, such as red and yellow ochre or black manganese. The oldest paints. Painting, drawing and printmaking
rows.134: passage: A technique, used by Cézanne and the Cubists, of leaving edges open so one plane flows into the next, blurring the boundaries between objects and space. Painting, drawing and printmaking
rows.135: disegno: Italian for both ‘drawing’ and ‘design’. The Florentine and Roman belief that great art begins with drawing and careful intellectual planning, praised in artists like Michelangelo. It was debated against Venetian colorito. Painting, drawing and printmaking 235 # Ans. Why Rule (category)
rows.136: folio: A single sheet or page of a manuscript or book. Folios are numbered with r (recto, the front) and v (verso, the back). Painting, drawing and printmaking
rows.137: dot painting: A style of contemporary Aboriginal Australian painting built up from many dabs or dots of color, connected to body painting and ceremonial designs about ancestral land. Painting, drawing and printmaking
rows.138: tarashikomi: A Japanese technique of dropping ink or paint onto an area that is still wet, so the colors pool and blur into soft, mottled patches. Painting, drawing and printmaking
rows.139: album page: A single painting or sheet of calligraphy made to be mounted in an album, rather than to illustrate the text of a book. Persian, Mughal and Ottoman collectors gathered such pages into albums called muraqqa. Painting, drawing and printmaking
rows.140: graphite: The soft gray carbon inside an ordinary pencil, used for drawing. Painting, drawing and printmaking
rows.141: plaque: A flat panel, often of metal or stone, decorated with relief and attached to a wall. Sculpture, objects and materials
rows.142: rock-cut: Carved directly out of a natural cliff or rock face, rather than built from separate blocks. Sculpture, objects and materials
rows.143: found object: An ordinary object, natural or manufactured, that an artist uses in a work of art, either as is or changed. Often called by the French ‘objet trouvé’. Sculpture, objects and materials
rows.144: featherwork: Art made by tying, gluing or sewing feathers onto a backing to create garments, headdresses or images. Rare, bright feathers were a sign of high rank in Polynesia and Mesoamerica. Sculpture, objects and materials
rows.145: ikenga: A carved wooden shrine figure of the Igbo people of Nigeria, with ram’s horns, honoring a man’s right hand, his personal drive and success. A man kept one and made offerings to it. Sculpture, objects and materials
rows.146: coiffure: An elaborate hairstyle. African masks often carve detailed coiffures to show beauty, status or the fashions of a time and place. Sculpture, objects and materials
rows.147: portrait: A likeness of a specific person, showing their appearance, status or character. It can be painted, carved, cast or photographed, and it can be naturalistic or symbolic. Sculpture, objects and materials
rows.148: tuff: A soft, porous rock formed from compacted volcanic ash. Rapa Nui’s moai were carved from it. The volcanic stone of the Roman catacombs, often called tufa, is geologically tuff too. Sculpture, objects and materials
rows.149: chiasmus: The crossing balance in a contrapposto figure: the tense, working parts sit diagonally across from each other, and so do the relaxed parts. In the Doryphoros the straight weightbearing right leg pairs with the bent, spear-holding left arm. Sculpture, objects and materials
rows.150: weft: The threads woven crosswise over and under the warp threads on a loom. In tapestry, colored wefts make the picture. Sculpture, objects and materials
rows.151: greywacke: A hard, dark gray sandstone. Egyptian sculptors used it for royal statues and objects because it could be polished to a smooth finish. Sculpture, objects and materials
rows.152: Pwo: A female mask of the Chokwe people (Angola and Congo) honoring the ideal woman and the founding ancestress. Ironically, it is danced by men, dressed as women. Sculpture, objects and materials 236 # Ans. Why Rule (category)
