rows.153: modular: Built from standard, interchangeable parts. The Terracotta Warriors were assembled from mold-made legs, torsos, arms and heads, then finished by hand so each looks individual. Sculpture, objects and materials
rows.154: sacrum: The large triangular bone at the base of the spine; the name is Latin for ‘sacred bone’. The Tequixquiac sacrum, from an extinct camelid, was carved so it looks like the head of a dog or coyote. Sculpture, objects and materials
rows.155: lamassu: A huge Assyrian guardian figure with a bull or lion body, eagle wings and a bearded human head, placed at palace gateways. Some have five legs so they look correct from the front and the side. Sculpture, objects and materials
rows.156: tooling: Pressing or punching small patterns into a surface, such as gold leaf, leather or metal, with small tools. The gold backgrounds of the Golden Haggadah are tooled. Sculpture, objects and materials
rows.157: andesite: A hard, gray volcanic stone. Borobudur in Java was built from enormous numbers of andesite blocks, and its long relief panels are carved into them. Sculpture, objects and materials
rows.158: plaster: A paste of lime or gypsum, sand and water that hardens as it dries. Used to coat walls (for fresco), to model details and to make casts. Sculpture, objects and materials
rows.159: subtractive: Making a sculpture by removing material, carving or cutting it away from a block. The opposite of additive. Sculpture, objects and materials
rows.160: warp: On a loom, the threads stretched lengthwise and held tight. The weft threads are woven over and under them. Sculpture, objects and materials
rows.161: soft sculpture: Sculpture made from soft materials like vinyl, cloth or foam, often making hard everyday things floppy. Claes Oldenburg is its best-known maker; Lipstick (Ascending) first had a soft vinyl tip that was pumped up with air. Sculpture, objects and materials
rows.162: life mask: A cast taken directly from a living person’s face, usually in plaster, so a sculptor can get a precise likeness. Houdon made a life mask of George Washington at Mount Vernon in 1785. Sculpture, objects and materials
rows.163: in the round: Sculpture that is fully three-dimensional and meant to be seen from all sides, not attached to a background like relief. Sculpture, objects and materials
rows.164: bust: A sculpture of a person’s head, neck and usually shoulders and upper chest. Sculpture, objects and materials
rows.165: sowei: A helmet mask of the Sande society of the Mende (Sierra Leone), worn by women leaders when initiating girls into adulthood, one of the few African masks danced by women. Its neck rolls signal health and beauty. Also called a Bundu mask. Sculpture, objects and materials
rows.166: openwork: Carving or metalwork pierced with holes so you can see through it, making a lacy pattern. Sculpture, objects and materials
rows.167: tesserae: The small cubes of stone, glass or tile used to make a mosaic. Singular: tessera. Glass tesserae backed with gold leaf make glittering gold backgrounds. Sculpture, objects and materials
rows.168: transformation mask: A mask of the Kwakwaka’wakw and other Northwest Coast peoples that opens with strings during a dance to reveal a second face inside, showing a being changing from animal to human or ancestor. Sculpture, objects and materials 237 # Ans. Why Rule (category)
rows.169: site-specific: Art made for one particular place, so that its meaning depends on that location. Moving it would change or destroy the work. Sculpture, objects and materials
rows.170: wood carving: Shaping wood with knives, adzes and chisels. Many of the 250 works from Africa and the Pacific are carved wood, often from a single piece. Sculpture, objects and materials
rows.171: paper mulberry: A tree whose inner bark is beaten into barkcloth (tapa) across Polynesia, and made into paper in East Asia. Sculpture, objects and materials
rows.172: embroidery: Decorating cloth by stitching designs onto it with colored thread. Sculpture, objects and materials
rows.173: lukasa: A hand-held wooden ‘memory board’ of the Luba people (Congo), covered in beads, shells and metal pins. Trained experts touched it while reciting history, king lists and sacred knowledge. Sculpture, objects and materials
rows.174: ivory: The hard, creamy-white material of elephant tusks (and some other animal teeth), prized for fine carving. Today the ivory trade is mostly banned to protect elephants. Sculpture, objects and materials
rows.175: sarsen: A hard sandstone found in southern England. Stonehenge’s huge outer circle and trilithons are sarsens; the smaller ‘bluestones’ came from Wales. Sculpture, objects and materials
rows.176: terracotta: Reddish-brown baked clay used for sculpture, pottery and roof tiles. Italian for ‘baked earth’. Sculpture, objects and materials
rows.177: bi: A flat jade disk with a round hole in the center, made in China from Neolithic times on and often buried with the elite. Later Chinese texts link the bi with heaven; on Lady Dai’s funeral banner two dragons loop through one. Sculpture, objects and materials
rows.178: titanium: A light, strong, silvery metal that does not rust. Gehry covered the Guggenheim Bilbao in thin titanium panels that shimmer like fish scales. Sculpture, objects and materials
rows.179: couching: An embroidery method in which threads are laid across the surface of the cloth and tied down with small stitches. The Bayeux Tapestry fills its figures with laid-andcouched work. Sculpture, objects and materials
rows.180: adlocutio: The pose of a Roman general or emperor with one arm raised, addressing his troops. The word is Latin for ‘speech’ or ‘address’. Sculpture, objects and materials
rows.181: ultramarine: A brilliant deep blue pigment made from ground lapis lazuli from Afghanistan. Before a synthetic version was invented in the 1820s it could cost more than gold; Vermeer used it lavishly. Sculpture, objects and materials
rows.182: veranda post: A carved wooden post that holds up the roof of a veranda (covered porch) of a palace. The Yoruba sculptor Olowe of Ise carved posts with figures that seem to carry the roof. Sculpture, objects and materials
rows.183: figurine: A small statue, usually of a person or animal, often small enough to hold in your hand. Sculpture, objects and materials
rows.184: cloisonné: A technique where thin metal strips are attached to a surface to make little walled cells (cloisons), which are then filled with colored enamel or cut stones like garnets. Sculpture, objects and materials 238 # Ans. Why Rule (category)
rows.185: imagines: Wax masks of a noble Roman family’s ancestors, kept in the atrium of the house and worn by actors in family funeral processions. They may help explain the stern realism of Roman portrait busts. Sculpture, objects and materials
rows.186: pyxis: A small round box with a lid, used for jewelry, cosmetics or perfume. Plural: pyxides. Sculpture, objects and materials
rows.187: relief: Sculpture that projects from a flat background instead of standing free. It can be low (bas-relief), high, or sunken. Sculpture, objects and materials
rows.188: lost-wax casting: A way to cast metal. The artist makes a model in wax, covers it in clay, and heats it so the wax melts out (‘is lost’). Molten metal is poured into the empty space, and the clay is broken away. Sculpture, objects and materials
rows.189: mother-of-pearl: The shiny, rainbow-colored inner layer of some seashells, cut and inlaid into wood, lacquer or paintings. Sculpture, objects and materials
rows.190: neon: Glowing, gas-filled glass tubes bent into lines or letters, as in signs. Paik outlined the U.S. states in neon in Electronic Superhighway. Sculpture, objects and materials
rows.191: tableau: A staged scene in which figures are arranged and frozen as if in a painting. Yinka Shonibare’s The Swing (after Fragonard) turns a painting into a three-dimensional tableau you can walk around. Sculpture, objects and materials
rows.192: alabaster: A soft, pale, slightly see-through stone that is easy to carve and polish. Sculpture, objects and materials
rows.193: assemblage: A three-dimensional work made by putting together found or ready-made objects and materials. The 3D cousin of collage. Sculpture, objects and materials
rows.194: equestrian: Showing a person on horseback. Equestrian statues of rulers were a classic way to show power and command. Sculpture, objects and materials
rows.195: ceramic: Any object made of clay and hardened by heat (firing). Includes earthenware, terracotta, stoneware and porcelain. Sculpture, objects and materials
rows.196: shell: Seashell and turtle shell used as a material for inlay, ornament, beads and, in the Pacific, even whole masks. Sculpture, objects and materials
rows.197: hood mask: A mask made of cloth, beads or fiber that is pulled over the whole head like a hood. The Bamileke Aka elephant mask is a beaded hood mask. Sculpture, objects and materials
rows.198: alloy: A metal made by melting two or more metals together, such as bronze (copper plus tin) or brass (copper plus zinc). Inka metalworkers used gold and silver alloys. Sculpture, objects and materials
rows.199: staff god: A carved wooden figure from Rarotonga (Cook Islands) with a god’s head at the top, wrapped in a huge roll of tapa cloth. Christian missionaries removed and destroyed many wrappings. Sculpture, objects and materials
rows.200: truth to materials: The modernist belief that a material should look like itself: stone should feel like stone, and wood should show its grain. Brancusi’s direct carving follows it. Sculpture, objects and materials
rows.201: pandanus: A tropical plant whose long leaves are dried, split and woven into mats, baskets and sails across the Pacific. Fine pandanus mats are valuable gifts. Sculpture, objects and materials
rows.202: gilding: Covering a surface with a thin layer of gold, as gold leaf or gold paint. Something gilded is called ‘gilt’. Sculpture, objects and materials 239 # Ans. Why Rule (category)
rows.203: kaolin: A fine white clay, the key ingredient of porcelain. Its name comes from Gaoling, a hill near the porcelain city of Jingdezhen in China. Sculpture, objects and materials
rows.204: bone: Animal bone used as a material for carving or shaping. One of the earliest art materials. Sculpture, objects and materials
rows.205: porcelain: Fine, hard, white ceramic made from a special clay (kaolin) fired at very high heat. It can be so thin light glows through it. First perfected in China. Sculpture, objects and materials
rows.206: direct carving: Carving straight into stone or wood without first making a clay model to copy, letting the material guide the shape. Championed by early modern sculptors like Brancusi. Sculpture, objects and materials
rows.207: pietra dura: Inlay of cut and polished colored stones fitted together into marble to make flowers, vines and patterns. Italian for ‘hard stone’. Sculpture, objects and materials
rows.208: sherd: A broken piece of pottery, also called a potsherd. Archaeologists use sherds to date sites and identify cultures, because fired clay survives well. Sculpture, objects and materials
rows.209: sunken relief: Relief where the figures are cut into the surface, so their highest points are level with (or below) the flat surface around them. Common in Egypt; it holds up well in bright sun. Sculpture, objects and materials
rows.210: combine: Robert Rauschenberg’s name for his works that combine painting with real objects attached to the surface, part painting and part sculpture. Jaune Quick-to-See Smith’s Trade follows the idea. Sculpture, objects and materials
rows.211: tenon head: A stone head with a long peg (tenon) on the back so it can be set into a wall. At Chavín de Huántar they show a human face changing step by step into a snarling jaguar. Sculpture, objects and materials
rows.212: red-figure: A Greek vase-painting technique where the background is painted black and the figures are left the red-orange color of the clay, with details drawn in with a brush. It allowed more lifelike detail than black-figure. Sculpture, objects and materials
rows.213: mold: A hollow form into which liquid material like clay, plaster or metal is pressed or poured to make a shape. Molds let makers produce many matching parts. Sculpture, objects and materials
rows.214: eﬀigy: A likeness of a person, especially a sculpture on a tomb or a figure used in a ritual. Among the cast-gold pieces hanging from the Golden Stool are eﬀigies of enemy rulers the Asante defeated. Sculpture, objects and materials
rows.215: Cor-Ten steel: A type of steel that forms a stable, rusty-orange outer layer, which protects the metal from further rust. Popular for outdoor sculpture since the 1960s. Sculpture, objects and materials
rows.216: helmet mask: A mask that covers the whole head like a helmet, rather than just the face. The Sande society’s sowei (Bundu) mask is a famous example. Sculpture, objects and materials
rows.217: brass: A gold-colored metal made by mixing copper and zinc. It can be hammered or cast, and it shines like gold when polished. Sculpture, objects and materials 240 # Ans. Why Rule (category)
rows.218: wet drapery: A carving style in which thin cloth seems wet and clings to the body, revealing it while forming rippling folds. It began on the Parthenon sculptures and continued in Hellenistic works like the Winged Victory. Sculpture, objects and materials
rows.219: closed-circuit video: Video sent live from a camera straight to monitors in the same place, without broadcasting it. Nam June Paik used it so viewers suddenly see themselves on screen inside the work. Sculpture, objects and materials
rows.220: carving: Shaping a sculpture by cutting, chiseling or scraping material away from a block of stone, wood, ivory or jade. Sculpture, objects and materials
rows.221: architectural sculpture: Sculpture made to be part of a building, such as figures on a roof, carved bands along a wall, or a carved panel over a doorway. Sculpture, objects and materials
rows.222: opus vermiculatum: Latin for ‘worm-like work’. The finest Roman mosaic technique, using tiny tesserae laid in curving rows that follow the outlines of forms, allowing painterly shading. Sculpture, objects and materials
rows.223: mosaic: A picture or pattern made by setting many small pieces of colored stone, glass or tile (tesserae) into plaster or cement. Sculpture, objects and materials
rows.224: quillwork: Native American decoration made from dyed porcupine quills, flattened and sewn or wrapped onto hide or birchbark. Glass beadwork, like that on the Lenape bandolier bag (No. 163), largely replaced it once trade beads were plentiful. Sculpture, objects and materials
rows.225: tie-dye: A resist-dye technique: cloth is tied, folded or bound so parts of it don’t take the dye, creating patterns. Faith Ringgold framed Dancing at the Louvre with tie-dyed fabric. Sculpture, objects and materials
rows.226: burnishing: Rubbing a surface hard with a smooth stone or tool to make it shiny. Potters burnish clay before firing to make it gleam; printmakers burnish metal plates to smooth out areas and lighten them. Sculpture, objects and materials
rows.227: public art: Art installed in public spaces, like parks, plazas or streets, where anyone can see it, often paid for by governments or communities. Sculpture, objects and materials
rows.228: joined-block construction: A Japanese technique (yosegizukuri) for making large wooden statues from many separately carved blocks fitted together, which makes them lighter and less likely to crack. Unkei and Kaikei’s Nio guardians at Todaiji were made this way. Sculpture, objects and materials
rows.229: filigree: Delicate ornament made from very fine twisted wires of gold or silver soldered into lacy patterns. Sculpture, objects and materials
rows.230: casting: Making a sculpture by pouring a liquid material, such as molten metal or plaster, into a mold and letting it harden. Many copies can come from one mold. Sculpture, objects and materials
rows.231: modeling (sculpture): Shaping a soft material like clay or wax with hands and tools to make a sculpture. It is additive, building form up. Sculpture, objects and materials
rows.232: fiber: Threads or strands from plants (cotton, bark, pandanus, coconut husk) or animals (wool, camelid hair, silk) used for weaving, netting, tying and binding. Sculpture, objects and materials 241 # Ans. Why Rule (category)
rows.233: polychromy: Painting a sculpture or building in many colors. Greek and Roman marble statues were originally painted; the color has mostly worn off. Adjective: polychrome. Sculpture, objects and materials
rows.234: mobiliary art: Portable prehistoric art, such as carved figurines or decorated stones that could be carried, as opposed to paintings fixed to cave walls. Also called portable art. Sculpture, objects and materials
rows.235: column: An upright post, usually round, that holds up a roof or beam. A classical column has three parts: a base at the bottom, a long shaft, and a decorated capital on top. Architecture
rows.236: applied ornament: Decoration attached to the surface of a building rather than growing out of its structure. In Postmodern architecture, like Venturi’s House in New Castle County, flat cut-out columns and arches are openly stuck on as signs. Architecture
rows.237: charbagh: A Persian-style garden divided into four parts by water channels or paths, often seen as an image of paradise, which the Qur’an describes as having four rivers. Architecture
rows.238: oval dome: A dome built over an oval rather than a circle, favored in the Baroque for its sense of movement and tension. Borromini’s San Carlo has one. Architecture
rows.239: cenotaph: A tomb-like monument that does not hold the body. In the Taj Mahal, the cenotaphs of Mumtaz Mahal and Shah Jahan sit in the main hall, while their real graves lie in a crypt below. Architecture
rows.240: cupola: A small dome, often on top of a roof or a larger dome, sometimes used as a lookout or to let in light. Architecture
rows.241: terrace: A flat, level step cut into a slope or built up as a platform. Inka farmers carved mountains into terraces; Hatshepsut’s temple and Borobudur rise in terraces. Architecture
rows.242: henge: A prehistoric circular area surrounded by a ditch and a bank of earth, sometimes with stones or timber posts set inside. Stonehenge is the famous example. Architecture
rows.243: ambulatory: A walkway that goes around something, such as the apse of a church or the central space of a round shrine. It let pilgrims circle relics without disturbing services. The Dome of the Rock has two ambulatories around its sacred rock. Architecture
rows.244: ashlar masonry: Walls made of stone blocks cut and smoothed so precisely that they fit tightly without mortar. Inka ashlar is so exact that a knife blade cannot slip between the stones. Architecture
rows.245: bracket system: In Chinese and Japanese wooden buildings, interlocking wooden blocks and arms (called dougong in Chinese) that sit on top of the columns and carry the heavy, overhanging tile roof. The more elaborate the brackets, the higher the building’s rank. Architecture
rows.246: stylobate: The top step of a Greek temple’s platform, the floor that the columns stand on. Architecture
rows.247: citadel: A fortified stronghold, often on high ground, protecting a city’s palace and temples. Sargon II’s palace at Dur Sharrukin stood within a walled citadel guarded by lamassu. Architecture
rows.248: metope: One of the square panels in a Doric frieze, set between triglyphs. Metopes were often carved with relief sculpture, such as battles on the Parthenon. Architecture 242 # Ans. Why Rule (category)
rows.249: cornice: The top, projecting layer of an entablature, or any strong ledge that sticks out along the top of a wall. It throws rainwater away from the wall and gives a building a firm ‘lid’. Architecture
rows.250: loculus: A long, shelf-like slot cut into a catacomb wall to hold a body, sealed with a slab or tiles. Plural: loculi. Architecture
rows.251: refectory: The dining hall of a monastery or convent. Leonardo painted the Last Supper on the refectory wall of Santa Maria delle Grazie, so the friars ate with Christ and the apostles. Architecture
rows.252: gopura: A monumental entrance gateway tower in the outer walls of a Hindu temple complex, especially in south India and Cambodia. Architecture
rows.253: mandapa: A hall or porch in a Hindu temple where worshippers gather before approaching the shrine. Larger temples have a series of them leading to the garbhagriha. Architecture
rows.254: quincunx: An arrangement of five things: four at the corners of a square and one in the middle, like the five dots on dice. Angkor Wat’s five towers form one, standing for the five peaks of Mount Meru. Architecture
rows.255: granary: A storehouse for grain. The Conical Tower at Great Zimbabwe may imitate a Shona granary, possibly as a symbol of the ruler’s generosity and wealth. Architecture
rows.256: Palladian: In the style of Andrea Palladio, a 16th-century Italian architect who designed symmetrical villas with templelike porticoes and pediments. His style spread to England and America, including Jefferson’s Monticello. Architecture
rows.257: glazed tile: Ceramic tiles covered in a shiny, colored glassy coat, used to cover walls and domes in bright patterns. Persian and Ottoman builders were masters of it. Architecture
rows.258: steel frame: A skeleton of steel beams and columns that carries a building’s whole weight, so walls do not have to. It made skyscrapers possible in the late 1800s. Architecture
rows.259: lunette: A half-moon-shaped wall area under an arch or vault, often filled with a painting or relief. The School of Athens fills one. Architecture
rows.260: pilgrimage church: A medieval church built to handle crowds of travelers visiting holy relics. It has wide aisles, an ambulatory, and radiating chapels so people can flow past the relics without disturbing Mass. Architecture
rows.261: archivolt: One of the curved bands that frame the tympanum of a church doorway, often carved with small figures. Architecture
rows.262: rotunda: A round building or round room, usually covered by a dome. Architecture
rows.263: hall: In East Asian architecture, a large rectangular wooden building on a stone platform, used for worship or government. The Great Buddha Hall at Todai-ji and the Hall of Supreme Harmony in the Forbidden City are famous examples. Architecture 243 # Ans. Why Rule (category)
rows.264: dry landscape garden: A Japanese Zen garden (in Japanese, karesansui, said kah-ray-sahn-SOO-ee) made of raked gravel and carefully placed rocks, with little or no water or plants. The gravel suggests water and the rocks suggest islands or mountains. It is for looking at and meditating on, not walking through. Architecture
rows.265: polygonal masonry: Stonework of many-sided blocks cut to fit together like a jigsaw puzzle, without mortar. The Inka walls of Cusco and Saqsaywaman are famous examples. Architecture
rows.266: earthen architecture: Buildings made mainly of earth, including mud brick, rammed earth and mud plaster. It stays cool in hot climates but must be repaired regularly. Architecture
rows.267: Chicago window: A wide window with a large fixed glass pane in the middle and a narrow window on each side that can open. A steel frame made it possible. Architecture
rows.268: rib vault: A vault supported by a framework of thin stone arches (ribs) that cross diagonally. The ribs carry the weight to specific points, so the panels between them can be thinner and lighter. Architecture
rows.269: optical refinements: Tiny, deliberate bends in a building that correct tricks of the eye. On the Parthenon the floor bulges up, the columns lean slightly inward, and the shafts swell, so the whole temple looks perfectly straight and alive. Architecture
rows.270: roof comb: A tall, often lacy stone crest built on the roof of a Maya temple to make it look taller and to display painted or sculpted images. Architecture
rows.271: amalaka: A ribbed, disk-shaped stone that caps the shikhara of a north Indian temple, shaped like a segmented fruit. Architecture
rows.272: serdab: A sealed room in an Egyptian tomb holding a statue of the dead person for their ka (life force), sometimes with a small slit so the statue could ‘see’ offerings. The Seated Scribe probably stood in a tomb chapel or serdab. Architecture
rows.273: formal garden: A garden laid out in strict geometric patterns, with straight paths, clipped hedges, pools and fountains arranged on an axis. Versailles’ gardens show the king controlling even nature. Architecture
rows.274: opus reticulatum: Latin for ‘net work’. Ancient Roman wall facing made of small square stones set diagonally in a diamond net pattern. Alberti imitated it at the base of the Palazzo Rucellai. Architecture
rows.275: arch: A curved structure that spans an opening. Wedgeshaped stones (voussoirs) press against each other and pass the weight down to the sides. Arches can span wider gaps than a single beam. Architecture
rows.276: qibla: The direction of Mecca, which Muslims face when they pray. The qibla wall of a mosque faces Mecca and holds the mihrab. Architecture
rows.277: compound pier: A pier with several thinner shafts attached to it. Each shaft lines up with an arch or rib above, so the wall’s structure reads as a set of lines rising to the vault. Architecture 244 # Ans. Why Rule (category)
rows.278: külliye: An Ottoman complex built around a mosque, which could also include schools, a hospital, a soup kitchen, baths and the founder’s tomb. Architecture
rows.279: triglyph: A block with three vertical grooves that alternates with metopes in a Doric frieze. It probably recalls the ends of wooden beams in earlier wooden temples. Architecture
rows.280: toron: Bundles of palm wood that stick out from the walls of West African mud buildings. They act as built-in scaffolding for the yearly re-plastering and also decorate the walls. Architecture
rows.281: hypostyle mosque: The earliest type of mosque: a large prayer hall filled with rows of columns, usually beside an open courtyard. It can be enlarged simply by adding more rows of columns. Architecture
rows.282: stained glass: Pieces of colored glass held together by strips of lead to form pictures in a window. In Gothic churches the colored light was meant to feel like heavenly light. Architecture
rows.283: form follows function: Louis Sullivan’s famous idea that a building’s shape should come from what it is used for. It became a motto of modern architecture. Architecture
rows.284: plaza: A large open public square in a town or ceremonial center, used for gatherings, markets or ritual. Architecture
rows.285: necropolis: Greek for ‘city of the dead’. A large ancient cemetery, often with tombs laid out like streets and houses. Architecture
rows.286: keystone: The wedge-shaped stone at the very top center of an arch. It is the last stone put in, and it locks the others in place. Architecture
rows.287: aisle: A long side passage that runs parallel to the nave of a church, separated from it by a row of columns or piers. Architecture
rows.288: dome: A rounded roof shaped like half a sphere (or taller, like an onion). A dome is basically an arch spun in a circle. Architecture
rows.289: less is more: Mies van der Rohe’s motto: simple, strippeddown design with no extra ornament is more powerful. Robert Venturi later joked back, ‘less is a bore.’ Architecture
rows.290: podium: A tall platform that an Etruscan or Roman temple stands on, with stairs only at the front. It makes the temple face one way, unlike a Greek temple you can approach from all sides. Architecture
rows.291: horseshoe arch: An arch that curves in past its widest point before meeting its supports, like a horseshoe. A hallmark of Islamic Spain. Architecture
rows.292: cast iron: Iron melted and poured into molds. Strong and cheap in the 1800s, it was used for building frames and for intricate ornament, like the swirling decoration over the entrance of Sullivan’s Carson, Pirie, Scott store. Architecture
rows.293: hypostyle hall: A large hall whose roof is held up by many rows of columns. The word means ‘under columns.’ Ancient Egyptians, Persians and early Islamic mosque builders all used it. Architecture
rows.294: bay: One repeated section of a building, marked off by columns, piers, or vault ribs. A Gothic nave is a row of identical bays. Architecture 245 # Ans. Why Rule (category)
rows.295: Iznik tile: Brilliant ceramic tiles made in the Ottoman town of Iznik (Turkey), famous for vivid blue, turquoise and tomatored flowers on white. Used inside Sinan’s mosques. Architecture
rows.296: temple-mountain: A temple designed as a model of a sacred mountain, usually Mount Meru, the center of the universe in Hindu and Buddhist belief, with towers or terraces rising to a high center. Architecture
rows.297: parametric design: Design in which computer formulas generate and adjust a building’s shapes. It is associated with the flowing, curving forms of Zaha Hadid. Architecture
rows.298: chevron pattern: A zigzag or V-shaped pattern. At Great Zimbabwe, a chevron band runs along the top of the Great Enclosure wall. Architecture
rows.299: skyscraper: A very tall building made possible by steel frames and elevators. It started in Chicago and New York in the late 1800s. Architecture
rows.300: architectural drawing: A precise line drawing, such as a plan, elevation or section, used to design or record a building. Julie Mehretu layers drawings of stadiums and buildings into her paintings. Architecture
rows.301: intihuatana: A carved stone outcrop at Inka sites, thought to be linked to the sun and the calendar. The name is often translated as ‘hitching post of the sun.’ Architecture
rows.302: cathedral: The main church of a bishop’s district, holding the bishop’s throne (the ‘cathedra’). Medieval cathedrals were the biggest, most expensive buildings in their towns. Architecture
rows.303: gable: The triangular upper part of a wall at the end of a pitched roof. In classical buildings, a decorated gable is a pediment. Venturi’s House in New Castle County hides behind a big farmhouse gable. Architecture
rows.304: entasis: A slight swelling in the middle of a column shaft. It makes columns look straight and strong rather than pinched, because perfectly straight columns can look thin in the middle from a distance. Architecture
rows.305: triclinium: The dining room of a Roman house, named for its three couches, arranged in a U, where diners reclined. The Etruscan Tomb of the Triclinium is named for its painted banquet scenes. Architecture
rows.306: barrel vault: A ceiling made by extending a round arch in a straight line, like a tunnel. Also called a tunnel vault. It is heavy and pushes outward along its whole length, so the walls below must be thick. Architecture
rows.307: papyrus capital: The top of an Egyptian column carved to look like a bundle of papyrus plants, either open like a flower or closed like a bud. It turns a stone hall into a symbolic marsh, where Egyptians believed creation began. Architecture
rows.308: banco: The fermented mud mixture used to build and plaster mosques and houses in Mali. At Djenné it is re-applied every year. Architecture
rows.309: prang: A tall, rounded, finger-like tower of a Thai or Khmerstyle temple, descended from Khmer prasats like those at Angkor Wat. Architecture 246 # Ans. Why Rule (category)
rows.310: feng shui: A Chinese system for siting and arranging buildings in harmony with the land, water and cosmic forces. The Forbidden City faces south, with protective hills to the north. Architecture
rows.311: entablature: Everything that sits on top of the columns in a classical building and below the roof: the architrave, the frieze, and the cornice, stacked in that order. Architecture
rows.312: adobe: Sun-dried brick made from clay, sand and straw, or the mud mortar and plaster made from the same mix. Used from Africa to the American Southwest. Architecture
rows.313: cladding: An outer covering or skin attached to a building’s frame, such as terra cotta, glass, stone or titanium. Architecture
rows.314: chamber tomb: A tomb with one or more rooms built or cut underground, often decorated like a house for the dead. Etruscan families were buried in painted chamber tombs. Architecture
rows.315: westwork: A massive, tower-flanked front block at the west end of Carolingian and Ottonian churches, holding an entrance, chapels and an upper gallery. Architecture
rows.316: colonnade: A long row of columns spaced at regular intervals, usually holding up a roof or entablature. Architecture
rows.317: oculus: A round opening at the top of a dome that lets in light (and rain). The Pantheon’s oculus is about 30 feet wide and is the only light source inside. Architecture
rows.318: trapezoidal doorway: A door, window or niche that is narrower at the top than at the bottom. The Inka used it because it is very stable in earthquakes. Architecture
rows.319: proto-doric: Columns that look like early versions of the Greek Doric column: plain, fluted and many-sided. Hatshepsut’s mortuary temple has them, about a thousand years before the first Greek Doric temples. Architecture
rows.320: hypogeum: An underground space. At the Colosseum, the hypogeum under the arena floor held tunnels, cages and lifts for animals and fighters. Architecture
rows.321: ziggurat: A huge stepped platform of mud brick built in ancient Mesopotamia (modern Iraq), with a temple on top. Raising the temple high lifted it closer to the gods and made it visible across the flat plain. Architecture
rows.322: dry-stone masonry: Stone walls built without any mortar. The stones hold together through careful fitting and their own weight. Architecture
rows.323: timber frame: A building structure made of a wooden skeleton of posts and beams, with the walls only filling the gaps. Traditional Chinese and Japanese temples and palaces use it. Architecture
rows.324: cloister: An enclosed garden courtyard surrounded by a covered walkway, part of a monastery or convent. The Spanish built a convent with a cloister on top of the Inka sun temple in Cusco. Architecture
rows.325: ribbed dome: A dome built on a framework of crossing arches or ribs, which often form a star pattern. The dome in front of Córdoba’s mihrab is a famous early example. Architecture
rows.326: valley temple: A temple at the edge of the Nile floodplain where a pharaoh’s funeral began, linked by a causeway to the mortuary temple beside his pyramid. Architecture 247 # Ans. Why Rule (category)
rows.327: spolia: Pieces taken from older buildings and reused in new ones, such as columns, capitals or carvings. It saves work and can also show victory over, or connection to, the past. Architecture
rows.328: mud brick: Bricks made of mud (often mixed with straw) and dried in the sun instead of fired in a kiln. Cheap and easy where stone and wood are scarce, but it wears away and needs constant repair. Architecture
rows.329: machine for living: Le Corbusier’s phrase for a modern house: an eﬀicient, functional object designed like a machine around how people actually live. Architecture
rows.330: pradakshina patha: The path for circumambulation, the ritual of walking clockwise around a holy object like a stupa or a temple’s sanctum. At Borobudur, pilgrims circle and climb through the terraces toward the top. Architecture
rows.331: multilobed arch: An arch whose inner edge is cut into a series of curves or ‘lobes’ like a scalloped edge. Used near the mihrab at Córdoba, sometimes in interlacing layers. Architecture
rows.332: iwan: A large vaulted hall that is walled on three sides and completely open on the fourth, usually facing a courtyard. A standard feature of Persian and later Islamic architecture. Architecture
rows.333: basilica: Originally a long Roman public hall used for law courts and business, with a central nave, side aisles and an apse at the end. Early Christians copied this plan for their churches. Architecture
rows.334: free facade: An outside wall that can be designed freely, with windows placed anywhere, because it carries no weight. One of Le Corbusier’s Five Points. Architecture
rows.335: International Style: A modern architecture style of the 1920s to 1960s, spread worldwide: boxy shapes, flat roofs, white walls or glass skins, steel and concrete frames, and no ornament. Architecture
rows.336: megalith: A very large stone used to build a monument, usually without mortar. ‘Megalithic’ describes structures made of such stones, mostly from prehistoric times. Architecture
rows.337: peristyle: A row of columns surrounding a building or a courtyard. A Greek temple like the Parthenon is wrapped in a peristyle; a Roman house has a peristyle garden, a courtyard ringed by columns. Architecture
rows.338: domus: A private townhouse of a wealthy Roman family. It turned inward around an atrium and a peristyle garden, with few windows on the street. Architecture
rows.339: mortar: A paste, such as mud, lime or cement, spread between stones or bricks to bind them. Mesa Verde’s sandstone blocks sit in mud mortar; Inka builders famously used none, fitting stones so tightly they did not need it. Architecture
rows.340: garbhagriha: The small, dark, innermost shrine of a Hindu temple, where the main image of the god is kept. Only priests may enter. Architecture
rows.341: hieroglyphic stairway: A Maya staircase whose steps are carved with writing (glyphs) and images that record a ruler’s history and deeds. Architecture 248 # Ans. Why Rule (category)
rows.342: parterre: A formal garden of flat, level beds laid out in symmetrical patterns, often edged with low clipped hedges and gravel paths, as at Versailles. Architecture
rows.343: stupa: A Buddhist monument shaped like a solid dome or mound that holds relics of the Buddha or a holy teacher. You cannot go inside; instead, worshippers walk around it clockwise. Architecture
rows.344: central plan: A building laid out around a central point, so all sides are equal or nearly so, such as a circle, square, octagon or Greek cross. It usually has a dome over the middle. Architecture
rows.345: martyrium: A church or shrine built over the grave of a martyr or at a site linked to Christ’s life, often with a central plan. San Vitale honors the martyr Saint Vitalis. Architecture
rows.346: octagonal plan: A building laid out as an eight-sided shape. San Vitale and the Dome of the Rock both use octagons, a shape halfway between a square (earth) and a circle (heaven). Architecture
rows.347: shikhara: The tall, curving tower that rises over the garbhagriha of a north Indian Hindu temple. Clusters of smaller towers climb toward it like a mountain range, evoking Mount Meru, home of the gods. Architecture
rows.348: apadana: A great audience hall of the ancient Persian kings, a hypostyle hall where the king received visitors and gifts. The one at Persepolis stood on a raised platform reached by staircases carved with processions of tribute bearers. Architecture
rows.349: congregational mosque: A large mosque where a whole community gathers for the Friday noon prayer and sermon. Also called a Friday mosque or, in Persian, masjid-e jameh. Architecture
rows.350: undulating facade: A building front that curves in and out in waves instead of being flat. Borromini’s San Carlo is the classic Baroque example. Architecture
rows.351: pishtaq: A tall rectangular frame around an iwan’s arched opening, which makes the entrance look bigger and grander. Persian and Mughal buildings use it; the Taj Mahal has one on each side. Architecture
rows.352: obelisk: A tall, thin, four-sided stone pillar that narrows as it rises and ends in a small pyramid point. Egyptian pharaohs set them up in pairs at temple entrances to honor the sun god. Architecture
rows.353: arcade: A row of arches held up by columns or piers. Architecture
rows.354: spire: A tall, pointed, cone- or pyramid-shaped structure on top of a tower, especially on a church. Architecture
rows.355: chapter house: A meeting room attached to a monastery or cathedral, where monks or clergy gathered to discuss business and hear readings. Architecture
rows.356: temenos: A sacred area set apart for a god, often walled, that contains temples, altars and offerings. Architecture
rows.357: concrete: A building material made by mixing lime, sand, water and rubble that hardens like stone. Romans used it to pour huge curved shapes like domes and vaults, which changed architecture forever. Architecture
rows.358: loggia: A gallery or porch that is open on one or more sides, usually with columns or arches, and part of a larger building. It is an indoor-outdoor space for shade and air. Architecture 249 # Ans. Why Rule (category)
rows.359: maqsura: A screened-off area in a mosque near the mihrab, reserved for the ruler to pray in safety and in style. Architecture
rows.360: anda: The solid, hemispherical dome of a stupa, which covers the relics and stands for the dome of heaven or the world mountain. Architecture
rows.361: gatehouse: A building that forms the guarded entrance to a temple or palace compound. Todai-ji’s Great South Gate holds two giant guardian figures. Architecture
rows.362: coffer: A sunken square or other shaped panel set into a ceiling or dome. Coffers make a dome lighter and decorate it with a grid pattern. Architecture
rows.363: architectural calligraphy: Beautiful writing used as decoration on a building, often Qur’an verses or poetry, carved in stone or stucco or laid in tile and mosaic. On the Taj Mahal the letters get larger near the top so they look the same size from the ground. Architecture
rows.364: impost block: An extra block placed between a column’s capital and the arch above it, helping to carry the weight. Used in Byzantine churches like San Vitale. Architecture
rows.365: pier: A thick, solid upright support, usually square or rectangular, bigger and stronger than a column. Architecture
rows.366: pagoda: A tall, many-storied tower with roofs at each level, found in Buddhist temples in China, Korea and Japan. It grew out of the Indian stupa and often holds relics. Todai-ji once had two huge pagodas, now lost. Architecture
rows.367: madrasa: A school for Islamic religious learning, often attached to a mosque. Architecture
rows.368: hipped roof: A roof that slopes down on all four sides. In China, a double-eaved hipped roof (two layers) was reserved for the most important imperial halls. Architecture
rows.369: kiva: A round, partly underground room used by Puebloan peoples for ceremonies and meetings. A small hole in the floor (the sipapu) stands for the place where people emerged into this world. Architecture
rows.370: impluvium: A shallow basin in the floor of a Roman atrium that caught rainwater falling through the opening in the roof above. Architecture
rows.371: animal style: An art tradition of the nomads of the Eurasian steppes and of early medieval northern Europe in which animals, such as birds of prey, beasts and fish, are twisted, stretched and woven into patterns on small, portable metal objects. Styles, periods and movements
rows.372: Constructivism: A Russian movement of about 1915 to the 1930s that wanted art to serve the new Soviet society, using geometric forms, industrial materials, graphic design and photomontage. Styles, periods and movements
rows.373: Futurism: An Italian movement founded in 1909 that celebrated speed, machines, cities, technology and even war, showing motion with repeated forms and fractured lines. Styles, periods and movements 250 # Ans. Why Rule (category)
rows.374: Proto-Renaissance: Italian art of about 1280 to 1400 that started to move toward the Renaissance, especially in Giotto’s frescoes, which give figures real weight, space around them and human emotion. Styles, periods and movements
rows.375: Neoplasticism: Piet Mondrian’s name for his pure abstract style: only straight horizontal and vertical lines, the three primary colors, and black, white and gray. He hoped it would express universal harmony. Styles, periods and movements
rows.376: Chandella: A Hindu dynasty of central India, 9th to 13th centuries C.E., which built the temples of Khajuraho with their towering shikharas and dense, sensual sculpture. Styles, periods and movements
rows.377: Nara period: Japan’s period from 710 to 794 C.E., when the capital was at Nara and emperors sponsored Buddhism as a state religion, building Todai-ji. Styles, periods and movements
rows.378: New York School: The Abstract Expressionist artists active in New York City in the 1940s and 1950s, such as Pollock, de Kooning and Rothko, who made New York the center of the art world. Styles, periods and movements
rows.379: Viceregal art: Art made in Spain’s American colonies (the viceroyalties of New Spain and Peru) from the 1500s to the early 1800s. It blends European styles with Indigenous materials, ideas and artists, from feather and shell inlay to casta paintings. Styles, periods and movements
rows.380: Academic art: Art made by the rules of oﬀicial art schools (academies), like the French Academy, from the 1600s to the 1800s: polished finish, perfect drawing and serious historical or mythological subjects. Shown at the yearly Salon in Paris. Styles, periods and movements
rows.381: Nasrid: The last Muslim dynasty in Spain, ruling Granada from 1232 until 1492, when it fell to Ferdinand and Isabella. It built the Alhambra palace. Styles, periods and movements
rows.382: color field painting: A type of Abstract Expressionism using large areas of flat or stained color to create calm, immersive, spiritual effects. Frankenthaler poured thinned paint into raw canvas. Styles, periods and movements
rows.383: Joseon: Korea’s longest dynasty, 1392 to 1910, guided by Confucian ideals. Oﬀicial portraits of scholars and oﬀicials show them formally and soberly in court dress. Styles, periods and movements
rows.384: Harlem Renaissance: A flowering of African American art, music and literature centered in Harlem, New York, in the 1920s and 1930s, celebrating Black identity, history and culture. Jacob Lawrence grew up in its world. Styles, periods and movements
rows.385: yamato-e: Japanese for ‘Japanese-style painting’. A style that grew up in the Heian period, with bright colors, high angled views, roofs left off to show interiors, and Japanese stories and places, in contrast to Chinese-style painting. Styles, periods and movements
rows.386: Modernism: The broad movement, from roughly the 1860s to the 1970s, of artists rejecting tradition to invent new forms suited to modern life. It includes Impressionism through Abstract Expressionism and the International Style. Styles, periods and movements 251 # Ans. Why Rule (category)
rows.387: Imperial Roman: Roman art under the emperors, starting with Augustus in 27 B.C.E. It mixes idealized Greek-style portraits of rulers with huge engineering projects in concrete, like the Colosseum and Pantheon, all promoting the emperor’s power. Styles, periods and movements
rows.388: synthetism: The approach Gauguin and his circle developed in the late 1880s: flat areas of bold color, strong outlines and simplified forms that combine what the artist saw with memory, feeling and symbols. Styles, periods and movements
rows.389: Liangzhu culture: A Neolithic culture in the Yangtze River delta of China, about 3300 to 2200 B.C.E., known for finely carved jade objects such as the cong, a square tube with a round hole. Styles, periods and movements
rows.390: Cubism: A revolutionary movement started in Paris around 1907 by Picasso and Braque. It breaks objects into flat, geometric pieces and shows them from several angles at once, abandoning single-point perspective. Styles, periods and movements
rows.391: Carolingian: Art under Charlemagne and his heirs, about 768 to 900 C.E., in France and Germany. It deliberately revived Roman and Early Christian models in manuscripts, metalwork and churches with westworks. Styles, periods and movements
rows.392: Heian period: Japan’s period from 794 to 1185 C.E., when the court in Heian (Kyoto) produced refined literature and painting. It ended in civil wars between the Taira and Minamoto clans, the war shown in the later Night Attack scroll. Styles, periods and movements
rows.393: proto-cubism: Work leading up to Cubism, especially Picasso’s Les Demoiselles d’Avignon (1907), which broke figures into flat, angular planes before Cubism was fully developed. Styles, periods and movements
rows.394: Mughal: The Muslim dynasty that ruled most of South Asia from 1526 to 1857, mixing Persian, Indian and Islamic traditions. Known for the Taj Mahal and refined, detailed miniature paintings. Styles, periods and movements
rows.395: Early Christian: Christian art from about 200 to 500 C.E. At first hidden in catacomb paintings with simple symbols, it became public after Christianity was legalized in 313, when churches were built on the basilica plan. Styles, periods and movements
rows.396: Expressionism: Art, especially in Germany around 1905 to 1925, that distorts form and color to express strong inner emotions such as anxiety, anger or spiritual feeling, rather than show the world accurately. Styles, periods and movements
rows.397: ukiyo-e: Japanese woodblock prints and paintings of the Edo period showing the ‘floating world’ of entertainment, actors, beauties and later landscapes. Cheap and popular, they deeply influenced European artists. Styles, periods and movements
rows.398: community-based art: Art made with and for a particular community, often through conversations, workshops and shared stories, and shown in that neighborhood rather than only in museums. Styles, periods and movements
rows.399: Synthetic Cubism: The second phase of Cubism (from about 1912). Instead of breaking objects down, artists built pictures up from flat, simpler shapes, brighter colors, and real materials glued on (collage). Styles, periods and movements 252 # Ans. Why Rule (category)
rows.400: Der Blaue Reiter: ‘The Blue Rider,’ a German Expressionist group founded in Munich in 1911 by Kandinsky and Franz Marc, which moved toward spiritual abstraction using color like music. Styles, periods and movements
rows.401: Sumerian: Art of Sumer, the world’s first civilization of cities, in southern Mesopotamia (modern Iraq), about 3500 to 2000 B.C.E. It includes ziggurats, wide-eyed praying statues and inlaid objects, and it invented writing (cuneiform). Styles, periods and movements
rows.402: Bauhaus: A German art and design school (1919 to 1933) that joined art, craft and industry. It taught clean, functional, geometric design and shaped modern architecture and furniture. Mies van der Rohe was its last director. Styles, periods and movements
rows.403: Surrealism: A movement launched in 1924 that explored dreams, the unconscious mind and strange combinations of images, inspired by Freud’s ideas. Styles, periods and movements
rows.404: Republican Roman: Roman art from 509 to 27 B.C.E., when Rome was a republic governed by elected oﬀicials. Portraits of older men are ‘veristic’: brutally realistic, showing wrinkles to signal wisdom and service. Styles, periods and movements
rows.405: Lapita: The seafaring culture, about 1500 to 500 B.C.E., that first settled the islands of the western Pacific. It is known for pottery decorated with stamped and incised patterns, many later found in Polynesian tattoo and tapa designs. Styles, periods and movements
rows.406: Merovingian: Art of the Franks under the Merovingian kings (about 481 to 751 C.E.) in what is now France and Germany, known for jeweled metalwork such as brooches (fibulae) with garnets and animal shapes. Styles, periods and movements
rows.407: High Renaissance: The peak of the Italian Renaissance, about 1495 to 1520 (longer in Venice). Leonardo, Michelangelo, Raphael and Titian created balanced, monumental, idealized works. Styles, periods and movements
rows.408: fête galante: French for ‘courtly party’. A Rococo type of painting showing elegant aristocrats flirting and amusing themselves in dreamy parks and gardens. Styles, periods and movements
rows.409: Rococo: A light, playful style of about 1720 to 1780, mostly in France. Pastel colors, curving lines, frothy decoration and flirty scenes of aristocrats at leisure. Styles, periods and movements
rows.410: Post-Impressionism: Art of about 1886 to 1905 by painters who began with Impressionism but went further in their own directions: Van Gogh (emotional color), Gauguin (flat symbolic color), Cézanne (solid geometric structure), Seurat (dots of color). Styles, periods and movements
rows.411: Neolithic: The New Stone Age, beginning around 10,000 to 8000 B.C.E. in the Near East and later elsewhere, when people started farming, raising animals and living in villages. It brought pottery, polished stone tools and huge stone monuments. Styles, periods and movements
rows.412: Classical Greek: Greek art of about 480 to 323 B.C.E., centered on Athens. It aims for ideal balance and calm: perfect human bodies in natural poses (contrapposto), harmonious proportions and the Parthenon. Styles, periods and movements 253 # Ans. Why Rule (category)
rows.413: Postmodernism: A movement from the 1970s on that rejects Modernism’s belief in purity and progress. It mixes styles, quotes the past, uses irony and questions ideas of originality and identity. Styles, periods and movements
rows.414: Predynastic Egypt: Egypt before and around the time its first kings united Upper and Lower Egypt, about 3000 B.C.E. The Narmer Palette already shows the conventions Egyptian art kept for 3,000 years. Styles, periods and movements
rows.415: anti-art: Art and attitudes that attack the very idea of art: its skill, beauty, museums and market. Dada artists, above all Marcel Duchamp with his readymades, made anti-art to question what counts as art at all. Styles, periods and movements
rows.416: Maya: A Mesoamerican civilization of southern Mexico and Central America, at its height about 250 to 900 C.E. Maya city-states built pyramid temples with roof combs and carved stone reliefs with hieroglyphic writing recording rulers’ histories. Styles, periods and movements
rows.417: Late Antique: The period from about 200 to 600 C.E., when the Roman world was turning Christian. Art becomes less naturalistic and more symbolic, with crowded or flattened figures, and Christian art begins in catacombs and basilicas. Styles, periods and movements
rows.418: caravaggisti: The many painters across Europe in the early 1600s who copied Caravaggio’s style: harsh light against deep darkness, ordinary-looking people and close-up, real-life drama. Caravaggio’s Calling of Saint Matthew (No. 85) shows the model they followed. Styles, periods and movements
rows.419: Mannerism: Italian art of about 1520 to 1600, after the High Renaissance. Figures are stretched and twisted, colors are strange, space is crowded or unclear, and the mood is tense: elegance and artificiality over balance. Styles, periods and movements
rows.420: Early Medieval: European art of about 500 to 1000 C.E., after the fall of Rome, made by peoples such as the Franks, Anglo-Saxons and Irish. Much of it is portable metalwork and illuminated manuscripts with dense interlaced patterns. Styles, periods and movements
rows.421: Northwest Coast: The Native American culture region along the Pacific coast of Canada and Alaska, home to peoples like the Kwakwaka’wakw, known for carved masks, totem poles and potlatch ceremonies. Styles, periods and movements
rows.422: installation art: Large artworks, from the 1960s on, that fill or transform a whole room or site, so viewers walk into and experience them. Styles, periods and movements
rows.423: Analytic Cubism: The first main phase of Cubism (about 1909 to 1912). Objects are broken into many small, overlapping facets in a narrow range of browns and grays, so the subject is hard to read. Styles, periods and movements
rows.424: Kamakura period: Japan’s period from 1185 to 1333, when samurai warlords (shoguns) took power. Art became more realistic and energetic, from narrative war scrolls to muscular guardian sculptures. Styles, periods and movements
rows.425: Fauvism: A short movement in France (about 1905 to 1908), led by Henri Matisse, using wild, bright, unnatural colors and loose brushwork to express feeling. Styles, periods and movements 254 # Ans. Why Rule (category)
rows.426: Silla: One of the Three Kingdoms of ancient Korea (57 B.C.E. to 935 C.E.), later ruling a unified Korea. Its royal tombs held spectacular gold crowns shaped like trees and antlers. Styles, periods and movements
rows.427: Venetian school: Renaissance painting in Venice, led by artists like Titian, which stressed rich color, soft light and the texture of oil paint more than precise drawing. Styles, periods and movements
rows.428: Safavid: The dynasty that ruled Iran from 1501 to 1736 and made Shia Islam the state religion. Its court produced dazzling illustrated manuscripts, carpets and tiled buildings. Styles, periods and movements
rows.429: performance art: Art in which the work is a live action by the artist, sometimes with the audience, rather than an object. It became a major form from the 1960s on. Styles, periods and movements
rows.430: Ottonian: Art of the German emperors named Otto and their successors, about 919 to 1024 C.E. It produced massive churches, bronze doors and solemn manuscripts that bridge Carolingian and Romanesque art. Styles, periods and movements
rows.431: Afrofuturism: An art and culture movement that mixes African and African diaspora history and myth with science fiction, technology and imagined futures, to picture Black life beyond the limits of the past and present. Styles, periods and movements
rows.432: Edo period: Japan’s period from 1615 to 1868, under the Tokugawa shoguns in Edo (Tokyo), when the country was largely closed to the outside world. A wealthy merchant class enjoyed Rinpa painting and ukiyo-e woodblock prints. Styles, periods and movements
rows.433: Romanesque: European art and architecture of about 1000 to 1150 C.E. Churches have thick walls, round arches, barrel vaults, small windows and sculpted portals, often built along pilgrimage roads. Styles, periods and movements
rows.434: Dutch Golden Age: The 1600s in the Dutch Republic, a rich Protestant trading nation. Artists sold to middle-class buyers on an open market, painting portraits, still lifes, landscapes and everyday scenes in exquisite detail. Styles, periods and movements
rows.435: Hellenistic: Greek art after Alexander the Great, 323 to 31 B.C.E., spread across a huge territory from Egypt to Asia. It is dramatic and emotional, shows twisting motion, and includes real people: the old, the poor and the suffering. Styles, periods and movements
rows.436: Gandharan: Buddhist art of Gandhara (today’s Pakistan and Afghanistan), about the first to eighth centuries C.E., which blended Indian Buddhism with Greek and Roman sculpture, giving the Buddha wavy hair and toga-like robes. Styles, periods and movements
rows.437: Babylonian: Art of Babylon in Mesopotamia. The Old Babylonian period (about 1900 to 1600 B.C.E.) under King Hammurabi produced the famous carved law code; a later NeoBabylonian empire flourished in the 600s B.C.E. Styles, periods and movements
rows.438: Yarlung dynasty: The early Tibetan kingdom (7th to 9th centuries C.E.) that brought Buddhism to Tibet. Its king Songtsen Gampo is linked to the arrival of the Jowo Rinpoche statue in Lhasa. Styles, periods and movements 255 # Ans. Why Rule (category)
rows.439: Nabataean: Art of the Nabataeans, Arab traders who controlled desert caravan routes and built the city of Petra (Jordan), about 400 B.C.E. to 106 C.E. They carved huge tomb facades into cliffs, mixing Greek and Roman forms with local taste. Styles, periods and movements
rows.440: monotheism: Belief in only one god, as in Judaism, Christianity and Islam, and briefly in Akhenaten’s Egypt. Religion, myth and symbols
rows.441: Bodhi tree: The fig tree under which the Buddha meditated and reached enlightenment. In early Buddhist art a tree can stand in for the Buddha himself. Religion, myth and symbols
rows.442: bloodletting: A Maya ritual in which rulers and nobles drew their own blood, for example through the tongue, as an offering to gods and to call up ancestors in visions. Religion, myth and symbols
rows.443: afterlife: Life after death. Belief in an afterlife drove huge amounts of art: tombs, coﬀins, grave goods and guardian figures meant to help or protect the dead. Religion, myth and symbols
rows.444: Entombment: The scene of Jesus’ body being carried to and laid in his tomb after the Crucifixion. Religion, myth and symbols
rows.445: ankh: An Egyptian symbol shaped like a cross with a loop on top, meaning ‘life’. Gods hold it to give life to the king. Religion, myth and symbols
rows.446: house altar: A small shrine or carved image set up in a private home for family worship. The relief of Akhenaton, Nefertiti and their daughters was a house altar honoring the royal family and the sun god Aten. Religion, myth and symbols
rows.447: Shinto: Japan’s native religion, honoring kami: spirits found in nature, places and ancestors. It coexists with Buddhism in Japan. Religion, myth and symbols
rows.448: horned crown: A crown with stacked pairs of horns, worn only by gods in Mesopotamian art. It tells you the figure is divine, like Shamash on the Code of Hammurabi. Religion, myth and symbols
rows.449: Aphrodite: Greek goddess of love and beauty, called Venus by the Romans. She was born from sea foam, and Julius Caesar’s family (including Augustus) claimed to descend from her. Religion, myth and symbols
rows.450: apu: A sacred mountain spirit in Andean belief. Inka sites were laid out to frame views of these holy peaks. Religion, myth and symbols
rows.451: Last Supper: Jesus’ final meal with his twelve apostles before his arrest. He announces that one of them (Judas) will betray him, and he shares bread and wine, which became the Christian rite of the Eucharist. Religion, myth and symbols
rows.452: Zen: A Japanese school of Buddhism (Chan in Chinese) that stresses meditation, simplicity and sudden insight over texts and rituals. Zen shaped Japanese gardens, ink painting and the tea ceremony. Religion, myth and symbols
rows.453: Gaia: The Greek goddess who is the Earth itself, mother of the Giants. Religion, myth and symbols
rows.454: Abraham: The founding father of Judaism, Christianity and Islam. God tested him by asking him to sacrifice his son (Isaac in the Bible, Ishmael in Muslim tradition). Muslims believe he and Ishmael built the Kaaba. Religion, myth and symbols
rows.455: Ahura Mazda: The supreme god of Zoroastrianism, the religion of ancient Persia’s kings, sometimes symbolized by a winged disk. Religion, myth and symbols 256 # Ans. Why Rule (category)
rows.456: lingam: An upright, rounded pillar that stands for Shiva’s creative energy. It is the main object of worship in most Shiva temples. Religion, myth and symbols
rows.457: dharmachakra mudra: The ‘turning the wheel of the law’ gesture, with both hands at the chest forming circles with the fingers. It stands for the Buddha’s first sermon. Religion, myth and symbols
rows.458: Nekhbet and Wadjet: The vulture goddess of Upper Egypt and the cobra goddess of Lower Egypt, protectors of the king. Together they stand for the united land. Religion, myth and symbols
rows.459: Exodus: The Bible story of the Israelites escaping slavery in Egypt, with the ten plagues and the parting of the Red Sea. Also the name of the second book of the Bible. Religion, myth and symbols
rows.460: phoenix: A mythical bird. In China it is a sign of peace, virtue and the empress, often paired with the dragon; in the West it is reborn from its own ashes. Religion, myth and symbols
rows.461: Book of the Dead: An Egyptian collection of spells and pictures, written on papyrus and buried with the dead to guide them safely through the underworld to the afterlife. Religion, myth and symbols
rows.462: Pantocrator: Greek for ‘ruler of all’. A Byzantine image of Christ as stern ruler of the universe, seen from the chest up, holding a book and blessing with his right hand. It usually fills the central dome of a Byzantine church. Religion, myth and symbols
rows.463: scriptorium: The room in a monastery where monks copied and decorated books by hand. Religion, myth and symbols
rows.464: calligraphy: The art of beautiful handwriting. In Islam it is the most honored art form because it records God’s words. Chinese and Japanese calligraphy is also a high art, done with brush and ink. Religion, myth and symbols
rows.465: meditation: Focusing and quieting the mind, a central practice in Buddhism and especially in Zen, which seeks enlightenment through direct experience. Zen gardens like Ryoan-ji are aids to quiet contemplation. Religion, myth and symbols
rows.466: moksha: In Hinduism, final release from the cycle of rebirth. Religion, myth and symbols
rows.467: Dreaming: In Aboriginal Australian belief, the time and ongoing reality in which ancestral beings created the land, laws and living things. Aboriginal art often maps a person’s Dreaming and country. Religion, myth and symbols
rows.468: weighing of the heart: The Egyptian judgment after death: the heart is weighed against the feather of Ma’at. A light heart (a good life) wins eternal life with Osiris; a heavy one is eaten by Ammit. Religion, myth and symbols
rows.469: apostle: One of the twelve chosen followers of Jesus, such as Peter, John, Matthew and Judas. The word means ‘one who is sent out’. Religion, myth and symbols
rows.470: Zephyr: The Greek god of the gentle west wind, often shown as a winged youth puﬀing air. Religion, myth and symbols
rows.471: Coyolxauhqui: Aztec moon goddess who led an attack on her mother Coatlicue and was killed and cut apart by her brother Huitzilopochtli. A stone disk of her broken body lay at the foot of the Templo Mayor. Religion, myth and symbols 257 # Ans. Why Rule (category)
rows.472: oracle: A priest or priestess through whom a god was believed to answer questions about the future, or the sacred place where this happened. Chavín de Huántar may have housed an oracle at the Lanzón. Religion, myth and symbols
rows.473: pharaoh: The king of ancient Egypt, believed to be a living god, the earthly form of Horus. Pharaohs are shown idealized, calm and young forever. Religion, myth and symbols
rows.474: Apollo: Greek and Roman god of the sun, light, music, poetry and prophecy, always shown young and handsome. Twin brother of Artemis. Religion, myth and symbols
rows.475: vision serpent: A giant snake in Maya art from whose mouth an ancestor or god appears, called up through bloodletting rituals. Religion, myth and symbols
rows.476: Buddhism: A religion founded in India around 500 B.C.E. by Siddhartha Gautama, the Buddha. It teaches that life is full of suffering caused by desire, and that one can escape the cycle of rebirth by reaching enlightenment. It spread across Asia along trade routes. Religion, myth and symbols
rows.477: cult: In art history, simply the worship and rituals given to a particular god, saint or image, as in ‘cult statue’. It does not mean a strange sect. Religion, myth and symbols
rows.478: polytheism: Belief in many gods, as in ancient Egypt, Greece, Rome, the Aztec Empire and Hinduism. Religion, myth and symbols
rows.479: relic: A holy object: part of a saint’s body (bones, hair) or something they touched (clothing). People believed relics could heal and protect, so churches that owned them drew crowds of pilgrims. Buddhists also honor relics of the Buddha. Religion, myth and symbols
rows.480: ancestor veneration: Honoring dead family members as spirits who still protect and guide the living. Many works are made to house, remember or honor ancestors. Religion, myth and symbols
rows.481: memento mori: Latin for ‘remember that you will die’. An object or image, like a skull or rotting fruit, that reminds viewers that life is short. Religion, myth and symbols
rows.482: serpopard: A modern name for the creature on the Narmer Palette that is part serpent (a long snaky neck) and part leopard (the body). Two with intertwined necks form the circle in the palette’s center. Religion, myth and symbols
rows.483: divination: Finding hidden knowledge or the future by ritual means, such as reading objects, casting lots or consulting spirits. Religion, myth and symbols
rows.484: dhyana mudra: The meditation gesture: both hands rest in the lap, palms up, one on top of the other. Religion, myth and symbols
rows.485: frigate bird: A large seabird that appears on Torres Strait masks and other Pacific art, linked to clans, ancestors and seafaring. Religion, myth and symbols
rows.486: shaykh: An Arabic title for a respected elder, religious scholar or Sufi master. Also spelled sheikh or shaikh. Religion, myth and symbols
rows.487: axis mundi: Latin for ‘axis of the world’: an imagined central pole connecting earth with heaven and the underworld. A mountain, tree, pillar or temple can play this role. Religion, myth and symbols 258 # Ans. Why Rule (category)
rows.488: Eucharist: The Christian ritual of sharing bread and wine in memory of the Last Supper. Catholics believe the bread and wine become Christ’s body and blood. Also called Holy Communion or the Mass. Religion, myth and symbols
rows.489: ushnisha: The bump on top of the Buddha’s head, a sign of his expanded wisdom. It is one of the fixed marks (lakshanas) of a Buddha. Religion, myth and symbols
rows.490: Santería: An Afro-Cuban religion blending Yoruba orisha worship with Catholic saints, created by enslaved Africans in Cuba. Religion, myth and symbols
rows.491: attribute: An object or feature that identifies a figure, like Zeus’s thunderbolt, a saint’s tool of martyrdom, or Shiva’s drum and flame. Religion, myth and symbols
rows.492: conclave: The closed meeting in which the Catholic cardinals elect a new pope. Today it is held in the Sistine Chapel. Religion, myth and symbols
rows.493: salat: The ritual prayer Muslims perform five times a day, facing Mecca. Mosques are designed around it. Religion, myth and symbols
rows.494: canopic jars: Four jars that held a mummy’s removed organs (liver, lungs, stomach, intestines), each lid often shaped as the head of a protective god. Religion, myth and symbols
rows.495: Shiva: One of the main Hindu gods, the destroyer and recreator of the universe. He is often shown with a third eye, matted hair, a snake and a trident, and is worshipped as the lingam. Religion, myth and symbols
rows.496: Thoth: Ibis-headed Egyptian god of writing and wisdom, who records the result of the weighing of the heart. Religion, myth and symbols
rows.497: Coatlicue: ‘Serpent Skirt’: the Aztec earth goddess, mother of the war god Huitzilopochtli. In the myth, she gave birth to him on Serpent Mountain (Coatepec) as her daughter Coyolxauhqui attacked her. The Templo Mayor re-creates that mountain. Religion, myth and symbols
rows.498: muezzin: The person who calls Muslims to prayer five times a day, traditionally from a minaret. Religion, myth and symbols
rows.499: Coatepec: ‘Serpent Mountain’: the mythical mountain where Huitzilopochtli was born and defeated Coyolxauhqui. The Templo Mayor’s Huitzilopochtli side was built as Coatepec. Religion, myth and symbols
rows.500: Counter-Reformation: The Catholic Church’s response to the Reformation, set out at the Council of Trent (1545 to 1563). It wanted art that was clear, emotional and dramatic to pull believers back to Catholicism. This fueled Baroque art. Religion, myth and symbols
rows.501: chador: A full-length cloak, usually black, worn by many women in Iran that covers the head and body but leaves the face open. Shirin Neshat’s Women of Allah photographs use it to explore Iranian women’s identity. Religion, myth and symbols
rows.502: katsina: A spirit being of the Hopi and other Pueblo peoples who brings rain and blessings. Masked dancers embody katsinas, and carved katsina dolls teach children about them. Also spelled kachina. Religion, myth and symbols
rows.503: samsara: In Hinduism and Buddhism, the endless cycle of birth, death and rebirth that a soul is trapped in until it is released. Religion, myth and symbols 259 # Ans. Why Rule (category)
rows.504: putto: A chubby, naked baby boy, often with wings, in European art. The plural is putti. They can be cupids or baby angels. Religion, myth and symbols
rows.505: allegory: A work in which characters and events stand for bigger ideas, so the whole thing carries a second, hidden meaning. Religion, myth and symbols
rows.506: mater dolorosa: Latin for ‘sorrowful mother’. The Virgin Mary grieving over Christ’s suffering and death, a favorite late medieval devotional subject. Religion, myth and symbols
rows.507: Five Pillars: The five basic duties of Islam: declaring faith in one God and Muhammad as his prophet, praying five times a day, giving to the poor, fasting in Ramadan, and making the hajj if possible. Religion, myth and symbols
rows.508: Hera: Queen of the Greek gods, wife of Zeus, goddess of marriage. The Romans called her Juno; her symbol is the peacock. Religion, myth and symbols
rows.509: offering: A gift given to a god, spirit or ancestor, such as food, flowers, precious objects or a statue. Religion, myth and symbols
rows.510: Dionysus: Greek god of wine, theater and wild celebration, called Bacchus by the Romans. His followers included frenzied women (maenads) and satyrs. Religion, myth and symbols
rows.511: deity: A god or goddess. Religion, myth and symbols
rows.512: Confucianism: A Chinese philosophy based on the teachings of Confucius (551 to 479 B.C.E.), stressing proper behavior, respect for elders and ancestors, loyalty to rulers, and education. It shaped government and family life in China and Korea. Religion, myth and symbols
rows.513: Inti: The Inka sun god, ancestor of the Inka ruler. His main temple was the Qorikancha in Cusco. Religion, myth and symbols
rows.514: power figure: A figure that holds spiritual power gathered by a ritual specialist, used to protect, heal, seal oaths or punish wrongdoers. The Kongo nkisi n’kondi is the best-known example. Religion, myth and symbols
rows.515: sacrifice: Offering something valuable, such as an animal, food, one’s own blood or even a human life, to a god. Mesoamerican religions held that the gods needed blood to keep the universe running. Religion, myth and symbols
rows.516: yakshi: A female nature spirit of fertility in Indian art, often shown as a curvy woman clinging to a tree. Yakshis decorate Buddhist and Hindu monuments. Religion, myth and symbols
rows.517: Gigantomachy: The mythical battle between the Greek gods and the Giants. Greeks used it as a symbol of civilization (or their own side) defeating chaos and barbarians. Religion, myth and symbols
rows.518: fasces: A bundle of rods tied around an axe, carried in front of ancient Roman oﬀicials as a sign of their power. Houdon’s George Washington rests his hand on a fasces of 13 rods, one for each original state. Religion, myth and symbols
rows.519: church (institution): Lower-case ‘church’ can mean a building for Christian worship; capital-C ‘the Church’ means the organization of Christianity itself, with its leaders (popes, bishops, priests). The Church was the biggest art patron in Europe for over a thousand years. Religion, myth and symbols 260 # Ans. Why Rule (category)
rows.520: nirvana: In Buddhism, the final state of peace in which desire and suffering are blown out and the cycle of rebirth ends. The Buddha’s death is called his parinirvana (‘complete nirvana’). Religion, myth and symbols
rows.521: dharma wheel: A wheel (dharmachakra) standing for the Buddha’s teaching, which he ‘set in motion’ with his first sermon. Early Buddhist art used it instead of showing the Buddha. Religion, myth and symbols
rows.522: apsara: A heavenly female dancer or nymph in Hindu and Buddhist belief. Hundreds of carved apsaras decorate the walls of Angkor Wat. Religion, myth and symbols
rows.523: Ra: Egyptian sun god, also spelled Re, who sails across the sky by day. He merged with other gods, as in Amun-Re. Religion, myth and symbols
rows.524: hubris: Excessive pride that challenges the gods; in Greek myth it is always punished. Religion, myth and symbols
rows.525: Gayumars: In the Shahnama, the first king of the world, who ruled from a mountaintop when people wore leopard skins and had not yet learned cooking or clothing. Religion, myth and symbols
rows.526: Neo-Confucianism: A revived form of Confucianism from the Song dynasty onward that blended in ideas from Daoism and Buddhism about the order of the universe. It became the oﬀicial philosophy of Joseon Korea. Religion, myth and symbols
rows.527: shrine: A holy place or container for a god, saint, relic or sacred image, from a tiny household altar to a whole building. Religion, myth and symbols
rows.528: iconoclasm: The destruction of religious images, or a belief that such images are wrong. The Byzantine Empire banned and destroyed icons in 726 to 843 C.E.; Protestants smashed church images in the 1500s; the Taliban blew up the Bamiyan Buddhas in 2001. Religion, myth and symbols
rows.529: baptism: The Christian ritual of washing or dipping in water to welcome a person into the faith and wash away sin. Religion, myth and symbols
rows.530: Quetzalcoatl: ‘Feathered Serpent’: a major Mesoamerican god of wind, learning and priests, worshipped from Teotihuacan to the Aztecs. Religion, myth and symbols
rows.531: devaraja: Sanskrit for ‘god-king’. A royal cult in the Khmer Empire that linked the king with a Hindu god, usually Shiva or Vishnu, so that royal temples were also the god’s palaces. Religion, myth and symbols
rows.532: karma: In Hinduism and Buddhism, the idea that your actions decide what happens to you in future lives. Good deeds bring a better rebirth. Religion, myth and symbols
rows.533: Hathor: Egyptian goddess of love, music and motherhood, shown as a cow or a woman with cow ears or horns. Religion, myth and symbols
rows.534: Trinity: The Christian belief that one God exists as three persons: the Father, the Son (Jesus) and the Holy Spirit (often shown as a dove). Religion, myth and symbols
rows.535: solstice: The longest or shortest day of the year. Many ancient monuments line up with the solstice sunrise or sunset. Religion, myth and symbols
rows.536: Islam: The religion founded in Arabia in the 600s C.E. by the Prophet Muhammad, who Muslims believe received God’s final message, the Qur’an. A follower is a Muslim. Islam spread quickly from Spain to India. Religion, myth and symbols
rows.537: mosque lamp: A glass or metal hanging lamp used in mosques and shrines. It echoes a famous Qur’an verse comparing God’s light to a lamp. Religion, myth and symbols 261 # Ans. Why Rule (category)
rows.538: apotheosis: The raising of a person to the status of a god, often shown as being carried up into heaven. Religion, myth and symbols
rows.539: ba: In Egyptian belief, a person’s personality or soul, shown as a bird with a human head. It could fly out of the tomb by day and return at night. Religion, myth and symbols
rows.540: cosmology: A people’s picture of how the universe is arranged: heaven, earth, underworld, and how they connect. Many buildings and objects are maps of a cosmology. Religion, myth and symbols
