rows.541: Athena: Greek goddess of wisdom, war strategy and crafts, and protector of Athens. The Romans called her Minerva. She wears a helmet and carries a shield and spear. Religion, myth and symbols
rows.542: halo: A ring or disc of light around a holy person’s head, showing their holiness or (for rulers) their god-given power. Also called a nimbus. Christ’s halo often has a cross in it. Religion, myth and symbols
rows.543: merit: In Buddhism, spiritual credit earned by good acts like paying for a temple or image. Rulers and donors sponsored Buddhist art partly to gain merit. Religion, myth and symbols
rows.544: menorah: A seven-branched lamp that stood in the ancient Temple in Jerusalem, a lasting symbol of Judaism. (A ninebranched version is used at Hanukkah.) Religion, myth and symbols
rows.545: monastery: A community where monks (or nuns, in a convent) live apart from the world to pray and work under strict rules. Medieval monasteries copied and decorated most books in Europe. Religion, myth and symbols
rows.546: tlacuilo: An Aztec painter-scribe who wrote by painting pictures in codices. Religion, myth and symbols
rows.547: Eros: Greek god of desire, called Cupid by the Romans: a winged boy with a bow whose arrows make people fall in love. Religion, myth and symbols
rows.548: consecration: A ceremony that makes a building or object sacred, setting it apart for religious use. Todai-ji’s Great Buddha was consecrated in 752 with an ‘eye-opening’ ceremony. Religion, myth and symbols
rows.549: Christianity: The religion built around Jesus of Nazareth, whom Christians believe is the Son of God who died and rose again to save people from sin. It became the main religion of Europe, so most European art from about 300 to 1700 C.E. is Christian art. Religion, myth and symbols
rows.550: Pietà: Italian for ‘pity’. An image of the Virgin Mary alone holding the dead body of Jesus across her lap. It is a close-up, private version of the Lamentation. Religion, myth and symbols
rows.551: mystery cult: An ancient religious group with secret rites revealed only to initiates, who were promised protection or a better afterlife. The Sanctuary of the Great Gods on Samothrace, where the Winged Victory stood, was the center of one. Religion, myth and symbols
rows.552: sutra: A sacred text recording the teachings of the Buddha (or, in Hinduism, short teachings). Copying sutras was a way to earn merit. Religion, myth and symbols
rows.553: Pure Land: A Buddhist paradise, especially Amida Buddha’s Western Paradise. Pure Land Buddhism, very popular in Japan, teaches that faith in Amida brings rebirth there. Religion, myth and symbols
rows.554: bhumisparsha mudra: The ‘earth-touching’ gesture: the right hand reaches down to touch the ground. It recalls the moment the Buddha called the earth to witness his enlightenment. Religion, myth and symbols 262 # Ans. Why Rule (category)
rows.555: the Fall: The Bible story in which Adam and Eve disobey God by eating the forbidden fruit and are thrown out of the Garden of Eden. Christians call this the origin of sin and death. Religion, myth and symbols
rows.556: bodhisattva: In Mahayana Buddhism, a being who has reached enlightenment but chooses to stay in the world to help others. Bodhisattvas are often shown as richly dressed princes, unlike the plain-robed Buddha. Religion, myth and symbols
rows.557: Kaaba: The cube-shaped shrine in Mecca, the holiest site in Islam. Muslims everywhere face it when they pray, and pilgrims walk around it seven times during the hajj. It is covered by a black cloth, the kiswa. Religion, myth and symbols
rows.558: Amida: The Buddha of Infinite Light (Amitabha in Sanskrit), who rules a Western Paradise called the Pure Land. Believers who call his name hope to be reborn there. Religion, myth and symbols
rows.559: masquerade: A performance with masks, full costumes, music and dance, in which the masker becomes a spirit or character. The mask is only one part of the work. Religion, myth and symbols
rows.560: Virgin of Guadalupe: A vision of the Virgin Mary that appeared to Juan Diego, an Indigenous man in Mexico, in 1531, leaving her image on his cloak. She became the patron of Mexico and a symbol of Mexican identity. Religion, myth and symbols
rows.561: underworld: The world of the dead, usually imagined below the earth. Religion, myth and symbols
rows.562: varada mudra: The gift-giving gesture: hand lowered, palm facing out, offering blessings or wishes granted. Religion, myth and symbols
rows.563: increase ceremony: A ritual meant to make crops, animals or fish multiply and the community prosper. Religion, myth and symbols
rows.564: mudra: A symbolic hand gesture in Buddhist and Hindu art. Each has a fixed meaning, so you can tell what a figure is ‘saying’ by its hands. Religion, myth and symbols
rows.565: Moses: The Hebrew prophet who led the Israelites out of Egypt and received the Ten Commandments (God’s law) on Mount Sinai. Religion, myth and symbols
rows.566: Sun Dance: A major summer ceremony of many Plains peoples involving fasting, dance and sacrifice for the renewal of the community. The U.S. government banned it in the late 1800s. Religion, myth and symbols
rows.567: Olympian gods: The twelve major gods of ancient Greece, believed to live on Mount Olympus. The Romans adopted them under Latin names (Zeus became Jupiter, Athena became Minerva, and so on). Religion, myth and symbols
rows.568: mosque: A Muslim building for communal prayer. Key parts: a wall facing Mecca (qibla) with a niche (mihrab), a pulpit (minbar), often a courtyard, and towers (minarets). ‘Masjid’ is the Arabic word. Religion, myth and symbols
rows.569: darshan: In Hinduism, seeing and being seen by a god through its sacred image. The exchange of looks is itself a blessing, which is why images have large, open eyes and are paraded in processions. Religion, myth and symbols
rows.570: Bible: The holy book of Christianity. It has two parts: the Old Testament (the Hebrew scriptures, shared with Judaism) and the New Testament (about Jesus and his followers). Most Christian art illustrates a Bible story. Religion, myth and symbols 263 # Ans. Why Rule (category)
rows.571: Madonna: Italian for ‘my lady’. A name for the Virgin Mary, and for any painting or statue of her, usually holding the baby Jesus. Religion, myth and symbols
rows.572: sun (symbol): Across cultures the sun stands for life, kingship and the divine: the Aten, Inti, the Mughal emperor’s halo, Mao as the ‘sun’ of China. Religion, myth and symbols
rows.573: nemes: The striped cloth headdress with side flaps worn by Egyptian kings. Religion, myth and symbols
rows.574: Crucifixion: The execution of Jesus by nailing him to a wooden cross, the central event of Christianity. Images range from calm and triumphant to bloody and painful. Religion, myth and symbols
rows.575: mysticism: The pursuit of direct, personal union with God through prayer, vision or trance, beyond ordinary thinking. Religion, myth and symbols
rows.576: spirit spouse: In Baule belief, a spirit husband or wife from the other world who can cause trouble in one’s life. A diviner may advise carving a figure of the spirit spouse and caring for it. Religion, myth and symbols
rows.577: Olokun: In Benin and Yoruba belief, the god of the sea and wealth. The Oba is linked to him through coral beads and river-leaf patterns. Religion, myth and symbols
rows.578: iconography: The meaning of the images and symbols in a work: who is shown, what the objects stand for, and what story is told. Also, the study of that meaning. Religion, myth and symbols
rows.579: nkisi: Among the Kongo peoples, any object filled with spiritual power and medicines by a ritual specialist (nganga). The nkisi n’kondi is one powerful type. Plural: minkisi. Religion, myth and symbols
rows.580: Hebrew Bible: The Jewish scriptures (the Tanakh), written mostly in Hebrew. Christians call it the Old Testament. Hebrew is read right to left, so Jewish manuscripts read right to left too. Religion, myth and symbols
rows.581: missionary: A person sent to spread their religion to other peoples. Christian missionaries in the Americas, Africa and the Pacific changed local art, often destroying or hiding ‘pagan’ objects. Religion, myth and symbols
rows.582: paradise garden: A garden divided into four parts by water channels, picturing the Qur’an’s description of paradise with its four rivers. The Persian name is charbagh (‘four gardens’). Religion, myth and symbols
rows.583: Resurrection: Christianity’s belief that Jesus rose from the dead three days after he died. In art he often bursts from the tomb surrounded by light. Religion, myth and symbols
rows.584: Sudano-Sahelian: The mud-brick building style of the Sahel region of West Africa, with thick walls, buttresses and wooden beams (toron) sticking out. Cultures, people and places
rows.585: Yoruba: A large West African people, mostly in southwest Nigeria and Benin, with city-kingdoms, orisha religion and famous carvers and bronze casters. Cultures, people and places
rows.586: Dogon: A people of Mali known for cliffside villages, granary doors, ancestor figures and masquerades. Cultures, people and places
rows.587: Mongol Empire: The largest connected land empire in history (1206 to 1368), founded by Genghis Khan, which linked China, Iran and Russia and boosted trade and artistic exchange. Cultures, people and places 264 # Ans. Why Rule (category)
rows.588: Normans: Vikings who settled in Normandy, France, and conquered England in 1066 under William the Conqueror. Cultures, people and places
rows.589: t’oqapu: Small squares of geometric pattern woven into Inka textiles, each probably standing for a place, group or rank. Also spelled tocapu. Cultures, people and places
rows.590: Austronesian: A huge language family, and the seafaring peoples who spoke it, who spread from Taiwan through Southeast Asia and across the Pacific to Madagascar and Rapa Nui. The Lapita people were early Austronesian voyagers. Cultures, people and places
rows.591: Rapa Nui: The Polynesian name for Easter Island and its people, famous for moai statues. Cultures, people and places
rows.592: kahu kiwi: A Māori cloak covered with kiwi feathers, worn by people of high rank. Cultures, people and places
rows.593: San Ildefonso Pueblo: A Tewa pueblo in New Mexico, home of the potters Maria and Julian Martínez. Cultures, people and places
rows.594: Theodora: Byzantine empress and wife of Justinian, a former actress who became a powerful co-ruler. Cultures, people and places
rows.595: Sinan: The chief Ottoman architect (c. 1490 to 1588), designer of hundreds of buildings, who sought to outdo Hagia Sophia’s dome. Cultures, people and places
rows.596: rock shelter: A shallow cave or overhanging rock that gives natural cover but stays open to daylight, unlike a deep cave. Much African rock art is found in them. Cultures, people and places
rows.597: Medici: A rich banking family that ruled Florence and spent huge sums on art in the 1400s to 1500s. Two Medici became queens of France and several became popes. Cultures, people and places
rows.598: atoll: A ring-shaped coral island, or a ring of small islets, surrounding a lagoon. Atolls are common in Micronesia and Polynesia. Cultures, people and places
rows.599: aliʻi: The chiefly ruling class of traditional Hawaiian society. Aliʻi held both political and sacred power, and only they could wear the red-and-yellow feather capes and cloaks called ʻahu ʻula. Cultures, people and places
rows.600: viceroyalty: A colony governed by a viceroy, who ruled on behalf of the Spanish king. New Spain and Peru were the two great viceroyalties. Cultures, people and places
rows.601: Assyria: A warlike empire of northern Mesopotamia (peak c. 900 to 612 B.C.E.) whose palaces had giant guardian figures and relief carvings. Cultures, people and places
rows.602: bwami: A Lega society with many ranks that men and women climb through by learning moral teachings, taught with small ivory and wood figures and masks. Cultures, people and places
rows.603: pope: The bishop of Rome and head of the Catholic Church, a giant art patron. Cultures, people and places
rows.604: Spartacists: German revolutionary socialists, led by Karl Liebknecht and Rosa Luxemburg, crushed in 1919. Cultures, people and places
rows.605: khipu: An Inka record-keeping device of knotted, colored cords, used for counting and possibly for stories. Also spelled quipu. Cultures, people and places
rows.606: Yuan: The Mongol dynasty that ruled China (1271 to 1368), founded by Kublai Khan. Cultures, people and places 265 # Ans. Why Rule (category)
rows.607: hieroglyph: A picture-sign in the ancient Egyptian writing system. Some signs stand for sounds, others for whole words or ideas. The Narmer Palette writes the king’s name with a catfish and a chisel. Cultures, people and places
rows.608: Grand Tour: A long trip through Europe, especially Italy, made by wealthy young British and northern Europeans in the 1600s to 1800s to study ancient ruins and Renaissance art. Cultures, people and places
rows.609: islet: A very small island. Nan Madol was built on nearly 100 artificial islets of stacked stone and coral fill off the coast of Pohnpei. Cultures, people and places
rows.610: Louis XIV: The ‘Sun King’ of France (reigned 1643 to 1715), who built Versailles as a stage for absolute royal power. Cultures, people and places
rows.611: Tibet: A high plateau region north of the Himalayas, center of Vajrayana Buddhism. Cultures, people and places
rows.612: Lega: A people of the eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo whose life is organized by the bwami society. Cultures, people and places
rows.613: bisj pole: A tall Asmat memorial pole carved from a mangrove tree, with stacked ancestor figures, made for a feast honoring the recently dead. Cultures, people and places
rows.614: Kwakwaka’wakw: A Northwest Coast people of British Columbia, Canada, known for dramatic transformation masks used in potlatch dances. Cultures, people and places
rows.615: New Ireland: An island province of Papua New Guinea where malagan ceremonies are held. Cultures, people and places
rows.616: Kuosi: A powerful Bamileke society of royals and wealthy titleholders who wear beaded elephant masks. Cultures, people and places
rows.617: Sephardi: Jews of Spain and Portugal and their descendants, who were expelled from Spain in 1492. Cultures, people and places
rows.618: Gandhara: An ancient region of today’s Pakistan and Afghanistan where Buddhist art mixed with Greek and Roman styles, as in the wavy drapery of Buddha statues. Cultures, people and places
rows.619: reservation: Land set aside by the U.S. government for a Native American nation, usually after forcing it off its homeland. Cotsiogo painted his elk hides on the Wind River Reservation in Wyoming. Cultures, people and places
rows.620: Samoa: A Polynesian island nation. Many Samoans now live in New Zealand, where artists like Michel Tuffery work. Cultures, people and places
rows.621: samurai: Japan’s hereditary warrior class, who served lords (daimyo) and followed a code of loyalty. Cultures, people and places
rows.622: casta: The Spanish colonial system of ranking people by their mix of Spanish, Indigenous and African ancestry, and the paintings that illustrated it as sets of family portraits. Cultures, people and places
rows.623: aurochs: A huge wild ox, the ancestor of modern cattle, that lived across Europe until the last one died in 1627. The giant bulls painted at Lascaux are aurochs. Cultures, people and places
rows.624: Asantehene: The title of the Asante king. Cultures, people and places
rows.625: Tehuana: A woman of the Isthmus of Tehuantepec in Oaxaca, Mexico, whose distinctive dress became a symbol of strong, Indigenous Mexican womanhood. Cultures, people and places 266 # Ans. Why Rule (category)
rows.626: creole: In colonial Spanish America, a person of Spanish descent born in the Americas (criollo). Creoles developed a proud local identity separate from Spain. Cultures, people and places
rows.627: Tate Modern: The modern art museum in London, in a former power station whose Turbine Hall hosts giant commissions. Cultures, people and places
rows.628: Hopi: A Pueblo people of northeastern Arizona, known for katsina ceremonies and carved katsina dolls. Cultures, people and places
rows.629: Pompeii: A Roman town buried and preserved by the eruption of Mount Vesuvius in 79 C.E. Cultures, people and places
rows.630: Angkor: The capital of the Khmer Empire in Cambodia, with Angkor Wat (Hindu) and Angkor Thom (Buddhist). Cultures, people and places
rows.631: Rococo patrons: The French aristocrats of the 1700s who commissioned playful, flirtatious, pastel art for private homes. Cultures, people and places
rows.632: Rarotonga: The main island of the Cook Islands in central Polynesia, known for wrapped staff gods. Cultures, people and places
rows.633: Country: For Aboriginal Australians, Country means the ancestral land a person belongs to and is responsible for, including its plants, animals, water, spirits and Dreaming stories. Painting it is a duty, not just a landscape. Cultures, people and places
rows.634: tā moko: Traditional Māori tattooing, especially of the face, carved into the skin with chisels. Each design records a person’s ancestry, rank and identity. Cultures, people and places
rows.635: Persia: The historic name for Iran and its empires, from the Achaemenids to the Safavids. Cultures, people and places
rows.636: nkisi n’kondi: A Kongo power figure that ‘hunts’ wrongdoers. A ritual specialist fills it with medicines, and people drive nails or blades into it to seal oaths, settle disputes or call for punishment. The plural of nkisi is minkisi. Cultures, people and places
rows.637: Torres Strait: The sea and islands between Australia and Papua New Guinea, whose peoples made masks from turtle shell. Cultures, people and places
rows.638: the Academy: An oﬀicial art school and society, like France’s Royal Academy of Painting and Sculpture (1648), which taught rules, ranked subjects and controlled the Salon. ‘Academic art’ means art following its rules. Cultures, people and places
rows.639: hei-tiki: A Māori neck pendant of greenstone (jade) shaped like a human figure, passed down as a family treasure. Cultures, people and places
rows.640: Pueblo peoples: Native peoples of New Mexico and Arizona, such as the Hopi and Tewa, who live in adobe or stone villages called pueblos. Cultures, people and places
rows.641: rangatira: A Māori chief or person of high rank. Tamati Waka Nene was a rangatira. Cultures, people and places
rows.642: Vatican: The pope’s headquarters and the smallest country in the world, inside Rome, with St. Peter’s Basilica and the Sistine Chapel. Cultures, people and places
rows.643: Song: A Chinese dynasty (960 to 1279) famous for monumental landscape painting, Neo-Confucianism and fine ceramics. Cultures, people and places
rows.644: Babylon: An ancient city of Mesopotamia, capital of King Hammurabi (c. 1792 to 1750 B.C.E.). Cultures, people and places
rows.645: ibol: A personal emblem carved on the front of a Kuba ndop that tells you which king it is. Cultures, people and places 267 # Ans. Why Rule (category)
rows.646: cuneiform: The writing of ancient Mesopotamia, made of wedge-shaped marks pressed into clay with a reed or carved into stone. It was used for about 3,000 years. Cultures, people and places
rows.647: Fang: A people of Gabon, Cameroon and Equatorial Guinea known for byeri reliquary guardian figures. Cultures, people and places
rows.648: Sumer: The first cities of southern Mesopotamia (c. 4500 to 1900 B.C.E.), such as Uruk and Ur, inventors of writing (cuneiform). Cultures, people and places
rows.649: Fiji: A Pacific island nation, a British colony from 1874 to 1970, where ceremonial gifts of mats and tapa build relationships. Cultures, people and places
rows.650: Etruscans: A people of central Italy (c. 800 to 100 B.C.E.) before the Roman takeover, known for lively tombs, terra cotta sculpture and temples. Cultures, people and places
rows.651: Luba: A people and former kingdom of the southeastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, known for royal art and the lukasa memory board. Cultures, people and places
rows.652: Pohnpei: An island in Micronesia, site of Nan Madol. Cultures, people and places
rows.653: Mexica: The people usually called the Aztecs, who ruled an empire from their island capital, Tenochtitlan, until the Spanish conquest in 1521. Cultures, people and places
rows.654: scholar-oﬀicial: A government oﬀicial in China or Korea chosen through exams on the Confucian classics, often also a poet, calligrapher or painter. Cultures, people and places
rows.655: Jingdezhen: China’s porcelain capital for over a thousand years, where imperial and export porcelain was made. Cultures, people and places
rows.656: Benin (kingdom): A West African kingdom in today’s southern Nigeria (not the modern country called Benin), ruled by the Oba. Its brass casters made plaques and heads for the royal palace. British troops looted it in 1897. Cultures, people and places
rows.657: Mbudye: A Luba society of ‘men of memory’ who kept and performed royal history and advised kings. Cultures, people and places
rows.658: Olowe of Ise: A famous Yoruba sculptor (c. 1875 to 1938), one of the few African artists of his time known by name, admired for his tall figures and deep undercutting. Cultures, people and places
rows.659: Justinian: Byzantine emperor (reigned 527 to 565 C.E.) who rebuilt Hagia Sophia and reconquered Italy. He appears in mosaic with his wife, Theodora. Cultures, people and places
rows.660: tatanua: A type of malagan mask with a crested fiber ‘hairstyle’ representing the spirit of a dead person. Cultures, people and places
rows.661: Chilkat: A Tlingit weaving style for ceremonial robes of mountain-goat wool and cedar bark, with formline crest designs and long fringes. Cultures, people and places
rows.662: Great Migration: The movement of about six million Black Americans from the rural South to Northern cities (c. 1910 to 1970) to escape segregation and find work. Cultures, people and places
rows.663: winter count: A Plains pictorial calendar, usually painted on a hide, with one picture for each year (‘winter’) recalling its main event. Cultures, people and places
rows.664: Igbo: A large people of southeastern Nigeria. Cultures, people and places 268 # Ans. Why Rule (category)
rows.665: tapa: Barkcloth made by beating the inner bark of paper mulberry trees into sheets, then painting, stamping or dyeing it. It is made mostly by women and used for clothing, gifts and ceremonies. Called ngatu in Tonga, masi in Fiji, hiapo in Niue, siapo in Samoa. Cultures, people and places
rows.666: whare: A Māori house. A carved meeting house (whare whakairo) is seen as the body of an ancestor. Cultures, people and places
rows.667: al-Andalus: The Arabic name for the parts of Spain and Portugal under Muslim rule (711 to 1492), a meeting place of Muslim, Christian and Jewish cultures. Cultures, people and places
rows.668: Khajuraho: A site in central India with Hindu and Jain temples famed for their dense, sometimes erotic sculpture. Cultures, people and places
rows.669: pastoralism: A way of life based on herding animals, such as cattle, sheep or goats, often moving with the seasons. Much later Saharan rock art shows herders and their cattle. Cultures, people and places
rows.670: Niue: A small Polynesian island nation known for hiapo barkcloth. Cultures, people and places
rows.671: Asante: A powerful kingdom and people of Ghana, rich from gold. Also spelled Ashanti. Their king is the Asantehene, and the Golden Stool is the soul of the nation. Cultures, people and places
rows.672: wayfinding: Traditional Pacific navigation without instruments, reading stars, swells, winds and birds. Cultures, people and places
rows.673: daimyo: A Japanese feudal lord who ruled a domain and commanded samurai under the shogun. Cultures, people and places
rows.674: Cuzco School: Painters in colonial Cusco and the Andes who made Catholic images with flat, gold-patterned surfaces, often mixing in local ideas. Cultures, people and places
rows.675: Cusco: The Inka capital in the Peruvian highlands, said to be laid out in the shape of a puma. Also spelled Cuzco. Cultures, people and places
rows.676: gogok: Comma-shaped jade or glass ornaments hung on Silla crowns, possibly standing for life, seeds or fertility. Cultures, people and places
rows.677: Melanesia: The region of the southwest Pacific including Papua New Guinea, the Solomon Islands, Vanuatu, the Torres Strait area and Fiji. Cultures, people and places
rows.678: Qin Shi Huang: The first emperor of a unified China, who standardized writing, money and measures, and was buried with the terra cotta army. Cultures, people and places
rows.679: Mississippian: Native cultures of the Mississippi valley and Southeast (c. 800 to 1600 C.E.) that built large earthen mounds and towns such as Cahokia. The College Board labels the Great Serpent Mound Mississippian, though some scholars credit earlier peoples (Adena or Fort Ancient). Cultures, people and places
rows.680: potlatch: A Northwest Coast ceremonial feast in which a host gives away goods and stages dances to confirm status, names and rights. Canada banned it from 1884 to 1951. Cultures, people and places
rows.681: refraction: The bending of waves as they pass around or over something. In Marshall Islands stick charts, curved sticks show ocean swells bending around islands. Context, ideas and the exam
rows.682: Old Masters: The great European painters from about 1300 to 1800, such as Leonardo, Rembrandt and Velázquez, and their works. Context, ideas and the exam 269 # Ans. Why Rule (category)
rows.683: didactic: Made to teach a lesson, usually moral or religious. Context, ideas and the exam
rows.684: mass media: Newspapers, magazines, radio, film, TV and the internet: forms that reach huge audiences at once. Context, ideas and the exam
rows.685: votive: Offered to a god as a gift or to fulfill a promise (a vow). Votive figures could ‘pray’ on the giver’s behalf. Context, ideas and the exam
rows.686: prestige object: An object whose main job is to signal that its owner is important, often made of rare materials or by rare skill. Context, ideas and the exam
rows.687: high and low art: The traditional split between ‘fine’ art for elites and museums (high) and popular culture, crafts or commercial images (low). Pop and later art erased the boundary. Context, ideas and the exam
rows.688: usury: Lending money at interest, which the medieval Church condemned as a sin. Enrico Scrovegni may have built the Arena Chapel partly to make up for his family’s usury. Context, ideas and the exam
rows.689: citation: A deliberate reference in a work to an earlier work, like a footnote in pictures. Context, ideas and the exam
rows.690: uncanny: Familiar but strangely disturbing. Freud described it as the eerie feeling when something homely turns strange, and the Surrealists sought it out, as in Oppenheim’s furcovered teacup. Context, ideas and the exam
rows.691: patron: The person or group who pays for and often directs the making of a work of art, such as a ruler, church, guild or rich family. Patrons usually decided the subject, size and materials. Context, ideas and the exam
rows.692: diplomacy: Relations between states. Art served it through gifts, portraits and ceremonies. Context, ideas and the exam
rows.693: continuity and change: How traditions carry on (continuity) and how they shift (change) over time. The AP continuity and change question asks how a work relates to earlier or later art traditions. Context, ideas and the exam
rows.694: explain: An AP task word: give reasons and show how or why, linking cause and effect. Most points on the exam need explaining, not just describing. Context, ideas and the exam
rows.695: commemorative: Made to honor and preserve the memory of a person or event. Context, ideas and the exam
rows.696: cultural patrimony: Objects and traditions that belong to a whole people or nation as their shared heritage, not to any one owner. Context, ideas and the exam
rows.697: global trade: Worldwide trade networks, especially after 1500, that moved silver, silk, porcelain, enslaved people and art between continents. Context, ideas and the exam
rows.698: kitsch: Cheap, sentimental, mass-market art or decoration seen as being in bad taste. Some artists use it on purpose. Context, ideas and the exam
rows.699: contextual analysis: Explaining how a work’s context (time, place, patron, function, audience, beliefs) shaped it and its meaning. One of the AP short-essay question types. Context, ideas and the exam
rows.700: satire: Using humor, exaggeration or irony to criticize people, habits or institutions. Context, ideas and the exam
rows.701: propaganda: Art or media made to spread a political or religious message and shape what people believe, often by glorifying a leader or cause. Context, ideas and the exam 270 # Ans. Why Rule (category)
rows.702: postcolonial: Describes the period after colonies won independence, and art or ideas that examine the lasting effects of colonialism on identity, power and culture. Context, ideas and the exam
rows.703: conservation: The science of protecting works from decay, damage and environment, preferably changing as little as possible. Context, ideas and the exam
rows.704: synesthesia: A mixing of the senses, such as seeing colors when hearing music. Kandinsky compared colors to musical tones and wanted his paintings to work on viewers like music. Context, ideas and the exam
rows.705: degenerate art: The Nazi label (in German, Entartete Kunst) for modern art they banned, including Expressionism and abstraction. In 1937 they seized thousands of works from German museums and mocked many of them in a touring exhibition. Context, ideas and the exam
rows.706: Neoplatonism: A philosophy based on Plato, revived in Renaissance Florence, that saw physical beauty as a reflection of divine, spiritual beauty. It let a nude pagan goddess like Botticelli’s Venus carry Christian-friendly meanings. Context, ideas and the exam
rows.707: style: The recognizable way something is made, which can belong to an artist, a workshop, a culture or a period. Learning styles lets you attribute unknown works. Context, ideas and the exam
rows.708: gender: The roles, behaviors and identities a society expects of women and men. Asking ‘how does this work show gender?’ is a powerful analysis tool. Context, ideas and the exam
rows.709: anonymous: Made by a maker whose name is not recorded. Most art in history is anonymous, which does not mean it was made without skill or individual style. Context, ideas and the exam
rows.710: heliocentric: Sun-centered: the idea, argued by Copernicus and confirmed by Galileo and Kepler, that the Earth and planets orbit the sun. Context, ideas and the exam
rows.711: secular: Not religious; worldly. Secular art includes portraits, scenes of daily life, entertainment masks and luxury objects for the court. Islamic art avoids figures mainly in religious settings, so secular Islamic objects are often full of people and animals. Context, ideas and the exam
rows.712: artist: The maker of a work. In many cultures makers were seen as skilled craftspeople, often anonymous, rather than celebrated geniuses; the idea of the famous individual artist became strong in Renaissance Europe. Context, ideas and the exam
rows.713: Mexicanidad: Spanish for ‘Mexicanness’. A movement after the Mexican Revolution to celebrate Mexico’s Indigenous and folk heritage as the heart of national identity. Frida Kahlo embraced it in her Tehuana dress and imagery. Context, ideas and the exam
rows.714: gravitas: Latin for ‘weight’ or ‘seriousness’. The Roman virtue of dignity, self-control and moral seriousness, shown in stern, wrinkled, veristic portraits. Context, ideas and the exam
rows.715: sovereignty: Supreme, independent power to govern. The Golden Stool embodies the sovereignty and soul of the whole Asante nation. Context, ideas and the exam
rows.716: cult of personality: Using propaganda, images and mass media to turn a political leader into an idolized, almost godlike hero. In Mao’s China his image was everywhere. Context, ideas and the exam 271 # Ans. Why Rule (category)
rows.717: homage: A work made to honor an earlier artist or work. Context, ideas and the exam
rows.718: entropy: A scientific idea: everything gradually breaks down into disorder. Robert Smithson welcomed it, letting Spiral Jetty sink, crust with salt and erode. Context, ideas and the exam
rows.719: regalia: The special clothing and objects that show royal or high rank, such as crowns, scepters, capes, stools and jewelry. Context, ideas and the exam
rows.720: bel composto: Italian for ‘beautiful whole’. Bernini’s idea of combining architecture, sculpture, painting and real light into one unified, theatrical experience. Context, ideas and the exam
rows.721: signature: The artist’s name written on a work. Signing was rare in many periods, so a signature can be a bold claim to fame or authorship. Context, ideas and the exam
rows.722: craft: Skilled handmade work, especially textiles, ceramics, metalwork and furniture, long ranked below painting and sculpture in Europe. That ranking is now widely questioned. Context, ideas and the exam
rows.723: quotation: Borrowing a recognizable pose, figure or composition from an earlier work. Context, ideas and the exam
rows.724: complexity: A more sophisticated argument, such as explaining both sides, several causes, or how a work both continues and breaks a tradition. The strongest AP long essays show it. Context, ideas and the exam
rows.725: commodification: Turning something (art, culture, identity, people) into a product to be bought and sold. Context, ideas and the exam
rows.726: decorative arts: Useful objects made beautifully: furniture, ceramics, textiles, metalwork, glass. Context, ideas and the exam
rows.727: guild: An association of craftsmen in a trade (such as painters or goldsmiths) that set standards, trained apprentices and controlled who could sell work in a city. Context, ideas and the exam
rows.728: atelier: French for an artist’s studio or workshop, especially a royal workshop of painters and calligraphers in Persian and Mughal courts. Context, ideas and the exam
rows.729: national identity: A shared sense of what makes a people a nation: history, land, language and heroes. Art from the 1800s on often tries to shape it, as in Velasco’s grand views of the Valley of Mexico. Context, ideas and the exam
rows.730: machismo: An exaggerated sense of masculine pride and toughness, including the idea that real men never show emotion. Pepón Osorio’s barbershop installation, titled No Crying Allowed in the Barbershop, questions it. Context, ideas and the exam
rows.731: genealogy: A family’s line of descent, traced back through generations of ancestors. Art often displayed genealogies to prove a ruler’s or chief’s right to power. Context, ideas and the exam
rows.732: limpieza de sangre: Spanish for ‘purity of blood’. A colonial idea that ranked people by ancestry, favoring ‘pure’ Spanish Christian descent. It underlay the casta system of New Spain. Context, ideas and the exam
rows.733: comparison: Discussing two or more works together, showing both similarities and differences and explaining why. The AP long-essay comparison question pairs a given work with one you choose. Context, ideas and the exam 272 # Ans. Why Rule (category)
rows.734: Royal Academy: The oﬀicial art academy of a kingdom: in France, the Royal Academy of Painting and Sculpture (1648); in Britain, the Royal Academy of Arts (1768). They trained artists, held exhibitions and ranked the genres. Vigée Le Brun was one of very few women admitted in France. Context, ideas and the exam
rows.735: attribution: Deciding who made a work, or when and where, based on style, materials, documents and comparison. On the AP exam, the attribution question shows you an unknown work and asks you to name the likely artist or culture and justify it. Context, ideas and the exam
rows.736: hybridity: The mixing of different cultures, styles or identities in one work or person, creating something new rather than simply one or the other. Context, ideas and the exam
rows.737: court art: Art made for a royal or princely court, usually by artists the ruler employed, to show the ruler’s wealth, taste and power. Safavid manuscripts and the Ardabil Carpet came from court workshops. Context, ideas and the exam
rows.738: Industrial Revolution: The change from hand production to machines and factories, starting in Britain around 1760, which brought railways, cities, new materials and photography. Context, ideas and the exam
rows.739: trade: The exchange of goods over distance. Trade brought new materials (brass, beads, cobalt, silk) and new ideas to artists. Context, ideas and the exam
rows.740: swell: A long, rolling ocean wave that travels far from the wind that created it. Marshall Islands navigators read swells, and how islands bend them, to find land. Context, ideas and the exam
rows.741: male gaze: A term from film critic Laura Mulvey (1975): images that present women as objects for a presumed male viewer. Context, ideas and the exam
rows.742: four humors: An old medical theory that health and personality depend on balancing four body fluids: blood, yellow bile, black bile and phlegm. Too much of one made a person sanguine (cheerful), choleric (angry), melancholic (sad) or phlegmatic (sluggish). Context, ideas and the exam
rows.743: contract: A written agreement between patron and artist listing what is to be made, materials (such as how much gold or blue), price and deadline. Context, ideas and the exam
rows.744: lex talionis: Latin for ‘law of retaliation’: punishment that matches the crime, ‘an eye for an eye’. Hammurabi’s laws apply it, though penalties also depended on the social rank of victim and offender. Context, ideas and the exam
rows.745: modernity: The condition of modern life after the Industrial Revolution: cities, railways, factories, crowds, speed and new technology. Artists like Monet made it their subject. Context, ideas and the exam
rows.746: art market: The system of buying and selling art through dealers, galleries, auctions and collectors. Context, ideas and the exam
rows.747: cultural exchange: The flow of ideas, materials, styles and beliefs between cultures through trade, travel, conquest or migration. On the exam it is one of the most useful themes for comparisons. Context, ideas and the exam 273 # Ans. Why Rule (category)
rows.748: global contemporary: Art made around the world from about 1980 to now, often dealing with globalization, identity, politics and new media, and shown at international biennials. Context, ideas and the exam
rows.749: wabi-sabi: A Japanese idea of beauty that values simple, imperfect, weathered and impermanent things, linked to Zen Buddhism and the tea ceremony. Context, ideas and the exam
rows.750: thesis: A clear, defensible claim that answers the question and that the rest of the essay proves. On the AP rubric it must do more than restate the question. Context, ideas and the exam
rows.751: claim: A statement you argue is true and back up with evidence. Context, ideas and the exam
rows.752: idealization: Showing a person or thing as more perfect than in real life, according to a culture’s ideal of beauty, virtue or power. Many ‘portraits’ outside Europe, and royal images everywhere, are idealized rather than true likenesses. Context, ideas and the exam
rows.753: visual analysis: Describing a work’s form (materials, technique, composition, color, line, scale) and explaining how those choices create meaning. One of the AP short-essay question types. Context, ideas and the exam
rows.754: looting: Stealing objects, especially in war or from archaeological sites without permission. Context, ideas and the exam 274
